local_feedback_text: Reduction of an aromatic nitro group to the aniline. The standard methods (H2/Pd, Fe/AcOH, SnCl2) all pose compatibility issues here: H2/Pd would reduce the alkene and cleave the vinyl triflate and the benzyl ether; dissolving-metal/SnCl2 conditions could affect the sulfonate ester and triflate. A chemoselective method (e.g., Zn, or transfer hydrogenation under carefully controlled conditions) would be required to avoid touching the vinyl triflate and the electron-poor alkene. The disconnection is logical but the highly functionalized, redox-sensitive substrate makes selective nitro reduction challenging.

Williamson-type benzylation (O-alkylation) of the free catechol phenol with benzyl bromide. Standard with K2CO3/Cs2CO3. The phenol being protected is the catechol that is sulfonylated on the other oxygen; selective mono-benzylation of the remaining free OH is straightforward. Compatible with the triflate, sulfonate, and nitro groups. Reasonable protecting-group operation.

This step proposes a Fischer esterification of the carboxylic acid with ethanol to give the ethyl ester. While esterification itself is feasible, the route is internally inconsistent: the immediate precursor (3e7e498fccb33584f19478d2cdbda11c3dfaeff3380f7f6e83c3a6c2146645da) is derived from a METHYL ester, yet here the disconnection converts a carboxylic ACID to an ETHYL ester. There is no logical reason to hydrolyze a methyl ester (3e7e498fccb33584f19478d2cdbda11c3dfaeff3380f7f6e83c3a6c2146645da) and then re-esterify with ethanol. If the target requires an ethyl ester, it should be carried as the ethyl ester throughout. Additionally, Fischer esterification under acidic conditions risks decomposition of the acid-sensitive pyrrole/dipyrrin-like chromophore and the enamine/azafulvene system. This is a poorly conceived, redundant transformation.

This step hydrolyzes a methyl ester to the free carboxylic acid, which is then re-esterified with ethanol in 9adb64aec42f442569c52b916935e6ab790682f5bcf63ea41e9f9d56846dd48e. This is a wasteful protect/deprotect-like detour. If the final target is the ethyl ester, the synthesis should simply use an ethyl ester from the start (transesterify or use ethyl-based building blocks). The free acid intermediate adds no strategic value and introduces an additional polar, difficult-to-handle intermediate. Furthermore, ester hydrolysis of this fully conjugated pyrrole-azafulvene system under basic or acidic conditions risks degradation. Recommend eliminating both 9adb64aec42f442569c52b916935e6ab790682f5bcf63ea41e9f9d56846dd48e and 3e7e498fccb33584f19478d2cdbda11c3dfaeff3380f7f6e83c3a6c2146645da and carrying the appropriate ester throughout.

Boc removal from the N-Boc pyrrole to reveal the free NH pyrrole is a standard, well-precedented transformation (TFA or thermal cleavage). The disconnection is appropriate and chemoselective. Care must be taken because the molecule contains an acid-sensitive azafulvene/dipyrromethene-type chromophore and a methyl ester; mild conditions (e.g., thermal Boc cleavage or controlled TFA) would be preferred over forcing acidic conditions. Overall a reasonable step.

This is a Suzuki-Miyaura coupling between an N-Boc-pyrrole-2-boronic acid and a 2-bromopyrrole fragment to form the bipyrrole linkage. The disconnection is strategically sound and bipyrrole formation via Suzuki is precedented. However, several concerns: (1) 2-pyrrole boronic acids (especially N-Boc) are notoriously unstable and prone to protodeboronation, often giving low yields; using the corresponding pinacol boronate or MIDA boronate would be more robust. (2) The 2-bromopyrrole partner bears a free NH and a sensitive azafulvene system; competing protodebromination and catalyst poisoning by the free NH/imine nitrogen are possible. (3) Chemoselectivity must be controlled to avoid interference from the extended conjugated dipyrrin-like system. Overall feasible but yield-limited and would benefit from optimized boron reagent.

Bromination of the pyrrole with NBS to install the 2-bromo substituent. Electrophilic bromination of electron-rich pyrroles with NBS is well-precedented, but regioselectivity is a major concern here: the pyrrole already bears a 3-OMe and is part of a highly electron-rich, extended conjugated azafulvene system. Multiple reactive positions (the methine bridge, the other pyrrole alpha position) could be brominated, and over-bromination is common with NBS on electron-rich pyrroles. The exocyclic methine (=CH-) and the azafulvene are also susceptible to electrophilic attack/addition. Strict control of stoichiometry (1.0 equiv), low temperature, and careful solvent choice would be required, and even then selectivity is uncertain. This step is the weakest in the route from a selectivity standpoint.

This step proposes a Fischer esterification of the carboxylic acid with ethanol to give the ethyl ester. However, the precursor in the route (3e7e498fccb33584f19478d2cdbda11c3dfaeff3380f7f6e83c3a6c2146645da) is itself the methyl ester (COC(=O)...), not the carboxylic acid. There is a fundamental inconsistency: the methyl ester is being converted to a carboxylic acid (3e7e498fccb33584f19478d2cdbda11c3dfaeff3380f7f6e83c3a6c2146645da), then re-esterified to an ethyl ester here. This transesterification/esterification sequence is redundant and chemically inefficient. Moreover, simple Fischer esterification with EtOH would face equilibrium limitations and would not be high-yielding without forcing conditions, which risk decomposing the sensitive dipyrromethene/azafulvene chromophore. The whole strategy of going methyl ester -> acid -> ethyl ester adds no value.

This step hydrolyzes the methyl ester to the carboxylic acid, only for the next step (9adb64aec42f442569c52b916935e6ab790682f5bcf63ea41e9f9d56846dd48e) to re-esterify it to an ethyl ester. If the final target is the ethyl ester, the most logical route would be to use ethyl acetoacetate-derived building blocks directly from the start, or perform a single transesterification. The acid intermediate serves no purpose here and introduces an unnecessary functional group interconversion. Additionally, ester hydrolysis on this electron-rich, conjugated system could risk side reactions, though the basic transformation is feasible.

This step is Boc deprotection of the pyrrole nitrogen using standard acidic conditions (e.g., TFA). This is a well-established and reliable transformation. The free NH-pyrrole is the target functionality. One minor concern is the acid-sensitivity of the methyl ether and the conjugated azafulvene system, but Boc removal with controlled conditions should be chemoselective and high-yielding.

This is a Suzuki-Miyaura coupling between a bromopyrrole and an N-Boc-pyrrole-2-boronic acid. While the disconnection forming the bipyrrole C-C bond is strategically sound, N-Boc-pyrrole-2-boronic acids are notoriously unstable and prone to protodeboronation, making this coupling low-yielding. Additionally, the free NH-pyrrole on the substrate may interfere with the Pd catalysis, and the electron-rich heteroaryl bromide can be sluggish. Chemoselectivity concerns exist with the conjugated enamine/azafulvene system. Consider using a more robust boronate (e.g., MIDA boronate or pinacol ester) or reversing the coupling partners (pyrrole halide + boronic acid on the other ring).

This step proposes NBS bromination of a pyrrole to install bromine selectively at the 5-position (alpha to NH, opposite the existing substituent). Pyrroles are highly reactive toward electrophilic halogenation, and selective monobromination at the desired position can be challenging—polybromination and bromination at undesired positions (including the electron-rich enamine/vinyl junction or the methoxy-bearing ring) are real risks. The conjugated azafulvene/dipyrrin-type chromophore presents multiple nucleophilic sites that could compete. Careful control (stoichiometry, low temperature, solvent) would be required. The basic disconnection is reasonable but selectivity is a genuine concern.

This step proposes Fischer esterification of the free carboxylic acid with ethanol to give the ethyl ester. However, the precursor itself is shown as the carboxylic acid which in turn is derived from the methyl ester (3e7e498fccb33584f19478d2cdbda11c3dfaeff3380f7f6e83c3a6c2146645da). This represents a self-defeating logic: converting a methyl ester to a free acid only to re-esterify to an ethyl ester. The transesterification/esterification is in principle feasible (Fischer conditions, acid catalysis), but the broader strategy is illogical. Furthermore, acid-catalyzed esterification conditions on this highly conjugated dipyrromethene/pyrrole-containing system risk decomposition. The disconnection as written (acid + EtOH -> ethyl ester) is chemically possible but the overall logic is flawed.

This step converts the methyl ester directly into the free carboxylic acid (saponification/hydrolysis), and the downstream step (9adb64aec42f442569c52b916935e6ab790682f5bcf63ea41e9f9d56846dd48e) then re-esterifies to the ethyl ester. This acid intermediate is entirely unnecessary; the target ethyl ester could be obtained directly via transesterification, or better, by building the ethyl ester from the outset. The hydrolysis-then-reesterification sequence adds two redundant steps. Moreover, hydrolysis of the methyl ester under basic or acidic conditions on this sensitive polypyrrolic conjugated system risks degradation of the methine bridge and pyrrole units.

This step is the removal of the Boc protecting group from the pyrrole nitrogen to reveal the free NH-pyrrole. Boc deprotection (e.g., TFA or thermal) is well-established and chemoselective. The methyl ester and the conjugated azafulvene system should tolerate mild acid or thermal Boc cleavage. Care must be taken to avoid acid-promoted decomposition of the sensitive chromophore, but conditions can be tuned (e.g., thermal Boc removal). Feasible.

This is a Suzuki-Miyaura coupling between a 2-bromopyrrole and a Boc-protected pyrrole-2-boronic acid. The disconnection (biaryl pyrrole-pyrrole bond formation) is reasonable in principle. However, several concerns arise: (1) N-Boc pyrrole-2-boronic acids are notoriously unstable and prone to protodeboronation, often giving low yields; (2) 2-bromopyrroles are also unstable; (3) the substrate has a free NH-pyrrole and an electron-rich, extended conjugated azafulvene system that could interfere with Pd catalysis or undergo side reactions; (4) chemoselectivity of coupling at the desired position. A Stille or Negishi alternative, or use of MIDA boronate, might improve outcomes. The disconnection is acceptable but realistically challenging.

This step is an NBS bromination of the electron-rich methoxypyrrole to install bromine at the 5-position (the free alpha-position). Pyrrole bromination with NBS is feasible, but regioselectivity is a major concern: the pyrrole has an open alpha-position and beta-positions, and the methine bridge connecting to the dipyrrinone-like core is electron-rich and highly susceptible to electrophilic attack/bromination. NBS could brominate the methine bridge or other activated positions rather than cleanly at the desired pyrrole alpha-carbon. Mono-selectivity and site selectivity would be difficult to control. Careful stoichiometry (1 equiv) and low temperature would be required, and yields are likely modest. Also note the precursor for this step is marked not in stock and not further disconnected, leaving the route incomplete.

This step proposes a Fischer esterification of the carboxylic acid with ethanol to give the ethyl ester. However, the immediate precursor in the route (3e7e498fccb33584f19478d2cdbda11c3dfaeff3380f7f6e83c3a6c2146645da) is derived from a methyl ester, and here the disconnection switches to an ethyl ester via the free acid. While Fischer esterification of a carboxylic acid with EtOH/acid catalyst is feasible in principle, the molecule contains a base/acid-sensitive dipyrromethene-type chromophore (the conjugated /C=C/ azafulvene/pyrrole-pyrrolenine system). Strong acidic conditions and prolonged heating could degrade this sensitive vinylogous system. More importantly, the route is internally inconsistent: it first makes the methyl ester target then later converts to the ethyl ester. A direct esterification with EtOH is plausible but the overall logic of generating an acid intermediate (3e7e498fccb33584f19478d2cdbda11c3dfaeff3380f7f6e83c3a6c2146645da hydrolyzing the methyl ester) only to re-esterify with ethanol is inefficient and risky. Consider building the ethyl ester directly from the start.

This step is a hydrolysis of the methyl ester to the free carboxylic acid, which is then re-esterified to the ethyl ester in 9adb64aec42f442569c52b916935e6ab790682f5bcf63ea41e9f9d56846dd48e. This protect/deprotect/re-esterify shuffle adds two unnecessary steps. If the final target is the ethyl ester, the synthesis should simply employ ethyl-ester-bearing building blocks throughout, avoiding the methyl ester entirely. Saponification of the methyl ester is chemically feasible (LiOH/NaOH), but the conjugated azafulvene and pyrrole NH systems may be sensitive to strongly basic, aqueous conditions, and the resulting carboxylic acid could promote decomposition. This is a non-strategic transformation.

This step is the removal of a Boc protecting group from the pyrrole nitrogen, revealing the free NH-pyrrole. Boc deprotection on pyrrole nitrogen typically proceeds cleanly under acidic conditions (TFA) or thermally. The transformation is well-precedented. Caution: the acid-sensitive conjugated dipyrromethene-like system and the methyl ester are generally compatible with mild TFA conditions, though monitoring is advised to avoid decomposition of the polyene chromophore. Overall a reasonable deprotection step.

This is a Suzuki-Miyaura cross-coupling between an N-Boc pyrrole-2-boronic acid and a 2-bromopyrrole intermediate to form the biaryl (pyrrole-pyrrole) linkage. The disconnection is strategically sound and pyrrole-2-boronic acids/esters are used in such couplings. However, several concerns: (1) N-Boc-pyrrole-2-boronic acids are prone to protodeboronation, lowering yields; (2) the heteroaryl bromide is part of a sensitive vinylogous azafulvene system that could interfere or decompose under Pd/base conditions; (3) the free pyrrole NH on the bromide partner (unprotected) may complicate the coupling or coordinate Pd. Protecting the NH of the bromopyrrole partner could improve outcomes. Regioselectivity of coupling should be fine (defined boronic acid and aryl bromide positions), but yield and chemoselectivity are concerns given the polyene system.

This step is an NBS bromination of an electron-rich pyrrole to install bromine at the 2-position (alpha to NH). While NBS brominations of pyrroles are well known, regioselectivity is a major concern here: the pyrrole bears an OMe substituent and a conjugated exocyclic vinyl group, and there are multiple potentially reactive positions including the electron-rich vinylidene/methylene of the azafulvene chromophore. Over-bromination and bromination of the activated methine/methylene bridge are likely competing pathways. Careful control of stoichiometry (1.0 equiv NBS), low temperature, and the choice of solvent would be required, and even then chemoselectivity is uncertain. The conjugated polyene is highly susceptible to electrophilic attack at sites other than the intended pyrrole alpha-carbon.

This is a standard sulfonylation of a secondary amine (bridgehead amine) with 4-cyanobenzenesulfonyl chloride. The reaction is well-precedented under mild basic conditions (Et3N, DCM or pyridine). The secondary amine is the only nucleophilic site after the amide nitrogen is engaged in the lactam, so chemoselectivity is good. The nitrile is unaffected. This is a clean final coupling step.

This represents the removal of a Cbz (benzyloxycarbonyl) protecting group from the secondary amine to reveal the free NH. Hydrogenolysis (H2, Pd/C) is the standard method. The dimethoxyaryl ring and lactam are compatible. No nitrile present at this stage. Straightforward deprotection.

local_feedback_text: This step proposes converting an N-benzyl amine into an N-Cbz carbamate directly with benzyl chloroformate. This is mechanistically problematic: a tertiary benzylamine does not simply convert to a Cbz carbamate by treatment with Cbz-Cl. To install Cbz one needs the free secondary amine. The route therefore has a redundant/contradictory protecting group sequence: it uses an N-benzyl group earlier (b572a37ba5f5aebb791645587ba5297332ad2157e15dd418b778f8471feff981), then proposes swapping it for Cbz. A direct debenzylation/reprotection would be needed, or simpler, the benzyl could be retained and removed directly. The proposed direct Bn-to-Cbz interconversion in a single step is non-standard and inefficient. This step proposes nitration of the N-phenyl group to install the para-nitro substituent using nitric acid. While aromatic nitration of the pendant phenyl is reasonable, the substrate contains a highly electron-rich/sensitive thiophene-fused quinone core (a pyridine-fused dithiole-quinone system) and multiple oxidation-sensitive functionalities. Strong oxidizing nitration conditions (HNO3) risk oxidation of the sulfide, degradation of the quinone, and potential nitration on other aromatic rings (the pyridine ring is deactivated, but the N-aryl ring nitrogen-attached phenyl is the most activated site). Regioselectivity for para is expected for an anilide-type N-aryl group, but chemoselectivity versus the sulfur and quinone is the dominant concern. A better strategy would be to introduce the para-nitrophenyl group already nitrated at an earlier stage (e.g., starting from 4-nitrophenylhydrazine) to avoid late-stage nitration of a sensitive scaffold.

This step proposes that the parent urazole NH compound derives from a PMB(para-methoxybenzyl)-protected urea nitrogen, i.e., removal of the PMB group to reveal the free N-H. However, the forward direction implies oxidative/acidic deprotection of an N-PMB amide/urea. While PMB removal from amide nitrogens is possible (CAN, DDQ, or acid), the bigger issue is that the route appears to introduce and then immediately remove this PMB protecting group with no apparent purpose (the nitrogen is just deprotected to NH). This protecting-group manipulation seems unnecessary if the NH is not engaged in any intervening chemistry. The disconnection itself (PMB on urea N) is chemically plausible but the strategic logic is questionable.

local_feedback: Protecting group strategy is wrong / non-optimal
local_feedback_text: This step methylates a phenol to a methyl ether (anisole) using methanol. First, direct conversion of a phenol to a methyl ether with MeOH alone is not feasible (requires MeI/base, Me2SO4, or Mitsunobu/diazomethane). Second, in the context of the whole route, the PMB group bears a free phenol that was just unmasked from a MOM ether in the prior step (02b0376bfacec782c81968672be94ba879f6a6575517855df0a74c61f3f50802), then methylated here (9df9b851e26c143661b430d089a4e10bded22161ad5eb713b9908f89915269ad), and the PMB is removed later (01e859b2f30d4c5769296b84f66d56a0ff23fc6b47ef405649844c27e061a7e3). This represents a convoluted and self-defeating protecting group cascade: MOM-protected phenol -> free phenol -> methyl ether -> PMB removal. The collection of steps 01e859b2f30d4c5769296b84f66d56a0ff23fc6b47ef405649844c27e061a7e3-e2e61a2532a8040f640a8b7d7a94a2797d9eb2b0f909f9c5566e1a3278326aa2 install and manipulate a PMB protecting group through multiple redundant transformations that serve no clear synthetic purpose and are non-optimal.

local_feedback: Protecting group strategy is wrong / non-optimal
local_feedback_text: This step removes a MOM (methoxymethyl) protecting group from a phenol (MOM ether -> free phenol), typically achieved under acidic conditions (HCl, TFA). The transformation itself is feasible. However, acidic MOM deprotection conditions may not be fully compatible with the sensitive quinone/sulfide scaffold, and again the strategic role is unclear since the phenol is subsequently methylated then the entire benzyl unit removed. This is part of a redundant protecting group sequence that should be eliminated.

This step proposes forming a MOM-protected phenol PMB-aryl ether linkage by combining MOMOH (methoxymethanol) with an aryl fluoride (4-fluorobenzyl-substituted substrate). The implied forward reaction is a nucleophilic aromatic substitution of an unactivated 4-fluorobenzyl fluoride by an alkoxide to give the MOM-aryl ether. SNAr on a simple para-fluoro benzyl arene without strong electron-withdrawing activation is not feasible under normal conditions. Furthermore, 'COCO' (methoxymethanol) is an unstable hemiacetal, not a practical reagent. This disconnection is chemically unsound.

This step proposes synthesizing methoxymethanol (COCO, an unstable hemiacetal of formaldehyde and methanol) from formaldehyde hydrate (OCO, methanediol) and dichloromethane (ClCCl). This transformation is not chemically sensible: dichloromethane is not a methyl/methoxy source under standard conditions, and methoxymethanol is an unstable species that cannot be reliably isolated. This is an invalid disconnection to nonsensical building blocks.

local_feedback: Problems with reaction type and functional group compatibility
local_feedback_text: Direct nitration with HNO3 on this complex substrate is highly problematic. The molecule contains an electron-rich thioether (sulfide), which is readily oxidized by nitric acid to sulfoxide/sulfone, and an azaquinone (pyridine-fused diketone) system. The urazole NH groups are also susceptible. Regioselectivity for para-nitration is plausible electronically, but chemoselectivity will be poor. This step should be performed early on a simple nitrobenzene-derived hydrazide building block rather than on the final complex molecule.

This step is written as converting a PMB-protected urazole nitrogen back to free NH-urazole, but it is presented as a forward synthesis disconnection that makes little strategic sense. If the intent is PMB deprotection on nitrogen, oxidative removal (DDQ/CAN) would be needed, but those conditions would damage the redox-sensitive azaquinone and sulfide. The overall logic of installing then removing a PMB group on this nitrogen is unclear and inefficient.

As written, this shows methanol (CO=MeOH) plus a free phenol substrate giving an aryl methyl ether (anisole-type, COc1ccc...). Direct O-methylation of a phenol with methanol alone is not feasible without an activating/dehydrating system (e.g., Mitsunobu, or MeI/base, or diazomethane). The SMILES strongly implies methyl ether formation, which contradicts the protecting group narrative. This transformation as written will not proceed.

MOM (methoxymethyl) ether deprotection to reveal the free phenol is a standard transformation, typically using mild acid (e.g., HCl, PPTS, or TFA). However, in this route the resulting free phenol is immediately methylated/protected differently, raising questions about strategic necessity. The deprotection itself is chemically sound, though acid sensitivity of the rest of the molecule should be verified.

This step proposes that MOMO (from COCO/MOM) reacts with a 4-fluorobenzyl-substituted substrate to install a MOM-protected phenol via displacement of the aryl fluoride. SNAr on a simple 4-fluorobenzyl arene is not feasible - the ring is not activated by strong electron-withdrawing groups ortho/para to fluorine. This bond disconnection is chemically implausible. A pre-formed 4-(MOM-oxy)benzyl building block should be used instead.

This step depicts MOM (COCO, methoxymethanol/MOM equivalent) being formed from methanediol (OCO) and dichloromethane (ClCCl). This is chemically nonsensical - dichloromethane and formaldehyde hydrate do not combine to give a MOM unit in any practical sense. MOM protection reagents (MOMCl, MOM-acetate, or dimethoxymethane) are commercially available building blocks and should be used directly. This is an invalid disconnection.

This is a standard Boc/tert-butyl ester deprotection to reveal the free carboxylic acid, typically done with TFA or HCl. The transformation is well-precedented. However, one must consider chemoselectivity: the molecule contains an aryl sulfonate ester (aryl OS(=O)2) and a sensitive bicyclic oxabicyclic alkene core. Acidic conditions (TFA) are generally compatible with sulfonate esters but the oxanorbornene oxygen bridge and the enol-type phenol should tolerate mild acid. Reasonable as the final deprotection step.

local_feedback: Protecting group strategy is wrong / non-optimal
local_feedback_text: This step proposes removal of an allyl ether (Pd(0)/scavenger) to reveal the phenol. The disconnection itself (allyl deprotection) is feasible. However, the protecting group strategy is questionable in context: the allyl group was installed on the phenol (f1a7664c0d33214bb7561cb27fea7eb2a145d5ab3958d34b4906c338a54a0a70) only to be removed here, yet the phenol does not appear to require protection for the intervening amide coupling (128015e7428783618b55e86b70dc9098ee8bc3c63d753ec728ea80c207a3a178) and acyl chloride steps. A free phenol can survive amide bond formation with an acyl chloride if controlled stoichiometry/conditions are used, but acyl chlorides could O-acylate the phenol — so SOME protection is justifiable. Still, allyl removal via Pd is incompatible concern with the electron-rich alkene of the oxanorbornene core, which could undergo competing coordination/isomerization. A more orthogonal phenol protecting group (e.g., benzyl removed by hydrogenation would be incompatible with the alkene; silyl ether would be cleaner) should be considered. Net: protecting group choice is non-optimal.

Amide coupling between the suberic acid mono-tert-butyl ester acyl chloride and the aniline. The transformation (acyl chloride + aniline → anilide) is well-established. The phenol is allyl-protected here, which addresses O- vs N-acylation selectivity, which is good. However, the free secondary alcohol on the oxabicyclic ring (the C-OH adjacent to the oxygen bridge) is unprotected and would compete with the aniline for acylation by the highly reactive acyl chloride. This is a significant chemoselectivity problem — esterification of the secondary alcohol is likely. A milder coupling (e.g., using the carboxylic acid with EDC/HATU, or a less reactive activated ester) under controlled conditions would favor the more nucleophilic aniline, but with an acyl chloride competing O-acylation of the aliphatic alcohol is a real risk. Recommend protecting the secondary OH or using milder amide coupling reagents.

Formation of the acyl chloride from suberic acid mono-tert-butyl ester using oxalyl chloride. This is a textbook transformation, typically with catalytic DMF in DCM. The tert-butyl ester is stable to oxalyl chloride. The selective mono-activation works because the other carboxyl is protected as the Boc/t-Bu ester. Well-precedented and high-yielding. Starting materials are accessible (mono-tert-butyl suberate is commercially available or readily made).

Williamson-type O-allylation of the phenol with allyl bromide (base, e.g., K2CO3). The disconnection is reasonable for installing the allyl protecting group. However, the substrate contains a free aniline (-NH2) which is more nucleophilic toward allyl bromide than the phenolate under many conditions, leading to competing N-allylation. Chemoselective O-allylation in the presence of a free aniline is problematic. Additionally, the secondary aliphatic alcohol could also react. The order of operations is questionable — protecting the phenol after the aniline is already free creates a selectivity conflict. Recommend revisiting the protection sequence so the phenol is protected before the aniline is unmasked, or use a phenol-selective method.

This step is the deprotection of a tert-butyl ester to reveal the free carboxylic acid, performed under acidic conditions (e.g., TFA in DCM). This is a well-established and reliable transformation. The phenol, sulfonate ester, vinyl ether (if still present), amide, and oxabicyclic ring should all tolerate mild acidic TFA conditions, though prolonged exposure could risk some sensitivity in the enol/diene-containing bicyclic system. Overall, a clean and standard final deprotection step.

local_feedback: Protecting group strategy is wrong / non-optimal
local_feedback_text: This step proposes removal of the O-allyl protecting group on the phenol (Pd-catalyzed deallylation) to reveal the free phenol. The transformation itself (allyl ether cleavage via Pd(0)/scavenger) is feasible. However, the strategic use of an allyl protecting group here is questionable. The molecule already contains a tert-butyl ester and an aryl methyl sulfonate; deallylation conditions using Pd(0) and nucleophilic scavengers are generally compatible. The bigger concern is that introducing and then removing the allyl group (f1a7664c0d33214bb7561cb27fea7eb2a145d5ab3958d34b4906c338a54a0a70 then 548b3e7b57ad47a6a70ad0e7011a2e207dc9f87b6530c38181e4a7716c168087) adds two steps purely to mask a phenol during a single amide coupling/acylation step, which may not be necessary if a milder acylation could tolerate the free phenol. The allyl protection is defensible but adds inefficiency to the route.

This step is an acylation of an aniline with an acid chloride (tert-butyl 8-chloro-8-oxooctanoate). The amide bond formation between the aniline NH2 and the acyl chloride is feasible. However, with a free aniline and the acid chloride, chemoselectivity should be fine since the aniline is the only strong nucleophile (phenol is allyl-protected). The main concern: the acid chloride is a mono-acid chloride of a tert-butyl ester diacid, so there is no risk of bis-acylation. Standard conditions (base such as Et3N or pyridine, DCM, 0 °C) should give clean monoamide. Minor risk if any free OH present. Overall feasible with attention to base/stoichiometry.

Formation of the acid chloride from the mono-tert-butyl ester of a diacid using oxalyl chloride is a standard, reliable transformation (typically with catalytic DMF in DCM). Chemoselectivity is excellent: only the free carboxylic acid reacts, while the tert-butyl ester is inert to oxalyl chloride. The starting mono-tert-butyl suberate is commercially available or readily prepared. A clean, well-precedented step.

Williamson ether synthesis / O-allylation of a phenol with allyl bromide (base such as K2CO3 in DMF/acetone). This is a robust and selective transformation. The phenol is the most acidic/nucleophilic site; the aniline NH2 could in principle compete via N-alkylation, but anilines are much less nucleophilic toward allyl bromide under mild base conditions and phenoxide formation with K2CO3 favors O-alkylation. Some N-allylation side product is possible but generally minor. Overall feasible; consider mild conditions to maximize O- vs N-selectivity.

This step is the removal of a tert-butyl ester to reveal the free carboxylic acid, achieved via standard acidic conditions (TFA, or HCl). The transformation is well-precedented and chemoselective for the Boc-type ester. However, one must consider that the molecule contains an aryl sulfonate ester, a free phenol, and an oxabicyclic system. The aryl sulfonate (sulfonate ester of a guaiacol derivative) and the oxabicyclic ether should both survive mild acidic tBu cleavage. The main concern is whether the strongly acidic conditions could affect the strained oxabicyclo[2.2.1] system; generally these survive TFA. Overall feasible.

This step proposes deprotection/removal of an allyl group from a phenol allyl ether to reveal the free phenol (the para-hydroxyphenyl). Pd(0)-catalyzed allyl deallylation (e.g., Pd(PPh3)4 with a scavenger such as morpholine or barbituric acid) is standard. However, the substrate contains a terminal allyl on the phenol AND a vinyl/alkene within the oxanorbornene system; the strained bicyclic alkene could be problematic but is unlikely to interfere with deallylation. A more significant concern is chemoselectivity: the aniline amide and the aryl sulfonate ester should survive, but the phenol allyl deprotection in the presence of a strained, electron-rich enol-ether type bicyclic alkene needs care. The disconnection itself (revealing the protected allyl phenol) is reasonable as a protecting group strategy. Feasible with attention to selectivity.

This is an amide bond formation between an aromatic amine (aniline) and an acid chloride (mono-tert-butyl ester of suberic/azelaic acid chloride). Acylation of anilines with acid chlorides is robust and high-yielding under Schotten-Baumann conditions or with an amine base (Et3N, pyridine). The free phenol is masked as the allyl ether, and the carboxylic acid is masked as the tBu ester, so chemoselective N-acylation should proceed cleanly. The aryl sulfonate ester is stable to these conditions. Well-designed step.

Formation of an acid chloride from a mono-tert-butyl protected diacid using oxalyl chloride. This is standard. The selectivity is governed by the fact that one carboxyl is masked as the tBu ester and the other is free; oxalyl chloride (with catalytic DMF) converts the free acid to the acid chloride without touching the tBu ester. Note: the mono-tBu ester diacid starting material is itself a known compound class but commercial availability of the specific chain length should be checked; otherwise it is readily made by mono-protection. Reaction is feasible.

This step is a Williamson-type O-allylation of a phenol with allyl bromide. The concern is chemoselectivity: the molecule contains both a free phenol AND a free aniline (aromatic amine). Under basic conditions with allyl bromide, the more nucleophilic aniline nitrogen would competitively undergo N-allylation (likely faster than O-allylation of the phenol). This would lead to undesired N-alkylation and over-alkylation of the aniline. As drawn, selective O-allylation of the phenol while leaving the free aniline untouched is not realistic. A protecting group on the aniline, or performing the allylation before introduction of the free amine, would be required. This is a genuine selectivity flaw in the route ordering.

This step is a Boc/tert-butyl ester deprotection of the carboxylic acid (TFA or acid-mediated). The transformation is well-established. However, note that the molecule contains an aryl sulfonate ester and an enol-ether-type (furanoid/oxabicyclic) framework; standard TFA conditions for tert-butyl ester cleavage are generally compatible with aryl sulfonates. The phenol (free OH on the para-hydroxyphenyl) is also tolerated. Reasonable as final deprotection step.

This step proposes removal of an O-allyl group from the phenol to reveal the free para-hydroxyphenyl. Allyl ether removal (e.g., Pd(0)/scavenger or Pd(PPh3)4) is generally feasible and chemoselective. The main concern is the presence of the strained oxabicyclic bridge and the aryl sulfonate ester, which should survive Pd-catalyzed deallylation. However, the molecule contains no other obvious competing allyl handles, so chemoselectivity for the O-allyl is reasonable. The greater question is why an allyl protecting group was introduced for a phenol that is ultimately free in the product — see protecting-group commentary in the overall route. Confidence moderate.

Amide bond formation between an aniline and an acid chloride (Schotten-Baumann type acylation). This is a robust, high-yielding transformation. The aniline is the most nucleophilic site; the phenol is protected as allyl ether, and the carboxylic acid is masked as the tert-butyl ester, so chemoselective N-acylation is well-controlled. Good disconnection.

Conversion of a mono-tert-butyl-protected diacid (mono-acid) to the corresponding acid chloride using oxalyl chloride. Standard and reliable. The tert-butyl ester is stable to oxalyl chloride under mild conditions (catalytic DMF, low temperature). The selective activation of the free acid over the ester is correct. Building blocks are commercially available.

This step proposes O-allylation of a phenol (Williamson ether synthesis with allyl bromide). The major chemoselectivity problem: the substrate also contains a free aniline (-NH2), which is more nucleophilic than the phenolate under many conditions and would compete for N-allylation. Under basic conditions (K2CO3), phenolate formation is favored and O-alkylation can be made selective, but N-alkylation of the aniline is a real risk and would require careful control. Additionally, introducing an allyl protecting group here, only to remove it two steps later (548b3e7b57ad47a6a70ad0e7011a2e207dc9f87b6530c38181e4a7716c168087), is questionable — if the phenol must be protected during the subsequent acylation, a more orthogonal/robust group could be considered, but the free phenol may in fact survive acid chloride acylation if the aniline is much more reactive, potentially making the allyl protection unnecessary.

This is a Hantzsch thiazole synthesis between the thiourea-bearing intermediate and 2-bromo-1-(2,4-dichlorophenyl)ethanone. While the disconnection is sound and well-precedented, there is a serious chemoselectivity concern: the reactant CCCCCCC(Sc1nc(Cl)cc(NC(N)=S)n1)C(=O)O contains a free carboxylic acid and an existing thioether, plus the aryl-Cl on the triazine ring. The thiourea will react with the α-bromoketone to build the thiazole as drawn, which is fine. However, the carboxylic acid could compete with O-alkylation/esterification of the α-bromoketone, and the cyclization regiochemistry to form the correct 2-aminothiazole (vs. linkage isomers) should be carefully controlled. Overall feasible but yields may suffer; consider doing the Hantzsch reaction before installing the carboxylic acid functionality.

This step proposes S-alkylation of the heteroaryl thiol (the 2-mercaptotriazine) with 2-bromooctanoic acid. The disconnection is reasonable, but the reactant NC(=S)Nc1cc(Cl)nc(S)n1 contains TWO sulfur nucleophiles: the ring thiol/thione AND the thiourea (NC(=S)N) group. Selective alkylation at only the ring thiol while leaving the thiourea sulfur intact is highly questionable - thiourea sulfur is a strong soft nucleophile and would compete. Additionally, there is a free carboxylic acid in the alkylating agent and the secondary α-bromide is sterically hindered and prone to elimination. This S-alkylation should likely be performed before the thiourea is introduced, or with protection. Significant chemoselectivity problem as written.

This is the basic/acidic hydrolysis of the N-benzoyl group from an acylthiourea to liberate the free thiourea (NC(=S)Nc1cc(Cl)nc(S)n1). This is a standard, well-precedented deprotection (typically K2CO3/MeOH or NaOH). The free thiol/thione on the triazine is compatible. Some risk that the aryl-Cl on the triazine could undergo competing hydrolysis/substitution under forcing basic conditions, but mild conditions should preserve it. Reasonable transformation.

Addition of an aminoheterocycle (Nc1cc(Cl)nc(S)n1) to benzoyl isothiocyanate to form the acylthiourea is a classic, robust reaction (PhC(O)NCS is commercially available). However, the aminotriazine reactant bears a free ring thiol (-SH), which is itself nucleophilic and could compete with the amino group for addition to the isothiocyanate, giving S-acyl/thioimidate byproducts. The exocyclic NH2 is the intended nucleophile and is generally favored for thiourea formation, but chemoselectivity vs. the thiol must be managed (e.g., the thiol may need protection). Otherwise the transformation type is well-established.

This is a Hantzsch thiazole synthesis disconnection. The forward reaction combines the alpha-bromoketone (O=C(CBr)c1ccc(Cl)cc1Cl) with the thiourea moiety to form the 2-aminothiazole ring. This is a well-established and reliable transformation. The thiourea on the pyrimidine nitrogen cyclizes with the alpha-haloketone to give the 2-(arylamino)thiazole. A key concern is chemoselectivity: the molecule contains a free carboxylic acid and a separate thioether sulfur. The thiourea sulfur should preferentially attack the bromoketone, but there is some risk of competing S-alkylation by the carboxylate or other nucleophiles. Mild conditions (EtOH, reflux) should favor the desired Hantzsch product. Overall feasible.

This disconnection proposes S-alkylation of the pyrimidine-2-thiol (NC(=S)Nc1cc(Cl)nc(S)n1) by 2-bromooctanoic acid (CCCCCCC(Br)C(=O)O). The chemoselectivity is highly problematic: the reactant contains both a pyrimidine-2-thiol (-SH, the desired alkylation site) AND a thiourea (NC(=S)) bearing a highly nucleophilic thiocarbonyl sulfur. Thiourea sulfur is one of the best soft nucleophiles and would compete strongly (likely outcompete) with the ring thiol for alkylation by the secondary alkyl bromide. Additionally, the secondary alkyl bromide adjacent to a carboxylic acid is sterically hindered and prone to elimination. The order of operations is questionable - installing the thiourea before the S-alkylation creates a selectivity conflict. Recommend performing the S-alkylation before introducing the thiourea, or protecting the thiourea.

This is a benzoyl deprotection of an acylthiourea to reveal the free thiourea (NC(=S)Nc1cc(Cl)nc(S)n1). Acylthioureas are commonly hydrolyzed under basic conditions (K2CO3/MeOH or NaOH) to liberate the free thiourea. This is a standard and reliable transformation. The aminopyrimidine-thiol substrate should tolerate these conditions, though care must be taken with the chloro substituent on the electron-poor pyrimidine, which could be susceptible to nucleophilic aromatic substitution under strongly basic/nucleophilic conditions. Mild conditions are advised.

This step forms an acylthiourea by reacting the aminopyrimidine (Nc1cc(Cl)nc(S)n1) with benzoyl isothiocyanate (O=C(N=C=S)c1ccccc1). Addition of the aryl/heteroaryl amine to the isothiocyanate is a classic, high-yielding reaction to make N-aroylthioureas. Benzoyl isothiocyanate is a standard reagent. One concern is the presence of the free pyrimidine-2-thiol, which could also react with the isothiocyanate; however, the 4-amino group is the intended and typically more reactive site for this benzoylthiourea formation. Some competition or need for selective conditions may arise. Generally a feasible and well-precedented step.

This is a classic Hantzsch thiazole synthesis: condensation of 2,4'-dichlorophenacyl bromide (an alpha-bromoketone) with a thiourea to construct the 2-aminothiazole bearing the 2,4-dichlorophenyl group at C4. The disconnection is appropriate and well-precedented. However, two concerns: (1) The thiourea fragment also bears a free carboxylic acid and a thioether linkage; the Hantzsch cyclization requires the N-aryl thiourea nitrogen to act as nucleophile, and chemoselectivity between the two thiourea-derived nitrogens (the aminopyrimidine N-H vs the terminal NH2) determines correct regiochemistry. The aminothiazole N must connect through the correct nitrogen to give the depicted Nc2nc... linkage. (2) The free thiol/thioether and carboxylic acid should be tolerated under typical Hantzsch conditions (EtOH, reflux). Mild conditions or buffering (Hantzsch-Holzapfel modification) recommended to avoid epimerization and HBr-mediated side reactions.

This step proposes S-alkylation of the pyrimidine thiol (NC(=S)Nc1cc(Cl)nc(S)n1) with 2-bromooctanoic acid. The major problem is severe chemoselectivity: the substrate contains BOTH a pyrimidine 2-thiol AND a thiourea (NC(N)=S), each presenting nucleophilic sulfur atoms. Selective S-alkylation at the pyrimidinyl thiol over the thiourea sulfur is not assured; thioureas are strongly nucleophilic at S and would compete. Additionally, the alpha-bromo acid is prone to elimination and the free carboxylate could promote O-alkylation/lactone-like side reactions. A protecting-group strategy for the thiourea, or installation of the thioether before the thiourea, would improve selectivity. As written, mixtures are likely. Note also that 2-bromooctanoic acid creates a stereocenter with no stereocontrol.

Hydrolytic cleavage of the benzoyl group from the N-benzoyl(acyl)thiourea to liberate the free monosubstituted thiourea is standard, typically achieved with K2CO3 in MeOH/H2O or NaOH. This is the conventional two-step sequence (acyl isothiocyanate addition then debenzoylation) for accessing N-aryl thioureas cleanly. The pyrimidine thiol and chloride should be tolerated under mild basic hydrolysis, though prolonged strong base could risk displacement of the pyrimidine chloride. Use controlled conditions.

Reaction of benzoyl isothiocyanate with the aminopyrimidine (Nc1cc(Cl)nc(S)n1) to give the N-benzoyl thiourea is a well-established transformation. However, the substrate contains a free pyrimidine-2-thiol in addition to the exocyclic amine. Benzoyl isothiocyanate is highly electrophilic and could react at the thiol (S-acylation / dithiocarbamate-type adduct) competing with the desired amine addition. Chemoselectivity for the amine is plausible (amine is a better nucleophile toward isothiocyanate to form thiourea) but not guaranteed given the thiol presence. Protection of the thiol or careful stoichiometry/low temperature is advisable. The starting aminopyrimidinethiol (4-amino-6-chloro-pyrimidine-2-thiol) commercial availability should be verified.

This is a Hantzsch thiazole synthesis: the thiourea moiety (NC(N)=S) condenses with the α-bromoketone O=C(CBr)c1ccc(Cl)cc1Cl to form the 2-aminothiazole ring bearing the 2,4-dichlorophenyl substituent. This is a well-established and reliable transformation. The aryl-substituted thiazole forms regioselectively with the aryl group at C4. The main concern is chemoselectivity: the substrate also contains a thioether (Sc1...) and a carboxylic acid, but the thiourea sulfur/nitrogen is far more nucleophilic and the reaction is selective for thiourea cyclization. Mild heating in ethanol typically suffices. Good disconnection.

This step proposes S-alkylation of NC(=S)Nc1cc(Cl)nc(S)n1 with the α-bromo acid CCCCCCC(Br)C(=O)O to install the alkyl thioether on the pyrimidine ring thiol. The major problem is chemoselectivity: the molecule contains TWO sulfur nucleophiles - the pyrimidine 2-thiol/thione and the thiourea (NC(=S)) sulfur, which is itself highly nucleophilic. S-alkylation could occur at the thiourea sulfur rather than (or in addition to) the desired pyrimidine thiol. Additionally, the carboxylic acid of the bromoacid is unprotected, and the secondary alkyl bromide is somewhat hindered/prone to elimination. To make this work, selective protection or a different sequence (alkylate the pyrimidine thiol BEFORE introducing the thiourea) would be advisable. As drawn, significant selectivity issues are expected.

This is the hydrolytic removal of the benzoyl group from an N-benzoylthiourea to reveal the free thiourea NC(=S)Nc1cc(Cl)nc(S)n1. Benzoylthioureas are commonly hydrolyzed (e.g., K2CO3/MeOH-H2O or NaOH) to give the corresponding thioureas. This is a standard and reliable deprotection. Care must be taken not to hydrolyze under harsh conditions that could affect the chloropyrimidine, but mild basic conditions are selective.

Addition of the aminopyrimidine Nc1cc(Cl)nc(S)n1 to benzoyl isothiocyanate (O=C(N=C=S)c1ccccc1) to give the N-benzoylthiourea is a textbook reaction. Aromatic/heteroaromatic amines add cleanly to acyl isothiocyanates. One consideration: the aminopyrimidine also bears a free thiol (2-mercapto), which could compete by adding to the isothiocyanate. However, the exocyclic NH2 is the intended and typically more reactive site for this benzoylthiourea formation; some competing S-addition is possible. Overall a feasible and standard step.

This is a Suzuki-Miyaura cross-coupling between an aryl boronic acid and an aryl bromide forming the biaryl bond. This is a well-precedented disconnection. The primary amide is compatible with standard Pd-catalyzed Suzuki conditions. The free carboxylic acid on the thiophene side chain is also tolerated. The boronic acid bearing an ortho-amide is commercially available (2-carbamoylphenylboronic acid). One minor consideration: the benzylic C-O ether (ArCH2-O-thiophene) could in principle undergo competing oxidative addition, but aryl bromides are far more reactive, so chemoselectivity strongly favors the desired coupling. Good convergent disconnection.

This step represents reduction/deoxygenation of a beta-keto acid (O=C(O)CC(=O)Ar) to the corresponding saturated propanoic acid (O=C(O)CCAr). This corresponds to a Wolff-Kishner or Clemmensen-type reduction of the aryl ketone to a methylene. While feasible in principle, harsh conditions (Wolff-Kishner: strong base/hydrazine/heat; Clemmensen: Zn/Hg, HCl) may be problematic for the benzylic aryl ether and the aryl bromide. A milder alternative would be to convert the route differently. Note also the thiophene is electron-rich and the benzylic ether linkage could be cleaved under strongly acidic Clemmensen conditions. The disconnection is reasonable but reagent/condition selection is critical.

Ester hydrolysis of the ethyl ester to the carboxylic acid (saponification). This is a standard, robust transformation. Mild base (LiOH/NaOH) selectively hydrolyzes the ethyl ester. The beta-keto ester is acidic and may be present partly as enol, but hydrolysis to the beta-keto acid is feasible, though beta-keto acids are prone to decarboxylation upon heating/acidification. Care needed to avoid premature decarboxylation. The aryl bromide and benzylic ether are stable under these conditions.

Claisen-type condensation between a methyl aryl ketone and diethyl carbonate to form the beta-keto ester. This is a classic and well-established transformation (acetophenone-type + diethyl carbonate with NaH or NaOEt base gives the beta-ketoester). Both starting materials are listed in stock. One consideration is that strong base could deprotonate/cause side reactions, but the substrate (acetylthiophene with benzylic ether and aryl bromide) should be reasonably compatible. The aryl bromide is stable to NaH/base. Good, efficient step with commercial starting materials.

This is a Suzuki-Miyaura cross-coupling between an aryl boronic acid bearing a primary amide and an aryl bromide. The disconnection of the biaryl bond is strategically sound and well-precedented. Both coupling partners are reasonable. Considerations: (1) The carboxylic acid on the thiophene side and the primary amide are both tolerated under standard Pd-catalyzed Suzuki conditions (e.g., Pd(PPh3)4 or Pd(dppf)Cl2 with K2CO3/Na2CO3 base). (2) The free carboxylic acid is generally compatible but may require slightly more base; protection is not strictly necessary. (3) Chemoselectivity for the aryl-Br over the thiophene ring is fine. Overall a robust, convergent final disconnection.

This step is a reduction/deoxygenation of a beta-keto acid (O=C(O)CC(=O)Ar) to the saturated acid (O=C(O)CCAr). This corresponds to removing the benzylic ketone carbonyl to a methylene. Such a transformation can be achieved by Clemmensen, Wolff-Kishner, or more practically by ionic hydrogenation/Et3SiH-TFA or catalytic hydrogenation. However, caution: the benzyl ether (ArCH2-O) and the aryl bromide are susceptible to hydrogenolysis under catalytic H2/Pd conditions, and Wolff-Kishner/Clemmensen harsh conditions may affect the thiophene-O-benzyl linkage. A milder selective deoxygenation (e.g., Et3SiH/BF3 or thioketal formation then Raney Ni - but Raney Ni would cleave C-Br and desulfurize thiophene) must be chosen carefully. The disconnection is reasonable but reagent selection is non-trivial given the aryl bromide that must survive for the subsequent Suzuki.

Saponification/hydrolysis of an ethyl ester to the carboxylic acid (beta-keto ester to beta-keto acid). Standard transformation with LiOH/NaOH. The beta-keto acid product is prone to decarboxylation, but isolation is feasible under controlled conditions. The aryl bromide and benzyl thioether ether are stable. Straightforward and feasible.

Claisen-type condensation of a methyl aryl ketone (acetylthiophene derivative) with diethyl carbonate to give the beta-keto ester. This is a classic transformation (using NaH or NaOEt as base). The acetyl group's alpha-protons are acidic and the enolate attacks diethyl carbonate. Feasible and well-precedented. Note that strong base (NaH/NaOEt) is compatible with aryl bromide and benzyl ether. Reagents are commercially available. Good step.

This is a Suzuki-Miyaura cross-coupling between 2-carbamoylphenylboronic acid and an aryl bromide to form the biaryl bond. The disconnection is strategically sound and well-precedented. The primary amide and the free carboxylic acid are generally tolerated under standard Pd-catalyzed Suzuki conditions (e.g., Pd(PPh3)4 or Pd(dppf)Cl2 with K2CO3/Na2CO3). One consideration: the boronic acid bearing an ortho-amide can sometimes be prone to protodeboronation, and the carboxylic acid may require a slight excess of base. Overall a robust convergent step.

This step proposes reduction of a beta-keto carboxylic acid (O=C(O)CC(=O)Ar) to the saturated carboxylic acid (O=C(O)CCAr), i.e., a deoxygenation of the aryl ketone to a methylene. This is a full ketone-to-methylene reduction (e.g., Wolff-Kishner, Clemmensen, or thiophene-tolerant catalytic conditions). The challenges: (1) Clemmensen (strong acid) and Wolff-Kishner (strong base/hydrazine, high temp) conditions risk cleaving the benzylic aryl-thioether (OCc) ether and could affect the aryl bromide; (2) catalytic hydrogenation would risk hydrodehalogenation of the ArBr and possible reduction/poisoning by the thiophene. A more controlled approach would be ketone reduction to the alcohol followed by deoxygenation, or use of Et3SiH/BF3 ionic hydrogenation. As drawn, chemoselectivity over the C-Br bond and benzylic ether is a real concern.

Hydrolysis of the ethyl ester to the free carboxylic acid of a beta-keto ester. This is straightforward; however beta-keto esters can undergo decarboxylation upon hydrolysis depending on conditions. Mild basic hydrolysis (LiOH) at low temperature followed by careful acidification should give the beta-keto acid, though the product is prone to decarboxylation. The aryl bromide and benzylic ether are stable under these conditions. Reasonable step.

Claisen-type condensation of the aryl methyl ketone with diethyl carbonate to install the beta-keto ester. This is a classic transformation using a strong base (NaH, NaOEt, or LDA). The acetyl methyl group is acidic enough to be deprotonated and acylated by diethyl carbonate. The aryl bromide and benzylic thioether ether are compatible. Standard and well-precedented. Watch for O- vs C-acylation but C-acylation dominates with diethyl carbonate. Good step.

This is a Suzuki-Miyaura cross-coupling between an aryl boronic acid bearing a primary amide and an aryl bromide. The disconnection at the biaryl bond is strategic and well-precedented. The free carboxylic acid and primary amide are generally tolerated under Pd-catalyzed Suzuki conditions (e.g., Pd(PPh3)4 or Pd(dppf)Cl2 with K2CO3/Na2CO3 base). The thiophene and benzylic ether are also compatible. One minor concern: the free carboxylic acid may require a slight excess of base, but no protecting group is strictly necessary. Selectivity is not an issue as there is only one aryl halide. A solid disconnection.

This step corresponds to reduction of a beta-keto acid to the saturated carboxylic acid (removal of the ketone carbonyl to give the CH2). This is a deoxygenation of an aryl ketone, achievable via Clemmensen, Wolff-Kishner, or more practically a two-step reduction (e.g., NaBH4 then ionic hydrogenation, or catalytic hydrogenation of the corresponding benzylic alcohol). However, caution: the benzylic aryl ether (ArCH2-O) and the aryl bromide could be problematic under hydrogenolytic conditions (debromination, benzyl ether cleavage). Wolff-Kishner or Clemmensen would avoid hydrogenolysis issues but Clemmensen's strongly acidic conditions could cleave the benzylic ether. A milder approach (e.g., Et3SiH/TFA ionic hydrogenation after ketone reduction) may be preferable. The transformation is feasible but reagent choice is critical to avoid C-Br loss and benzyl ether cleavage.

Ester hydrolysis of an ethyl beta-keto ester to the free beta-keto acid. This is straightforward saponification (LiOH or NaOH, aqueous THF/MeOH). Beta-keto acids are prone to decarboxylation, so mild conditions and careful workup are needed. The aryl bromide and benzylic ether are stable under basic hydrolysis. Feasible, though decarboxylation risk should be noted.

This is a Claisen-type condensation forming a beta-keto ester from an aryl methyl ketone and diethyl carbonate, typically using a strong base (NaH or NaOEt). This is a classic and reliable transformation to install the -C(=O)CH2CO2Et moiety. The aryl bromide and benzyl thiophenyl ether are compatible with these conditions. Selectivity favors deprotonation of the acetyl methyl group. Both starting materials (the acetylthiophene derivative and diethyl carbonate) are reasonable; diethyl carbonate is commercially available. The acetylthiophene building block is marked in stock. Good, well-precedented step.

This step proposes an intramolecular Suzuki-type coupling between an arylboronic acid and an aryl bromide (on the imidazole C-Br) to forge the biaryl bond and form the fused tetracyclic system. While intramolecular Suzuki couplings to form biaryls are precedented, there are serious problems here: (1) The boronic acid and the C-Br are on the same molecule and the geometry would have to allow a 5-membered-ring-forming biaryl coupling - this is highly strained and atypical. (2) Critically, the product imidazo[1,5-a]-fused system requires C-C bond formation directly between the benzene ring and the imidazole C, but the boronic acid is on the benzene and the Br is on the imidazole - a standard Pd(0) intramolecular Suzuki could in principle do this, but a free secondary alcohol and the basic imidazole nitrogen complicate matters. The atom count and connectivity between starting material and product also appear inconsistent (the product loses the boronic acid and forms the ring). The disconnection is plausible in concept as an intramolecular Suzuki but the strained 5-membered biaryl closure makes success doubtful. I categorize as unlikely as drawn.

A protecting-group/orthogonal-leaving-group strategy or stepwise installation is required.

However, the overall protecting-group logic is questionable: the THP was installed (ab893909a2c8e0350ab55364b00200f30a400720f42ff38c7b9f358b1bd6c15a) and then carried through a nitro reduction (67342e89cf256506f2f86201d3cd378491660d19c746fa237fb6baf0a7df808c), only to be removed here, then the freed alcohol is mesylated (ccd64bdf697e16f51b5a1a89c79d1e9abd1605f0b6705917939eb7ce82bade0e). The same OH ends up as a leaving group, so an orthogonal strategy or direct use of a halide/leaving group would be more efficient. Also note: THP creates a new stereocenter giving diastereomer complications. Non-optimal protecting group sequencing.

local_feedback: Problems with reaction type and functional group compatibility
local_feedback_text: This is a nitro-to-amine reduction. The substrate contains an O-methyl oxime ether (C=N-OMe) and an alkyl bromide, both of which are highly sensitive to common nitro reduction conditions. Catalytic hydrogenation (H2/Pd) would reduce/cleave the oxime ether (N-O bond hydrogenolysis) and cause dehalogenation of the C-Br bond. Dissolving-metal or Fe/Zn reductions might be more chemoselective but still risk the oxime and alkyl halide. Achieving clean ArNO2 → ArNH2 while preserving the oxime ether AND the alkyl bromide is a serious chemoselectivity/compatibility challenge. Consider transfer hydrogenation alternatives or reordering steps; even so, the alkyl bromide and oxime survival are doubtful.

THP protection of a primary alcohol using dihydropyran (shown as the enol ether C1=COCCC1) under acid catalysis (PPTS/cat. acid) is a standard transformation and should proceed. The free primary OH is the nucleophile. Minor concern: acidic conditions could affect the O-methyl oxime, but PPTS conditions are typically mild enough. The transformation is reasonable, though it introduces an unnecessary protecting group (see c36154dea280772ccebdffc5a871d4358106face928c22ec399475a0a9dba88e commentary). Overall the protection chemistry is sound but the strategy is questionable.

This step proposes formation of the piperidine ring via double N-alkylation: a primary amine (after displacement of the mesylate by the amine, and the existing secondary amine bearing the cyclohexylmethyl group) closing onto the ring. The retrosynthetic logic is that the 4-substituted piperidine is constructed by intramolecular cyclization of a secondary amine onto a pendant mesylate. This is mechanistically plausible (intramolecular N-alkylation to form a 6-membered ring is favorable), but the precursor is drawn as an open-chain bis-functionalized compound and there is a concern that intramolecular vs intermolecular alkylation selectivity could be problematic, and competing reactions with the free aniline (-NH2) and oxime functionalities are likely. The free aromatic amine could also be alkylated. Overall a reasonable but non-standard disconnection requiring careful control.

This step couples (aminomethyl)cyclohexane with a substrate bearing BOTH a primary alkyl bromide AND a primary mesylate. Both are good leaving groups; selective mono-alkylation of the amine at only one of these is highly unlikely. The amine would react with either electrophile non-selectively and likely over-alkylate (forming the tertiary amine/ring prematurely or polymerizing). Additionally, the free aniline could interfere. This disconnection sets up the later cyclization (8c5ea146d998b718ad21ff505929cccc1f2ba099797f1dad4e2856aa02f560c9) but the chemoselectivity between Br and OMs is a serious flaw. A differentiated leaving-group strategy or reductive amination approach would be far more robust.

Mesylation of a primary alcohol with MsCl is straightforward chemistry. However, the substrate already contains a primary alkyl bromide and a free aniline. The free aniline (-NH2) is nucleophilic and could be sulfonylated by MsCl, competing with the desired O-mesylation. Use of a mild base (Et3N) at low temperature and controlled stoichiometry would be needed; selectivity for O over N is uncertain. The alcohol mesylation itself is fine, but chemoselectivity with the unprotected aniline is a concern.

Formation of methanesulfonyl chloride from methanesulfonic acid and oxalyl chloride is a well-established transformation. However, this is a reagent preparation step that is typically unnecessary in a synthetic route since MsCl is inexpensive and commercially available. As a chemical transformation it is valid.

Removal of the THP protecting group to reveal the primary alcohol is standard (mild acid, e.g., PPTS/MeOH or dilute acid). This is chemically sound. The alkyl bromide and oxime ether are compatible with mild acidic THP deprotection conditions, though prolonged strong acid could affect the oxime ether — mild conditions are advised.

Reduction of an aromatic nitro group to an aniline is a well-established transformation. The challenge here is chemoselectivity: standard catalytic hydrogenation (H2/Pd) would also reduce the alkyl bromide (hydrodehalogenation), cleave the C-Br bond, and could reduce the oxime ether (C=N) and the aryl chloride. Therefore a chemoselective method (e.g., Fe/NH4Cl, SnCl2, or Zn/AcOH) must be used to preserve the alkyl bromide, aryl-Cl, and the O-methyl oxime. With proper reagent choice this is feasible.

THP protection of a primary alcohol using dihydropyran (3,4-dihydro-2H-pyran) under acid catalysis (e.g., PPTS) is standard and high-yielding. Compatible with the alkyl bromide, nitroarene, and oxime ether. Note this creates a new stereocenter (THP acetal) giving diastereomers, but this is inconsequential for a transient protecting group.

This step forms the piperidine ring via double N-alkylation (intramolecular cyclization). The retrosynthesis disconnects the piperidine to a precursor with a secondary amine and a mesylate leaving group. In the forward direction, the secondary amine (N-benzyl-type, actually N-cyclohexylmethyl) displaces the mesylate to close the 6-membered ring. This is a reasonable cyclization to form the piperidine. However, regiochemistry of the resulting piperidine is important: the precursor as drawn (CCC(CCNCC1CCCCC1)CCOMs) would cyclize to give a 4-substituted piperidine, which matches the target. Mild base and dilution would favor cyclization over oligomerization. The free aniline and oxime ether are compatible. Confidence reflects that intramolecular alkylation to form the piperidine is sound, though competing intermolecular reactions are possible.

This step proposes mono-alkylation of cyclohexylmethylamine (a primary amine) with a substrate bearing BOTH a primary alkyl bromide AND a primary mesylate. The retrosynthesis intends selective displacement of the bromide while leaving the mesylate intact for the subsequent cyclization. However, primary mesylates and primary bromides have very similar reactivity toward amine nucleophiles, so achieving chemoselective substitution of only the bromide over the mesylate would be extremely difficult. Both leaving groups would react competitively, leading to mixtures and premature cyclization/polymerization. Additionally, primary amines tend to over-alkylate (dialkylation). This is a significant selectivity flaw. A better strategy would use orthogonal protection or sequential introduction with differentiated leaving groups.

Mesylation of a primary alcohol with MsCl is a standard, well-precedented transformation. However, the substrate contains a free aniline (-NH2), which is far more nucleophilic than the alcohol and would be sulfonylated preferentially, leading to N-mesylation rather than O-mesylation. Chemoselectivity is therefore problematic without protecting the aniline. With appropriate base (e.g., Et3N) and low temperature, partial O-selectivity is possible but the aniline competition is a real concern. The transformation itself (alcohol to mesylate) is sound, but the order/protection strategy is flawed.

This step shows the preparation of methanesulfonyl chloride from methanesulfonic acid and oxalyl chloride. MsCl is an inexpensive, ubiquitous commercial reagent and need not be synthesized. This step adds unnecessary complexity to the retrosynthetic tree.

This step represents THP protection of a primary alcohol (forward: alcohol + dihydropyran -> THP ether; shown here as deprotection in retro). The transformation of THP removal/installation is standard with PPTS or acid catalysis. The concern is chemoselectivity: the substrate also contains a primary alkyl bromide and an oxime ether. THP protection under acidic conditions could potentially affect the acid-sensitive oxime ether, but generally THP/DHP chemistry is mild enough. The bigger conceptual issue is that protecting one primary alcohol as THP while leaving a bromide elsewhere requires the diol-type intermediate handling to be carefully orchestrated. Reasonable but selectivity must be watched.

local_feedback_text: This step is the reduction of an aromatic nitro group to an aniline. While nitro reduction is well-established, the substrate contains an O-methyl oxime ether (C=N-OMe) and a primary alkyl bromide, both of which are highly sensitive to common reduction conditions. Catalytic hydrogenation (H2/Pd) would reduce the oxime ether and likely hydrogenolyze the C-Br bond. Dissolving metal or even SnCl2/Fe conditions could be partially tolerated, but the oxime ether is at risk under many reductive conditions, and the C=C/C=N double bond geometry could be affected. A chemoselective nitro reduction (e.g., Fe/NH4Cl, or Zn) would be needed and even then competing dehalogenation/oxime reduction is a serious risk. This is a significant compatibility concern.

This step shows THP protection of a primary alcohol using dihydropyran (3,4-dihydro-2H-pyran). The reaction is standard (acid-catalyzed). However, the substrate bears a primary alkyl bromide, an acid-sensitive O-methyl oxime ether, and a nitroarene. Selective mono-THP protection of the single free alcohol in the presence of these groups is achievable but the acid catalyst could affect the oxime ether. The fundamental transformation is sound, but reagent/condition selection must avoid disturbing the oxime. Note that the substrate already has a Br and an OH on the same fragment—differentiating them and the overall functional density makes this synthesis very crowded.

This is an amide bond formation between the indoline N-H of 4-(trifluoromethyl)indoline and an acid chloride. The acylation of a secondary amine (indoline nitrogen) with an acyl chloride is well-precedented and should proceed smoothly with a base (e.g., Et3N, DIPEA). The major concern, however, is the use of the acid chloride bearing an unprotected pyrimidinone N-H and a heteroaryl-attached morpholine; these are tolerated, but see comments on the acid chloride formation step. Chemoselectivity should favor acylation of the more nucleophilic indoline nitrogen over the pyrimidinone N-H/lactam.

The disconnection to form the acid chloride from the carboxylic acid is reasonable, but the choice of oxalyl chloride is problematic here because the substrate is an alpha-(heteroaryl)acetic acid bearing an acidic pyrimidinone N-H and a tautomerizable hydroxypyrimidine/pyrimidinone. Oxalyl chloride (typically with cat. DMF) can work, but the free lactam N-H and the carbonyl of the pyrimidinone could be chlorinated (formation of chloropyrimidine) as a competing side reaction. Thionyl chloride or oxalyl chloride could convert the pyrimidinone C=O to a chloro-pyrimidine. A milder activation strategy for the subsequent amide coupling (e.g., direct coupling of the carboxylic acid with the indoline using a peptide coupling reagent such as HATU/T3P/EDC) would avoid isolating this unstable, polyfunctional acid chloride and reduce side reactions. Confidence reflects the genuine risk of competing chlorination of the heterocycle.

Saponification/hydrolysis of an ethyl ester to the carboxylic acid is straightforward (LiOH or NaOH, aqueous THF/MeOH). The pyrimidinone and morpholine are stable under basic hydrolysis. Care is needed not to use forced conditions that could hydrolyze/decompose the aminopyrimidinone, but standard mild conditions should cleanly afford the acid. The alpha-CH2 is somewhat acidic but no epimerizable stereocenter is present, so no stereochemical concern.

local_feedback: Problems with reaction type and functional group compatibility
local_feedback_text: This is an amide coupling between the indoline NH and an acyl chloride. The disconnection itself is reasonable (forms the amide bond between the indoline secondary amine and the acetyl group). However, the acyl chloride reactant bears an unprotected pyrimidinone NH and a carbonyl/lactam system that would compete for acylation. The acid chloride could also react with the lactam NH or the ring nitrogen. Selectivity for the indoline NH over the pyrimidinone NH is not guaranteed. A safer approach would be a coupling-reagent-mediated amidation (e.g., HATU/DIPEA or T3P) directly from the carboxylic acid, avoiding the acid chloride and its handling issues entirely. Also note that 2-(substituted) pyrimidinone acetic acids of this type can be prone to tautomeric/chelation effects that reduce reactivity.

Formation of an acyl chloride from the carboxylic acid using oxalyl chloride is a standard transformation. However, this substrate contains an unprotected pyrimidinone (lactam) with both NH and C=O functionality. Oxalyl chloride can react with the lactam oxygen/NH and could chlorodehydroxylate the pyrimidinone ring (forming a chloropyrimidine) as a competing side reaction. The morpholine and pyrimidinone are sensitive functionalities. If an acid chloride route is desired, this is mechanistically plausible, but for this polar heterocyclic acid, direct activation with a peptide coupling reagent (HATU, T3P, CDI) is more selective and reliable than going through the isolated acyl chloride. Thionyl chloride or oxalyl chloride with catalytic DMF is the conventional choice if an acid chloride is truly needed.

Saponification/hydrolysis of the ethyl ester to the carboxylic acid is a well-established and robust transformation (e.g., LiOH or NaOH in THF/H2O/MeOH). The morpholine and pyrimidinone are stable under basic hydrolysis conditions, although care should be taken with prolonged exposure to avoid degradation of the activated methylene/heterocycle. The starting ethyl ester is listed as in stock, providing a good entry point. This is a clean, reliable step.

local_feedback_text: This is an amide coupling between an indoline N-H and an acyl chloride to form the final amide. The disconnection is strategically sound and the indoline starting material is commercially available. However, there is a significant chemoselectivity concern: the acyl chloride partner (O=C(Cl)Cc1nc(N2CCOCC2)cc(=O)[nH]1) contains a pyrimidinone N-H and a heterocyclic system with multiple nucleophilic nitrogen sites. The amide N-H of the pyrimidinone could compete for acylation, and the basic morpholine nitrogen is present. A safer and more practical approach would be to avoid the acid chloride entirely and use a direct amide coupling (e.g., HATU/DIPEA, T3P, or EDC/HOBt) between the carboxylic acid (O=C(O)Cc1nc(N2CCOCC2)cc(=O)[nH]1) and the indoline. The CF3-substituted indoline is also a somewhat hindered, electron-poor secondary amine, which will slow acylation but should still proceed. Recommend revising to a coupling-reagent-mediated amidation.

Formation of the acyl chloride from the carboxylic acid is depicted using oxalyl chloride (O=C(Cl)C(=O)Cl), which is a reasonable reagent (typically with catalytic DMF). However, the substrate is highly polar and contains a pyrimidinone N-H, a carbonyl, and a morpholine; the acid is also an alpha-CH2 acid adjacent to the heterocycle, raising risk of side reactions and poor solubility. More importantly, generating and isolating this acyl chloride is unnecessary if a direct coupling is used (see 92ed09f3254cae63270b66407728138bedd7b4a162d57dc16329c71a9a2f10ab). If an activated species is genuinely required, oxalyl chloride or SOCl2 with DMF catalysis are standard, but the free pyrimidinone N-H may consume reagent. Consider in-situ activation rather than isolating the acid chloride.

Saponification/hydrolysis of the ethyl ester (CCOC(=O)Cc1nc(N2CCOCC2)cc(=O)[nH]1) to the corresponding carboxylic acid is a well-established transformation (LiOH or NaOH, aqueous THF/MeOH). The pyrimidinone, morpholine, and CH2 linker are all compatible with mild basic hydrolysis. The ethyl ester precursor is reasonable as a building block. Minor caution: the alpha-CH2 is acidic and prolonged strong base could cause some epimerization/side reactions, but there is no stereocenter here, so this is not an issue. Good step.

local_feedback: Problems with reaction type and functional group compatibility
local_feedback_text: This is an amide coupling between the indoline NH and an acyl chloride. The disconnection itself is sound and well-precedented. However, the acyl chloride partner contains a pyrimidinone with an acidic N-H (the lactam/hydroxypyrimidine tautomer) and an electron-rich morpholine, which can compete for acylation. The acidic NH and the pyrimidinone oxygen could react with the acyl chloride leading to chemoselectivity issues. A milder amide coupling (e.g., using the carboxylic acid directly with HATU/EDC) would be far preferable to avoid the unstable, polyfunctional acyl chloride. As written with the acyl chloride, competing O- or N-acylation on the pyrimidinone is a genuine concern.

Conversion of the carboxylic acid to the acyl chloride using oxalyl chloride is in principle straightforward, but here the substrate bears a pyrimidinone with an acidic N-H/OH tautomer that can react with oxalyl chloride, and the morpholine nitrogen could also interfere. The active methylene adjacent to both the carbonyl and the heteroaromatic ring may also be prone to side reactions. More importantly, isolating and handling this acyl chloride is problematic given its polyfunctional nature. A better strategy is to skip acyl chloride formation entirely and use a direct amide coupling reagent (HATU, T3P, EDC/HOBt) on the carboxylic acid. Thionyl chloride or oxalyl chloride/cat. DMF could work but is non-optimal here.

Ester hydrolysis of the ethyl ester to the carboxylic acid is a robust, well-established transformation. Standard conditions (LiOH or NaOH in aqueous THF/MeOH) would cleanly furnish the acid. The pyrimidinone, morpholine, and active methylene are all compatible. The starting ethyl ester is listed as in stock, providing a clean entry point. Care should be taken to use mild base/controlled conditions to avoid decarboxylation of the malonyl-type/active methylene acid, but the hydrolysis itself is fine.

This step proposes debenzylation of an O-benzyl ether to reveal the free phenol as the final step. While O-debenzylation itself is feasible (hydrogenolysis with H2/Pd-C, or Lewis acid mediated), the substrate contains a highly reducible exocyclic alkylidene (the benzylidene-rhodanine type system) and a thioether/thiocarbonyl-type rhodanine core. Catalytic hydrogenolysis (H2/Pd-C) would reduce the C=C alkylidene and potentially poison the catalyst with sulfur. The exocyclic alkene is the pharmacophore and must survive. A non-hydrogenolytic debenzylation (e.g., BCl3, TMSI) might work chemoselectively but is risky given the electron-rich dimethylaminobenzylidene and the acid/Lewis-acid-sensitive imine (N=C) on the rhodanine. The protecting group strategy as a whole is also questionable since the phenol could simply be retained free during the Knoevenagel condensation.

This step constructs the aryl benzyl ether via what appears to be an SNAr displacement of an aryl fluoride by benzyl alcohol. While SNAr on the fluoro-anisole ring is conceivable, the ring is not sufficiently activated (it bears only an electron-donating methoxy and a downstream imine substituent, not strong electron-withdrawing groups ortho/para to F), so SNAr with benzyloxide would be very sluggish or fail. More importantly, the logic is inverted: typically one would install the benzyl ether by Williamson etherification on a phenol, not by displacing fluoride. The retro-disconnection to ArF + BnOH is mechanistically dubious for this substrate.

This step proposes converting an aryl bromide (on the benzylidene ring) to a dimethylamino group via reaction with dimethylamine. While Buchwald-Hartwig amination of aryl bromides with HNMe2 is feasible in principle, the substrate is a rhodanine bearing a free N-H, an exocyclic alkene, a thioether, and an arylimine — all potentially incompatible with Pd-amination conditions (catalyst poisoning by sulfur, competing N-arylation of the rhodanine N-H). The product C=C-aryl-NMe2 push-pull chromophore is best installed by Knoevenagel of the rhodanine with 4-(dimethylamino)benzaldehyde directly, rather than late-stage amination. This disconnection is strategically poor.
