The protecting group strategy is non-optimal given these compatibility concerns.

This step interconverts an N-TFA-protected free carboxylic acid into the corresponding ethyl ester (acid + EtOH). Again the route is shuffling ester identity without strategic gain. More seriously, this is yet another redundant ester interconversion that does not advance the synthesis toward simpler building blocks. The combination with the parallel methyl ester branch (44c059ad64b23e8f60ea445a89a998d454cfcb4cbe33342de9c0709a2e7763da) shows the route is circular and inconsistent. Carboxylic acid + ethanol esterification is feasible per se, but the disconnection serves no purpose.

This step converts an N-TFA methyl ester (product) from an N-TFA free carboxylic acid (reactant) - i.e. a methyl esterification. While methyl ester formation from a carboxylic acid is chemically achievable, this branch duplicates the same redundant ester interconversion seen elsewhere and does not simplify the molecule. The route keeps switching between methyl and ethyl esters of essentially the same intermediate, which is non-productive and indicates a poorly conceived retrosynthesis.

This step proposes generating the chloromethyl group (CH2Cl) from a hydroxymethyl precursor (CH2OH) with dichloromethane (ClCCl) shown as the chlorinating reagent. DCM is not a chlorinating agent for converting primary alcohols to alkyl chlorides; it serves only as a solvent. The correct reagents would be SOCl2, PCl3, or the Appel conditions (CCl4/PPh3 or NCS/PPh3). As written, the disconnection (alcohol + DCM -> chloride) is mechanistically impossible. Note also that the primary benzylic-type chloride from this strained cyclopenta-fused system may be prone to elimination or solvolysis.

This step proposes forming a methyl ester from a carboxylic acid using carbonic acid (O=C(O)O) as the methyl source. Carbonic acid cannot serve as a methylating agent for ester formation. A proper methyl esterification would require methanol (with acid catalyst or coupling reagents) or a methylating agent like MeI/TMS-diazomethane. The disconnection logic to a carboxylic acid is reasonable, but the reagent (carbonic acid) is chemically incorrect for delivering a methyl group.

This step interconverts a carboxylic acid (with free NH) into an ETHYL ester. The problem is a fundamental inconsistency: the final target (e20522ac9e5ceadf8f68291ed7919696c85177f0477a2f1947223550e6378938) bears a METHYL ester, yet this intermediate route introduces an ethyl ester. Carrying an ethyl ester forward when the goal is a methyl ester is illogical and forces unnecessary ester interconversions later. Furthermore, the free secondary amine (indoline NH) would be a far more nucleophilic/reactive site than the carboxylic acid under esterification conditions, creating chemoselectivity problems. This disconnection is poorly conceived.

local_feedback: Protecting group strategy is wrong / non-optimal
local_feedback_text: This represents removal of a trifluoroacetamide protecting group to reveal the free secondary amine. While TFA-amide removal (mild base hydrolysis, K2CO3/MeOH) is well precedented, the issue is the protecting group strategy in context: the route protects the amine as TFA-amide, then deprotects, while simultaneously juggling ester interconversions. The sequence is convoluted. Also, basic deprotection conditions for the TFA group could risk transesterification or saponification of the adjacent ester and could affect the primary alkyl chloride. The strategy needs rationalization.

This step forms an ethyl ester from a carboxylic acid plus ethanol. Beyond requiring an acid catalyst/coupling reagent (not just EtOH), the deeper flaw is that the route oscillates between methyl ester (44c059ad64b23e8f60ea445a89a998d454cfcb4cbe33342de9c0709a2e7763da) → carboxylic acid → ethyl ester (69fb4cb668241de49b02e83496c56ab91f64da2bc10942eafd0f553ca07cfc42), which is wholly redundant and self-defeating. There is no synthetic rationale for converting a methyl ester to an acid to an ethyl ester and ultimately back to a methyl ester. These interconversions add no value and should be eliminated.

This converts a methyl ester (TFA-protected) into a carboxylic acid (saponification), which is then re-esterified to an ethyl ester in 69fb4cb668241de49b02e83496c56ab91f64da2bc10942eafd0f553ca07cfc42. Since the methyl ester is already the desired functionality in the final target, performing saponification here only to re-esterify (and later interconvert again) is entirely unnecessary and counterproductive. Additionally, ester hydrolysis conditions could compromise the alkyl chloride and the TFA amide. This step should be removed; the methyl ester should simply be carried through.

This step converts a primary alcohol (hydroxymethyl) to a primary alkyl chloride. The disconnection (alcohol → chloride) is sound and common. However, the reagent shown is dichloromethane (ClCCl), which is NOT a chlorinating agent for alcohols—it is merely a solvent. The correct reagents would be SOCl2, (COCl)2, PPh3/CCl4 (Appel), or MsCl then chloride. With proper reagents this transformation is very feasible. Note also the electron-poor nitroarene and TFA amide should be compatible with these chlorination conditions.

This step proposes forming a methyl ester (COC(=O)) from a carboxylic acid using carbonic acid (O=C(O)O) as a reagent. Carbonic acid cannot serve as a methylating agent to form a methyl ester. This is chemically nonsensical - there is no carbon source for the methyl group. A proper esterification would require methanol/acid catalysis, MeI/base, TMS-diazomethane, or DMS. The disconnection itself (acid to methyl ester) is reasonable, but the proposed reagent (carbonic acid) is impossible. Moreover, this entire step appears redundant given the route already converts to the ethyl ester (62e03488a97c257b6052c13bf18efa7e2e28e539dbea936c6f6c8cd21d098674).

This step proposes converting an ethyl ester into a carboxylic acid (forward direction). However, the retrosynthetic logic here creates a confusing situation: the target is a methyl ester (e20522ac9e5ceadf8f68291ed7919696c85177f0477a2f1947223550e6378938 root), but this step interconverts a free acid with an ethyl ester. The route oscillates between methyl ester, free acid, and ethyl ester without coherent strategy. Ester hydrolysis itself is feasible, but the chloromethyl group (CCl) and the secondary amine (NH) would be problematic under typical hydrolysis conditions - the chloride could be displaced intramolecularly by the amine to form an aziridine or pyrrolidine ring. This route segment is also logically circular and inefficient.

local_feedback: Problems with reaction type and functional group compatibility
local_feedback_text: This step represents TFA (trifluoroacetyl) deprotection of the amine. Removing the electron-withdrawing trifluoroacetamide regenerates the free secondary amine adjacent to a primary alkyl chloride (CH2Cl) on the same dihydropyrrole ring system. The free nucleophilic amine will readily undergo intramolecular cyclization with the pendant chloromethyl group, forming an aziridinium/bridged system. This is a serious chemoselectivity/stability problem. The TFA group was presumably installed to prevent this very cyclization, so deprotecting it while CH2Cl is still present is poorly timed in the synthetic sequence.

This step proposes esterification of a carboxylic acid with ethanol (EtOH) to form an ethyl ester. While Fischer esterification with EtOH is feasible per se, the route makes no sense overall: the final target (e20522ac9e5ceadf8f68291ed7919696c85177f0477a2f1947223550e6378938) bears a METHYL ester, yet here an ETHYL ester is formed, then later hydrolyzed back (62e03488a97c257b6052c13bf18efa7e2e28e539dbea936c6f6c8cd21d098674), then re-esterified. This is a wasteful interconversion loop. Additionally, the substrate contains an acid-labile/base-labile chloromethyl group and a TFA amide; standard acid-catalyzed esterification could partially cleave the TFA group or promote elimination/substitution at the CH2Cl. A direct methyl ester strategy would be far more efficient.

This step proposes converting a methyl ester directly into a carboxylic acid (forward), but it is written so that the methyl ester is the product and the free acid is the reactant - i.e., methyl esterification. Together with 69fb4cb668241de49b02e83496c56ab91f64da2bc10942eafd0f553ca07cfc42 (ethyl esterification of the same acid) and 764fbad847b09d52ed8b07bad5a95f653589e6caaeec453aa83ddc104f27d9f9 (methyl esterification), the route contains multiple, mutually redundant ester-forming/cleaving steps that serve no purpose. The whole methyl/ethyl/acid interconversion network is logically incoherent and adds unnecessary steps. A single ester throughout the synthesis would suffice.

This step proposes forming the alkyl chloride (CH2Cl) from the primary alcohol (CH2OH) with dichloromethane (ClCCl/DCM) listed as the reagent/byproduct. DCM is NOT a chlorinating agent for converting primary alcohols to chlorides - it is merely a solvent. The intended transformation (alcohol to chloride) is chemically reasonable and well-precedented, but the reagent is wrong. Appropriate reagents would be SOCl2, MsCl/LiCl, PPh3/CCl4 (Appel), or PPh3/NCS. As written with DCM, the reaction is impossible. The disconnection direction is sound; only the reagent is incorrect.

This convergent step joins the indole-acetic acid fragment (containing a free phenol on the 7-position of indole) with the alkyl chloride fragment via Williamson ether synthesis (O-alkylation of the phenol with the primary chloride). The disconnection of the OCCCO ether linkage is strategically sound and convergent. However, a significant chemoselectivity issue exists: the indole fragment carries a free carboxylic acid (CC(=O)O), which under basic Williamson conditions (K2CO3/Cs2CO3) will be deprotonated and could compete as a nucleophile (O-alkylation of carboxylate to form an ester), and the phenol vs carboxylate selectivity must be addressed. Performing this coupling on the carboxylic acid rather than an ester is non-optimal; the ester should ideally be carried through and hydrolyzed last. Additionally, primary alkyl chlorides are sluggish; a bromide or iodide (or NaI/Finkelstein) would be preferable. The intramolecular vs intermolecular selectivity is fine, but free-acid + phenol coexistence is the main concern.

Saponification of the ethyl ester to the carboxylic acid (LiOH or NaOH, aqueous/THF/MeOH) is a well-established, high-yielding transformation. The free indole phenol and indole N-CH2 are compatible. No issues. Note this ordering (hydrolyzing the ester before the ether coupling) is what creates the chemoselectivity concern in 8b98ceaa34b21f70c71c1553aa0dcb61cb074984a0c889cb690b81f874f241ab; carrying the ester forward and hydrolyzing as the final step would be cleaner.

Debenzylation of a benzyl-protected phenol to reveal the free phenol via hydrogenolysis (H2, Pd/C) is standard and reliable. Care must be taken because the indole ring can in principle undergo reduction under forcing conditions, but standard mild hydrogenolysis (1 atm H2, Pd/C) selectively cleaves the O-benzyl group while leaving the indole and the ethyl ester intact. Transfer hydrogenation or BCl3/Lewis-acid mediated debenzylation are alternatives. Overall a sound, well-precedented step.

This is a Friedel-Crafts acylation of the naphthalene with benzoyl chloride (AlCl3). The disconnection of the diaryl ketone is reasonable. However, regioselectivity is a major concern: installing the benzoyl group specifically at the 6-position of the 1-propyl-2-(alkoxy)naphthalene is not guaranteed. The electron-rich (alkoxy-bearing) ring is activated, and FC acylation would preferentially occur on the same ring as the alkoxy group (ortho/para to OR), not necessarily the distal position drawn. Additionally, the alkyl chloride (OCCCCl) tether is present during the AlCl3-mediated acylation and could suffer Friedel-Crafts side reactions or AlCl3-promoted ether cleavage. Performing the acylation before installing the sensitive chloroalkyl ether chain, or using milder conditions, would be advisable. Regiochemical control is the dominant risk.

Williamson ether synthesis between 1-propyl-2-naphthol and 1-bromo-3-chloropropane is a sensible, well-precedented transformation. Selective reaction of the more reactive bromide over the chloride (mild base, K2CO3) gives the chloro-ether product cleanly. Some bis-alkylation/cyclization side products are possible but readily controlled by using excess dihalide. Good step with cheap, commercially available starting materials.

This is a Williamson ether synthesis coupling a 7-hydroxyindole (with free carboxylic acid) and a primary alkyl chloride. The disconnection is strategically reasonable as the final convergent step. However, two issues arise: (1) The indole partner bears a free carboxylic acid (O=C(O)Cn1...), which under basic O-alkylation conditions (K2CO3, Cs2CO3) could lead to competing O-alkylation of the carboxylate, generating an ester byproduct. The acid should ideally remain protected (as the ethyl ester) until after the ether coupling, then be hydrolyzed. (2) Primary alkyl chlorides are relatively unreactive in Williamson etherification; a bromide or iodide (or NaI/Finkelstein in situ) would be preferred. As written with the free acid, chemoselectivity is a real concern.

Saponification/hydrolysis of the ethyl ester to the free carboxylic acid (LiOH or NaOH, aqueous/THF/MeOH) is a well-established, high-yielding transformation. The free phenol and indole are compatible with mild basic hydrolysis. Note, however, that the order of operations in the overall route is suboptimal—performing this hydrolysis before the ether coupling (8b98ceaa34b21f70c71c1553aa0dcb61cb074984a0c889cb690b81f874f241ab) creates the chemoselectivity problem flagged there. The reaction itself is sound.

Hydrogenolytic debenzylation of the O-benzyl-protected phenol (H2/Pd-C) to reveal the free phenol is a standard, reliable transformation. The ethyl ester and the indole ring are tolerant of these conditions. One minor caution: indoles can occasionally undergo partial reduction under forcing hydrogenation conditions, but standard Pd/C with H2 at 1 atm is generally chemoselective for benzyl ether cleavage. Good choice.

Friedel-Crafts acylation of the naphthalene with benzoyl chloride (AlCl3) to install the aroyl group. While F-C acylation on electron-rich alkoxy-naphthalenes is feasible, regioselectivity is a serious concern. The substrate already bears an alkoxy and propyl substituent; controlling acylation at the desired 6-position of the naphthalene ring will be difficult and likely give regioisomeric mixtures. Additionally, Lewis acid (AlCl3) conditions could cleave the alkyl-aryl ether or react with the chloropropyl chain. A milder acylation or an alternative directed strategy would improve selectivity and functional group tolerance.

Williamson ether synthesis between 2-propyl-1-naphthol and 1-bromo-3-chloropropane is a sound, well-precedented transformation. Use of the dihalide with a bromide leaving group ensures selective alkylation at the more reactive bromide terminus, leaving the chloride intact for the subsequent coupling. Standard base (K2CO3, Cs2CO3) in acetone/DMF works well. Both starting materials are accessible. Minor concern is potential bis-alkylation/oligomerization, but excess dihalide minimizes this.

This is a Williamson ether synthesis joining the indole-4-ol phenol with the alkyl chloride to form the propyl-ether linkage. The disconnection is reasonable and convergent. However, two concerns: (1) The carboxylic acid on the indole N-CH2CO2H is unprotected and would compete/interfere under the basic O-alkylation conditions (carboxylate could be alkylated to form an ester). It would be better to keep this as the ethyl ester until the final step and hydrolyze afterward, or carry the acid as a salt. (2) Alkyl chlorides are poor leaving groups for Williamson ether synthesis; reaction would be sluggish and likely require iodide catalysis (Finkelstein) or use of the corresponding bromide/iodide. With these caveats the bond disconnection itself is sound.

Saponification/hydrolysis of an ethyl ester to the free carboxylic acid using aqueous base (LiOH/NaOH) is a well-established, reliable transformation. The phenol and indole are stable under these conditions. Straightforward and high-yielding.

Hydrogenolytic cleavage of a benzyl (Bn) ether to reveal the phenol (H2/Pd-C) is a standard, robust deprotection. The ethyl ester and indole are compatible with hydrogenolysis conditions. Note that the indole double bond is generally stable to mild Pd/C hydrogenation but care should be taken to avoid over-reduction; selective debenzylation is well precedented. Good step.

Friedel-Crafts acylation of the naphthalene with benzoyl chloride/Lewis acid (e.g., AlCl3). The disconnection is logical, but regioselectivity is a serious concern: the substituted naphthalene has multiple reactive positions, and controlling acylation to the specific 6-position (as drawn) is difficult. Additionally, the alkyl chloride (OCCCCl) and the aryl ether are present; AlCl3 could promote side reactions including cleavage of the ether or chemistry at the chloride. A more controlled acylation strategy or installing the ketone earlier on a simpler arene would improve selectivity. The bond disconnection is acceptable but selectivity/compatibility risks are significant.

Williamson ether synthesis between the naphthol and 1-bromo-3-chloropropane. Selective reaction at the more reactive bromide over the chloride is well precedented (differential reactivity of Br vs Cl), giving the chloro-ether. Base such as K2CO3 in acetone/DMF works well. Both starting materials are commercially available. Solid step.

This is a Williamson ether synthesis coupling the indole phenol (O=C(O)Cn1ccc2c(O)cccc21) with the alkyl chloride. The disconnection is reasonable, but two major problems exist: (1) The free carboxylic acid on the indole fragment is a competing nucleophile (O-alkylation of the carboxylate vs. the phenol), which would lead to ester byproducts. The acid should be protected (as in earlier steps, the ethyl ester was used) and the saponification done LAST. (2) The alkyl chloride is a poor leaving group for SN2 etherification; primary alkyl bromide or iodide (or in situ Finkelstein) would be far superior. Using K2CO3/DMF or Cs2CO3 conditions, selectivity for phenol over carboxylate is uncertain. Recommend protecting the acid and using the bromide/iodide.

Ester hydrolysis (saponification) of the ethyl ester to the carboxylic acid using LiOH/NaOH. The free phenol is fully compatible. This is a robust, well-precedented transformation. Note: strategically, this deprotection is best performed at the very end of the synthesis to avoid the carboxylate interfering with the subsequent Williamson ether step (see 8b98ceaa34b21f70c71c1553aa0dcb61cb074984a0c889cb690b81f874f241ab feedback).

Debenzylation of an O-benzyl phenol ether to reveal the free phenol. Standard hydrogenolysis (H2, Pd/C) would cleanly remove the benzyl group. The ethyl ester and the indole are compatible with hydrogenolysis conditions (indoles are generally stable to mild Pd/C hydrogenation, though over-reduction of the indole ring should be monitored). Transfer hydrogenation or BCl3 are alternatives if indole reduction becomes problematic. Disconnection is sound.

Friedel-Crafts acylation of the naphthalene with benzoyl chloride (AlCl3 or other Lewis acid). The disconnection at the aryl ketone is sound retrosynthetically, but regioselectivity on the substituted naphthalene is a serious concern—the product shows acylation at a specific position (6-position), but Friedel-Crafts on alkoxy/alkyl-substituted naphthalenes can give mixtures of regioisomers. Additionally, the alkyl chloride side chain (OCCCCl) may undergo competing reactions or the Lewis acid could cleave/complicate the aryl alkyl ether. Strong Lewis acids (AlCl3) can also cleave the ether linkage. Milder conditions or careful Lewis acid choice needed; regioselectivity should be verified experimentally.

Williamson ether synthesis between the naphthol (CCCc1c(O)ccc2ccccc12) and 1-bromo-3-chloropropane (ClCCCBr). The bromide is selectively displaced over the chloride due to higher reactivity, leaving the terminal chloride intact for later functionalization. Standard K2CO3/DMF or Cs2CO3 conditions work well. Both starting materials are commercially available. Good, well-precedented step.

local_feedback: Problems with reaction type and functional group compatibility
local_feedback_text: This step is the reduction of an aromatic nitro group to an aniline in the final step. The major problem is chemoselectivity: the molecule contains a stilbene-type C=C double bond that is highly susceptible to reduction under common nitro-reduction conditions (e.g., H2/Pd-C). Catalytic hydrogenation would reduce the alkene preferentially or concomitantly. A chemoselective method (e.g., Fe/NH4Cl, SnCl2, Zn/AcOH, or Na2S2O4) would be required to preserve the alkene. Additionally, this is an [18F]-radiotracer synthesis, so the nitro reduction should ideally precede or be carefully ordered relative to the [18F] incorporation given the short half-life of F-18 (~110 min). Reducing the nitro group as the LAST step after [18F] labeling adds time, which is undesirable in radiochemistry. Strategically, the free aniline could also have been carried as a protected/labeled precursor instead. Use of Fe/AcOH or Na2S2O4 recommended.

This is the key radiofluorination/alkoxylation step forming the OCH2CH2[18F] aryl ether via nucleophilic aromatic substitution (SNAr) of an aryl fluoride by the alkoxide of 2-[18F]fluoroethanol. The aryl fluoride is ortho to a nitro group and para to the vinyl substituent, making it activated toward SNAr. The ortho-nitro group strongly activates the position for displacement by the alkoxide nucleophile. This is a sensible and well-precedented disconnection. However, note that in actual radiochemistry one would typically introduce [18F] in the LAST step due to F-18's short half-life; here the OCC[18F] synthon is brought in pre-labeled, which is acceptable if 2-[18F]fluoroethanol is the labeled prosthetic group. Selectivity is good since only one activated aryl-F is present. Competing O- vs base-mediated side reactions are minor.

This is a Heck coupling between 4-fluoro-3-nitrostyrene (or the corresponding vinyl arene) and an aryl bromide (4-(sec-butylamino)bromobenzene) to construct the (E)-stilbene. Heck reactions reliably give the trans/E-alkene as the major product, consistent with the depicted stereochemistry. The aryl bromide is a suitable oxidative-addition partner with Pd catalysis. One concern: the secondary aniline N-H is a free amine, which could weakly coordinate Pd but is generally tolerated in Heck reactions. The nitro and aryl fluoride groups are compatible. Regioselectivity for the terminal (linear) Heck product is expected for a styrene-type substrate. Both starting materials are reasonable building blocks.

This step is a nitro reduction to an aniline. The transformation itself is well-established (e.g., Fe/NH4Cl, SnCl2, or catalytic hydrogenation). However, the substrate contains a stilbene-type (E)-alkene which is highly susceptible to reduction under catalytic hydrogenation conditions (H2/Pd). To preserve the alkene, a chemoselective reagent must be used (e.g., Fe/AcOH, SnCl2, Zn/NH4Cl, or Na2S2O4). With proper reagent selection this step is feasible, but reagent choice is critical to avoid concomitant alkene reduction. Additionally, for an [18F]-radiotracer synthesis, the nitro reduction should ideally precede or be carefully timed, since carrier-free [18F] chemistry requires rapid, late-stage steps. Performing reduction after [18F] incorporation adds time-sensitive manipulations to short-lived isotope (t1/2 ~110 min).

This is an aromatic nucleophilic substitution (SNAr) where 2-[18F]fluoroethanol displaces an aromatic fluoride ortho to the nitro group to form the aryl ether. The disconnection is chemically reasonable since the F is activated by the ortho-nitro group. However, two concerns: (1) The nucleophile is the [18F]-labeled fluoroethanol — using a precious [18F] reagent as the nucleophile in an SNAr means a separate fluorination is needed to make it, and competing displacement of the aliphatic [18F] is unlikely but the regiochemistry of building the radiolabel into the ether is acceptable. (2) More importantly, in practice the radiolabeled fluoroethyl group would typically be installed via O-alkylation of a phenol precursor with [18F]fluoroethyl tosylate/bromide rather than SNAr with [18F]fluoroethanol, which is a poor nucleophile and would require strong base. The secondary alkylamine (NH) could also compete. An alternative and more standard route: make the phenol, then alkylate with 2-[18F]fluoroethyl tosylate. As written, SNAr of an alcohol nucleophile is feasible but non-optimal for a radiochemistry context.

This is a Heck reaction between a vinyl arene (4-fluoro-3-nitrostyrene) and an aryl bromide (4-(sec-butylamino)bromobenzene) to form the (E)-stilbene. Heck couplings of aryl halides with styrenes are well-precedented and give predominantly the (E)-product, consistent with the drawn stereochemistry. The secondary alkylamine is generally tolerated under Pd catalysis. Minor concern: the free secondary amine could coordinate Pd or undergo competing N-arylation (Buchwald-Hartwig), but with appropriate ligand/conditions Heck olefination is favored. Both building blocks are reasonable; 4-bromo-N-(sec-butyl)aniline may require synthesis (reductive amination) but is accessible. Overall a sound disconnection.

local_feedback: Problems with reaction type and functional group compatibility
local_feedback_text: The transformation is a nitro reduction to an aniline (ArNO2 -> ArNH2). The disconnection itself is reasonable, but reagent/condition selection is critical. The molecule contains a styryl (stilbene-type) C=C double bond which is highly susceptible to reduction under standard catalytic hydrogenation (H2/Pd-C), which would saturate the alkene as a competing reaction. A chemoselective reduction that preserves the alkene is required — e.g., Fe/NH4Cl, SnCl2, Zn/AcOH, or Na2S2O4. This is especially important given the [18F] PET context where this would be the final step on a radiolabeled intermediate; harsh or non-selective conditions would compromise the product. Selective conditions exist, so the step is achievable, but the obvious default (H2/Pd) is incompatible with the alkene.

This step is a nucleophilic aromatic substitution (SNAr) where 2-fluoro-18F-ethanol displaces an aryl fluoride to install the -OCH2CH2[18F] ether. Mechanistically this is sound: the aryl-F is activated by the ortho/para nitro group (here ortho to F), making SNAr by an alkoxide feasible. However, two concerns: (1) Chemoselectivity of deprotonation/alkoxide formation — the primary alcohol of OCC[18F] must be deprotonated to act as nucleophile, but the secondary amine (CCC(C)NH-Ar) is also present and could compete or be deprotonated/interfere. (2) In a radiochemistry context this would be a late-stage step using a precious [18F]-fluoroethanol building block as the nucleophile, which is unusual — typically the [18F] is introduced LAST via [18F]fluoride displacement of a tosylate/mesylate on the ethylene tether to minimize handling of the short-lived isotope. Using [18F]fluoroethanol as a multi-step reagent is not practical for 18F (t1/2 ~110 min). Strategically the [18F] should be introduced in the final step. The bond disconnection (Ar-O-alkyl via SNAr on the activated fluoroarene) is chemically valid though.

This is a Heck reaction (or Mizoroki-Heck coupling) between 4-fluoro-3-nitrostyrene (vinyl arene) and the aryl bromide CCC(C)Nc1ccc(Br)cc1 to form the trans-stilbene. The disconnection is sound and Heck coupling of an aryl halide with a styrene to give the E-configured 1,2-diarylethylene is well-precedented (Pd catalysis, base). The E-selectivity is favored, consistent with the drawn geometry. Both starting materials are reasonable building blocks. Minor consideration: the free secondary aniline N-H is generally tolerated under Heck conditions, though it could mildly coordinate Pd; no protection strictly required. Regiochemistry of Heck addition favors the terminal/beta-aryl product giving the stilbene, as drawn.

This step proposes reduction of an aromatic nitro group to an aniline as the final transformation. The chemistry itself (nitro reduction) is well-established. However, there are significant chemoselectivity concerns: (1) the molecule contains a stilbene-type C=C double bond that is highly susceptible to over-reduction under common nitro-reduction conditions (H2/Pd-C). (2) The secondary aniline N-H and the [18F]-alkyl group must survive. Selective nitro reduction in the presence of an alkene requires careful reagent choice such as Fe/NH4Cl, SnCl2, Na2S2O4, or Zn/AcOH, which can leave the alkene intact. Additionally, this is a radiochemistry context (18F PET tracer); performing nitro reduction AFTER 18F incorporation adds a step to the radiosynthesis, which is undesirable given the short half-life of 18F (~110 min). Strongly recommend introducing the free aniline (protected) earlier and placing 18F labeling as the LAST step. Otherwise the chemistry can work with a chemoselective reductant.

This step is an O-alkylation/etherification forming the aryl alkyl ether via reaction of 2-[18F]fluoroethanol with the aryl fluoride (SNAr displacement of the activated ortho-fluoro by the alcohol/alkoxide). The disconnection is reasonable: the aryl-F is ortho to a strongly activating nitro group, so SNAr by an alkoxide is feasible. However, two concerns: (1) regiochemically, using 2-[18F]fluoroethanol as a nucleophile in a late-stage radiosynthesis is problematic because the 18F is already incorporated and the alkoxide displacement step adds time/loss. More commonly the order is reversed: build the 2-hydroxyethyl ether, convert to a leaving group (tosylate/mesylate), and perform [18F]fluoride displacement LAST. (2) Chemoselectivity: the alkoxide of 2-fluoroethanol could compete with elimination, and the basic conditions must tolerate the secondary amine and stilbene. The SNAr disconnection is chemically sound but the radiochemistry strategy is non-optimal.

This is a Heck coupling between 4-bromo-N-(sec-butyl)aniline and 2-fluoro-4-vinyl-1-nitrobenzene to form the trans-stilbene. The Mizoroki-Heck reaction with a terminal vinyl arene and an aryl bromide is well-precedented and reliably affords the E-alkene with good selectivity using Pd(OAc)2/phosphine and base. Functional groups (nitro, aryl-F, secondary aniline) are compatible. The secondary amine N-H may require mild conditions but generally tolerated. Good convergent disconnection. Both starting materials are reasonable; 4-bromo-N-sec-butylaniline is readily accessible by reductive amination of 4-bromoaniline with 2-butanone.

This is a Suzuki-Miyaura cross-coupling between the thiophene-bromide and 2-hydroxyphenylboronic acid. The disconnection at the biaryl C-C bond is sound and well-precedented. The 2-hydroxyphenylboronic acid is a known, commercially available reagent, though ortho-hydroxy boronic acids can be prone to protodeboronation; mild conditions (e.g., Pd(PPh3)4, K2CO3, aqueous dioxane) are advised. The free phenol on the boronic acid partner and the free phenol/ketone on the thiophene partner are generally tolerated under Pd catalysis. Chemoselectivity for the aryl-Br over the other positions is good as it is the only halide reactive toward oxidative addition. A minor concern is the electron-rich nature of the thiophene 5-bromide, but this typically couples readily.

This step is a demethylation of an aryl methyl ether to reveal the free phenol (BBr3 or similar). The disconnection is logical - protecting the phenol as a methyl ether during the upstream Friedel-Crafts acylation. The transformation is well-established. Caution: BBr3 demethylation on a substrate bearing a diaryl ketone and a C-Br thiophene is generally compatible, though strongly Lewis-acidic conditions could be screened against alternatives (e.g., AlCl3/thiol, or pyridine·HCl). No major selectivity issues since only one OMe is present.

This step proposes a Friedel-Crafts acylation between 2-bromothiophene and a polyfluorinated/methoxylated benzoyl chloride. While Friedel-Crafts acylation of thiophenes is feasible and gives good 2,5-selectivity (acylation at the 5-position of 2-bromothiophene, consistent with the product), there are concerns: (1) The acyl chloride is highly electron-poor (three fluorines + ortho positions), which is favorable for acylation but the electron-rich thiophene should still react. (2) Regioselectivity for the 5-position is generally good but 2-bromothiophene can give some 4-isomer/deactivation considerations. (3) A more significant concern is whether a standard Lewis acid (AlCl3) is compatible with the aryl methyl ether (risk of partial demethylation) - milder conditions or SnCl4 may be preferable. Overall the disconnection is reasonable but selectivity and FG compatibility warrant attention. Both starting materials (2-bromothiophene and the benzoyl chloride) are commercially available or readily accessible.

This is a Suzuki-Miyaura cross-coupling between 2-hydroxyphenylboronic acid and the aryl bromothiophene. The disconnection at the biaryl (thiophene-phenol) bond is appropriate and well-precedented. The bromothiophene is the electrophilic partner and the boronic acid bears a free ortho-phenol, which is generally tolerated in Suzuki couplings (free phenols and even free OH groups on the boronic acid are commonly used). The free phenol on the fluorinated ring and the ketone are also compatible. One consideration: 2-hydroxyphenylboronic acids can be prone to protodeboronation and may form cyclic boroxines, so slightly elevated boronic acid loading and a mild base (e.g., K2CO3 or K3PO4) with Pd(PPh3)4 or Pd(dppf)Cl2 would be advisable. Overall a sound and reliable final step.

This step is a demethylation of an aryl methyl ether to reveal the free phenol. Given the highly electron-poor, fluorinated aromatic ring with an ortho/para-ketone, the methyl ether is activated and could be cleaved by BBr3, or even by nucleophilic conditions. BBr3 is a robust standard choice. The aryl-bromothiophene and the diaryl ketone are compatible with BBr3. Chemoselectivity is good since there is only one methyl ether present. The strategy of carrying a protected phenol (as the methyl ether) through the acylation and unmasking it late is reasonable, though one could question whether a removable protecting group like MOM or benzyl might be milder than the harsh BBr3 conditions; nevertheless BBr3 demethylation here is feasible.

This is a Friedel-Crafts acylation of 2-bromothiophene (or equivalently bromothiophene) with the polyfluorinated benzoyl chloride. Thiophenes are activated toward electrophilic acylation and Friedel-Crafts acylation proceeds readily, typically with AlCl3 or SnCl4 as Lewis acid. Regioselectivity is a consideration: 2-bromothiophene would direct acylation to the 5-position (the desired product shows the 2-bromo-5-acyl pattern), which is the favored position, so regioselectivity is good. The electron-poor acyl chloride is suitably reactive. The methyl ether on the fluorinated ring is compatible with Lewis-acid acylation conditions (BBr3-type cleavage is avoided with milder Lewis acids and controlled conditions). Overall a feasible, well-precedented step with good regiocontrol.

This is a Suzuki-Miyaura coupling between 2-hydroxyphenylboronic acid and the aryl bromide (on the thiophene). The disconnection at the biaryl/heterobiaryl bond is strategically sound and well-precedented. However, two issues: (1) 2-hydroxyphenylboronic acids are notoriously prone to protodeboronation and cyclic boroxine/benzoxaborole formation due to the intramolecular ortho-OH, which can lower coupling yields; (2) the free phenol on the difluoro/fluoro-trisubstituted arene and the free phenol on the boronic acid partner are both unprotected. Suzuki coupling tolerates free phenols, but yields may be improved with optimized Pd catalyst (e.g., Pd(dppf)Cl2 or SPhos/XPhos systems) and aqueous base. Chemoselectivity favors the C-Br bond over the aryl C-F bonds, so that is fine. Overall feasible but yield-limiting protodeboronation is a real concern.

local_feedback: Protecting group strategy is wrong / non-optimal
local_feedback_text: This step is a demethylation of the aryl methyl ether to reveal the free phenol (BBr3 or similar). The transformation itself is feasible. However, in the context of the whole route, the methyl protecting group was carried through the Friedel-Crafts acylation (799af4b729c59abad8e1ce0c374981a0537d9fd5b7bfc2302872c8b28e27d2f6) and would now require harsh demethylation conditions (BBr3, or HI/HBr). The ketone and the bromothiophene are generally compatible with BBr3, though prolonged exposure can risk some side reactions. The bigger concern: why protect as a methyl ether at all if the phenol could simply be installed later or carried through? The methyl group requires forcing deprotection conditions which is non-optimal. A more labile protecting group (MOM, benzyl) or carrying the free phenol could be considered, though the free phenol could interfere with the Friedel-Crafts step. Acceptable but non-optimal choice.

This is a Friedel-Crafts acylation of 2-bromothiophene with a polyfluorinated/methoxy benzoyl chloride. The disconnection is reasonable and Friedel-Crafts acylation of thiophenes is well-established (thiophene is highly reactive toward electrophilic acylation). Regioselectivity: acylation of 2-bromothiophene would occur at the 5-position (alpha to sulfur, para-like to the bromine), giving the desired 5-acyl-2-bromothiophene, which is the expected major product - this is favorable. The electron-poor (polyfluorinated) benzoyl chloride is a less reactive acylating agent but should still work with a Lewis acid catalyst (AlCl3). Compatibility concern: the methyl ether could be cleaved by AlCl3 under forcing conditions, and the electron-deficient ring reduces acylium electrophilicity, possibly requiring more vigorous conditions. Overall feasible with attention to regioselectivity (favorable) and catalyst loading. Both starting materials appear commercially accessible.

This is a Friedel-Crafts acylation of 2-bromothiophene with the aroyl chloride. The transformation is feasible and well-precedented in principle (thiophenes are highly reactive toward Friedel-Crafts acylation). However, two concerns exist: (1) Regioselectivity - acylation of 2-bromothiophene will preferentially occur at the 5-position (alpha to sulfur, para-like to Br), which matches the desired product, so this is actually favorable. (2) The main concern is the electron-poor, highly fluorinated acyl chloride combined with a Lewis acid catalyst (AlCl3) which could demethylate the aryl methyl ether (anisole-type OMe) under forcing conditions. Milder Lewis acids or careful control would be needed. Overall feasible but watch for demethylation side reactions and ensure correct regiochemistry on thiophene.

local_feedback: Protecting group strategy is wrong / non-optimal
local_feedback_text: This step represents demethylation of the aryl methyl ether to reveal the free phenol. The reagent is appropriate (BBr3 or similar). However, in the context of the whole route, the methyl protecting group is questionable. The phenol is on a highly fluorinated ring; one of the fluorines (ortho to OH) could potentially be installed/displaced. More importantly, the OMe protection introduces an extra protection/deprotection pair (the methylation must have happened earlier, not shown, or the methyl ether is from the starting building block COc1c(F)c(F)cc(C(=O)Cl)c1F which is commercial). Demethylation with BBr3 is feasible, but harsh conditions risk cleaving the aryl-aryl/ketone framework or affecting the thiophene. The disconnection itself (phenol <- methyl ether) is chemically sound.

This is a Suzuki-Miyaura cross-coupling between 2-(bromothienyl) ketone and 2-hydroxyphenylboronic acid. This is a well-established disconnection. The bromothiophene is a good coupling partner, and the free phenol on the boronic acid is tolerated under standard Pd-catalyzed Suzuki conditions (Pd(PPh3)4 or Pd(dppf)Cl2 with base). The free phenol on the fluorinated ring should also be tolerated. One minor concern: ortho-hydroxyphenylboronic acids can be prone to protodeboronation, so excess boronic acid or boronic ester (e.g., pinacol or MIDA boronate) may improve yield. Chemoselectivity favors C-Br over the C-F bonds. Overall a sound, convergent final step.

This is the global deprotection of a diethyl phosphonate ester to the free phosphonic acid. This is standard and reliable, typically done with TMSBr (McKenna conditions) followed by hydrolysis, or with concentrated HCl. The free amines and the pyrimidinone are compatible with TMSBr. The cyclopropyl group is stable. This is a well-precedented final step in nucleoside phosphonate chemistry (cf. tenofovir, adefovir syntheses).

This step proposes alkylation of diethyl (hydroxymethyl)phosphonate's hydroxyl with the alkyl bromide to form the ether (Williamson-type O-alkylation forming the O-CH2-P linkage). While the disconnection of the P-CH2-O-CH2CH2 ether is reasonable, there are serious selectivity concerns: the substrate contains two free primary aromatic amines (NH2) that are far more nucleophilic toward alkyl halides than an alkoxide-deprotonated hydroxymethylphosphonate oxygen under most conditions. Competing N-alkylation is highly likely. In practice, the standard approach reverses the order — the phosphonate ether oxygen is installed first (e.g., via diethyl tosyloxymethylphosphonate reacting with the alcohol under base), and the amines are protected or the heterocycle is built afterward. As written, chemoselectivity would be poor without amine protection.

local_feedback: Problems with reaction type and functional group compatibility
local_feedback_text: Conversion of the primary alcohol to the bromide using PBr3 is conceptually fine for the alcohol itself, but the substrate bears two free aromatic amino groups and an amide-like pyrimidinone carbonyl. PBr3 is a harsh, electrophilic reagent that can react with amines (forming aminophosphines/salts) and with the lactam carbonyl. Chemoselective bromination of the alcohol in the presence of unprotected diaminopyrimidinone would be problematic. Milder methods (Appel: CBr4/PPh3, or MsCl/LiBr) would be preferable, and ideally with amine protection. The bromide intermediate is also prone to intramolecular cyclization with the ring nitrogen/amine.

This step is a demethylation of a methyl ether to the free primary alcohol (COCCn... -> HOCCn...). O-demethylation of a simple alkyl methyl ether is harsh (requires BBr3, TMSI, or strong acid), and these conditions are incompatible with the free amines and would risk degrading the heterocycle. More fundamentally, this step appears unnecessary and awkward: if the alcohol is the desired functionality, one should not introduce a methyl ether (5f151bdae6486403d78ef6acb50a190227c2a6fe6264d5db104670b92f9cdca0) and then cleave it. The strategy of installing COCCBr (2-bromoethyl methyl ether) and later demethylating is inefficient. A protected alcohol (e.g., as a silyl or THP ether, or simply using the bromoethanol with appropriate protection) would be far better.

N-alkylation of the 2,4-diamino-5-cyclopropyl-pyrimidin-6(1H)-one with 2-bromoethyl methyl ether. The disconnection to commercially available pieces is reasonable, but regioselectivity is a major concern: this diaminopyrimidinone tautomer has multiple nucleophilic sites — the ring N1 (amide N), the ring N3, and two exocyclic NH2 groups. Selective N1-alkylation (the desired site) typically requires specific conditions (e.g., Cs2CO3/DMF, or prior silylation) and often gives mixtures of N- vs O-alkylation and regioisomers. This is a known challenge in guanine/diaminopyrimidinone alkylation chemistry. The transformation is feasible but selectivity must be carefully controlled and yields are often modest.

This is a standard phosphonate diester deprotection to the free phosphonic acid. Treatment with TMSBr (McKenna procedure) followed by methanolysis/hydrolysis is the typical method for cleaving phosphonate ethyl esters without harming the diaminopyrimidinone core or the cyclopropyl group. Direct acidic hydrolysis is also possible but harsher. The transformation is well-precedented for acyclic nucleotide phosphonate (ANP) chemistry, of which this molecule is clearly a member. Reagent should be specified (TMSBr) but the disconnection is correct.

This step proposes a Williamson-type ether formation (O-alkylation) coupling diethyl (hydroxymethyl)phosphonate with the primary alkyl bromide (CCBr on the side chain) to form the O-CH2-P linkage. While the bond disconnection (C-O ether bond formation) is correct and characteristic of ANP synthesis, there are serious chemoselectivity concerns: the substrate contains two free primary aromatic amino (guanidine-like) groups. Under basic conditions (NaH or similar required to deprotonate the hydroxymethylphosphonate), the exocyclic amines could compete as nucleophiles, and N-alkylation byproducts are likely. In practice, ANP syntheses typically alkylate the heterocycle FIRST with the preformed phosphonate-containing chain, or use protected amino groups. The free diamines here make this O-alkylation poorly selective and low-yielding. Protection of the amines is advisable.

local_feedback: Problems with reaction type and functional group compatibility
local_feedback_text: Conversion of the primary alcohol to the bromide using PBr3 is conceptually reasonable, but the substrate bears two free exocyclic amino groups on the pyrimidinone. PBr3 reacts with amines and with the amide/lactam carbonyl, and the basic amines will consume the reagent and may form bromophosphoramidates. This makes the transformation low-yielding and non-chemoselective. Milder activation (e.g., MsCl/base then bromide, or Appel conditions with CBr4/PPh3) would still face amine interference. Amine protection is needed for this to be practical.

This step proposes converting a methyl ether (COCCn..., i.e., CH3-O-CH2CH2-N) into a free primary alcohol (HO-CH2CH2-N). Cleavage of a simple methyl ether to reveal a primary alcohol selectively is very difficult and would require harsh conditions (BBr3, TMSI) that are incompatible with the free diaminopyrimidinone and could degrade the substrate. More fundamentally, introducing a methyl ether in the prior step only to cleave it here is a poor protecting-group strategy. The methyl group is not an appropriate protecting group for a primary alcohol intended for later activation. This disconnection is non-strategic and the deprotection is unlikely to be clean.

N-alkylation of the 2,4-diamino-cyclopropyl-pyrimidinone with 2-bromoethyl methyl ether targets the ring N1 (lactam nitrogen). However, this ambident nucleophile (diaminopyrimidinone) can alkylate at multiple sites: the exocyclic amines, the ring nitrogen, or O-alkylation at the carbonyl. Achieving selective N1-alkylation requires careful base/conditions control and typically gives mixtures. While N1-alkylation is the thermodynamically favored/literature-precedented site for such guanine-like systems under basic conditions, regioselectivity is a genuine concern and yields are often modest. Additionally, the choice of a methyl ether-protected bromide is non-optimal since the methyl group cannot be readily removed later (see 62586090b7c21dffdf2dc968c78788bbb738dae9a9ede1f1e7aa6603d4f9bba6).

N-alkylation of the 2,4-diamino-pyrimidinone (an isocytosine/guanine-like core) with 2-bromoethyl methyl ether targets the ring N1 nitrogen. However, this substrate contains two exocyclic NH2 groups and a ring NH, presenting a serious regioselectivity challenge. Alkylation could occur at the exocyclic amines, the ring N-H (the desired N1), or O-alkylation. While N1 alkylation is often thermodynamically preferred under basic conditions (e.g., K2CO3/DMF, Cs2CO3), competitive N-alkylation of the more nucleophilic exocyclic amines is a well-documented problem in purine/pyrimidine chemistry. Selectivity would likely require careful optimization and may give modest yields. The choice of leaving group (Br) and reagent is reasonable. Starting material Nc1nc(N)c(C2CC2)c(=O)[nH]1 needs verification of commercial availability — it is a specialized building block.

This step proposes converting a methyl ether (COCCn...) to a free primary alcohol (HOCCn...). Demethylation of a simple primary alkyl methyl ether to reveal the alcohol is not a clean, practical transformation — it requires harsh conditions (e.g., BBr3, TMSI, strong Lewis acids) that are entirely incompatible with the sensitive 2,4-diaminopyrimidinone core (would cleave/degrade the heterocycle and other functionality). Strategically, this is a poor protecting-group choice: a methyl ether is essentially a permanent protecting group, not one removable under mild conditions. The retrosynthesis would be far better served by introducing the 2-haloethanol or a 2-(protected-hydroxy)ethyl group (e.g., THP, acetate, benzyl, or directly the bromoethanol) instead of methyl ether, avoiding this implausible demethylation entirely.

local_feedback: Problems with reaction type and functional group compatibility
local_feedback_text: Appel-type bromination of the primary alcohol using PBr3 is in principle a reasonable conversion of a primary alcohol to a primary bromide. However, the substrate carries two free exocyclic primary amines and a lactam carbonyl. PBr3 reacts readily with primary amines and amide/lactam functionalities, so chemoselectivity is a major concern; the free NH2 groups would likely interfere or be consumed. A milder approach (e.g., Appel conditions CBr4/PPh3, or mesylation/tosylation followed by displacement) with appropriate amine protection would be required. As drawn, without protection of the amines, this step is unlikely to be selective.

Williamson-type ether formation / O-alkylation coupling diethyl (hydroxymethyl)phosphonate with the primary alkyl bromide to form the O-CH2-P(O)(OEt)2 linkage is a well-precedented approach used in the synthesis of acyclic nucleoside phosphonates (cf. cidofovir/adefovir/tenofovir chemistry). Deprotonation of the hydroxymethylphosphonate (NaH) and reaction with the bromide gives the ether. The main caveat is competing reactivity/poor selectivity from the unprotected exocyclic amines on the heterocycle, which could lower yield. Reagent diethyl (hydroxymethyl)phosphonate is commercial and in stock. Overall a sound disconnection consistent with literature ANP syntheses.

Global deprotection of the diethyl phosphonate ester to the free phosphonic acid is a standard, well-established transformation, typically accomplished with TMSBr (McKenna procedure) followed by aqueous/methanol workup, or with conc. HCl. This is the standard final step in acyclic nucleoside phosphonate syntheses. The 2,4-diaminopyrimidinone core and cyclopropyl group are compatible with TMSBr conditions. Appropriate and feasible.

Phosphonate diethyl ester deprotection to the free phosphonic acid using TMSBr (McKenna procedure) followed by hydrolysis is a well-established transformation. The amino groups and pyrimidinone core should tolerate these conditions. This is a standard final-step deprotection commonly used in acyclic nucleoside phosphonate synthesis (e.g., cidofovir-type compounds). Selectivity is not an issue. Note the only concern is potential over-reaction with cyclopropyl, but that is inert under TMSBr/H2O.

This step proposes formation of the P-CH2-O-CH2 ether linkage by combining diethyl (hydroxymethyl)phosphonate with the primary alkyl bromide (CCBr on the side chain). The retrosynthetic logic implies a Williamson ether synthesis between the phosphonate -CH2OH and the alkyl bromide. However, the regiochemistry is inverted relative to a typical ANP synthesis: normally one alkylates a side-chain alcohol with a phosphonate-bearing electrophile (e.g., diethyl tosyloxymethylphosphonate or chloromethyl phosphonate), not the reverse. Using the hydroxymethylphosphonate as nucleophile against a primary alkyl bromide is feasible in principle via NaH-mediated Williamson etherification, but competing N-alkylation/O-alkylation on the diaminopyrimidinone (multiple NH/N nucleophiles) is a serious chemoselectivity problem. The free amino groups would compete and likely require protection. As drawn, this is a problematic disconnection.

local_feedback: Problems with reaction type and functional group compatibility
local_feedback_text: Conversion of the primary alcohol to the bromide using PBr3 is in principle a standard Appel-type/PBr3 transformation. However, the substrate bears two free primary aromatic amino groups and a lactam (pyrimidinone) carbonyl. PBr3 is incompatible with free amines (forms aminophosphines/salts) and can react with the amide/lactam. The free NH2 groups would need protection. As drawn, this step would suffer from poor chemoselectivity. A milder activation (MsCl/then bromide, or Appel with CBr4/PPh3) on a protected substrate would be preferable.

This step proposes demethylation of a methyl ether (COCCn... = CH3-O-CH2CH2-N) to the free primary alcohol (HOCH2CH2-N). Cleaving a simple methyl ether to a primary alcohol requires harsh conditions (BBr3, TMSI), which would be incompatible with the diaminopyrimidinone and would not be a clean way to reveal this alcohol. More importantly, this is a wasteful/illogical disconnection: installing a methyl-protected ethanol then demethylating is non-strategic. One would directly alkylate with 2-bromoethanol (or a protected variant) to install the hydroxyethyl side chain. The methyl ether protecting strategy is poorly chosen and the demethylation is impractical.

N-alkylation of the 2,4-diamino-pyrimidin-6(1H)-one (a diaminopyrimidinone) with 2-bromoethyl methyl ether. The intended site is N1 (the lactam nitrogen). However, this scaffold has multiple competing nucleophilic sites: the two exocyclic amino groups, the ring N, and the O of the amide (O- vs N-alkylation). Achieving clean N1-selective alkylation is non-trivial and typically gives mixtures of N- and O-alkylation plus exocyclic amine alkylation. Base choice (e.g., K2CO3/Cs2CO3 in DMF) and protection of the amino groups are usually required. The starting pyrimidinone is a reasonable, likely commercially accessible building block, but the alkylation selectivity is the principal concern.

This is an SNAr displacement of the final chlorine on the trisubstituted triazine by a primary amine (NCCN1CCOCC1). After two substituents (pyridyl and piperidine) are installed, the remaining C-Cl is less activated, but triazine systems are sufficiently electron-poor that displacement by a primary amine proceeds under mild heating. Chemoselectivity is excellent because the primary amine is far more nucleophilic than the morpholine tertiary amine, which is already tied up. No protecting groups needed. Minor concern: prolonged heating could lead to bis-amination, but with the mono-chloro substrate this is not an issue.

SNAr of one chlorine on the 2,4-dichloro-6-(pyridyl)triazine intermediate by the secondary amine of 4-morpholinopiperidine. The remaining two chlorines on the dichlorotriazine are differentiated by reactivity, and sequential, temperature-controlled mono-substitution of dichlorotriazines/pyrimidines is well precedented (first substitution at 0 °C, second at RT/heat). Selectivity for mono-substitution is achievable using 1 equiv amine and low temperature. The morpholine nitrogen is tertiary and non-competing, so the piperidine NH is the reactive site. Good chemoselectivity.

Suzuki-Miyaura coupling of pyridin-3-ylboronic acid with 2,4,6-trichloro-1,3,5-triazine (cyanuric chloride) to install the pyridyl group with mono-selectivity. Mono-arylation of cyanuric chloride is achievable with controlled stoichiometry (1 equiv boronic acid) and low temperature, exploiting the deactivation after the first substitution. Both starting materials are commercially available and inexpensive. Potential concerns: pyridin-3-ylboronic acids are prone to protodeboronation, and over-coupling to give di/tri-aryl products is possible, so careful control of conditions and stoichiometry is required. Standard Pd(PPh3)4/base systems should work.

This is the final SNAr displacement of the last chloride on the triazine/pyrimidine core by the primary amine of 2-morpholinoethylamine. The product depicted is a pyrimidine (six-membered ring with two N, c2cc...nc...n2), and the displacement of an activated chloride alpha to ring nitrogens is well-precedented. The primary amine reacts chemoselectively over the morpholine tertiary amine. Mild heating (60-100 °C) in alcohol or with a base such as DIPEA should provide clean monosubstitution since this is the least reactive (last) chloride after two prior substitutions. Good feasibility.

SNAr of 4-morpholinopiperidine onto a dichloropyrimidine (Clc1cc(-aryl)nc(Cl)n1) bearing two activated chlorides. The secondary amine of the piperidine displaces one chloride selectively. Mono-substitution selectivity can be achieved by controlling stoichiometry (1 equiv amine) and temperature; the morpholine nitrogen is sterically/electronically less nucleophilic and tertiary, so the piperidine N is the reactive site. The regiochemistry between the two equivalent-ish chlorides ortho/para to the aryl group could pose a mild selectivity concern, but both positions are activated and the subsequent step installs the second amine, so this is acceptable. Standard DIPEA/heating conditions apply.

Suzuki-Miyaura coupling of 3-pyridylboronic acid with 2,4,6-trichloropyrimidine (written here as Clc1cc(Cl)nc(Cl)n1, a trichloropyrimidine). The disconnection is chemically reasonable and well-precedented, but mono-arylation selectivity on a trichloropyrimidine is the key challenge: the C4 position is most reactive, so mono-coupling can be controlled with careful stoichiometry (1 equiv boronic acid), low temperature, and Pd(PPh3)4/base. However, over-coupling (bis-arylation) and protodeboronation of the electron-poor 3-pyridylboronic acid are real concerns and may limit yield. The product retains two chlorides for the subsequent amine substitutions, consistent with the route. Recommend using milder conditions and possibly a pyridyl boronic ester or controlled addition to improve selectivity. Starting materials (3-pyridylboronic acid, 2,4,6-trichloropyrimidine) are commercially available.

This is an SNAr displacement of the final chloride on the triazine/pyrimidine ring by the primary amine of 2-morpholinoethylamine. The disconnection is appropriate and well-precedented. The aminoethylmorpholine reacts selectively through its primary amine rather than the tertiary morpholine nitrogen, so chemoselectivity is not an issue. Note: the core is a pyrimidine (2,4,6-trisubstituted with N at 1,3 positions per SMILES nc...n), and the remaining C-Cl is reasonably activated for SNAr by the two ring nitrogens. Mild heating with an amine base (DIPEA) in a polar aprotic solvent (NMP, dioxane, n-BuOH) should suffice. Selectivity between the two original chlorides was handled in the prior step.

SNAr displacement of one of the two equivalent/near-equivalent chlorides of the dichloropyrimidine by the secondary amine of 4-morpholinopiperidine. This is a sound, well-precedented transformation. The main concern is mono- vs bis-substitution selectivity: since both chlorides are activated, controlled addition (1 equiv amine, low temperature, DIPEA) is needed to favor mono-substitution and avoid double displacement. Regiochemistry between the two chlorides may give minor positional isomers but they are electronically similar. Overall feasible with careful stoichiometry/temperature control.

This is a Suzuki–Miyaura coupling of pyridin-3-ylboronic acid with 2,4,6-trichloro-1,3,5-triazine (cyanuric chloride) — note the starting material drawn (Clc1cc(Cl)nc(Cl)n1) is actually a trichloropyrimidine, not symmetric cyanuric chloride. The mono-Suzuki coupling on a polychlorinated electron-poor heteroarene is feasible but achieving clean mono-arylation with selectivity for the desired position over di/tri-coupling is challenging. Cyanuric chloride/trichloropyrimidines are highly reactive toward both Pd insertion and SNAr; the boronic acid and aqueous base conditions could also promote SNAr-type hydrolysis of C-Cl bonds. Careful control (low temperature, 1 equiv boronic acid, mild base, selective catalyst) is required, and product is the desired aryl-dichloride. Regioselectivity for the correct chlorine and chemoselectivity against over-coupling are the key risks. Pyridin-3-ylboronic acid is also prone to protodeboronation.

This is an SNAr reaction of a primary amine (NCCN-morpholine) with a chloro-triazine to install the aminoethyl-morpholine sidechain. Triazines are highly activated toward SNAr, and the remaining chloride is the most reactive position after the two amine/aryl substituents are in place. The primary amine is more nucleophilic and will react preferentially over the morpholine nitrogen (which is tertiary). Mild heating in the presence of a base (e.g., DIPEA) should give clean substitution. Chemoselectivity is good as the morpholine N's are already substituted/tertiary.

Sequential SNAr on a dichloro-triazine with the secondary amine of 4-morpholinopiperidine. Triazines undergo stepwise SNAr with good temperature-controlled mono-selectivity. The piperidine NH is the reactive nucleophile (morpholine N is tertiary). Running at low temperature (0 °C to rt) with one equivalent of amine and a base typically gives the mono-substituted product selectively, leaving one chloride for the subsequent step. Feasible and well-precedented.

Suzuki coupling of 2,4,6-trichlorotriazine (cyanuric chloride) with 3-pyridylboronic acid. While the C–B/C–Cl coupling is feasible, achieving mono-arylation selectively on cyanuric chloride is challenging—the three positions are highly reactive and similar, and over-arylation (bis/tris) is a major competing pathway. Additionally, cyanuric chloride is extremely reactive toward hydrolysis/SNAr; the boronic acid and basic Suzuki conditions could promote substitution side reactions and protodeboronation of the electron-poor pyridylboronic acid. Careful stoichiometry, low temperature, and mild base are required. A more selective alternative would be to perform the Suzuki coupling later or use a dichloro-pyridyltriazine building block directly. Note also the product retains two chlorides matching the next step, but selectivity for exactly one coupling is the main concern.

SNAr displacement of the remaining chloride on the triazine by N-methylisobutylamine (CNCC(C)C) is a well-established transformation. Aminotriazines are highly activated toward nucleophilic aromatic substitution, and the second (less reactive) chloride is displaced under slightly more forcing conditions (mild heating, base such as DIPEA). The secondary amine is a competent nucleophile. Chemoselectivity is good since the first amino group is already installed and deactivates the ring somewhat, allowing controlled monosubstitution of the final chloride. The alkyne is compatible. Feasible and sensible disconnection.

Selective mono-SNAr of a dichlorotriazine with a primary amine (isobutylamine) to install the first amino substituent. Trichlorotriazine/dichlorotriazine chemistry is classic and highly selective: the first substitution occurs at low temperature (0 °C) with good mono-selectivity. Here one chloride is already replaced by the alkyne-bearing aryl group, leaving a dichloro-substituted position pattern; the primary amine will displace one chloride selectively at low temperature. The disconnection is appropriate and well-precedented. Stoichiometry and temperature control are needed to avoid bis-amination.

Sonogashira coupling between 1-ethynylnaphthalene and cyanuric chloride (2,4,6-trichloro-1,3,5-triazine) to install the alkyne at one ring position. The chlorotriazine is an excellent electrophilic coupling partner, and a single Sonogashira coupling can be achieved selectively at low temperature with controlled stoichiometry (Pd/Cu catalysis). The main concern is selectivity for mono-coupling on the highly reactive trichlorotriazine and avoiding Glaser homocoupling of the terminal alkyne (use of mild conditions, controlled Cu, inert atmosphere). Both starting materials are commercially available. Reasonable disconnection though selectivity for mono-coupling requires careful optimization.

SNAr substitution of the remaining chloride on the triazine with N-methylisobutylamine (CNCC(C)C). Chloro-triazines are highly reactive toward sequential SNAr displacements, and the final/least reactive chloride is displaced under slightly more forcing conditions (mild heating, base). The selectivity for the third substitution is well-established in triazine chemistry. Compatibility with the alkyne and the existing secondary amine is fine. Good step.

SNAr of one chloride on the dichlorotriazine intermediate with isobutylamine (CC(C)CN). Mono-selective displacement on a dichloro-triazine is achievable at low temperature (0 °C to RT) with controlled stoichiometry/base, exploiting the decreasing reactivity after the first substitution. The amine is a good nucleophile and primary amines react cleanly. Standard cyanuric chloride-type chemistry. Minor risk of bis-substitution can be controlled by temperature and equivalents.

This step proposes a Sonogashira coupling between 1-ethynylnaphthalene and 1,3,5-trichlorotriazine (cyanuric chloride) to install the alkyne on a single position. While Sonogashira on chloro-heteroarenes activated by the triazine is feasible, the chemoselectivity is the major concern: cyanuric chloride bears three equivalent, highly electrophilic C-Cl bonds. The terminal alkyne (and the Cu-acetylide) would also be prone to react with the highly electrophilic triazine via SNAr-type pathways, and controlling mono-coupling versus multiple couplings/side reactions is difficult. Additionally, free terminal alkynes can undergo Glaser homocoupling under Cu/O2 conditions. A more robust strategy would be to install the alkyne after partial amination (when fewer reactive chlorides remain) or to use a halonaphthalene + ethynyltriazine surrogate. Mono-selective Pd-coupling on cyanuric chloride is non-trivial.

Disconnection of the C(triazine)-N(C)CC(C)C bond to install the N-methylisobutylamine via SNAr on the chloro-triazine. Aminotriazines are classically built by sequential SNAr displacement of chlorines on cyanuric chloride, and at this stage the remaining chloride is displaced by a secondary amine. This proceeds well but typically requires somewhat elevated temperature for the third (least reactive) substitution. The N-methylisobutylamine (CNCC(C)C) is commercially available. The existing isobutylamino group and alkyne are compatible. Good step.

SNAr displacement of one chloride of the dichlorotriazine with isobutylamine (CC(C)CN). This is the second substitution on the triazine and proceeds under mild conditions (0 degC to RT with a base such as DIPEA). Selectivity for mono-substitution leaving one chloride intact is well established for cyanuric-chloride-derived systems by temperature control. The alkyne is compatible. Building block isobutylamine is commercial.

This step proposes a Sonogashira coupling between 1-ethynylnaphthalene and 2,4,6-trichloro-1,3,5-triazine (cyanuric chloride) to give the mono-alkynylated dichlorotriazine. While Sonogashira coupling on chloro-heteroarenes activated by adjacent ring nitrogens is feasible, cyanuric chloride is extremely electrophilic and highly susceptible to side reactions (hydrolysis, homocoupling/Glaser of the terminal alkyne, multiple substitution). Achieving clean mono-coupling on a symmetric trichlorotriazine while preserving exactly two chlorides for downstream SNAr is challenging - controlling mono- vs di-/tri-coupling regioselectivity and avoiding competing displacement by the amine/copper acetylide is problematic. A more reliable approach would be to first install the alkyne onto a less reactive, partially-substituted triazine, or to use a halo-naphthalene + alkynyl-triazine variant. Consider reordering so the SNAr aminations occur before the metal-catalyzed alkynylation. Mild conditions (Pd, CuI, amine base) needed to avoid Glaser homocoupling. The building blocks (1-ethynylnaphthalene, cyanuric chloride) are commercially available.

This step is the SNAr displacement of the remaining chloride on the triazine by N-methylisobutylamine (CNCC(C)C). Chlorotriazines are classic substrates for sequential SNAr amination, and the third substitution typically requires somewhat elevated temperature. The secondary amine is appropriately nucleophilic. Chemoselectivity is fine because the only electrophilic site is the triazine chloride; the alkyne and the existing secondary amine substituent are unreactive. Well-precedented transformation in cyanuric chloride chemistry.

Second SNAr amination of a dichlorotriazine intermediate with isobutylamine (primary amine). Sequential substitution of cyanuric-chloride-derived systems is well established, with temperature control providing selectivity between the first, second, and third substitution. At this stage one chloride remains for the subsequent (20ebde92234aa545e43ed4d1ac848c9848af290dc341ffd8d110df5ef0763fad) substitution. Note there is a subtle ordering concern across 20ebde92234aa545e43ed4d1ac848c9848af290dc341ffd8d110df5ef0763fad/6e733e9b1271d9bd707701cb4adabaf211e42b02347bf365cffc0ada8e25129d: introducing the alkyne (Sonogashira) on a chlorotriazine before amination requires that the chloride used for coupling be differentiated from those used for amination — see comments on a59c04b0bdff7fcd63476f3ae36387152809e1295ac0b0959ade76e277a9fd6f. The amination itself is feasible and standard.

This step proposes a Sonogashira coupling of 1-ethynylnaphthalene with 2,4,6-trichloro-1,3,5-triazine (cyanuric chloride) to install the alkyne on one position, leaving two chlorides. While Sonogashira coupling on chlorotriazines is chemically possible (triazinyl chlorides are activated toward both Pd-catalyzed coupling and SNAr), there is a serious selectivity/chemoselectivity concern: cyanuric chloride is extremely electrophilic and the terminal alkyne/copper acetylide, as well as the amine bases (e.g., Et3N) typically used in Sonogashira conditions, will compete by direct SNAr on the triazine, leading to multiple substitutions and poor mono-selectivity. Achieving clean mono-Sonogashira on cyanuric chloride is difficult. A better strategy would be to perform the aminations first (to deactivate/differentiate the ring) and install the alkyne last, or to use a halotriazine where the coupling position is differentiated. As written, controlling which of three equivalent C-Cl positions reacts and avoiding amine/alkyne SNAr side reactions is a real problem.

SNAr of a dichlorotriazine (bearing the alkynylnaphthalene) with isobutylamine to install the first alkylamino group. SNAr on activated chlorotriazines with primary amines proceeds readily at low temperature with good mono-selectivity (statistical/temperature control). The alkyne is compatible with these mild basic conditions. Feasible, though see the global ordering concern: if the alkyne is installed first (a59c04b0bdff7fcd63476f3ae36387152809e1295ac0b0959ade76e277a9fd6f), the subsequent aminations are fine, but the a59c04b0bdff7fcd63476f3ae36387152809e1295ac0b0959ade76e277a9fd6f step itself is the weak link.

This is a Suzuki-Miyaura coupling installing the 4-hydroxyphenyl group onto a vinyl triflate. The disconnection is reasonable for constructing the trisubstituted alkene of the oxabicyclic core. However, there is a serious chemoselectivity concern: the substrate contains a free carboxylic acid, a free phenol, AND a second aryl sulfonate ester (the catechol monosulfonate, O=S(=O)Oc2ccccc2O). Under Pd(0)/base Suzuki conditions, aryl sulfonate esters can also undergo oxidative addition/coupling, and the catechol sulfonate ester could be cleaved or react. The vinyl triflate is more reactive than the aryl sulfonate, so chemoselectivity may be achievable, but the free phenol on the boronate partner and free COOH are not ideal and would likely require protection. There is also a risk of protodeboronation of the electron-rich 4-hydroxyphenylboronate. Recommend protecting the carboxylic acid and free phenols during this coupling.

This step is removal of a tert-butyl ester to reveal the free carboxylic acid (TFA or acid-mediated Boc/tBu ester cleavage). This is a well-established, high-yielding transformation. Note the molecule contains acid-sensitive functionality (vinyl triflate, sulfonate ester, the oxabicyclic ether) but these are generally stable to TFA. Standard and reliable.

This is a debenzylation (hydrogenolysis) of a benzyl-protected catechol phenol to reveal the free phenol. H2/Pd-C would normally accomplish this; however the substrate contains a vinyl triflate and an alkene-bearing oxabicyclic core that would be reduced/cleaved under hydrogenolysis conditions. Therefore the benzyl group cannot be removed by hydrogenation here — a non-hydrogenolytic method (e.g., BCl3, Lewis acid) would be needed. The disconnection itself (PG removal) is valid, but reagent choice is constrained by the alkene and triflate.

This is an O-benzylation of the free phenol of the catechol monosulfonate using benzyl bromide/base. The intent is reasonable as a protecting-group step. However, the molecule also contains a vinyl triflate that is base-sensitive and could undergo elimination or substitution under the basic alkylation conditions (e.g., K2CO3/Cs2CO3). Mild base and careful conditions needed to preserve the triflate and sulfonate ester.

This is a Suzuki-Miyaura coupling installing the 4-hydroxyphenyl group via vinyl triflate. The major problem is severe chemoselectivity: the molecule contains TWO sulfonate ester leaving groups (the vinyl triflate AND the aryl sulfonate on the catechol-derived 2-hydroxyphenyl ester), both of which are competent electrophiles in Pd-catalyzed coupling. Aryl sulfonates of catechol monoesters can undergo oxidative addition. Additionally, the free phenol on the boronate and the free carboxylic acid are unprotected, which can complicate the coupling (protodeboronation of electron-rich p-hydroxyphenyl boronate is a known issue, and free acid can poison the catalyst). The vinyl triflate on an enol of a strained oxabicyclic system is also prone to elimination/decomposition. Selective coupling at the vinyl triflate over the aryl sulfonate is plausible (vinyl triflates are usually more reactive), but not guaranteed. Recommend protecting the carboxylic acid and reconsidering the order so the free phenol coupling partner is less prone to protodeboronation.

This is a Boc/tert-butyl ester deprotection (TFA-mediated) revealing the free carboxylic acid. Standard and reliable. One caution: the molecule contains acid-sensitive functionality (the strained 7-oxabicyclic ether/oxetane-like ring and vinyl triflate); strong acid conditions could promote ring opening or triflate solvolysis. Mild controlled TFA conditions should be acceptable, but monitor for the sensitive bicyclic ether.

Debenzylation (hydrogenolysis) of the benzyl-protected catechol phenol to reveal the free phenol. The transformation itself is standard. However, in the FORWARD direction there is a major chemoselectivity concern: H2/Pd hydrogenolysis would also reduce the vinyl triflate-bearing tetrasubstituted alkene and could cleave the vinyl triflate, and the nitro-derived aniline and other groups are sensitive. The benzyl ether on a catechol is also somewhat redundant given the late-stage manipulations. A non-hydrogenolytic deprotection (e.g., Lewis acid) would be safer here to preserve the alkene and triflate.

Amide bond formation between the aniline and the acid chloride of the mono-tert-butyl suberate. This is a straightforward Schotten-Baumann/acyl chloride amidation. The aniline is the most nucleophilic site, and the reaction should be selective. Mild base (pyridine/Et3N) recommended. Compatible with the protected functional groups present.

Conversion of the mono-tert-butyl suberate to the corresponding acid chloride using oxalyl chloride. Standard transformation. Caution: oxalyl chloride conditions are typically mild enough to leave the tert-butyl ester intact, but acidic byproducts/HCl can risk Boc/t-Bu ester cleavage; catalytic DMF and controlled conditions advised. Both starting materials are commercially available.

local_feedback_text: Reduction of the aryl nitro group to the aniline. The standard reagents (H2/Pd) would cleave the benzyl ether and reduce/cleave the vinyl triflate and the tetrasubstituted alkene - serious chemoselectivity problems. Chemoselective nitro reduction avoiding the alkene/triflate/OBn requires non-hydrogenative methods (e.g., Fe/AcOH, SnCl2, or Zn). Even then, the vinyl triflate and the catechol sulfonate ester may not survive strongly reducing or acidic conditions.
