Williamson-type O-benzylation of the catechol monoester (the free phenol of the 2-hydroxyphenyl sulfonate ester) with benzyl bromide/base. The transformation is feasible in principle, but selectivity is a concern: the substrate is an aryl SULFONATE ESTER of a catechol mono-OH. Base required for benzylation could promote transesterification/cleavage of the labile catechol sulfonate or attack the vinyl triflate. Also, no other strongly acidic OH should compete here, so regioselectivity for the single phenol is acceptable, but FG compatibility under basic alkylation conditions is the real risk.

This is a Suzuki-Miyaura coupling between a vinyl triflate and an arylboronic ester (4-hydroxyphenyl pinacol boronate). The disconnection of the C=C-aryl bond from the vinyl triflate is reasonable in principle. However, there is a serious chemoselectivity problem: the molecule contains an aryl sulfonate ester (catechol arylsulfonate, ArO-SO2-) which is itself a viable Pd cross-coupling electrophile and competing leaving group. Additionally, the free carboxylic acid and free phenol may complicate the Pd catalysis (catalyst poisoning by carboxylate). Doing this Suzuki coupling on the fully deprotected substrate (free COOH and free phenol present) is non-optimal. One would expect chemoselectivity issues between the vinyl triflate and the aryl sulfonate ester. Confidence is moderate.

This step is the deprotection of a tert-butyl ester to reveal the free carboxylic acid (TFA or acid-mediated). This is a well-established and robust transformation. The concern is that the substrate also bears a vinyl triflate and an aryl sulfonate ester; acidic conditions (e.g., TFA) are compatible with these. The vinyl triflate and sulfonate are stable to acidic Boc/tBu ester cleavage. Feasible and standard.

Debenzylation of the catechol O-benzyl ether to reveal the free phenol. Typically done by hydrogenolysis (H2/Pd-C). However, the substrate contains a vinyl triflate and an alkene-like enol ether/strained bicyclic olefin (C2=C3 oxabicyclic system) plus an aryl-O-SO2 ester; hydrogenolysis conditions (H2/Pd) would reduce the alkene AND likely cleave/reduce the vinyl triflate. This is a significant chemoselectivity concern. A Lewis-acid mediated debenzylation (e.g., BCl3) might be preferable to preserve the alkene and triflate. As written with the implicit hydrogenolysis, this step is problematic. I will flag this as a feasibility/selectivity concern.

Amide bond formation between an acid chloride (mono-tBu suberyl chloride) and an aniline. This is a standard Schotten-Baumann type acylation and should proceed well. The aniline is the most nucleophilic site; chemoselective acylation of the amine over the phenolic ether (protected as Bn) is fine. Standard and reliable.

Conversion of a mono-tert-butyl-protected suberic acid to its acid chloride using oxalyl chloride. This is a standard activation. The tBu ester is compatible with oxalyl chloride (mild, no acid generated beyond CO/CO2 and HCl which is fine briefly). The mono-tBu suberic acid is a known/accessible building block. Feasible.

local_feedback: Problems with reaction type and functional group compatibility
local_feedback_text: Reduction of the aromatic nitro group to an aniline. The classic methods (H2/Pd, SnCl2, Fe/AcOH) raise compatibility concerns: the substrate contains a vinyl triflate, a strained alkene within the oxabicyclic core, and an aryl sulfonate ester. Catalytic hydrogenation would reduce the alkene and/or cleave the triflate. Dissolving-metal or hydride reductions could also affect the sulfonate ester or triflate. A chemoselective method (e.g., Fe/NH4Cl, Zn, or SnCl2) would be needed and even then selectivity over the vinyl triflate is questionable. Significant compatibility issues.

Benzylation of the free catechol phenol with benzyl bromide (Williamson ether synthesis, base-mediated). This is a standard O-alkylation. The remaining catechol OH that bears the sulfonate is already capped, so selective benzylation of the free phenol is fine. Mild base (K2CO3) should be compatible with the vinyl triflate and sulfonate. Feasible.

This Suzuki-Miyaura coupling installs the 4-hydroxyphenyl group via the vinyl triflate. The disconnection is reasonable in principle, but there are serious chemoselectivity concerns: the molecule contains TWO sulfonate ester functionalities (the aryl sulfonate on the catechol-derived O and a free phenol on the catechol). The free phenol and free carboxylic acid are also present unprotected. More critically, the boronic ester is an UNprotected 4-hydroxyphenylboronic pinacol ester, and the substrate bears an aryl sulfonate (ArOSO2-) which can itself undergo Pd-catalyzed coupling under Suzuki conditions, competing with the vinyl triflate. Vinyl triflate is generally more reactive than aryl sulfonate, so chemoselectivity may be achievable, but the unprotected carboxylic acid and free phenol are not ideal under basic Pd conditions. Performing this as the final step on a highly functionalized substrate with a free acid is risky.

TFA-mediated (or acid-mediated) cleavage of the tert-butyl ester to reveal the free carboxylic acid is a well-established transformation. The other functionalities (triflate, sulfonate ester, amide) are generally compatible with acidic Boc/tBu deprotection conditions, though prolonged strong acid exposure could risk the vinyl triflate. Standard and reliable disconnection.

local_feedback_text: This step is the hydrogenolytic (or otherwise) removal of the benzyl ether protecting the catechol phenol. The problem is that hydrogenolysis (H2/Pd) of a benzyl ether would be incompatible with the vinyl triflate (which would undergo reduction/hydrogenolysis) and could also reduce the alkene/aryl systems. Since the substrate contains a vinyl triflate that must survive to the next coupling step, using a benzyl-protected catechol that requires hydrogenolytic removal is a poor protecting-group choice. A more orthogonal protecting group (e.g., MOM, TBS, or acetate) that can be removed without H2/Pd would be far more appropriate here. As written, the deprotection method is non-optimal given downstream/upstream functionality.

local_feedback_text: Reduction of the aromatic nitro group to the aniline. The chemoselectivity problem is severe: the substrate contains a vinyl triflate and an oxabicyclic epoxide. Standard nitro reduction conditions (H2/Pd, SnCl2, Fe/AcOH) are problematic - catalytic hydrogenation would reduce/cleave the vinyl triflate and the benzyl ether, and could open the strained ring. A chemoselective reduction (e.g., Fe/NH4Cl or Zn) avoiding the triflate would be required, but even these may not be fully selective. This is a high-risk step as drawn given the vinyl triflate present.

O-benzylation of the catechol phenol with benzyl bromide under basic conditions. The substrate already bears an aryl sulfonate ester on the adjacent catechol oxygen, so only one free phenol remains - mono-benzylation is therefore plausible. However, basic conditions (K2CO3/Cs2CO3) needed for O-alkylation could also attack the activated aryl sulfonate ester or the vinyl triflate, and the sulfonate ester on a catechol is somewhat labile. Regioselectivity is not an issue (single free OH), but chemoselectivity vs. the sulfonate/triflate is a concern.

This step proposes the target ethyl ester is made by Fischer esterification of the free carboxylic acid with ethanol. The fundamental problem is that the immediate precursor (3e7e498fccb33584f19478d2cdbda11c3dfaeff3380f7f6e83c3a6c2146645da product) is the METHYL ester, not the free acid. Yet here the disconnection switches to a free carboxylic acid + EtOH. This is internally inconsistent with the route: the methyl ester would need to be hydrolyzed first to the acid (which is exactly what 3e7e498fccb33584f19478d2cdbda11c3dfaeff3380f7f6e83c3a6c2146645da does), and then re-esterified to the ethyl ester. This methyl->acid->ethyl ester shuffle is chemically nonsensical and wasteful. Moreover, Fischer esterification under acidic conditions on this highly functionalized dipyrromethene-type chromophore (with two NH pyrroles, an enamine/imine system, and a vinylogous bridge) would risk decomposition. A direct ethyl ester should simply be carried through from an ethyl ester building block. This disconnection is not justified.

This step converts the methyl ester to the free carboxylic acid (ester hydrolysis in the retrosynthetic sense). Combined with 9adb64aec42f442569c52b916935e6ab790682f5bcf63ea41e9f9d56846dd48e, this generates an unnecessary methyl ester -> acid -> ethyl ester sequence. If the target is the ethyl ester, the synthesis should employ an ethyl ester throughout rather than installing a methyl ester, hydrolyzing it, and re-esterifying. This interconversion adds steps and risks decomposing the sensitive vinylogous/dipyrrin-like core under hydrolysis or esterification conditions. Strategically redundant.

This step is a Boc deprotection of the N-Boc pyrrole to reveal the free NH pyrrole. Boc removal from pyrrole nitrogen is well-established (TFA or thermal). The free NH pyrrole, methyl ester, and the conjugated pyrromethene/azafulvene system should tolerate mild acidic Boc cleavage, though strong acid could affect the sensitive chromophore. Overall a reasonable and standard protecting-group removal. Note the Boc was used to enable the Suzuki coupling in 47825577bde9cde6833b0c5404527504e912898c54a9b70985f4e65531300fcb, which is a logical strategy.

This is a Suzuki–Miyaura coupling between a 2-bromopyrrole and an N-Boc-pyrrole-2-boronic acid. The bond disconnection (forming the inter-pyrrole C–C bond) is reasonable and a sound convergent strategy. However, several practical concerns: (1) 2-boronic acids of N-Boc pyrroles are notoriously prone to protodeboronation, which limits yields. (2) The brominated coupling partner contains a free NH pyrrole and an electron-rich, conjugated azafulvene/methylene-bridged system that could coordinate Pd or undergo side reactions. (3) Chemoselectivity of oxidative addition is fine (only one aryl bromide), but the boronic acid stability is the main risk. A pinacol boronate or MIDA boronate of the N-Boc pyrrole, or reversing the coupling partners (brominate the pyridinone-substituted ring), would improve robustness. Feasible but with notable selectivity/stability caveats.

This step is an NBS bromination of a methoxypyrrole to install the 2-bromo (alpha) position selectively. The major concern is regioselectivity and chemoselectivity: the substrate is an electron-rich pyrrole already bearing a methoxy substituent and conjugated to an extended azafulvene/exocyclic alkene system. NBS could brominate at multiple electron-rich positions (the open alpha-position of the pyrrole, the beta-positions, or even add across/halogenate the electron-rich exocyclic vinylogous double bond). Controlling mono-bromination at the desired alpha position would be challenging without careful conditions (low temperature, stoichiometric control, radical vs. ionic conditions). The proposed regiochemistry is plausible (alpha to NH, para-like to OMe) but selectivity is a real risk.

This step proposes a Fischer esterification of the carboxylic acid with ethanol to give the ethyl ester. The disconnection itself (acid + EtOH -> ethyl ester) is chemically reasonable in isolation. However, the problem is that the immediate precursor in the route (3e7e498fccb33584f19478d2cdbda11c3dfaeff3380f7f6e83c3a6c2146645da) is derived from a METHYL ester. The route methylates/demethylates inconsistently: the carboxylic acid here was supposedly obtained by hydrolysis of a methyl ester (3e7e498fccb33584f19478d2cdbda11c3dfaeff3380f7f6e83c3a6c2146645da), only to be re-esterified to an ethyl ester. This is a non-strategic transmutation of esters (methyl -> acid -> ethyl) that adds two unnecessary steps. Furthermore, the molecule contains multiple acid-sensitive moieties (dipyrromethene-type/azafulvene system, two pyrrole NH, enol ether), and Fischer esterification (strong acid, reflux) would risk decomposition. A direct ethyl ester would be preferable from the start, avoiding the hydrolysis/re-esterification cycle entirely.

This step is the ester hydrolysis (methyl ester -> carboxylic acid). Combined with 9adb64aec42f442569c52b916935e6ab790682f5bcf63ea41e9f9d56846dd48e (re-esterification to the ethyl ester), this constitutes a wasteful methyl->acid->ethyl ester interconversion. If the target bears an ethyl ester, the synthesis should simply install the ethyl ester at the outset. Saponification of the methyl ester is feasible chemically, but exposing the base-sensitive azafulvene/methine-bridged bis-heterocyclic chromophore to hydrolytic conditions risks E/Z isomerization of the exocyclic alkene and possible retro-condensation. The step adds no strategic value.

This is a Boc deprotection of the N-Boc pyrrole to reveal the free NH pyrrole. Boc removal from pyrrole nitrogen is well precedented (TFA or thermal). The other functional groups (esters, enol ether, methine bridge) are generally compatible with mild acidic Boc cleavage, though care is needed to avoid alkene isomerization. The disconnection is sound and the protecting group logic (Boc to enable clean Suzuki coupling on the boronic acid pyrrole) is reasonable.

This is a Suzuki–Miyaura coupling between an N-Boc-pyrrole-2-boronic acid and a 2-bromopyrrole-containing fragment to form the inter-ring C-C bond. The disconnection is strategically attractive and well-precedented for biaryl/bis-heteroaryl linkages. However, several concerns arise: (1) N-Boc-pyrrol-2-yl boronic acids are notoriously prone to protodeboronation under basic Pd conditions, lowering yield; an MIDA boronate or pinacol ester would be more robust. (2) Chemoselectivity: the substrate contains a base-sensitive azafulvene/methine system and an ester; Pd/base conditions could induce isomerization of the exocyclic alkene. (3) The 2-bromopyrrole partner (free NH) may need protection to ensure clean oxidative addition and to avoid catalyst poisoning. Overall feasible but with notable optimization required.

This step is the regioselective bromination of a pyrrole (with NBS) to install the 2-bromo substituent. NBS bromination of electron-rich pyrroles is feasible, but selectivity is a major concern here: the substrate already bears an electron-rich, methine-bridged azafulvene chromophore and an enol ether-substituted pyrrole, both highly activated toward electrophilic halogenation. Bromination could occur on the exocyclic methine, on the second pyrrole/pyrrolinone ring, or give poly-bromination. Controlling mono-bromination at the desired pyrrole C-position would be very challenging. Low-temperature, controlled stoichiometry NBS could work, but chemo-/regioselectivity is a real risk.

This step proposes a Fischer esterification of the carboxylic acid with ethanol to give the ethyl ester. However, the disconnection is problematic. First, the molecule contains an extremely sensitive bis-pyrrole methine (dipyrrin-like) chromophore with multiple acid-sensitive NH heterocycles. Fischer esterification requires strong acid catalysis and reflux conditions that would likely degrade or protonate the basic azafulvene/pyrromethene system and promote E/Z isomerization of the exocyclic alkene. More critically, selective mono-esterification of the carboxylic acid in the presence of the free 2H-pyrrole NH groups would be straightforward chemoselectively, but the harsh conditions are incompatible. A milder esterification (e.g., EtBr/base, or DCC/DMAP coupling) would be preferred. The disconnection itself (acid + EtOH) is reasonable in principle but the chosen reagent/conditions are non-optimal.

This step proposes converting the methyl ester to the carboxylic acid (hydrolysis) as a forward step, but in the synthesis this introduces an unnecessary redox/protecting-group shuffle: a methyl ester is hydrolyzed to acid (3e7e498fccb33584f19478d2cdbda11c3dfaeff3380f7f6e83c3a6c2146645da), then re-esterified to the ethyl ester (9adb64aec42f442569c52b916935e6ab790682f5bcf63ea41e9f9d56846dd48e). This is highly inefficient and chemically illogical—if the final target is the ethyl ester, one should not pass through methyl ester then acid then ethyl ester. Furthermore, basic hydrolysis (saponification) of the methyl ester risks competing decomposition of the labile pyrromethene system. This step should be eliminated; the ethyl ester could be installed directly or carried through.

This step is a Boc deprotection of the N-Boc pyrrole to reveal the free NH pyrrole. Boc removal under acidic conditions (TFA) or thermal conditions is well-established. The main concern is the acid sensitivity of the dipyrrin/azafulvene chromophore and potential E/Z isomerization of the methine bridge under acidic conditions, plus possible protodeboronation byproduct issues are not relevant here. Thermal Boc removal is a milder alternative. Overall the disconnection is sound and standard.

This is a Suzuki-Miyaura cross-coupling between an N-Boc-pyrrole-2-boronic acid and a 2-bromopyrrole intermediate. The disconnection strategy (forming the bipyrrole C-C bond via Suzuki) is reasonable and well-precedented for pyrrole couplings. However, several concerns: (1) N-Boc pyrrole-2-boronic acids are notoriously prone to protodeboronation, often giving low yields; (2) the brominated coupling partner contains a free pyrrole NH and the sensitive azafulvene/methine system, which may not tolerate the Pd catalysis/base conditions well; (3) chemoselectivity should be acceptable since there is only one aryl halide. Use of a boronate ester (pinacol or MIDA boronate) would improve stability. Overall feasible but yield-limited.

This step proposes regioselective bromination of the pyrrole using NBS at the 2-position (alpha to NH, distal from the methoxy). Regioselectivity between the two free alpha/beta positions of this 3-methoxy pyrrole would be a concern; the 5-position (where Br is installed) vs other positions must be controlled. Additionally, the electron-rich pyrrole bearing the conjugated azafulvene system could undergo bromination at the methine bridge or on the second heterocyclic ring. Careful stoichiometry (1.0 equiv NBS, low temperature) and the directing effect of the methoxy group are needed. Selectivity is the major risk.

This step proposes a Fischer esterification of a free carboxylic acid with ethanol to give the ethyl ester. This is a redundant/illogical transformation. Standard Fischer esterification would also be complicated by the acid-sensitive functionalities (enamine/azafulvene system, two NH-pyrroles, vinylogous system).

This is a simple methyl ester to carboxylic acid conversion (saponification/hydrolysis). This step is a Boc deprotection of the N-Boc pyrrole to reveal the free NH-pyrrole. Boc removal under mild acidic conditions (TFA) is well-precedented and reliable. The main concern is the acid sensitivity of the polypyrrole/azafulvene system, but transient TFA treatment is generally compatible. A reasonable, well-established transformation.

This is a Suzuki-Miyaura cross-coupling between an N-Boc-pyrrole-2-boronic acid and a 2-bromopyrrole-containing substrate. Suzuki couplings of pyrrole boronic acids/halides are feasible, though pyrrole-2-boronic acids and 2-bromopyrroles can be unstable/prone to protodeboronation and protodehalogenation. The N-Boc protection on the boronic acid coupling partner helps stabilize it. Regioselectivity is defined by the halide position. Standard Pd(0) catalysis with mild base should work. Minor concern about protodeboronation of the electron-rich pyrrolylboronic acid, but acceptable. Good convergent disconnection.

This step proposes NBS bromination of a methoxypyrrole to install bromine selectively at the 5-position (alpha) of the pyrrole. While electrophilic bromination of pyrroles with NBS is feasible, regioselectivity is a serious concern: the pyrrole already bears a 3-OMe substituent and a 2-vinyl(azafulvene) substituent, leaving only the 5-position open, which helps selectivity. However, the highly electron-rich conjugated azafulvene/dipyrrin-like system is very prone to over-bromination and bromination at the activated methine bridge or the second ring. Controlling mono-bromination at the desired position will be challenging. Careful stoichiometry (1.0 equiv NBS) at low temperature would be required. Chemoselectivity over the electron-rich vinyl bridge is the main risk.

The final step is a sulfonylation of a secondary amine (bridgehead N-H of the bicyclic diamine) with 4-cyanobenzenesulfonyl chloride. The secondary amine is the only nucleophilic site (the lactam N is acylated and non-nucleophilic), so chemoselectivity is good. The nitrile is fully compatible. A reasonable and high-yielding endgame disconnection.

Removal of the Cbz protecting group to reveal the secondary amine. Hydrogenolysis (H2/Pd-C) is standard. One caution: the substrate contains two electron-rich aryl methyl ethers and a benzylic C-N/C-H environment, but Cbz hydrogenolysis is selective and aryl methyl ethers are stable under these conditions. The lactam and aromatic ring are untouched. Feasible and routine.

Good step.

This is mechanistically implausible: (1) Nucleophilic aromatic substitution of a simple aryl fluoride by an oxygen nucleophile would require strong activation (ortho/para EWG) which the 4-fluorobenzyl ring lacks. (2) MOM-OH (the hemiacetal of formaldehyde and methanol) is not a stable/standard reagent and would not serve as the nucleophile source here. This disconnection is not viable.

This step proposes that MOM-OH (COCO = methoxymethanol) is formed from formaldehyde hydrate/methanediol (OCO) and dichloromethane (ClCCl). This is chemically incorrect - dichloromethane is not a methanol/methyl source under normal conditions, and this combination does not produce methoxymethanol. The disconnection is nonsensical. Methoxymethyl reagents (MOMCl, MOM ethers) are made from formaldehyde + methanol/HCl, not via DCM.

This step proposes a direct nitration of the N-phenyl ring to install a para-nitro group. While electrophilic aromatic nitration of an aniline-derived N-phenyl urazole is plausible, there are several serious concerns: (1) The substrate is extremely electron-poor and contains numerous oxidatively/acid-sensitive functionalities (two quinone-type/diketone carbonyls on a pyridine-fused system, a thioether/sulfide which is highly susceptible to oxidation under strong nitrating conditions like HNO3, and the bicyclic semicarbazide/urazole core). Concentrated HNO3 (shown as the nitrating agent) would likely oxidize the sulfide to sulfoxide/sulfone and could degrade the sensitive quinone system. (2) Regioselectivity: nitration on an N-aryl urea-type phenyl is moderately para-selective, but mixtures of ortho/para are common. (3) Better practice would be to introduce the p-nitrophenyl group already nitrated from a pre-functionalized building block (e.g., use 4-nitrophenylhydrazine in constructing the urazole) rather than late-stage nitration of a complex, sensitive intermediate. Confidence in feasibility as written is low.

local_feedback_text: This step removes a 4-methoxybenzyl (PMB) group from the urazole nitrogen to reveal the free N-H. local_feedback_text: This step is a MOM (methoxymethyl) deprotection of a phenol on the benzyl group. Again this is part of a chain of protecting-group manipulations (MOM on/off, PMB, O-methyl) on a benzyl substituent that, taken together, are redundant. This step proposes converting a 4-fluorobenzyl group to a 4-(MOM-oxy)benzyl group, i.e. an aromatic nucleophilic substitution of an aryl fluoride by a MOM-oxy oxygen nucleophile (COCO = methoxymethanol). A simple, unactivated 4-fluorobenzyl aryl fluoride is not activated toward SNAr (no ortho/para electron-withdrawing groups on that ring), so direct displacement of fluoride by an alkoxide/MOM-O nucleophile will not proceed. This disconnection is chemically implausible as written. Additionally, methoxymethanol is not a competent nucleophile reagent for installing a MOM ether on a phenol.

This step depicts the formation of methoxymethanol (COCO) from formaldehyde hydrate (OCO) and dichloromethane (ClCCl). This is not a real synthetic transformation: dichloromethane does not serve as a methyl source here, and the proposed combination does not produce methoxymethanol cleanly. Methoxymethanol/MOM sources are normally derived from formaldehyde + methanol or from MOM-Cl/DMM. The disconnection is chemically invalid.

Direct nitration with nitric acid (HNO3) on this highly functionalized substrate would face severe chemoselectivity problems. The molecule contains an electron-poor pyridine-fused quinone (azaanthraquinone) system, multiple amide/urea carbonyls, and a thioether. The thioether is highly susceptible to oxidation under nitration conditions. While regioselectivity for para-nitration on the aniline-derived N-phenyl ring is reasonable (activated by N), the harsh oxidizing conditions would degrade the sensitive quinone and oxidize sulfur. A late-stage nitration on such a complex molecule is risky; better to introduce the nitro group earlier on a simple aniline building block.

This step proposes forming a 4-methoxybenzyl (PMB) protected product from a 4-hydroxybenzyl compound plus methanol (CO). Methylation of a phenol to form an aryl methyl ether does not proceed by simply combining the phenol with methanol (CO) - it requires a methylating agent (MeI/base, Me2SO4, or Mitsunobu). The SMILES disconnection as written (release of CO/methanol) is not a valid representation of O-methylation. Moreover, the strategic logic is flawed: protecting a phenol as a methyl ether is poor practice since methyl ethers require harsh deprotection (BBr3) incompatible with this sensitive substrate.

local_feedback_text: MOM protection of the phenol is chemically feasible (MOMCl/DIPEA), but in the context of the route it is redundant. The pathway protects the phenol as MOM (02b0376bfacec782c81968672be94ba879f6a6575517855df0a74c61f3f50802), then somehow converts it to a methyl ether (9df9b851e26c143661b430d089a4e10bded22161ad5eb713b9908f89915269ad), then to free phenol again... The protecting group choreography is convoluted and internally inconsistent. A single, well-chosen protecting group strategy on the building block would be far more efficient. The MOM group is also acid-labile and may not survive other steps.

This disconnection is chemically nonsensical. It proposes that a MOM-protected phenol arises from 'COCO' (methoxymethanol) plus a 4-FLUORObenzyl-containing substrate. Converting an aryl fluoride into a MOM-protected aryl ether via reaction with methoxymethanol is not a real transformation - aromatic C-F to C-O exchange would require harsh SNAr conditions (and the ring is not activated for SNAr) or transition-metal catalysis, not a hemiformal. The disconnection logic and reagents are invalid.

This step proposes synthesizing methoxymethanol/MOM precursor ('COCO') from methylene glycol (OCO) and dichloromethane (ClCCl). This is not a valid chemical reaction - DCM is a solvent, not a methoxy source under normal conditions, and the product connectivity makes no sense. MOM-protecting reagents (MOMCl, MOM-acetate) are commercially available and would not be made this way. This is an artifact of the retrosynthetic algorithm.

This is an aromatic nitration using nitric acid to convert the N-phenyl group to a para-nitrophenyl group. While electrophilic aromatic nitration is well-established, there are serious selectivity and chemoselectivity concerns here. The substrate contains a highly electron-poor heterocyclic quinone (azaanthraquinone) system, multiple amide/urea carbonyls, a thioether, and an electron-rich vs electron-poor aromatic landscape. The N-phenyl ring attached to nitrogen would be activated/directed, but strong nitrating conditions (HNO3) could oxidize the thioether to sulfoxide/sulfone, and could potentially nitrate the pyridine-fused quinone or cause decomposition of the sensitive spiro-fused triazinedione/thiophene system. Para-selectivity on the N-aryl amide is reasonable but regiocontrol and over-nitration are concerns. Milder conditions (e.g., HNO3/AcOH or acetyl nitrate at low temperature) would be preferable. Performing nitration at this late stage on a complex, sensitive polyfunctional molecule is strategically risky; nitration of an early building block would be wiser.

local_feedback_text: This step represents removal of a 4-methoxybenzyl (PMB) group from the urea/triazinedione nitrogen to give the free N-H. The disconnection (debenzylation) is conceptually sound, but the overall strategy of installing a PMB group on this urea nitrogen and then removing it is questionable. Standard PMB removal (DDQ, oxidative; or acidic conditions; or hydrogenolysis) would face compatibility problems: DDQ oxidation could affect the electron-rich systems, hydrogenolysis would reduce the nitro-free precursor's quinone and pyridine, and strong acid could cleave the spiro-thiophene. More fundamentally, debenzylation of a benzyl group on an amide/urea N (rather than an O or simple amine) is more difficult. The whole PMB protection sequence (01e859b2f30d4c5769296b84f66d56a0ff23fc6b47ef405649844c27e061a7e3-e2e61a2532a8040f640a8b7d7a94a2797d9eb2b0f909f9c5566e1a3278326aa2) appears unnecessary if the goal N-H is simply revealed at the end.

This step proposes converting a free phenol (4-hydroxybenzyl) to a methyl ether (4-methoxybenzyl) using methanol. Simple O-methylation of a phenol with MeOH alone is not feasible without an activating agent (MeI/base, Me2SO4, or Mitsunobu with MeOH). As written, MeOH as the only reagent will not methylate the phenol. Additionally, this transformation seems strategically pointless - converting a phenol to an anisole only to later remove the entire benzyl group. This represents an unnecessary functional group interconversion within an already questionable protecting group sequence.

local_feedback: Protecting group strategy is wrong / non-optimal
local_feedback_text: This step is an MOM (methoxymethyl) ether deprotection, converting MOM-protected phenol to free phenol. The transformation itself (acidic hydrolysis of MOM ether) is standard and feasible. However, in the context of the route this is part of a convoluted and self-defeating protecting group cascade (MOM on a phenol, then deprotection, then methylation, then full debenzylation). Acidic MOM removal conditions may be incompatible with the acid-sensitive spiro-fused thiophene/triazinedione scaffold. The strategy lacks coherent logic.

This step proposes forming a MOM-protected 4-hydroxybenzyl group from a 4-fluorobenzyl precursor plus MOM-OH (methoxymethanol). The disconnection implies a nucleophilic aromatic substitution of an aryl fluoride by a MOM-protected oxygen nucleophile (or hemiacetal), which is mechanistically implausible: (1) the 4-fluorobenzyl arene is not sufficiently activated for SNAr (no ortho/para EWG); (2) methoxymethanol (MOMOH) is an unstable hemiacetal and a poor nucleophile; (3) this would not install both the aryl-O bond and the MOM group simultaneously. This transformation as written is chemically unfeasible.

This step proposes synthesizing methoxymethanol (COCO, i.e., CH3OCH2OH) from formaldehyde hydrate (OCO, methanediol) and dichloromethane (ClCCl). This disconnection is nonsensical: dichloromethane is not a methoxy source, and the combination shown does not provide a viable route to methoxymethanol. Methoxymethanol is itself an unstable hemiacetal and is not a useful, isolable reagent. This entire branch reflects a flawed retrosynthetic logic. The starting materials being 'in stock' does not redeem an unfeasible transformation.

This step is the deprotection of a tert-butyl ester to reveal the free carboxylic acid (TFA or HCl). The transformation is standard and well-precedented. However, note the molecule contains an aryl mesylate-type sulfonate ester and an oxabicyclic system; acidic conditions (TFA) are generally compatible with these. The free phenol present is also stable under these conditions. A potential concern is that strongly acidic conditions could affect the strained oxanorbornene/oxabicyclic ether, but standard TFA conditions are typically mild enough.

This step is a deallylation of an allyl aryl ether (O-allyl) to reveal the free phenol. The forward direction (Pd(0)/scavenger, e.g., Pd(PPh3)4 with morpholine/dimedone) is well-established and chemoselective. The main concern is chemoselectivity: the molecule also bears an alkene-free framework but contains a tert-butyl ester and a sulfonate ester, both of which are compatible with Pd-catalyzed allyl deprotection. The transformation is feasible, but one should be careful about possible interference of the diene/enol system; overall a reasonable deprotection. Slight selectivity concern flagged but generally workable.

Amide bond formation between an aniline and an acid chloride (mono-tert-butyl-protected azelaic/suberic acid chloride). This is a standard Schotten-Baumann type acylation and is highly reliable. The aniline is the most nucleophilic site; the free phenol has been protected as an allyl ether, avoiding competing O-acylation, which justifies the protecting group strategy. Use of a mild base (Et3N, pyridine) recommended. Well-precedented and high-yielding.

Conversion of the mono-tert-butyl-protected diacid to its acid chloride using oxalyl chloride (with catalytic DMF). This is a classic, robust transformation. The tert-butyl ester is stable to oxalyl chloride at low temperature. Care must be taken to avoid excess heating that could degrade the tert-butyl ester, but the transformation is standard and selective for the free carboxylic acid. Good choice of reagent.

Williamson ether synthesis: O-allylation of the phenol with allyl bromide (K2CO3, DMF/acetone). The phenol is selectively alkylated over the aniline nitrogen under basic conditions favoring phenolate formation. There is a minor concern that the aniline nitrogen could compete, but phenols typically react faster as O-nucleophiles with allyl bromide/K2CO3, and the aniline is less acidic/less reactive under these conditions. The sulfonate ester is stable. Overall feasible and standard.

This step represents tert-butyl ester deprotection to reveal the free carboxylic acid (forward direction). TFA-mediated Boc/tBu ester cleavage is well-established and chemoselective. The other functional groups (sulfonate ester, free phenol, vinyl ether... actually here the phenol is free) are compatible with acidic deprotection. One caution: the aryl sulfonate ester and the oxabicyclic ether are generally stable to TFA. This is a sound terminal deprotection.

In the forward direction this corresponds to removal of an O-allyl protecting group on the phenol to reveal the free phenol (the product has free OH on the phenol, while the precursor bears an O-allyl ether). Pd(0)-catalyzed deallylation (e.g., Pd(PPh3)4 with a scavenger like morpholine/dimedone) is standard and chemoselective. However, the substrate contains a sensitive oxabicyclic alkene system and an electron-rich diene; competing reactions or coordination issues are possible. Overall feasible but selectivity should be checked. Note: the allyl ether seems an unnecessary protecting group if the phenol could be carried through other steps, so the strategy adds steps.

Amide bond formation between the aniline and the acid chloride (mono-tert-butyl suberyl chloride) is a standard Schotten-Baumann type acylation. Selective acylation of the aromatic amine is expected; the free aryl OH (here protected as allyl ether) and sulfonate ester are compatible. Use of base (Et3N/pyridine) recommended. Good disconnection.

Conversion of the mono-tert-butyl suberate (mono-acid) to the corresponding acid chloride using oxalyl chloride is standard. Selectivity for the free acid over the tert-butyl ester is excellent since the ester is unreactive toward oxalyl chloride. Catalytic DMF accelerates the reaction. Building blocks are commercially accessible. Well-precedented.

This is the O-allylation of the phenol with allyl bromide (Williamson ether synthesis, K2CO3). The major selectivity concern is chemoselectivity between the phenol OH and the aniline NH2 present in the same molecule. Allyl bromide can alkylate the aromatic amine (N-allylation), leading to mixtures. The free aniline would likely need protection, or one must rely on the higher acidity/nucleophilicity differences with careful base/conditions (phenoxide formation favored with mild carbonate base). As drawn, competing N-allylation is a real risk, reducing yield and complicating purification.

This is a standard tert-butyl ester deprotection to reveal the free carboxylic acid (TFA or HCl in dioxane). The transformation is well-precedented and chemoselective. The phenol, sulfonate ester, and amide should all tolerate acidic deprotection conditions. The benzylic ether (oxabicyclic) and aryl sulfonate are stable. No issues expected.

This step proposes removal of an allyl protecting group from a phenol to reveal the free phenol. The allyl deprotection (Pd(0)/scavenger such as morpholine or barbituric acid) is generally feasible and chemoselective. However, the molecule also contains an N-allyl-type vinyl ether and importantly the substrate bears a sensitive sulfonate ester and an amide; Pd-catalyzed deallylation conditions are usually compatible. The main concern is chemoselectivity if the Pd catalyst engages other functionalities, but the allyl aryl ether is the standard substrate for this reaction. Reasonable but monitor for side reactions.

Amide bond formation between the aromatic amine (aniline) and the acid chloride of the mono-tert-butyl suberic acid (Schotten-Baumann type acylation). This is a robust, high-yielding, and chemoselective coupling. The aniline is the only strong nucleophile present (phenol is protected as allyl ether), so selectivity is good. The sulfonate ester is stable under these conditions. Well-designed step.

Conversion of mono-tert-butyl suberate to the corresponding acid chloride using oxalyl chloride. This is standard and chemoselective — the tert-butyl ester is stable toward oxalyl chloride while the free carboxylic acid is converted to the acid chloride. Catalytic DMF can be used. Both starting materials are reasonable; mono-protected suberic acid (8-(tert-butoxy)-8-oxooctanoic acid) is a known building block. Good step.

This is an O-allylation of a phenol with allyl bromide (Williamson ether synthesis, base such as K2CO3). The disconnection is reasonable for protecting the phenol. However, the substrate also contains a free aniline (aromatic amine) which is a competing nucleophile and could undergo N-allylation under basic conditions. This presents a chemoselectivity problem — selective O-allylation in the presence of a free aniline NH2 is non-trivial and would likely require careful control or protection. Consider acylating the aniline first or using milder/selective conditions. The phenol is more acidic so with K2CO3 phenoxide formation can favor O-alkylation, but competing aniline alkylation remains a real risk.

This step is the deprotection of a tert-butyl ester to the free carboxylic acid (TFA, or formic acid). This is a well-established and reliable transformation. The acid-labile tert-butyl ester is selectively removed, and the other functional groups (sulfonate ester, aryl ethers, amide, phenol) are stable under standard acidic conditions (TFA/DCM). One minor concern is that the strongly acidic conditions could potentially affect the strained oxabicyclic (7-oxanorbornene-type) system, but generally tert-butyl deprotection is mild enough. This is a logical final-step revealing of the acid.

This step proposes removal of an allyl ether (deallylation) to reveal the free phenol on one of the aryl rings. The disconnection itself (allyl protecting group on a phenol, removed via Pd(0)/scavenger) is a standard and feasible transformation. However, the strategic question is why the phenol was protected as an allyl ether in the first place (see f1a7664c0d33214bb7561cb27fea7eb2a145d5ab3958d34b4906c338a54a0a70). Pd-catalyzed deallylation is generally chemoselective and compatible with the amide, sulfonate ester, and the alkene of the oxabicyclic core (the internal trisubstituted alkene is far less reactive toward Pd-allyl chemistry than the allyl-O bond). The transformation should work, but the strained bicyclic alkene and the sulfonate ester could be sensitive to the reaction conditions. Overall acceptable but the protecting group strategy adds steps.

This is an amide bond formation between an aniline (free aryl amine) and an acid chloride (mono-tert-butyl suberoyl chloride). Acylation of the aniline with the acid chloride is straightforward and high-yielding, typically run with a base (Et3N, pyridine) at low temperature. The aniline is the most nucleophilic site; the phenol is protected as allyl ether, which avoids competing O-acylation. Chemoselectivity is good. Feasible as drawn.

Conversion of a mono-tert-butyl ester of a diacid (suberic/azelaic-type) to the corresponding acid chloride using oxalyl chloride. This is standard. The tert-butyl ester is stable to oxalyl chloride under mild conditions (catalytic DMF, 0 °C to rt), allowing selective conversion of the free carboxylic acid to the acid chloride. Good chemoselectivity. The mono-tert-butyl suberate starting material is commercially available or readily prepared.

local_feedback_text: This step is an O-allylation of a phenol with allyl bromide (Williamson-type, base-mediated). The chemistry is feasible. However, the strategic problem is severe chemoselectivity: the starting material contains BOTH a free phenol AND a free aniline. Under basic O-alkylation conditions with allyl bromide, the more nucleophilic aniline nitrogen would be competitively (and likely preferentially) N-allylated, leading to mixtures. This makes selective mono-O-allylation of the phenol in the presence of a free aniline very problematic. The protecting-group logic is also questionable: the phenol is protected as allyl ether only to be removed later (548b3e7b57ad47a6a70ad0e7011a2e207dc9f87b6530c38181e4a7716c168087), adding two steps. A cleaner strategy would be to install the amide/acyl chain first and avoid protecting the phenol, or to use orthogonal protection. As written, the chemoselectivity issue undermines this step.

This is a Hantzsch thiazole synthesis disconnecting the thiazole ring into an α-bromoketone (2,4-dichlorophenacyl bromide, commercially available) and a thiourea-bearing fragment. The forward reaction (condensation of α-haloketone with thiourea) is well-precedented to form 2-aminothiazoles, and here the 2-position bears the aminopyrimidine via the thiourea nitrogen. The regiochemistry (aryl at C4, H at C5) is consistent with Hantzsch mechanism. One concern: the molecule also contains a thioether (Sc1nc...) and a carboxylic acid, but these should be compatible with Hantzsch conditions. Good disconnection.

This step proposes an S-alkylation of the dithiol/thione pyrimidine fragment (NC(=S)Nc1cc(Cl)nc(S)n1) with 2-bromooctanoic acid to install the thioether at the pyrimidine 2-mercapto position. The major selectivity problem: the molecule contains TWO sulfur nucleophiles — the pyrimidine-2-thiol AND the thiourea thione sulfur. Alkylation would compete between these two soft nucleophilic sulfurs, with the thiourea sulfur often being more nucleophilic, leading to undesired S-alkylation of the thiourea. Chemoselectivity for the ring thiol over the thiourea is not guaranteed and would likely require protection or careful control. Additionally, the α-bromo acid is a secondary halide, so alkylation may be sluggish and compete with elimination. This step needs reconsideration of the order of operations.

Hydrolytic/aminolytic cleavage of the benzoyl group from an acylthiourea to reveal the free thiourea (NC(=S)Nc...) is a standard transformation. Benzoyl isothiocyanate adducts are routinely deprotected with base (K2CO3/MeOH or NaOH) to give the free monosubstituted thiourea. This is a well-established protecting-group/activation strategy for thiourea synthesis. Feasible.

Addition of an amine (2-amino-4-chloro-6-mercaptopyrimidine) to benzoyl isothiocyanate (commercially available) to form an acylthiourea is a classic, robust reaction proceeding under mild conditions in good yield. The aminopyrimidine NH2 is the expected nucleophile. One minor consideration is the presence of the free pyrimidine thiol, which could potentially also react with the isothiocyanate (S-addition), so chemoselectivity for N vs S should be watched, but typically the aromatic amine reacts cleanly. Generally feasible.

This is a Hantzsch thiazole synthesis disconnection. The forward reaction combines an α-bromoketone (2,4-dichlorophenacyl bromide) with a thiourea (the aminopyrimidine-thiourea) to form the 2-aminothiazole linked via the C-N bond. This is a well-established transformation. The 2,4-dichlorophenyl substituent ends up at the 4-position of the thiazole, consistent with regiochemistry. One concern: the free carboxylic acid and the secondary thioether are present, but these should be tolerated under Hantzsch conditions (typically EtOH, heat). The thiourea nitrogen attached to the pyrimidine becomes the exocyclic amine of the 2-aminothiazole. Feasible.

This step proposes S-alkylation of a 2-mercaptopyrimidine bearing a thiourea substituent with 2-bromooctanoic acid. The major chemoselectivity problem: the substrate NC(=S)Nc1cc(Cl)nc(S)n1 contains BOTH a thiourea (with a nucleophilic sulfur) AND a ring mercapto/thione group. Alkylation with 2-bromooctanoic acid would not be selective for the ring thiol over the thiourea sulfur (thioureas are excellent S-nucleophiles). Additionally, the 2-bromo carboxylic acid is alpha to a carboxylate, so the carboxylate could compete or the alkylation could be sluggish. The intended S-alkylation at the pyrimidine-2-thiol position is reasonable in principle (thiopyrimidines undergo S-alkylation readily), but competing alkylation of the more nucleophilic thiourea sulfur is a serious selectivity issue. A protecting/order-of-operations strategy would be needed.

Removal of the benzoyl group from an acyl thiourea to reveal the free thiourea (N-debenzoylation). Benzoyl isothiocyanate-derived acylthioureas are commonly hydrolyzed under basic conditions (K2CO3/MeOH/H2O) to give the free thiourea. This is a standard and reliable transformation. Compatible with the chloropyrimidine and ring thiol. Feasible.

Addition of an aminopyrimidine to benzoyl isothiocyanate to form an acyl thiourea is a classic, high-yielding transformation (benzoyl isothiocyanate is commercially available and reactive toward primary amines). The amino group of 2-mercapto-4-amino-6-chloropyrimidine adds to the isothiocyanate carbon. One concern: chemoselectivity between the ring thiol (SH) and the amine; however, amines typically react faster with isothiocyanates than thiols under these conditions, and the aromatic amine is the intended nucleophile. The product regiochemistry is consistent. Feasible, though the presence of a free pyrimidine thiol could lead to some competing S-addition.

This is a Hantzsch thiazole synthesis, disconnecting the thiazole ring into an α-bromoketone (2,4-dichlorophenacyl bromide) and a thiourea. The thiourea moiety is present on the aminopyrimidine fragment. The condensation of α-haloketones with thioureas to form 2-aminothiazoles is a robust, well-precedented transformation. The 2,4-dichlorophenyl substituent ends up correctly at the 4-position of the thiazole. One concern: the free carboxylic acid and the multiple basic/nucleophilic sites (pyrimidine, thioether) are generally compatible with Hantzsch conditions. Mild heating in EtOH should give clean cyclization. Good disconnection.

This step proposes S-alkylation of a pyrimidine-2-thiol (the mercapto group of NC(=S)Nc1cc(Cl)nc(S)n1) with 2-bromooctanoic acid to install the thioether. However, the reactant bears BOTH a ring 2-mercaptopyrimidine (-SH) AND a thiourea (-NC(=S)NH2) functional group, each containing nucleophilic sulfur. Selective S-alkylation at the pyrimidine thiol over the thiourea sulfur is questionable; thioureas are excellent S-nucleophiles and would compete strongly, leading to a mixture of S-alkylation products. Additionally, the free carboxylic acid of 2-bromooctanoic acid could promote competing reactions. The order of operations is problematic: installing the thiourea before the thioether risks chemoselectivity failure. Consider performing the thioether alkylation first, then introducing the thiourea, or protecting one of the sulfur nucleophiles.

local_feedback: Protecting group strategy is wrong / non-optimal
local_feedback_text: This step is a deprotection/hydrolysis of an N-benzoyl thiourea (acylthiourea) to the free thiourea. Benzoyl thioureas are commonly hydrolyzed under basic conditions (K2CO3/MeOH) to reveal the free thiourea. The transformation itself is feasible. However, in the context of this route the benzoyl group on the thiourea is used as a means to access the thiourea via the isothiocyanate addition (f685be38a0b78ea5a3e6bd9e3ac8e1ded937ac3351c3fcc8ff81ebb2f3c379fc), but the molecule already contains a free pyrimidine-2-thiol (-SH) which would be incompatible/competitive during both the benzoylthiourea formation and the hydrolytic deprotection (base may cause side reactions with the thiol or the ring chloride). The protecting/installation strategy adds steps and creates selectivity liabilities. A more direct route to the aminothiourea pyrimidine should be considered.

local_feedback: Problems with reaction type and functional group compatibility
local_feedback_text: This step proposes addition of the aminopyrimidine (Nc1cc(Cl)nc(S)n1) to benzoyl isothiocyanate to form the acylthiourea. The reaction of amines with acyl isothiocyanates to form N-acyl thioureas is well-established. However, the substrate contains a free pyrimidine-2-thiol (-SH) which is a much stronger nucleophile than the ring amino group; the thiol would react preferentially with the electrophilic isothiocyanate carbon, leading to S-addition rather than the desired N-acylthiourea formation. This is a significant chemoselectivity problem. The thiol would need protection, or the reaction would give undesired products. Furthermore, the aminopyrimidine NH2 is weakly nucleophilic due to the adjacent ring nitrogens and chloride. The starting material Nc1cc(Cl)nc(S)n1 itself (2-mercapto-4-amino-6-chloropyrimidine) availability should also be verified.

This is a Hantzsch thiazole synthesis disconnecting the thiazole ring into an alpha-bromoketone (2,4-dichlorophenacyl bromide) and a thiourea fragment. The disconnection is well-precedented and chemically sound for forming the 2-aminothiazole. However, the thiourea precursor 'CCCCCCC(Sc1nc(Cl)cc(NC(N)=S)n1)C(=O)O' contains both a free carboxylic acid and a thioether linkage on the pyrimidine. The major selectivity concern is that the thiourea sulfur is the intended nucleophile for thiazole formation, but the molecule also contains a reactive thioether (the alpha-thio carboxylic acid attached to the pyrimidine). The Hantzsch reaction conditions (heating with alpha-haloketone) should preferentially engage the thiourea, so chemoselectivity is likely manageable, but the free carboxylic acid may need attention. Overall a reasonable forward step.

This step proposes SNAr displacement of a chloropyrimidine by the thiol of an alpha-bromo carboxylic acid (2-bromooctanoic acid). The problem: the building block 'NC(=S)Nc1cc(Cl)nc(S)n1' has a free thiol (or thione/thiol tautomer) on the pyrimidine and TWO chlorine-bearing positions are NOT present — actually the pyrimidine has one Cl and one SH. The intended reaction forms a thioether between the pyrimidine-SH and the alkyl bromide. However, there is a major chemoselectivity issue: the thiourea group (NC(=S)N) also bears a nucleophilic sulfur that could compete in S-alkylation with the alkyl bromide. Additionally, the carboxylic acid of 2-bromooctanoic acid could undergo intramolecular issues. The disconnection (S-alkylation of pyrimidinethiol with secondary alkyl bromide) is reasonable but secondary alkyl bromides give sluggish SN2 and possible elimination. Selectivity between the thiourea-S and pyrimidine-S is a real concern.

Benzoyl isothiocyanate is a standard reagent (commercially available or prepared in situ from KSCN and benzoyl chloride). The aminopyrimidine has a free thiol which could in principle react with the isothiocyanate, but the aromatic amine is the more typical/intended nucleophile. The exocyclic amine is the most nucleophilic site, so the reaction should proceed selectively. Good step.

This is a Suzuki-Miyaura coupling between 2-carbamoylphenylboronic acid and an aryl bromide. The disconnection at the biaryl bond is strategically sound and the boronic acid partner is commercially available. However, there are two notable concerns: (1) The aryl bromide partner contains a benzylic ether (ArCH2-O-thiophene) which is generally stable under Suzuki conditions, but the primary carboxamide can engage in undesired interactions/coordination with Pd, and free carboxylic acids can lower yields. (2) Chemoselectivity is the main issue - the molecule has both an aryl-Br and could potentially have competing reactivity; however with only one C-Br present, the coupling should be reasonably selective. The free -COOH and -CONH2 are tolerated in modern Suzuki protocols (Pd(PPh3)4 or SPhos/Pd, aqueous base). Overall feasible but yields may be moderate without protection of the polar groups.

This step is a reduction/deoxygenation of a beta-keto acid (O=C(O)CC(=O)Ar) to the corresponding propanoic acid (O=C(O)CCAr). This represents a ketone-to-methylene reduction. This is feasible via Wolff-Kishner or Clemmensen, but those harsh conditions could affect the benzylic aryl ether and the C-Br. A milder approach (e.g., Et3SiH/TFA, or catalytic hydrogenation with care toward the C-Br) would be preferred. The benzyl thienyl ether and aryl bromide pose chemoselectivity risks under hydrogenation (potential hydrogenolysis/dehalogenation). A non-hydrogenolytic deoxygenation (e.g., ionic reduction) is advisable. Disconnection logic is sound for building the propanoic acid chain.

Saponification of the ethyl ester to give the free carboxylic acid (beta-keto acid). This is a standard ester hydrolysis (LiOH or NaOH). One caveat: beta-keto acids are prone to decarboxylation, so the free acid may not be stable and could spontaneously lose CO2 to give the methyl ketone. Mild basic hydrolysis followed by careful acidification at low temperature is needed. The transformation itself is feasible and the disconnection is reasonable.

Claisen-type condensation: the methyl ketone (CC(=O)Ar) is acylated with diethyl carbonate (CCOC(=O)OCC) under basic conditions (NaH or NaOEt) to form the beta-keto ester. This is a well-precedented transformation for making aryl beta-keto esters from aryl methyl ketones. Both starting materials are listed in-stock. The base could potentially affect the benzylic ether, but enolate acylation with diethyl carbonate is standard and reliable. Good disconnection.

This is a Suzuki-Miyaura coupling between 2-carbamoylphenylboronic acid and an aryl bromide to form the biaryl bond. The disconnection is strategically sound and the biaryl linkage is a classic Suzuki target. However, there are two key concerns: (1) The primary amide (carboxamide) on the boronic acid component is generally compatible with Suzuki conditions, though ortho-substituted boronic acids with ortho carboxamides can suffer from protodeboronation and slower transmetalation. (2) More importantly, the free carboxylic acid on the thiophene-propanoic acid fragment is tolerated but may require careful base selection. Overall feasible but optimization needed; consider using the boronic ester (pinacol) or controlled conditions (Pd(PPh3)4 or SPhos/XPhos Pd, K2CO3 or K3PO4). The ortho-carbamoyl group can also act as a directing/chelating group affecting yield.

This step represents the reduction of a beta-keto carboxylic acid to the corresponding methylene (CH2), converting O=C(O)CC(=O)-thiophene to O=C(O)CCH2-thiophene. This is essentially a deoxygenation of an aryl ketone (Wolff-Kishner or Clemmensen-type, or more practically a two-step reduction). Such ketone-to-methylene reduction adjacent to a carboxylic acid is achievable, though direct conditions must be chosen carefully. The aryl bromide must survive; Wolff-Kishner (hydrazine/base) and Clemmensen (Zn-Hg/HCl) generally tolerate aryl bromides. A milder alternative would be reduction to alcohol then deoxygenation, or catalytic hydrogenation (which risks dehalogenation). Feasible but reagent choice is critical to preserve the C-Br bond.

Saponification/hydrolysis of the ethyl ester to the free carboxylic acid in a beta-ketoester. This is a standard, high-yielding transformation. For beta-ketoesters, mild hydrolysis (LiOH/aqueous) works well, though decarboxylation of the resulting beta-keto acid can be a competing concern under acidic or thermal conditions. The aryl bromide and thioether ether linkage are stable. Straightforward step.

Claisen-type condensation between the methyl ketone (acetyl thiophene) and diethyl carbonate to install the beta-ketoester. This is a classic transformation (NaH or NaOEt base, diethyl carbonate) to generate beta-ketoesters from methyl ketones. The aryl bromide and benzyl thioether ether are compatible. Note that strongly basic conditions could risk deprotonation/elimination but the benzylic ether should be stable. Both starting materials are reasonable; CC(=O)c1ccc(OCc2cccc(Br)c2)s1 is listed as in stock. Good, well-precedented step.

This is a Suzuki-Miyaura cross-coupling between an aryl bromide and a 2-(aminocarbonyl)phenylboronic acid to form the biaryl bond. The disconnection is strategically sound and well-precedented. The primary amide and the free carboxylic acid are both tolerated under standard Pd-catalyzed Suzuki conditions (e.g., Pd(PPh3)4 or Pd(dppf)Cl2 with K2CO3/Na2CO3 base). The benzylic aryl ether (the COc2 thiophene linkage) is stable. One consideration: ortho-substituted boronic acids bearing an amide can be prone to protodeboronation; using the pinacol boronate or careful base/temperature control may improve yields. Overall a robust, convergent final step.

This step corresponds to reduction of a beta-keto acid (O=C(O)CC(=O)Ar) to the saturated acid (O=C(O)CCAr), i.e., removal of the carbonyl. Practically this is a deoxygenation of an aryl ketone to a methylene, which is commonly achieved via Wolff-Kishner (hydrazine/KOH) or Clemmensen, or via thioketal formation/Raney Ni desulfurization. Note the free carboxylic acid and benzyl aryl ether must tolerate the conditions; the benzylic C-Br could be problematic under Clemmensen (Zn/HCl) or Raney Ni (potential dehalogenation). Wolff-Kishner is harsh but generally compatible. A more reliable route may be to reduce the ketone to alcohol then deoxygenate, or to perform the deoxygenation before installing sensitive groups. The disconnection itself is reasonable but reagent selection requires care to preserve the aryl bromide.

Saponification/hydrolysis of the ethyl ester to the free carboxylic acid. This is a standard, high-yielding transformation (LiOH or NaOH in aqueous THF/MeOH). The beta-keto ester is compatible, though under strongly basic conditions a beta-keto acid can undergo decarboxylation upon acidic workup/heating. Mild conditions and controlled temperature recommended. Straightforward step.

Claisen-type condensation of an aryl methyl ketone (acetylthiophene derivative) with diethyl carbonate to install the beta-keto ester. This is a well-established transformation using a strong base (NaH or NaOEt). The disconnection is appropriate and the starting acetylthiophene with the benzyl bromide ether is reasonable. Caution: NaH/strong base in presence of a benzylic bromide could lead to side reactions (alkylation or elimination); the enolate could displace the benzylic bromide intermolecularly. Use of a controlled stoichiometry and lower temperatures advised. Note that the building block 'CC(=O)c1ccc(OCc2cccc(Br)c2)s1' may not be truly commercially available and would itself require synthesis (O-alkylation of a hydroxyacetylthiophene with 3-bromobenzyl bromide), so 'in_stock: True' is questionable.

This is a Suzuki-Miyaura cross-coupling between an aryl boronic acid (2-carbamoylphenylboronic acid) and an aryl bromide. The disconnection of the biaryl bond is strategically sound and is a robust, well-precedented transformation. The primary amide and carboxylic acid are generally tolerated under Suzuki conditions, though the free carboxylic acid may require a slight excess of base. Standard Pd catalysis (e.g., Pd(PPh3)4 or Pd(dppf)Cl2 with K2CO3/Na2CO3) should work well. The boronic acid is commercially available. Minor concern: potential for protodeboronation of the ortho-substituted boronic acid, but this is manageable.

This step proposes reduction of a beta-keto acid (3-aryl-3-oxopropanoic acid) to the corresponding 3-arylpropanoic acid, i.e., complete deoxygenation of the aryl ketone to a methylene. This is a Wolff-Kishner or Clemmensen-type reduction. The chemoselectivity is a concern: the aryl bromide is susceptible to reduction/hydrogenolysis under many conditions, and the benzylic ether (OCH2Ar) linkage could also be cleaved under strongly reducing or acidic conditions. Wolff-Kishner (strongly basic, hydrazine/KOH, high temp) or Clemmensen (Zn/HCl) conditions risk degrading the benzyl thienyl ether and the C-Br bond. Also, beta-keto acids are prone to decarboxylation. A milder route (e.g., reduction to alcohol then deoxygenation, or thioketal formation/Raney Ni desulfurization — but Raney Ni would cleave C-Br) is problematic given the substrate. This transformation, while conceptually a single disconnection, is not clean for this substrate.

Ester hydrolysis of the ethyl ester to the carboxylic acid (beta-keto ester to beta-keto acid). This is straightforward, though beta-keto acids are prone to decarboxylation. Mild basic hydrolysis (LiOH) followed by acidification, or selective saponification, should work. Care must be taken to avoid decarboxylation of the resulting beta-keto acid during workup. Acid-mediated hydrolysis could risk the benzyl ether. The aryl bromide is stable. Overall feasible but the intermediate beta-keto acid is somewhat unstable.

This is a Claisen-type condensation/acylation of an aryl methyl ketone with diethyl carbonate to form the beta-keto ester. This is a well-established transformation (e.g., NaH or NaOEt as base with diethyl carbonate). The acetylthiophene substrate with the benzyl ether and aryl bromide should tolerate these conditions, though strong base could potentially cause issues with the aryl bromide via benzyne formation (unlikely at the meta-Br position without ortho-activation). The methyl ketone alpha-protons are acidic and well-suited for this acylation. Both starting materials are reasonable; the acetylthiophene building block is listed as in stock. Good, standard step.

This step proposes an intramolecular Suzuki-type/Pd-mediated biaryl coupling between an aryl boronic acid and the imidazole C-Br to form the dibenzazepine-fused biaryl ring system. While intramolecular C-C bond formation to close the central ring is conceptually reasonable, the regiochemistry is problematic: the boronic acid is on the benzene ring ortho to the CH(imidazolyl) center, and the bromide is on the imidazole. An intramolecular Suzuki coupling forming the biaryl C-C bond between the arene and imidazole carbons would create the fused tetracyclic system. The concept is plausible but the precise connectivity (forming a 5-membered or strained ring depending on geometry) needs scrutiny. The free secondary alcohol and free boronic acid would tolerate Pd conditions. The bigger concern is whether the boronic acid survives the upstream Grignard chemistry (see below). The disconnection itself for ring closure is reasonable but the boronic acid handling makes it questionable.

THP protection of a primary alcohol using dihydropyran (DHP) under acid catalysis is standard chemistry. However, the substrate contains a free primary alcohol AND a primary alkyl bromide on a similar position - the starting material 'CO/N=C(\CCC(CCO)CCBr)...' already differentiates these as drawn, so selective THP protection of the alcohol over the bromide is fine since bromide doesn't react with DHP. The main concern is acid sensitivity of the O-methyl oxime under DHP/acid conditions. Generally feasible with mild acid (PPTS).

This step forms the piperidine ring via double N-alkylation: the secondary amine displaces the mesylate (intramolecular) and presumably also closes the ring. However, as written, the precursor contains a secondary amine (NHCH2Cy) and a mesylate but the carbon framework does not clearly support a 6-membered ring closure to form the 4-substituted piperidine. The connectivity (CCC(CCNCC...)CCOMs) implies the nitrogen and mesylate are positioned to cyclize into a piperidine. This is a known strategy (double alkylation/cyclization to form piperidines), but it requires a single nitrogen attacking two electrophilic carbons. Here only one leaving group (mesylate) is present plus the existing C-N bond, so ring closure is plausible via intramolecular N-alkylation. The regiochemistry must give the 4-substituted piperidine. Feasible but somewhat non-obvious; competing intermolecular oligomerization and the free aniline NH2 acting as competing nucleophile are concerns. The aryl-NH2 could also be alkylated, requiring protection.

This disconnection installs the benzylamine onto an alkyl bromide (SN2) while leaving the mesylate intact for the subsequent cyclization (8c5ea146d998b718ad21ff505929cccc1f2ba099797f1dad4e2856aa02f560c9). Achieving chemoselective amination of the primary alkyl bromide over the primary alkyl mesylate is extremely difficult since both are good leaving groups toward amine nucleophiles; the amine would not discriminate well, leading to mixtures and premature cyclization. Additionally, the free aryl-NH2 (aniline) is a competing nucleophile. This two-electrophile strategy with poor differentiation is a major weakness. A cleaner approach would be to assemble the full piperidine ring (e.g., via reductive amination or a preformed piperidinone) rather than relying on selective mono-displacement of one of two near-equivalent leaving groups.

Standard mesylation of a primary alcohol with methanesulfonyl chloride. The alkyl bromide, oxime ether, aniline, and aryl chloride are all compatible under typical mesylation conditions (MsCl, Et3N, 0 °C). The free aniline NH2 could potentially be sulfonylated, so use of a slight excess of base and controlled stoichiometry/low temperature is advisable; mild conditions generally favor O-mesylation of the more nucleophilic alcohol, though aniline competition is a minor risk.

THP deprotection to reveal the primary alcohol. Standard acid-catalyzed removal (e.g., PPTS or mild acid, MeOH). The O-methyl oxime ether is reasonably stable to mild acidic conditions, though strongly acidic conditions could hydrolyze the oxime ether or epimerize/cleave; mild conditions (PPTS) recommended. Aryl bromide and other groups compatible.

Methanesulfonyl chloride is a cheap, commercially available bulk reagent. Synthesizing it from methanesulfonic acid and oxalyl chloride is unnecessary in a retrosynthetic plan; MsCl should simply be treated as a stock reagent.

This step proposes formation of the piperidine ring via double N-alkylation (intramolecular cyclization) of a primary/secondary amine onto a mesylate and an implied second leaving group. The retrosynthesis shows the product piperidine being formed from an acyclic amino-mesylate, but the precursor as drawn (CCNCC...CCOMs) only contains ONE leaving group (the mesylate) plus a secondary amine. To close a 6-membered piperidine ring you need two C-N bonds, requiring two leaving groups on the carbon chain. The drawn intermediate has the secondary amine already attached to one carbon arm and only one mesylate on the other arm — this geometry would give the correct ring closure (intramolecular N-alkylation) to form the piperidine. While the cyclization is plausible, intramolecular N-alkylation to form piperidines competes with intermolecular oligomerization and elimination; high dilution and base (K2CO3/Cs2CO3) would be needed. Stereochemistry/regiochemistry of the substituted piperidine should be considered. Moderate feasibility.

This step couples cyclohexylmethylamine (NCC1CCCCC1) with a substrate bearing BOTH a primary alkyl bromide AND a primary mesylate. A primary amine reacting with a molecule containing two distinct alkylating groups will show poor chemoselectivity — the amine could displace either the bromide or the mesylate, and over-alkylation (tertiary amine formation) is highly likely with a primary amine. The intended outcome (selective substitution of the bromide leaving the mesylate intact for subsequent cyclization) is questionable since both are competent leaving groups. Additionally, the free aniline (NH2) on the aromatic ring is a competing nucleophile. This step has serious chemoselectivity problems. A better strategy would protect/differentiate leaving groups or use a protected amine with controlled mono-alkylation.

Mesylation of a primary alcohol with MsCl is a standard, robust transformation. However, the substrate also contains a free aniline (NH2) which is nucleophilic and would compete for the sulfonyl chloride, forming a sulfonamide. Without protection of the aniline, chemoselective O-mesylation over N-sulfonylation is not guaranteed. Using a slight excess of MsCl with Et3N at low temperature may favor the alcohol but aniline sulfonamide formation is a real concern. Consider protecting the aniline or performing mesylation before aniline unmasking.

Preparation of methanesulfonyl chloride from methanesulfonic acid and oxalyl chloride is a well-established transformation. However, this step is unnecessary to include in a retrosynthesis since MsCl is a cheap, commercially available reagent. It does not detract chemically but adds no synthetic value.

Removal of a THP protecting group from the primary alcohol under mild acid conditions (e.g., PPTS/MeOH or dilute acid) is standard and reliable. Chemoselectivity is generally good. The alkyl bromide and oxime ether should be stable under mild acidic THP-removal conditions, though strongly acidic conditions could affect the O-methyl oxime — use mild conditions (PPTS).

This step proposes conversion of an aryl bromide to a dimethylamino group using dimethylamine. While Buchwald-Hartwig amination of aryl bromides with HNMe2 is feasible, the aryl bromide here is on the styryl ring of a vinylogous Michael-acceptor rhodanine. Pd-catalyzed amination conditions (strong base, elevated temperature) are likely incompatible with the base-sensitive rhodanine NH, the exocyclic alkene, and the imine. Moreover, retrosynthetically the p-(dimethylamino)benzaldehyde is far more sensibly introduced directly in the Knoevenagel condensation rather than via late-stage C–N coupling on a fragile scaffold. The disconnection direction is non-optimal.

This step proposes preparing dimethylamine (HNMe2) by reduction of N-methylformamide. Dimethylamine is an extremely cheap, commercially available bulk chemical (available as gas, aqueous solution, or salts). Preparing it from N-methylformamide is wholly unnecessary and also chemically odd as written. This node should simply be a commercial building block.

This step proposes para-bromination of an unsubstituted phenyl ring (styryl group) using NBS. Aromatic bromination of a simple benzene ring with NBS does not occur readily without a radical initiator/strong activation, and even then would not be regioselective for the para position. More critically, NBS in the presence of an electron-rich enol/enamine and an activated exocyclic alkene would preferentially brominate the alkene or the activated heterocycle rather than the unactivated aryl ring. This disconnection is unselective and unlikely to give the desired aryl bromide. The bromo-substituent should instead derive from 4-bromobenzaldehyde used in the Knoevenagel condensation.

This step proposes deprotection of a benzyl ether to reveal the free phenol, but the disconnection direction is wrong/non-productive. The SMILES shows the product as the free phenol and reactant as the benzyl ether, which is a debenzylation (correct direction for forward synthesis). However, standard benzyl deprotection uses hydrogenolysis (H2/Pd-C), which would be catastrophic for this substrate: it would reduce both the exocyclic C=C of the rhodanine arylidene and potentially the C=N imine, destroying the chromophore/pharmacophore. Lewis-acid or acidic deprotection (e.g., BCl3, TFA) could be used to avoid reduction, but these are harsh and may attack the thiohydantoin/rhodanine system. More fundamentally, the benzyl protection of this phenol is unnecessary (see af133b73429531ef163e26c846288b4a37171cf02acaf98271375715d1ec3de6 comments), so this entire deprotection step is superfluous.

This protecting group sequence (introduce Bn, then remove Bn) adds two steps with no clear benefit.

The imine/thiazolidinone is too remote to activate this position. Therefore SNAr would be very sluggish or fail. A Cu- or Pd-catalyzed C-O coupling (Ullmann/Buchwald-type) would be more appropriate, but the overall protecting-group rationale remains questionable. Additionally, benzyl alkoxide could deprotonate/attack the rhodanine NH and the activated Michael acceptor.

This step proposes installing the N,N-dimethylamino group onto an aryl bromide using dimethylamine (CNC). The disconnection (Buchwald-Hartwig amination of aryl bromide with HNMe2) is reasonable in principle.
