Mono-silylation (TBSCl) of a primary alcohol in the presence of a tertiary alcohol is well-precedented and generally chemoselective for the less-hindered primary position with TBSCl/imidazole. This is a reasonable protecting-group operation. The principal caveat is again the presence of acid/base-sensitive epoxides and the butenolide, but standard imidazole/DMF conditions are mild enough. The disconnection (1,2-diol with differentiation) is sensible and likely feasible.

This step represents removal of an N-mesyl protecting group on the indole nitrogen as the forward direction. Cleavage of N-sulfonyl indoles is well precedented under basic hydrolysis (NaOH/KOH) or with fluoride/reductive conditions. The free indole NH is the desired final product feature. The transformation is chemically sound and chemoselective with respect to the tertiary amine and the fused ring system.

In the forward sense this is a reductive dehalogenation (debromination) of an aryl bromide to give the unsubstituted arene. This can be accomplished by hydrogenolysis (Pd/C, H2) or via halogen-metal exchange/protonation. The N-mesyl group is compatible. However, one should note that introducing a bromide earlier only to remove it later (see 89daec0e2a7d63f1138a5d851767fe9e514b6d61e29049ca15928a8c96a6891b and 2d56735ec710da31798a856fa4a7334d23b47c31cb89fc17f117a8839126cf29) is strategically wasteful — the bromine appears to serve only as a regiochemical directing/blocking element, which adds steps. Otherwise the individual transformation is feasible.

This is an N-sulfonylation of the indole nitrogen with methanesulfonyl chloride (forward direction). The mesylation of an indole NH is feasible with MsCl/base (e.g., NaH or n-BuLi then MsCl). The concern is chemoselectivity: the molecule contains a secondary/tertiary aliphatic amine within the fused azepine ring. Wait—the nitrogen here is tertiary (part of the ring system), so over-reaction at amine is less of an issue, but deprotonation/sulfonylation must be selective for the indole NH versus other nucleophilic positions. Generally feasible but base and stoichiometry require care.

This depicts the synthesis of methanesulfonyl chloride from methanesulfonic acid and oxalyl chloride. Methanesulfonyl chloride is a cheap, ubiquitous commercial reagent and need not be synthesized. This step is unnecessary in a retrosynthesis as the reagent is a standard stock item.

In the forward direction this is an intramolecular cyclization: the secondary amine displaces the benzylic chloride (intramolecular N-alkylation) to close the azepine ring and form the tertiary amine, concomitant with loss of HCl. Benzylic chloride substitution by an amine to form the C–N bond is well precedented and would form the polycyclic core. Ring-size and conformational feasibility appear reasonable. Possible competing elimination of the benzylic chloride could lower yield, but the disconnection is sound.

local_feedback: Problems with reaction type and functional group compatibility
local_feedback_text: This step proposes removal of a trifluoroacetamide (TFA) protecting group to reveal the secondary amine, while a benzylic chloride and an unprotected indole NH remain present. Trifluoroacetamide cleavage typically requires basic hydrolysis (K2CO3/MeOH, NaOH) or reduction; under such basic/nucleophilic conditions the reactive benzylic chloride would likely undergo solvolysis or intramolecular cyclization prematurely. Thus exposing a free amine in the presence of an intact benzylic chloride is problematic — the deprotection and the subsequent cyclization (0c0133d4363ed3173585481fe732bb7e22309cc99da30ceadc713bbdcb9f2ee4) may not be cleanly separable, and the benzylic chloride is unlikely to survive deprotection conditions. Order of operations needs reconsideration.

This is an aromatic bromination using NBS on an electron-rich indole-containing arene. The C3 position of indole is the most nucleophilic site; here C3 is substituted, but NBS bromination of indoles is notoriously prone to attacking the pyrrole ring (C2/C3) rather than the desired benzenoid position. Achieving regioselective bromination at the specified aromatic carbon (para to the fused position) over indole C2 bromination is challenging. Additionally, the benzylic C–H/benzylic chloride could be susceptible to radical bromination under NBS/radical conditions. Significant regio- and chemoselectivity concerns.

This step represents removal of a methanesulfonyl (Ms) protecting group from the indole nitrogen. Mesyl groups on indole nitrogen are readily cleaved under basic conditions (NaOH/MeOH, K2CO3, or TBAF). This is a chemically sound deprotection as the final step. However, the question arises whether the N-Ms group was strategically necessary in the forward direction. As a final deprotection step it is feasible and clean.

This step proposes reductive removal of an aryl bromide (debromination of an aryl-Br to aryl-H). While dehalogenation (e.g., via hydrogenolysis, Bu3SnH, or Pd-catalyzed reduction) is feasible, introducing a bromide only to remove it later (in the forward sense the Br is installed then removed) suggests it served as a blocking/directing group. The disconnection is chemically reasonable but the overall logic of installing and removing Br must be justified. Chemoselectivity in removing the aryl-Br without affecting the N-Ms group or the saturated framework is generally achievable. Moderate confidence due to the synthetic logic of an apparently superfluous halogen.

This step is N-mesylation of the indole nitrogen using methanesulfonyl chloride. N-sulfonylation of indoles with MsCl in the presence of base (NaH, Et3N, or DMAP) is a well-established, high-yielding transformation. The free indole N-H is the most nucleophilic site and reacts selectively. Functional group compatibility with the aryl bromide and the tertiary amine is acceptable, though the tertiary amine could potentially compete; using mild base and controlling stoichiometry favors N-indole sulfonylation. Overall feasible.

Synthesis of methanesulfonyl chloride from methanesulfonic acid and oxalyl chloride is a standard, well-precedented activation. However, MsCl is itself a cheap commercial reagent, so this step is trivial/unnecessary as a synthetic disconnection. As written, the chemistry is correct and proceeds readily.

This step is an electrophilic aromatic bromination using NBS on a free (N-H) indole bearing a fused tetracyclic framework. The indole C-3 position is already substituted (part of the ring fusion), so bromination is directed to the indole benzene ring. NBS bromination of indoles typically occurs at C-3 first; with C-3 blocked, ring bromination at C-4/C-6/C-7 may compete and regioselectivity for the specific position shown (para to the alkyl, ortho to ring fusion) is uncertain. The presence of a benzylic chloride is a concern—NBS can promote radical side reactions or the benzylic C-Cl could be labile. Regiochemical control is the major issue here.

local_feedback: Problems with reaction type and functional group compatibility
local_feedback_text: This step proposes removal of a trifluoroacetyl (TFA) protecting group from the secondary amine to reveal the free amine, with concomitant retention of a benzylic chloride. The problem is severe: removing the TFA group typically requires basic hydrolysis (K2CO3/MeOH, NaOH) or reduction, conditions under which the benzylic chloride (alpha to the indole, highly activated) would not survive—intramolecular cyclization onto the liberated secondary amine is essentially inevitable (indeed that appears to be intended in step 0c0133d4363ed3173585481fe732bb7e22309cc99da30ceadc713bbdcb9f2ee4). Therefore having both a free amine and a benzylic chloride coexisting as a stable isolable intermediate (the product Cl-amine) is implausible; they would immediately cyclize. The disconnection logic is muddled.

This step constructs the central ring via intramolecular N-alkylation of a secondary amine onto a benzylic chloride (forming the C-N bond and closing the azacycle). This is a reasonable Friedel-Crafts-type or simple SN1/SN2 benzylic amination cyclization. The benzylic chloride is highly activated (benzylic and alpha to indole), making cyclization facile. However, this disconnection is intimately tied to 73423bce4c8be854131d5892d431469c3465c87aee99103013b4e1568041f643—the free amine and benzylic chloride cannot realistically be isolated together without spontaneous cyclization, so the separation into 0c0133d4363ed3173585481fe732bb7e22309cc99da30ceadc713bbdcb9f2ee4/73423bce4c8be854131d5892d431469c3465c87aee99103013b4e1568041f643 is artificial. As a ring-forming amination the chemistry itself is sound.

This step represents removal of a methanesulfonyl (mesyl) protecting group from the indole nitrogen. Reductive or basic cleavage of N-SO2Me from indoles is well-precedented (e.g., aqueous NaOH, K2CO3/MeOH, or TBAF). The transformation should proceed cleanly with the rest of the polycyclic framework intact. Note that mechanistically this is a deprotection rather than introduction; in the forward direction it is straightforward.

This step is the reductive removal (hydrodehalogenation) of an aryl bromide to give the unsubstituted arene. While catalytic hydrogenation/transfer hydrogenation or Pd-mediated dehalogenation can remove an aryl bromide, the strategic logic is questionable: a bromide was installed (presumably for regiochemical control earlier) and then removed here, adding two non-productive steps. Furthermore, chemoselective dehalogenation in the presence of the indole and tertiary amine should be feasible but requires care. The bigger issue is the overall necessity of carrying a Br that is later removed.

Mesylation of the indole N-H using methanesulfonyl chloride and base (e.g., NaH or Et3N/DMAP) is well established. The indole nitrogen is the most acidic/nucleophilic N-H site, and N-sulfonylation is selective. The aryl bromide and tertiary amine are compatible. Note: the tertiary amine could compete by forming a salt with MsCl, but using a base to deprotonate the indole N-H first mitigates this.

Synthesis of methanesulfonyl chloride from methanesulfonic acid and oxalyl chloride is a standard, well-precedented transformation. However, MsCl is inexpensive and commercially available, so this step is typically unnecessary in a synthetic route. Marked as feasible since the chemistry is sound.

This step proposes forming the fused polycyclic framework (closing the central ring with C-N bond formation and concomitant loss of the benzylic chloride and the secondary amine) from a benzylic chloride/secondary amine precursor. While intramolecular N-alkylation of a benzylic chloride by a secondary amine to form the C-N bond is plausible in principle, the way the product is drawn (a fully fused indole-containing pentacyclic with a benzylic C-H) requires both ring closure AND reductive dehalogenation of the benzylic chloride, which cannot occur in a single simple operation. The disconnection conflates two distinct transformations and is mechanistically inconsistent. Reconsider the order: intramolecular alkylation should give a quaternary or C-N closed product retaining functionality, not a reduced benzylic position.

local_feedback: Problems with reaction type and functional group compatibility
local_feedback_text: This step proposes removal of a trifluoroacetyl (TFA) amide protecting group to liberate the secondary amine while retaining a benzylic chloride. TFA amide cleavage typically requires basic hydrolysis (K2CO3/MeOH, NaOH) or reduction; under these conditions a reactive benzylic chloride adjacent to an indole would readily solvolyze, eliminate, or be displaced (especially intramolecularly by the liberated amine). Therefore retaining the benzylic chloride during deprotection of the amine is problematic—the freed amine would immediately cyclize onto the benzylic chloride. The chemoselectivity here is highly questionable.

Bromination with NBS on the indole-containing substrate is proposed to occur on the carbocyclic benzene ring of the indole (at the position para to nitrogen). However, NBS preferentially brominates the most electron-rich/nucleophilic position, which for indoles is C-3 (here already substituted) or C-2; aromatic ring bromination on the benzo ring is less favored. Achieving the desired regioselectivity for benzo-ring bromination over the indole C-2 or other activated positions would be challenging. Additionally, the benzylic chloride present could compete in radical processes. Regiocontrol is a significant concern.

This step represents removal of a methanesulfonyl (mesyl) protecting group from the indole nitrogen to reveal the free N-H indole. Cleavage of N-sulfonyl indoles is well-precedented (typically using base such as NaOH/KOH, TBAF, or Mg/MeOH). The transformation is chemically reasonable and chemoselective for the sulfonamide. Confidence is high that this final deprotection would succeed without affecting the tertiary amine or aromatic rings.

This step proposes a reductive removal of an aryl bromide (debromination) to convert the brominated arene into the parent arene. While dehalogenation (e.g., hydrogenolysis, Bu3SnH) is feasible chemistry, its presence here is highly questionable from a synthetic logic standpoint: a bromine was installed only to be removed later. If the bromine serves no functional purpose in the target, then both the bromination (89daec0e2a7d63f1138a5d851767fe9e514b6d61e29049ca15928a8c96a6891b reactant) and this debromination are unnecessary detours. More importantly, in the forward direction this is a wasteful protecting/blocking strategy. As an actual disconnection it is logically inconsistent and likely represents an artifact. The transformation itself (debromination) is feasible but the strategy is flawed.

This step combines two operations: N-mesylation of the indole N-H using methanesulfonyl chloride AND implies the parent has a bromine. The N-sulfonylation of indole with MsCl/base is feasible. However, the disconnection bundles N-protection with an aryl bromide present, and the chemoselectivity of mesylation (indole N-H vs. the secondary/tertiary amine) needs careful base control. In this polycyclic system with both a basic tertiary amine and an indole N-H, selective N-mesylation of the indole over O/N competing sites requires careful conditions. The presence of the aryl bromide compounds the concern about why bromine is carried through. Overall feasible but with selectivity caveats.

This step proposes forming the final tetracyclic C-ring (closing the tertiary amine ring and forming the C2-C3 indole bridge) by intramolecular reaction of a benzylic chloride with a secondary amine, with concomitant loss of HCl, generating the fused indole system. The product shown (fully aromatic indole fused polycycle) versus the chloro-amine precursor implies a Friedel-Crafts-type or N-alkylation/cyclization. The benzylic chloride alkylation of the secondary amine to form the azepine ring is plausible, but the simultaneous formation of the fully conjugated indole-fused ring and loss of the C-Cl as written is mechanistically muddled. The mapping suggests two bonds forming at once which is not a clean single disconnection. This step needs to be decomposed and clarified; as written it is dubious.

This step is the removal of the trifluoroacetyl (TFA) protecting group from the secondary amine to reveal the free amine. TFA amide cleavage (mild base hydrolysis, K2CO3/MeOH or NaOH) is well-established and chemoselective. The benzylic chloride present could be a liability under basic hydrolytic conditions (potential for elimination or substitution), representing a functional group compatibility concern, but the core deprotection is feasible.

This step is an aromatic bromination of the indole-containing arene using NBS (N-bromosuccinimide). NBS bromination of electron-rich (hetero)aromatics is feasible, but in an indole system NBS strongly prefers the C3 (or C2) position of the indole over the benzenoid ring. Here the desired bromination is on the carbocyclic ring (peri position), and the indole C3 is already substituted in the fused system, but achieving regioselective bromination on the specific benzene-ring carbon over other reactive positions (and over the benzylic C-H/C-Cl) is a significant concern. Also the benzylic chloride may react with NBS via radical pathways. Regioselectivity is the main issue.

This step shows the synthesis of methanesulfonyl chloride from methanesulfonic acid and oxalyl chloride. While this transformation is chemically valid (oxalyl chloride converts sulfonic acids to sulfonyl chlorides), MsCl is an inexpensive, ubiquitous commercially available reagent. This step is entirely unnecessary in a retrosynthetic analysis and should be treated as a stock building block.

Saponification of the methyl ester to the free acrylic acid using LiOH or NaOH is straightforward. The free phenol is compatible with mild basic hydrolysis. No issues with the alkene geometry under these conditions. This is a reasonable final deprotection step.

Suzuki-Miyaura cross-coupling between the aryl pinacol boronate and the 2-bromothiophene (vinylogous benzothiophene) is a well-precedented C-C bond formation. The disconnection at the biaryl bond is sound and convergent. Potential concern: the free phenol on the benzothiophene could be tolerated, but protection might improve yields; the acrylate ester is compatible. The bromide is at the activated 2-position of the thiophene/benzothiophene which couples well. Overall a good convergent disconnection.

Miyaura borylation of the aryl bromide with bis(pinacolato)diboron (B2pin2) using Pd catalysis and a base (KOAc) is standard and reliable. The benzylic C-F is compatible with these conditions. Good preparation of the boronate coupling partner.

This represents a Sandmeyer-type conversion of an aniline to an aryl bromide. While the transformation (ArNH2 -> ArBr) is feasible, the depicted reagent 'Br' (HBr/Br2) alone is insufficient. Proper conditions require diazotization (NaNO2/HBr or t-BuONO) followed by CuBr (Sandmeyer). The disconnection itself is reasonable but the reagent set is incomplete/non-optimal. Note also the benzylic C-F could potentially be sensitive under strongly acidic diazotization conditions.

Reduction of an aromatic nitro group to the corresponding aniline is a well-established transformation (H2/Pd, Fe/AcOH, SnCl2). Chemoselectivity is good; the benzylic C-F should survive mild reduction conditions, though hydrogenolysis of the benzylic C-F could be a minor concern with Pd/H2 - using Fe or SnCl2 would avoid this. Overall feasible.

Deoxyfluorination of a benzylic secondary alcohol with DAST (Et2NSF3) to install the benzylic C-F is well-precedented. The ortho-nitro group is electron-withdrawing and compatible with DAST. Some risk of elimination to styrene byproduct with benzylic substrates, but generally workable. Both starting materials are commercially available.

Demethylation of the aryl methyl ether to the free phenol using BBr3 or similar. The acrylate methyl ester and the vinyl bromide are potential complications: BBr3 can also cleave esters and may be harsh. Milder demethylation (e.g., LiCl, or thiolate) might be preferred to preserve the methyl acrylate. Functionally feasible but reagent choice matters; consider doing the demethylation at a later/earlier stage to avoid ester cleavage.

Bromination with NBS at the benzothiophene 2-position (alpha to S). The regioselectivity here is the concern: the electron-rich methoxy-substituted benzothiophene with an additional 3-aryloxy substituent could undergo competing ring bromination on the activated arene or on the styryl/acrylate system. NBS could also add to the electron-rich alkene (acrylate is electron-poor, so less likely there, but the aryloxy ring is electron rich). Directed electrophilic bromination to the desired 2-position is plausible given the 3-position is occupied, but selectivity needs verification.

This is a Heck reaction between methyl acrylate and the aryl bromide. However, the depicted starting material 'COc1ccc2c(Oc3ccc(Br)cc3)csc2c1' contains an aryl bromide on the pendant phenoxy ring, which is the correct site for the Heck coupling to give the E-cinnamate. This is feasible and gives good E-selectivity. One concern: the benzothiophene also has reactive C-H positions, but the aryl bromide is the dedicated coupling site. Generally feasible Heck with good E-selectivity. Note this building block is listed as in_stock which simplifies the route.

Final step is saponification (ester hydrolysis) of the methyl cinnamate to the free acrylic acid. This is straightforward using LiOH or NaOH in THF/water/MeOH. The free phenol is compatible. The benzylic C-F should survive mild basic hydrolysis. Good final deprotection step.

This is a Suzuki-Miyaura cross-coupling between the aryl pinacol boronate and the 2-bromobenzothiophene. The disconnection is reasonable to install the ortho-substituted biaryl. However, the free phenol on the benzothiophene is present (not protected) which is tolerated under Suzuki conditions. The main concern is steric hindrance: coupling at the 2-position of the benzothiophene (which is flanked by the 3-O-aryl ether) with an ortho-substituted (CHFCH3) aryl boronate is quite congested, potentially leading to low yields. Protodeboronation of the electron-rich/hindered boronate is also a risk. SPhos/RuPhos-type ligands recommended. Feasible but selectivity/yield concerns warrant attention.
Miyaura borylation of the aryl bromide with bis(pinacolato)diboron (B2pin2) using Pd catalyst and KOAc base. Well-established transformation. The benzylic C-F is compatible. Standard and reliable.

This represents a Sandmeyer-type conversion of the aniline to the aryl bromide, shown as 'Br + aniline'. The bare HBr is not the actual reagent; a proper Sandmeyer requires diazotization (NaNO2/HBr) then CuBr. The disconnection (ArNH2 -> ArBr) is valid and useful, but the reagent depiction is non-optimal. The benzylic C-F should survive. Recommend explicit diazotization/CuBr conditions.

Reduction of the aromatic nitro group to the aniline. Standard transformation (H2/Pd, Fe/AcOH, SnCl2, etc.). For substrate bearing a benzylic C-F, milder conditions like Fe/NH4Cl or SnCl2 are preferable to avoid hydrogenolysis of the C-F bond under H2/Pd. Overall feasible.

Deoxyfluorination of the benzylic secondary alcohol with DAST (Et2NSF3). This is a well-precedented transformation to convert benzylic alcohols to benzylic fluorides. Some risk of elimination (styrene formation) or carbocation rearrangement with benzylic substrates, but generally workable. Deoxofluor would be a safer alternative. Both starting materials commercially available.

local_feedback: Protecting group strategy is wrong / non-optimal
local_feedback_text: Demethylation of the aryl methyl ether to free phenol (e.g., BBr3). The issue is sequence/strategy: the methyl-protected phenol is carried then deprotected here, BUT this then leaves a free phenol that must survive the subsequent Suzuki coupling (df91de862d06067d834a1320ac43f907aa04a972ec807832bb7911423dae3eb1). More importantly, BBr3 demethylation conditions are harsh and could cleave the diaryl ether linkage and react with the acrylate ester. The benzylic C-F (in later steps) is not yet present here so that is fine. The protecting group choice (methyl) requiring harsh deprotection in the presence of a sensitive diaryl ether and Michael-acceptor ester is non-optimal; a more readily removable group (MOM, Bn) would be preferable.

Electrophilic bromination at the 3-position of the benzothiophene using NBS. The 3-position is activated and this is a common, regioselective bromination for benzothiophenes (2-position blocked here by O-aryl, so bromination at C2... note connectivity). The regiochemistry should be controlled by the existing substitution pattern. The acrylate alkene could be a competing site for radical/electrophilic addition, so conditions (NBS, polar solvent, no radical initiator) should be chosen carefully to favor aromatic substitution. Generally feasible.

Heck reaction between the aryl bromide and methyl acrylate to install the (E)-cinnamate. Pd-catalyzed Heck couplings give high E-selectivity. The aryl bromide on the pendant phenyl ether is the reactive site. Standard Pd(OAc)2/phosphine/base conditions. Good convergent coupling. Note the benzothiophene C-H positions are present; chemoselectivity for the ArBr over C-H is expected.

Saponification of the methyl ester to the free acrylic acid is a standard transformation (e.g., LiOH or NaOH in THF/MeOH/H2O). The free phenol and aryl thiophene ether are compatible. The E-geometry of the acrylate is preserved under mild basic hydrolysis. No major concerns.

This is a Suzuki-Miyaura coupling between an aryl pinacol boronate and a 2-bromothiophene bearing a free phenol and an enoate. The disconnection is reasonable to install the biaryl bond. However, two concerns: (1) the free phenol on the benzothiophene is left unprotected during the Pd coupling, which is generally tolerated but can slow the reaction and complicate purification; (2) the Michael acceptor (cinnamate) is present, and while Suzuki conditions usually leave acrylates intact, there is some risk of side reactions/competing Heck-type processes. The bromothiophene C-Br is a competent electrophile. Overall feasible but selectivity/yield may be moderate; protecting the phenol could help.

Miyaura borylation of an aryl bromide with bis(pinacolato)diboron (B2pin2) using Pd catalysis and a base (e.g., KOAc, Pd(dppf)Cl2) is a robust, well-precedented transformation. The benzylic C-F is stable under these conditions. Good disconnection.

This represents conversion of the aniline (CC(F)c1ccccc1N) to the aryl bromide, shown as reacting with 'Br'. Mechanistically this would be a Sandmeyer-type sequence (diazotization then CuBr/HBr), not simple reaction with bromine. The single 'Br' fragment is not a realistic reagent representation. The transformation itself (aniline -> aryl bromide via diazonium) is feasible, but the depicted reagent is non-optimal/incomplete; proper conditions are NaNO2/HBr then CuBr.

Reduction of the nitroarene to the aniline is a standard transformation (H2/Pd-C, Fe/AcOH, SnCl2). The benzylic C-F is generally stable under mild reduction conditions, though hydrogenolysis of benzylic C-F is a possible minor side reaction; non-hydrogenative methods (Fe/AcOH, SnCl2) are preferred to preserve the fluoride. Overall feasible.

Deoxofluorination of a benzylic secondary alcohol with DAST (Et2NSF3) to give the benzylic fluoride is well-precedented. The ortho-nitro group is compatible with DAST. Possible side reactions include elimination to styrene, but benzylic secondary alcohols typically convert well. Both starting materials are commercially available. Good step.

local_feedback: Protecting group strategy is wrong / non-optimal
local_feedback_text: This step is a demethylation of the aryl methyl ether to reveal the phenol (e.g., BBr3). In the context of the route, the methyl ether is installed/carried as a protecting group, but BBr3 demethylation conditions are harsh and could affect the methyl ester (converting/cleaving) and the aryl-aryl thioether ether linkage. Given a methyl ester is present elsewhere in the molecule, harsh Lewis-acid demethylation risks chemoselectivity problems. A more orthogonal phenol protecting group (e.g., MOM, benzyl, TBS) would be preferable. The strategy of carrying a methyl phenol ether through is non-optimal.

Electrophilic bromination of the benzothiophene at C-2 (or C-3, here the position alpha to S) using NBS is standard. The electron-rich heteroaromatic ring is activated and NBS gives clean monobromination at the most nucleophilic position. The methyl ester and cinnamate are tolerated. Regioselectivity for the desired position should be favorable given the substitution pattern.

This is a Heck reaction between an aryl bromide and methyl acrylate to install the E-cinnamate. The aryl bromide substrate (COc1ccc2c(Oc3ccc(Br)cc3)csc2c1) contains an electron-rich benzothiophene with a free C-H alpha to sulfur, plus an aryl ether. Heck on the para-bromophenyl ether is feasible and typically gives E-selectivity. However, chemoselectivity is a concern: the benzothiophene C-H position could undergo competing C-H functionalization/arylation under Pd conditions, and the heteroarene could coordinate Pd. Still, standard Heck conditions (Pd(OAc)2, phosphine, base) should favor the aryl-Br oxidative addition. The E-geometry is well-precedented. Minor risk noted.

Ester hydrolysis of the methyl cinnamate to the free acrylic acid is a standard transformation (LiOH/NaOH, THF/H2O). The free phenol is tolerated. The α,β-unsaturated ester hydrolyzes cleanly under mild basic conditions without affecting the aryl ether or thiophene. Good final deprotection step.

Suzuki-Miyaura coupling between the aryl bromide on the benzothiophene C2 position and the pinacol boronate of the ortho-fluoroethyl aryl group. This is a well-precedented disconnection. Concerns: the boronate bears a secondary benzylic C-F which is stable under Suzuki conditions; the free phenol on the benzothiophene is tolerated (may slightly slow coupling but usually fine). The electron-rich/hindered ortho-substituted boronate may require an optimized catalyst (SPhos/XPhos Pd) but is feasible. Note the methyl ester might benefit from retention until coupling—route does keep it, which is sensible.

Miyaura borylation of the aryl bromide with bis(pinacolato)diboron (B2pin2), Pd catalyst and base (KOAc) is standard. The benzylic C-F is stable. Good disconnection to access the boronate coupling partner.

This step proposes converting an aryl amine (CC(F)c1ccccc1N) into an aryl bromide via reaction with 'Br' (HBr). A direct amine-to-bromide substitution on an aromatic ring is not a single step. In practice this requires diazotization (NaNO2/HBr) followed by a Sandmeyer-type reaction (CuBr). The disconnection as written (ArNH2 + HBr -> ArBr) is mechanistically incomplete/incorrect. Should be represented as a Sandmeyer reaction with explicit diazonium intermediate and CuBr.

Reduction of an aromatic nitro group to the corresponding aniline is a standard transformation (H2/Pd-C, Fe/AcOH, SnCl2, or Zn). The benzylic C-F is stable under most reduction conditions (use Fe/AcOH or SnCl2 to avoid potential hydrogenolysis of the benzylic C-F under H2/Pd-C). Feasible with appropriate reagent choice.

Deoxofluorination of a benzylic secondary alcohol to the corresponding fluoride using DAST (Et2NSF3) is well-established. Both starting materials are commercially available. Potential side reactions include elimination to styrene and SN1-type rearrangements given the benzylic activation, which may limit yield, but the transformation is sound. Deoxo-Fluor would be a milder alternative.

Demethylation of the aryl methyl ether to the free phenol (BBr3, or other Lewis acids). Caution: BBr3 could potentially cleave the diaryl ether linkage and the methyl ester is also at risk. Milder selective conditions (e.g., NaSEt, LiCl/DMF, or BCl3) may be needed to differentiate the methyl aryl ether from the diaryl ether and to preserve the methyl ester. Chemoselectivity is the main concern here.

Bromination of the benzothiophene C3 position with NBS. The regiochemistry needs to be controlled—NBS bromination of a benzothiophene bearing an aryloxy substituent at the open ring position should occur at the remaining electron-rich heteroaromatic position, but selectivity vs allylic/benzylic bromination of the cinnamate or ring bromination of the electron-rich anisole ring is a concern. NBS could also brominate the activated arene. Radical conditions could attack the cinnamate vinyl. Careful condition control required.

Heck reaction between an aryl bromide and methyl acrylate to install the (E)-cinnamate is a classic, high-yielding transformation (Pd(OAc)2, phosphine, base). Excellent E-selectivity is typical. The aryl ether/benzothiophene are compatible. Good disconnection. Note the listed starting material COc1ccc2c(Oc3ccc(Br)cc3)csc2c1 is marked in stock—plausibility of commercial availability of this complex benzothiophene should be verified.

This step proposes global deprotection of two isopropyl phosphonate/phosphate esters to reveal the free phosphonic acid-phosphate (pyrophosphate-type) linkage. The disconnection (deprotection of isopropyl esters on P) is chemically reasonable; isopropyl esters of phosphonates can be cleaved with TMSBr/TMSI followed by aqueous workup. However, the regioselectivity of cleaving exactly two of three esters while leaving the overall diphosphate intact is questionable, and the chlorouracil ring and the diphosphate are sensitive to the strong silylating/acidic conditions. The mismatch in the number of isopropyl groups between product (free acid) and reactant (still bearing some P-OiPr) suggests an inconsistent intermediate. TMSBr deprotection is the standard approach but selectivity here is dubious.

This step interconverts a methyl phosphonate ester (COP...) into the free phosphonic acid (OP(=O)(O)...) selectively, while leaving two isopropyl esters intact on the adjacent phosphate. Selective mono-demethylation in the presence of two isopropyl esters is difficult to control; standard TMSBr/TMSI deprotection conditions tend to cleave all alkyl phosphate/phosphonate esters non-selectively (methyl esters are typically MORE labile, so selective methyl cleavage is plausible with thiolate nucleophiles, but full chemoselectivity over the chlorovinyl uracil is uncertain). This selective single-ester unmasking is the main weak point of the route.

N-alkylation of 5-chlorouracil with the allylic bromide. The disconnection is sound (N1-alkylation of uracil via allylic halide). However, uracils possess two nitrogen atoms (N1 and N3) and the regioselectivity between N1 vs N3 alkylation is a well-known issue. Typically N1 selectivity is achievable under basic conditions (e.g., K2CO3/DMF) but O-alkylation and N3-alkylation are competing pathways. Additionally, the allylic bromide bearing a labile phosphonate-phosphate diester linkage may suffer from elimination or phosphate participation. Some optimization (e.g., silylation of uracil, Vorbruggen-type conditions, or protection) would improve N1-selectivity.

This step proposes forming a P-O-P (pyrophosphate-type) linkage by reacting a phosphorochloridate with isopropanol. However, the SMILES shows isopropanol simply displacing chloride to give a P-OiPr ester, NOT forming the anhydride bridge present in both species. Mechanistically, treating a phosphorochloridate with isopropanol gives the isopropyl phosphate ester (P-Cl + iPrOH -> P-OiPr), which is reasonable as an esterification. But the retro-disconnection here is confusing because the P-O-P bridge is preserved in both. If the intent is simple chloride-to-isopropoxide substitution, it is feasible with iPrOH/base; the allylic bromide elsewhere in the molecule is a chemoselectivity liability under basic alcoholysis conditions. Reagent (neat iPrOH) would need base activation.

Appel-type bromination of an allylic primary alcohol using CBr4 (here shown with CBr4; typically requires PPh3 as co-reagent which is missing from the SMILES). Conversion of allylic primary alcohol to allylic bromide via Appel conditions (CBr4/PPh3) is well-established and proceeds with high yield and retention of alkene geometry. The phosphorochloridate functionality is a concern — P-Cl is moisture sensitive and PPh3/CBr4 conditions are mild and anhydrous, so should be tolerated, though the highly electrophilic P-Cl could react with PPh3 or liberated species. Note PPh3 should be explicitly included as co-reagent.

This step represents the global deprotection of a phosphonate-phosphate diester to reveal the free pyrophosphonate (bisphosphonate-type) acid. The disconnection (removing two isopropyl groups) is chemically reasonable - isopropyl phosphate esters are typically cleaved with TMSBr (McKenna reaction) followed by hydrolysis. However, the product shown loses ALL three remaining protecting groups in a single retro-step, while the precursor still bears two iPr groups AND one free OH on the proximal phosphorus. The stereochemistry of the trans double bond and the chlorouracil are likely stable to TMSBr conditions. A more careful sequence of deprotections is preferred, and the reagent choice (implied) should be explicitly TMSBr/2,6-lutidine then water. Acceptable disconnection but reagent/conditions need specification.

This step proposes selective mono-demethylation of a methyl phosphonate ester (COP -> HOP) while leaving the two isopropyl esters intact. Selective cleavage of a single methyl ester in the presence of isopropyl esters is challenging but feasible (methyl esters are more labile to nucleophiles like LiBr/thiolates or TMSBr under controlled conditions). The chemoselectivity (methyl vs isopropyl) is the main concern, and over-deprotection to the free acids is a real competing pathway. The use of differentiated alkyl groups (Me vs iPr) is a deliberate strategy to enable selective deprotection, which is sound in principle but practically delicate.

This is an N-alkylation of 5-chlorouracil with an allylic bromide bearing a phosphonate-phosphate tail. The disconnection is reasonable (N1-alkylation of uracil with an allylic halide). However, 5-chlorouracil has two NH positions (N1 and N3), and regioselective N1-alkylation is required - N1 is the more nucleophilic/kinetically favored site, so selectivity is generally achievable but not guaranteed without protection or careful base/conditions (e.g., using a silylated uracil/Vorbruggen-type or controlled K2CO3/DMF). O-alkylation is also a competing pathway with allylic halides. The allylic bromide could also undergo SN2'/allylic rearrangement, potentially scrambling the trans-alkene geometry. Overall feasible but selectivity must be addressed.

This step proposes formation of a P-O-P (pyrophosphate-type) linkage by reaction of isopropanol with a P-chloridate, while simultaneously the precursor already contains the P-O-P linkage. As written, the retro-disconnection has isopropanol + a phosphono-chloridate giving the diisopropyl pyrophosphonate. Esterification of a P-Cl with iPrOH to give a P-OiPr is feasible chemically (standard phosphorochloridate alcoholysis, typically needs a base such as pyridine/Et3N). However, performing this on a molecule that ALREADY bears a reactive allylic bromide is problematic - the alkyl bromide and the chlorophosphate are both electrophilic and the alcohol/base could lead to side reactions. The bigger issue is the order: installing the labile allylic bromide before completing the phosphate esterification invites elimination/substitution. The disconnection itself (P-Cl + ROH) is valid but the molecular context makes it poorly conceived.

This is an Appel-type bromination of an allylic alcohol (C/C=C/CO -> C/C=C/CBr) using CBr4. The Appel reaction normally requires CBr4 together with PPh3; CBr4 alone is not sufficient. More critically, performing an Appel reaction on a substrate bearing a P-Cl (phosphorochloridate) is highly problematic - the PPh3 and the alcohol would react with the chlorophosphate, and the free OH of an allylic system adjacent to a phosphonate may not survive. Allylic alcohols can also undergo SN2' rearrangement under Appel conditions, threatening the E-alkene geometry. PPh3 must be added; alternative milder allylic brominations (MsCl then LiBr, or PBr3) might be considered. Functional group incompatibility with the chlorophosphate is a real concern.

This step proposes global deprotection of the isopropyl phosphonate/phosphate esters to reveal the free phosphonate-phosphate (pyrophosphate analogue). Deprotection of isopropyl phosphate esters typically requires TMSBr (McKenna conditions) or strong acid. The transformation is feasible in principle, but note that the product shown has THREE free P-OH groups whereas the precursor only bears TWO isopropyl groups plus one free P-OH; the mass balance/oxygen count must be carefully checked. The chemodifferentiation between cleaving both isopropyl esters while leaving the acid-sensitive allylic system and chlorouracil intact is plausible with TMSBr. Overall feasible but specify proper deprotection reagent.

This step represents selective demethylation of a methyl phosphonate ester (P-OMe to P-OH) while leaving the two isopropyl esters intact. Selective mono-demethylation in the presence of isopropyl esters is challenging - TMSBr or thiolate (e.g., LiBr, thiourea, or NaI in acetone) can cleave methyl esters preferentially due to steric accessibility, but achieving clean chemoselectivity between methyl and isopropyl P-esters is non-trivial and may give mixtures. The strategy of having differentiated ester groups (methyl vs isopropyl) is reasonable for sequential deprotection but selectivity remains a real concern.

N-alkylation of 5-chlorouracil with the allylic bromide. The major concern is regioselectivity: 5-chlorouracil has two N-H sites (N1 and N3). N1-alkylation is typically favored, and the product correctly shows N1-alkylation, but O-alkylation and N3-alkylation are competing pathways and clean selectivity requires careful base/conditions (e.g., using the bis-silylated uracil under Vorbrüggen-type conditions, or controlled base such as K2CO3/DMF). Additionally, the allylic bromide is reactive and the (E)-geometry must be preserved. Feasible but selectivity needs optimization.

This step represents esterification/substitution of a phosphorochloridate (P-Cl) with isopropanol to install the second isopropoxy group. Reaction of P-Cl with an alcohol in the presence of base (e.g., pyridine, Et3N) is a well-established phosphorylation. The allylic bromide should be compatible under mild, non-nucleophilic-base conditions, though excess isopropoxide could potentially displace the bromide - mild conditions and controlled stoichiometry recommended.

This proposes an Appel-type conversion of an allylic alcohol to the allylic bromide using CBr4. However, the Appel reaction requires CBr4 PLUS a phosphine (typically PPh3); CBr4 alone will not effect this conversion efficiently. More critically, the substrate retains a reactive P-Cl (phosphorochloridate) which is highly moisture/nucleophile sensitive and would be incompatible with the alcohol present elsewhere and with Appel conditions. The order of operations is problematic - bromination should ideally precede installation of the labile P-Cl, or the P-Cl should already be converted. Reagent specification (missing PPh3) and FG compatibility are concerns.

This step represents global deprotection of the isopropyl phosphonate/phosphate esters to reveal the free phosphonic acid/phosphate. The disconnection of the final product from a tri-isopropyl-protected precursor is reasonable for phosphonate chemistry. However, the precursor shown (CC(C)OP(=O)(OC(C)C)OP(=O)(O)...) already has ONE free P-OH, meaning the deprotection is partial/inconsistent. For phosphonate ester cleavage, TMSBr (McKenna reaction) is the standard reagent, which would cleave all isopropyl esters simultaneously and indiscriminately - making the selective retention of one free OH in the precursor implausible. The protecting group state is inconsistent across the disconnection.

This step proposes selective demethylation of a methyl phosphonate ester (COP) to give P-OH while retaining the two isopropyl esters. Selective cleavage of a methyl ester in the presence of isopropyl esters on a pyrophosphonate is extremely difficult to achieve cleanly. TMSBr and similar reagents cleave methyl esters faster, but full chemoselectivity over isopropyl in this mixed system is not reliable, and the chlorouracil and pyrophosphate linkage add lability concerns. The mixed methyl/isopropyl protecting scheme is awkward and poorly justified.

This is an N-alkylation of 5-chlorouracil with an allylic bromide. 5-Chlorouracil has two nitrogen atoms (N1 and N3), and alkylation regioselectivity between N1 and N3 is a well-known issue. N1 alkylation is typically favored but mixtures often form, requiring careful base/conditions (e.g., via silylation/Vorbrüggen-type or controlled basic conditions). The transformation is feasible and a sensible convergent C-N disconnection, but regioselectivity must be controlled. The allylic bromide is reactive and the E-geometry should be retained.

This step forms a phosphate isopropyl ester from a P-Cl (phosphorochloridate) and isopropanol. Reaction of P-Cl with alcohols to give phosphoesters is well-established and typically proceeds in the presence of a base (e.g., pyridine, Et3N). The allylic bromide and methyl phosphonate ester should be compatible. A reasonable and feasible transformation.

This is an Appel-type conversion of an allylic alcohol to the allylic bromide using CBr4 (Appel normally requires CBr4/PPh3 - PPh3 is not shown). More importantly, performing the Appel reaction in the presence of a reactive phosphorochloridate (P-Cl) is problematic: the P-Cl would react with the alcohol or be hydrolyzed, and PPh3 could interact with the chloridate. The order of operations is questionable - converting the alcohol to bromide before installing the chloridate ester would be cleaner. Also, the reagent list omits PPh3. Functional group compatibility with the P-Cl is a real concern.

This is a Suzuki-Miyaura coupling between bromobenzene and an arylboronic acid to form the biaryl. The disconnection itself is sound and well-precedented. However, the coupling partner choice is non-optimal: aryl bromide (bromobenzene) is used as the electrophile while the more complex fragment bears the boronic acid. A more strategic and convergent approach would reverse this (use bromobenzene as the ArBr but it is the simpler partner - generally one would prefer to install boron on the simpler arene). Either way, the reaction should proceed with Pd(0)/base. The free secondary amine (NHCH2CH2OMe) is a minor concern but typically tolerated. Confidence moderate due to selectivity/practical considerations.

Miyaura borylation of the aryl bromide to give the boronic acid. Using triisopropyl borate (B(OiPr)3) typically requires a strong organometallic intermediate (e.g., via lithium-halogen exchange or Grignard formation), which would be incompatible with the sensitive thienopyrimidinone, the secondary amine, and the ether. A Pd-catalyzed Miyaura borylation with bis(pinacolato)diboron (B2pin2) and Pd catalyst followed by hydrolysis would be far more functional-group tolerant for this complex substrate. As written, organolithium/Grignard chemistry would destroy the carbonyl/heteroaromatic system. Recommend B2pin2/Pd(dppf)Cl2/KOAc conditions instead.

Reductive amination between methoxyacetaldehyde and the primary amine to install the N-(2-methoxyethyl) group. This is a well-established transformation (NaBH(OAc)3 or NaBH3CN). The primary amine reacts cleanly with the aldehyde; the heteroaromatic and aryl bromide are compatible. Good disconnection and high likelihood of success. One minor consideration: over-alkylation to tertiary amine is possible but controllable with stoichiometry.

Boc deprotection of the carbamate to reveal the primary amine. Standard acidic conditions (TFA/DCM or HCl/dioxane). The thienopyrimidinone, aryl bromide, and benzyl group are all stable to these conditions. Straightforward and reliable.

N-alkylation of the pyrimidinone NH with 3-bromobenzyl bromide. This is a standard alkylation (base such as K2CO3 or Cs2CO3 in DMF). Chemoselectivity favors the more acidic/nucleophilic ring nitrogen. One concern is potential O- vs N-alkylation of the amide/lactam tautomer, but N-alkylation typically predominates under these conditions. The benzylic bromide is appropriately more reactive than the aryl bromide, ensuring selective benzylation. The Boc group is stable. Good step.

Construction of the pyrimidinone ring from a 2-aminothiophene-3-carboxylic acid ester via cyclocondensation with formamide (Niementowski-type synthesis). This is a classic, well-precedented method to build the fused 4-oxo-pyrimidine ring from o-aminoester precursors. Heating with formamide installs the C2-H and ring nitrogens. The Boc group may be partially labile at high temperatures used for formamide cyclizations (often >150 °C), which is a concern - it could be cleaved. Otherwise the disconnection is correct and standard. Consider performing cyclization before Boc protection to avoid this issue.

local_feedback: Problems with reaction type and functional group compatibility
local_feedback_text: Miyaura borylation of the aryl bromide using triisopropyl borate (or pinacolborane/B2pin2) to give the boronic acid. The transformation is feasible, but conducting it with a free secondary amine (methoxyethylamino) present is suboptimal - the amine can interfere with lithiation/Pd-mediated borylation. With B(OiPr)3 borylation typically proceeds via lithium-halogen exchange (n-BuLi), which is incompatible with both the free N-H amine and the lactam/aminothiophene system (deprotonation, side reactions). A Pd-catalyzed Miyaura borylation with B2pin2 would be more appropriate here, and even then amine protection is advised. Reagent choice (triisopropyl borate via organolithium route) is non-optimal for this substrate.

Reductive amination of methoxyacetaldehyde with the primary amine to install the methoxyethyl secondary amine. This is a standard, robust transformation (NaBH(OAc)3 or NaBH3CN). The primary aliphatic amine and the aldehyde are well-matched. Chemoselectivity is good as the other carbonyl is a stable lactam. Feasible as written.

Boc deprotection of the carbamate to reveal the primary amine. Standard acidic conditions (TFA or HCl). The aryl bromide, lactam, and thiophene are all stable to these conditions. Straightforward and high-yielding. Note: the sequence Boc removal then reductive amination is logical and clean.

N-alkylation of the lactam/pyrimidinone N-H with 3-bromobenzyl bromide. The fused thienopyrimidinone has an acidic N-H that can be deprotonated (K2CO3, Cs2CO3) and alkylated by the benzylic bromide. Chemoselectivity favors N-alkylation over O-alkylation under appropriate base/solvent, though some O-alkylation is possible. The use of a symmetric-ish dibromide (one benzylic, one aryl) gives good chemoselectivity for the more reactive benzylic position. The Boc group is stable. Feasible, with minor O- vs N-alkylation selectivity to monitor.

Note: the hash b7486e2e31cc6459b9553d067d38ae34e8456e70871d3dee9ebb184daf6d826c reaction as written represents the N-alkylation (the 907210f1aa422f564ec52dff260d6b74f714ab76b472669772c29b08e63a93b6 entry actually shows Boc protection). This step is the alkylation of the thienopyrimidinone N-H with 3-bromobenzyl bromide using the benzylic position selectively. The aryl bromide remains intact (no competing aryl reactivity under SN2 conditions). Standard base-mediated N-alkylation, feasible. Watch for over-alkylation/O-alkylation.

Construction of the thienopyrimidinone ring from a 2-aminothiophene-3-carboxylate (ester) and formamide (Niementowski-type cyclization). Heating an o-aminoester with formamide is a classical route to fused 4(3H)-pyrimidinones (analogous to quinazolinone synthesis). The Boc carbamate may be partly labile under the high temperatures typically required (150-200 °C) for formamide cyclization - this is a potential issue, as Boc groups can cleave thermally. Consider performing the cyclization before Boc installation, or using formamidine acetate at lower temperature. Mechanistically the disconnection is sound; reagent/thermal compatibility with Boc is the concern.

This is a Suzuki coupling between bromobenzene and an arylboronic acid to form the biaryl. The disconnection is reasonable, but the polarity is reversed from optimal: typically one would couple the aryl halide bearing the more complex fragment with phenylboronic acid (commercially available), rather than installing the boronic acid on the complex fragment. The boronic acid on the complex substrate is harder to make and prone to protodeboronation. The secondary amine and ether are compatible. A better approach would be to keep the aryl bromide on the complex fragment and use commercially available PhB(OH)2. Otherwise the chemistry is sound.

Miyaura borylation using triisopropyl borate to convert the aryl bromide to a boronic acid. This is feasible (Pd-catalyzed or via halogen-metal exchange/lithiation), but with a free secondary amine and a sensitive heterocyclic thienopyrimidinone, the lithiation route would be problematic. Bis(pinacolato)diboron (B2pin2) with Pd catalysis is the more standard and milder reagent for this Miyaura borylation. Note also that this step combined with 226acd229f03a6228127c32298678ad654c399b6d2cdb64c4fece7772ed16ec5 is inefficient — the boronic acid is generated only to be coupled; a direct Suzuki with PhB(OH)2 on the bromide would be preferable.

Reductive amination between methoxyacetaldehyde and the primary amine to install the 2-methoxyethyl group on nitrogen. This is a well-precedented transformation using NaBH(OAc)3 or NaBH3CN. The aryl bromide, thioether, and heterocyclic carbonyl are all compatible. Mono-alkylation selectivity is good with reductive amination. Straightforward step.

Boc deprotection of the carbamate to reveal the primary amine. Standard transformation with TFA or HCl. The thienopyrimidinone, aryl bromide, and benzyl group are all stable under acidic deprotection conditions. Well-precedented and reliable.

N-alkylation of the pyrimidinone NH with 3-bromobenzyl bromide. The disconnection is sensible and the benzylic bromide is a good electrophile, but there is a regioselectivity concern: alkylation could occur at N vs O (O-alkylation of the amide/lactam tautomer) and there may be ambiguity over which ring nitrogen is alkylated. With appropriate base (K2CO3 or Cs2CO3 in DMF) N-alkylation typically dominates for such pyrimidinones, but this should be verified. Also note 3-bromobenzyl bromide has two reactive sites — the aryl bromide is much less reactive than the benzylic bromide so chemoselectivity should be acceptable.

Construction of the pyrimidinone ring by cyclization of the 2-aminothiophene-3-carboxylate with formamide (Niementowski-type cyclization). This is a classic, well-established route to thieno[2,3-d]pyrimidin-4(3H)-ones — heating an ortho-aminoester with formamide directly furnishes the fused pyrimidinone. The Boc carbamate may be at risk under the high temperatures (typically 150-200 °C) required for formamide cyclization, which could lead to Boc loss; this is a potential issue but the disconnection itself is correct and high-yielding. Consider doing the cyclization before introducing Boc.

Miyaura borylation converting the aryl bromide to the boronic acid using triisopropyl borate. While isopropyl borate is a viable reagent for lithiation/borylation sequences, the substrate contains many sensitive functionalities (free secondary amine, thienopyrimidinone, second aryl bromide motif). A halogen-metal exchange route is unlikely to be chemoselective here. The standard approach would be a Pd-catalyzed Miyaura borylation with bis(pinacolato)diboron (B2pin2) and KOAc to give a Bpin ester rather than the free boronic acid via B(OiPr)3, which requires strongly basic organolithium/Grignard conditions incompatible with this substrate. Reagent choice is non-optimal.

Reductive amination of methoxyacetaldehyde with the primary amine to install the N-(2-methoxyethyl) group. This is a standard transformation (NaBH(OAc)3 or NaBH3CN) and should proceed selectively. The aryl bromide, thiophene, and pyrimidinone are all compatible. Mono-alkylation is favored using the aldehyde under reductive amination conditions. Well-precedented.

Boc deprotection of the carbamate to reveal the primary amine. Standard acidic conditions (TFA/DCM or HCl/dioxane) will accomplish this cleanly. All other functional groups (aryl bromide, thioether, pyrimidinone) are stable to these conditions. Straightforward and necessary step preceding the reductive amination.

N-Alkylation of the pyrimidinone NH with 3-bromobenzyl bromide. The benzylic bromide is selectively reactive over the aryl bromide, so chemoselective N-alkylation is expected using a base (K2CO3 or Cs2CO3, DMF). One consideration: regioselectivity between N-alkylation and O-alkylation of the amide/pyrimidinone tautomer; N-alkylation is usually favored under these conditions but O-alkylation is a possible competing pathway. Overall feasible with standard precedent.

Cyclization/condensation of the 2-aminothiophene-3-carboxylate ester with formamide to construct the fused pyrimidin-4(3H)-one ring (Niementowski-type synthesis). Heating an o-aminoester with formamide is a classic, reliable method to build 4-oxo-pyrimidine rings. The Boc carbamate may be partially labile at the high temperatures typically required (150-200 °C) for formamide cyclizations, which is a concern - a Boc group may not survive and could be lost during the cyclization. Otherwise the disconnection is sound and well-precedented.

Gewald-type product disconnection: the 2-aminothiophene-3-carboxylate with the fused cyclohexane (carrying a Boc-protected amine) is a classic Gewald thiophene precursor. The forward direction (assembling the aminothiophene ester) from a ketone, ethyl cyanoacetate and sulfur is standard. Here the molecule is shown reacting with formamide (this entry overlaps with b7486e2e31cc6459b9553d067d38ae34e8456e70871d3dee9ebb184daf6d826c in description). The aminothiophene ester building block is reasonable and accessible. Boc-protected 4-aminocyclohexanone derivatives are known. Feasible.

This is a C–N coupling (Buchwald-Hartwig type or SNAr) installing the phenethylamine onto a 2-bromopyrimidinone. The bond disconnection is reasonable, as 2-aminopyrimidinones can be made from 2-halopyrimidinones via SNAr/amination. However, the molecule contains a free acylguanidine/aminooxyguanidine (NCCONC(=N)N) and an amide, both of which present competing nucleophiles. The primary amine NCCc1ccc(C(F)(F)F)cc1 must out-compete the guanidine nitrogen for chemoselective coupling, which is questionable. A protecting group strategy for the guanidine would be required. Pd-mediated amination may also be complicated by the free guanidine. Confidence moderate.

local_feedback: Problems with reaction type and functional group compatibility
local_feedback_text: Bromination with NBS at the pyrimidinone C-H to give the 2-bromo derivative is mechanistically plausible for an electron-rich heteroaromatic position. However, the substrate contains a highly nucleophilic guanidine/aminooxyguanidine group, which is readily oxidized/brominated by NBS. Achieving chemoselective ring bromination in the presence of this free guanidine and the secondary amide is highly problematic. The guanidine would need protection. Additionally, the regiochemistry of bromination on the ring should be confirmed. Recommend installing the halogen earlier, before elaborating the sensitive guanidine moiety.

This is an amide coupling between the carboxylic acid Cc1cncc(=O)n1CC(=O)O and the amine N=C(N)NOCCN. The disconnection is sound and standard (EDC/HATU coupling). However, the aminooxyguanidine partner has multiple nucleophilic sites (the guanidine NH groups vs. the primary amine), raising chemoselectivity concerns; the primary amine should be the most reactive but guanidine acylation is a known side reaction. Protection of the guanidine (e.g., Boc) would improve selectivity. The overall disconnection is reasonable but reagent/protection optimization is needed.

This step proposes converting a nitrile N#CCONC(=N)N into the primary amine/guanidine N=C(N)NOCCN by reduction of the nitrile to a CH2NH2. While nitrile reduction to a primary amine is a known transformation (LiAlH4, H2/catalyst, borane), doing so selectively in the presence of the free guanidine (which would be reduced/decomposed or interfere) is very problematic. Furthermore, the retrosynthetic logic here also seems inconsistent with the Boc-protected sequence below it (11ed91f4801aa431a047645f803286607823c7d3a1a14e753abcee95bc5696fb), where the actual reduction would be performed on the Boc-protected nitrile, not the free guanidine. As written (free guanidine present), chemoselective nitrile reduction is unlikely. Reduction should be done on the bis-Boc-protected intermediate.

This represents installation/manipulation of Boc groups on the guanidine of the aminooxynitrile. The forward direction (bis-Boc guanidine) is a well-precedented protection of guanidines, and the retro disconnection to mono-Boc + Boc2O is standard. Boc protection of guanidines with Boc2O is routine. Feasible.

Boc protection of a guanidine NH using Boc2O (di-tert-butyl dicarbonate) to give the bis-Boc protected guanidine. This is a standard, well-precedented transformation. Both reactants are reasonable, and Boc2O is commercially available. Feasible.

Boc ester deprotection (acidolysis, TFA) to reveal the free carboxylic acid. This is a standard, robust transformation. The pyrimidinone and methyl substituents are stable to TFA. Feasible and appropriate.

N-alkylation of the pyrimidinone NH with tert-butyl bromoacetate. This is a standard N-alkylation; the ambident pyridinone/pyrimidinone could in principle give O- vs N-alkylation, but N-alkylation typically predominates with soft alkyl halides under basic conditions (K2CO3/Cs2CO3, DMF). Both building blocks are commercially available. Minor O/N-selectivity caveat but generally feasible.

This is a Buchwald-Hartwig/SNAr amination of an aryl bromide on a 2-bromopyrimidinone (or pyridinone) core with a primary amine. The disconnection itself is reasonable (C–N bond formation to install the phenethylamine), and the activated C-Br adjacent to the ring nitrogen/carbonyl should be displaceable by SNAr. However, there is a significant chemoselectivity concern: the substrate contains an acylguanidine/aminooxyguanidine (N=C(N)N) moiety with multiple nucleophilic NH/NH2 groups that could compete with the external phenethylamine for the aryl bromide, leading to intramolecular or intermolecular side reactions. The free guanidine is also a potential ligand-poisoning group under Pd catalysis. Performing this amination earlier (before installing the unprotected guanidine) would be advisable. Confidence reflects the inherent risk of competing amination by the polar polyfunctional fragment.

NBS bromination of the pyridinone/pyrimidinone ring to install the C-Br handle. Electrophilic bromination of electron-rich pyridinones is feasible, but regioselectivity is a concern — the position alpha to the ring nitrogen vs. other ring positions must be controlled, and the methyl-bearing ring carbon could also be a site for benzylic bromination by NBS (radical conditions). More critically, the substrate bears a free guanidine and an aminooxy group, both highly oxidizable/electron-rich functionalities that would likely be brominated or oxidized preferentially by NBS. This step would suffer from poor chemoselectivity unless the guanidine is protected. Strongly recommend introducing the bromide much earlier on the simple heterocycle before elaborating sensitive functionality.

local_feedback: Problems with reaction type and functional group compatibility
local_feedback_text: Amide coupling between the carboxylic acid (Cc1cncc(=O)n1CC(=O)O) and the aminooxy-amine fragment N=C(N)NOCCN. The disconnection is logical (forming the glycinamide bond). However, the coupling partner contains a free, unprotected guanidine AND a free aminooxy group, both of which present serious selectivity issues: the guanidine NH and the primary amine will both compete for the activated acid, and standard coupling reagents (HATU, EDC) could acylate the guanidine. The free aminooxy/guanidine should ideally be protected (e.g., Boc) during the coupling. As written, expect poor selectivity and side-product formation. Suggest performing the amide coupling on a Boc-protected guanidine intermediate.

This step maps N=C(N)NOCCN (an amine) to N#CCONC(=N)N (a nitrile), implying reduction of a nitrile to a primary amine. While nitrile-to-amine reduction is a real transformation, the precursor nitrile here also bears a free guanidine. More problematic, the retrosynthetic relationship as written (forward: reduce N#CCONC(=N)N to N=C(N)NOCCN) requires selective reduction of the nitrile in the presence of the guanidine/oxime-type functionality; catalytic hydrogenation could reduce the N-O bond of the aminooxy linkage, cleaving the key O-N connectivity. This is a poorly chosen step — the N-O bond is labile under hydrogenation. A borane or alternative chemoselective reduction would be needed, and even then N-O cleavage is a real risk. The disconnection logic is questionable.

This step corresponds to removal/manipulation of Boc groups on the bis-Boc protected guanidine to reveal N#CCONC(=N)N. The forward direction (going from bis-Boc guanidine N#CCONC(NBoc)... to free guanidine nitrile) is a standard Boc deprotection (TFA). The transformation is feasible chemically, though the mapping is a bit unusual. Boc deprotection with TFA on this substrate is reasonable; selection of conditions is fine. Minor concern that the aminooxy O-N could be sensitive but generally stable to TFA.

Boc protection of a mono-Boc guanidine using Boc2O to give the bis-Boc protected guanidine. This is a well-established transformation for guanidine protection. Boc2O is commercial and the reaction proceeds reliably under basic conditions (e.g., with DMAP or NaH/base). Standard and feasible.

N-alkylation of the pyridinone NH with tert-butyl bromoacetate. This is a standard, reliable N-alkylation of an ambident pyridinone/amide. The main consideration is O- vs N-selectivity (pyridinones can alkylate on O or N), but with these substrates N-alkylation typically predominates under basic conditions (K2CO3/Cs2CO3 in DMF). Both reagents are commercially available. Feasible with attention to regioselectivity (O/N).

Acidic cleavage of the tert-butyl ester to reveal the free carboxylic acid. Standard TFA-mediated Boc/t-Bu ester removal. Clean and reliable transformation. The substrate has no competing acid-sensitive groups at this stage (the bromide/guanidine not yet installed in this branch), so the deprotection is straightforward.

local_feedback: Problems with reaction type and functional group compatibility
local_feedback_text: This is an SNAr/Buchwald-type amination of a 2-bromopyrimidinone with a primary amine. The disconnection is reasonable since 2-halopyrimidinones are activated toward amine substitution. However, the molecule contains a free aminoguanidine/hydroxyguanidine (NOC(=N)N) functionality, which is highly nucleophilic and would compete strongly with the desired amine for either SNAr or Pd-catalyzed coupling, leading to chemoselectivity problems. The guanidine should be protected (e.g., Boc) during this coupling. Additionally, free guanidines can poison Pd catalysts. Recommend installing the amine earlier or protecting the guanidine.

NBS bromination of the pyrimidinone ring to install bromide at the position alpha to the ring nitrogen. While electrophilic halogenation of electron-rich pyrimidinones is feasible, regioselectivity is a concern given the multiple ring positions and the methyl substituent. More critically, the substrate bears a free guanidine and amide-tethered chain; NBS could brominate or oxidize these nucleophilic/electron-rich sites (e.g., N-bromination of guanidine, alpha-bromination of activated positions). Chemoselectivity is poor without protection. The C-H to C-Br conversion at this specific ring position via NBS is also not strongly precedented for this substitution pattern.

local_feedback: Problems with reaction type and functional group compatibility
local_feedback_text: Amide coupling between the carboxylic acid (Cc1cncc(=O)n1CC(=O)O) and the amine of the aminooxy-guanidine (N=C(N)NOCCN). The amide bond disconnection is sound, but the free guanidine and aminooxy moiety present compatibility/chemoselectivity issues. The primary amine being acylated must be differentiated from the guanidine NH groups. Standard coupling reagents (HATU/EDC) could activate and cause intramolecular cyclization or react with the guanidine. Protection of the guanidine (Boc) would be advisable. The transformation is in principle feasible but needs careful selectivity control.

This step proposes converting a nitrile-containing guanidine (N#CCONC(=N)N) to the amine product (N=C(N)NOCCN), i.e., reduction of nitrile to a primary amine (CH2CN -> CH2CH2NH2). The disconnection adds a carbon implicitly? Actually CH2-C#N reduces to CH2-CH2-NH2 which is consistent atom-wise. Nitrile reduction to primary amine is feasible (e.g., H2/catalyst, LiAlH4, borane). HOWEVER, the substrate contains an O-N bond (aminooxy/hydroxyguanidine) which is labile to hydrogenolysis and to strong hydride reductions; the weak N-O bond would likely cleave under most nitrile reduction conditions. The guanidine is also incompatible with LiAlH4. This makes the proposed transformation problematic and selectivity-poor.

Removal of two Boc groups from the bis-Boc guanidine to give the free guanidine nitrile (N#CCONC(=N)N). Boc deprotection with TFA or HCl is well-established. The main concern: the product is a free guanidine bearing a nitrile and an O-N bond, all of which survive acidic Boc deprotection. The transformation is chemically reasonable. Standard acidic conditions are appropriate; the nitrile and weak N-O bond tolerate mild acid. Minor risk of N-O cleavage under prolonged strong acid.

Boc protection of a mono-Boc guanidine with Boc2O to give the bis-Boc guanidine. This is standard guanidine protection chemistry and proceeds readily with Boc2O and base (e.g., DMAP/Et3N). Well-precedented. The nitrile and aminooxy ether are stable under these conditions.
tert-Butyl ester deprotection to the carboxylic acid using TFA or HCl. Standard and reliable transformation. The pyrimidinone ring tolerates these acidic conditions. No major issues.

N-alkylation of the pyrimidinone NH with tert-butyl bromoacetate. This is a standard N-alkylation; both starting materials are commercially available. Regioselectivity (N- vs O-alkylation) of ambident pyrimidinone anions can be a minor concern, but N-alkylation typically dominates with soft alkyl halides and appropriate base (K2CO3/Cs2CO3). Generally feasible.

This is a Buchwald-Hartwig type or SNAr amination of an aryl/heteroaryl bromide with a primary amine. The disconnection itself (C-N bond formation at the C-Br position of the pyrimidinone) is reasonable. However, the molecule contains a free aminoguanidine/amidoxime-type O-NH-C(=N)N moiety which is highly nucleophilic and would compete with the desired phenethylamine for coupling, plus it could poison Pd catalysts. The substrate also has an amide N-H. Chemoselectivity is a serious concern - the guanidine should be protected. Better executed with protected guanidine intermediates as done elsewhere in the route. Consider doing this amination before installing the sensitive guanidinyloxy fragment.

Bromination of the pyrimidinone with NBS to install the bromide at the position adjacent to the ring nitrogen. NBS brominations on electron-rich heteroarenes are feasible, but regioselectivity on this polysubstituted pyrimidinone is uncertain, and the methyl group on the ring is prone to benzylic (Wohl-Ziegler) bromination under radical conditions. More importantly, the free guanidine/aminooxy group is highly susceptible to oxidation/halogenation by NBS, leading to side reactions. This step would be much cleaner with protecting groups on the guanidine and performed earlier in the sequence on a simpler substrate.

local_feedback: Problems with reaction type and functional group compatibility
local_feedback_text: Amide coupling between the carboxylic acid and the primary amine of N=C(N)NOCCN. The disconnection is logical (standard amide bond formation, e.g., EDC/HOBt or HATU). However, the free, unprotected aminoguanidine-oxy group contains multiple nucleophilic nitrogen centers (guanidine NH/NH2) that will compete with the desired primary amine, leading to poor chemoselectivity and possible acylation of the guanidine. A protected guanidine (e.g., Boc-protected) would be strongly preferred here for selective coupling at the primary amine.

This step proposes converting a nitrile (N#CCONC(=N)N) to a primary amine (N=C(N)NOCCN), i.e., reduction of -CH2-C#N to -CH2-CH2-NH2. While nitrile reduction to a primary amine is a known transformation (e.g., LiAlH4, catalytic hydrogenation, borane), doing so selectively in the presence of an unprotected guanidine (also containing C=N) is highly problematic, and the O-N bond of the aminooxy linkage is labile to many reducing conditions and could be cleaved. The retrosynthetic mapping is also questionable - the starting nitrile already bears the free guanidine yet the earlier steps (11ed91f4801aa431a047645f803286607823c7d3a1a14e753abcee95bc5696fb) carry Boc protection. There is an inconsistency: the Boc groups present in 11ed91f4801aa431a047645f803286607823c7d3a1a14e753abcee95bc5696fb product are not removed before this reduction. This disconnection as written is unlikely to work cleanly.

The reaction as written shows N#CCONC(=N)N (free guanidine) being formed from a bis-Boc protected precursor CC(C)(C)OC(=O)N=C(NOCC#N)NC(=O)OC(C)(C)C. This is a Boc-deprotection (TFA), which is feasible chemically. However, the SMILES transform direction/notation here is confusing and the product (free guanidine nitrile) would then be reduced in 7a43bdb9384fff6ef2d5ea9bed7dadf9b42929fe75fd0d5c9da913c00dc45f4c - placing a free guanidine ahead of a nitrile reduction is poor strategy. The deprotection itself is fine, but its placement in the sequence is non-optimal; Boc groups should be retained until after the nitrile reduction and subsequent couplings.

This step is the Boc protection of a guanidine using Boc2O to give the bis-Boc guanidine. Mono-Boc guanidine + Boc2O to make bis-Boc is feasible but achieving clean bis-protection of a guanidine often requires specific conditions (base such as DMAP/Et3N, and the regiochemistry of N-acylation on guanidines can be capricious). A more standard approach would use a pre-formed bis-Boc-protected guanidinylation reagent (e.g., N,N'-di-Boc-1H-pyrazole-1-carboxamidine or N,N'-di-Boc-S-methylisothiourea) reacting with the aminooxy nitrile, rather than building the guanidine then Boc-protecting. The transformation can work but reagent/strategy is non-optimal.
Boc ester deprotection (tert-butyl ester to carboxylic acid) using TFA or HCl. This is a robust, well-precedented transformation and fully compatible with the pyrimidinone substrate. No issues.

N-alkylation of the pyrimidinone NH with tert-butyl bromoacetate. This is a standard N-alkylation; the ambident nucleophile (N vs O) could in principle give some O-alkylation, but N-alkylation typically dominates for such pyrimidinones under basic conditions (K2CO3, Cs2CO3 in DMF). Both starting materials are commercially available. Minor N/O selectivity caveat but generally a reliable step.

This is the key convergent step assembling the tricyclic quinolone-type core. The reaction between a cyclic secondary amine (3,4-dihydro-2H-benzo[b][1,4]oxazine derivative) and the diethyl ethoxymethylenemalonate-type donor (here an alpha-(thiazolylcarbamoyl) acrylate) is a classic Gould-Jacobs-type sequence. The enamine forms by displacement of the ethoxy group by the secondary amine, followed by intramolecular Friedel-Crafts-type/thermal cyclization (Conrad-Limpach/Gould-Jacobs) onto the aromatic ring to form the 4-oxo-quinolone fused ring. This disconnection is well-precedented in fluoroquinolone/pyridoquinolone chemistry (e.g., levofloxacin synthesis, which uses a very similar benzoxazine + ethoxymethylenemalonate strategy). The regiochemistry of cyclization onto the position ortho to oxygen is consistent with electron-rich activation. One concern: the amide on the thiazole nitrogen is carried through the cyclization rather than being installed afterward; in the levofloxacin route the ester is typically retained and cyclized, then the carboxylic acid is coupled to the amine last. Cyclizing with the pre-formed thiazole amide could be problematic (the amide carbonyl may compete, and harsh cyclization conditions e.g. polyphosphoric acid/high temperature could degrade the aminothiazole amide). Still, the bond disconnection is sound and mirrors established quinolone chemistry.

Reduction of the aromatic nitro group followed by intramolecular reductive amination (or imine formation/reduction) to give the 2-substituted 3,4-dihydrobenzoxazine. Catalytic hydrogenation (H2/Pd-C) of the nitro group generates the aniline, which condenses with the adjacent ketone to form a cyclic imine that is reduced in situ to the dihydrobenzoxazine. This tandem nitro reduction/reductive cyclization is well-precedented for benzoxazine synthesis. A stereocenter is created at C2 (the ethyl-bearing carbon); the product will be racemic unless asymmetric methods are applied, which matches the (unspecified) stereochemistry of the target. Minor risk of over-reduction or incomplete cyclization, but overall a reasonable transformation.

Williamson-type O-alkylation of 2-nitrophenol with 1-bromo-2-butanone (CCC(=O)CBr) under basic conditions (K2CO3, DMF/acetone). The phenol is acidified by the ortho-nitro group, making O-alkylation facile. The alpha-bromoketone is a good electrophile. Chemoselectivity favors O-alkylation over C-alkylation. Both starting materials are commercially available and inexpensive. Straightforward and high-yielding step.

Condensation of an active methylene compound (ethyl 3-oxo-3-(thiazol-2-ylamino)propanoate, i.e., the malonamic ester) with triethyl orthoformate to give the ethoxymethylene derivative. This is the classic preparation of ethoxymethylenemalonate-type building blocks, typically run with acetic anhydride as dehydrating agent at elevated temperature. The active methylene flanked by ester and amide is sufficiently acidic to undergo this condensation. The geometry of the resulting enol ether (E/Z) is not critical since it is consumed in the subsequent cyclization. Both starting materials are accessible (the malonamic ester from monoethyl malonate/Meldrum's acid + 2-aminothiazole). Well-precedented.

This is the key disconnection of the tricyclic pyridoquinolone core. The forward reaction is a classic Gould-Jacobs-type annulation: the secondary amine of the dihydrobenzoxazine (3,4-dihydro-2H-1,4-benzoxazine) condenses with the alkoxymethylene malonate-type Michael acceptor (CCOC=C(C(=O)Nc1nccs1)C(=O)OCC), followed by intramolecular thermal (or acid/base-mediated) cyclization onto the aromatic ring to form the 4-oxo-pyridine ring annulated onto the benzene. This type of chemistry is well precedented in fluoroquinolone-related syntheses. The use of a pre-formed amide bearing the thiazol-2-yl group on the malonate is a reasonable convergent choice, though there is some risk that the more activated diester would be preferred and one might instead build the amide after cyclization. Overall a sound, convergent disconnection. Note the formed ring also generates the C-N bond closing the bridgehead, consistent with the bicyclic amine geometry.
