Reduction of the o-nitro aryl ether ketone (CCC(=O)COc1ccccc1[N+]([O-])=O) gives the 2-substituted 3,4-dihydro-2H-1,4-benzoxazine via reduction of the nitro group followed by intramolecular reductive amination/cyclization onto the ketone. This is a well-established tandem reduction-cyclization (e.g., H2/Pd-C, Fe/AcOH, or SnCl2 followed by reductive amination). The product CCC1COc2ccccc2N1 is the expected dihydrobenzoxazine. A minor concern is that the intermediate imine/enamine must be reduced to give the saturated ring, which typically works under catalytic hydrogenation. Feasible.

Williamson-type O-alkylation of 2-nitrophenol with 1-bromobutan-2-one (CCC(=O)CBr) under basic conditions (K2CO3/DMF or acetone) gives the aryl ether ketone cleanly. The phenol is acidic (nitro-activated) and the alpha-bromoketone is a good electrophile. Both starting materials are commercially available and inexpensive. Chemoselective O-alkylation predominates. A minor competing pathway is self-condensation of the alpha-haloketone, but standard conditions minimize this. Feasible and efficient.

Condensation of the malonamide ester (ethyl 3-oxo-3-(thiazol-2-ylamino)propanoate, CCOC(=O)CC(=O)Nc1nccs1) with triethyl orthoformate (CCOC(OCC)OCC), typically with acetic anhydride at elevated temperature, gives the ethoxymethylene derivative. This is a standard, well-precedented transformation to generate alkoxymethylene malonate-type Michael acceptors used in quinolone syntheses. Both building blocks are readily available. The active methylene between the ester and amide carbonyls is sufficiently acidic to react. Feasible. Note the stereochemistry of the enol ether double bond (E/Z) is not critical since it is consumed in subsequent cyclization.

This is the key disconnection of the tricyclic pyrido[1,2-a]benzoxazine-quinolone core into a 3,4-dihydro-2H-1,4-benzoxazine (with the ethyl substituent) and an ethoxymethylene malonate-type building block bearing the thiazole amide. This is the classic Gould-Jacobs / enaminone cyclization strategy used widely in fluoroquinolone-type syntheses (e.g., levofloxacin, ofloxacin). The secondary amine of the benzoxazine condenses with the ethoxymethylenemalonate (displacing the ethoxy group to form the enamine), followed by thermal/base-mediated intramolecular cyclization onto the aromatic ring (Gould-Jacobs cyclization) and concomitant loss of ethanol to build the 4-oxoquinoline core. The retained ester here is the amide to the aminothiazole. This is a well-precedented and convergent disconnection. One concern: typically the malonate has two esters, and cyclization onto the ring forms the C-4 ketone while keeping the C-3 carbonyl as the carboxylic acid/amide; here the amide is preinstalled which is plausible but the regiochemistry of which carbonyl cyclizes vs remains as amide should be verified. Overall sound.

Reductive cyclization of an ortho-nitro aryl ether bearing a pendant ketone to give the 2-ethyl-3,4-dihydro-2H-1,4-benzoxazine. Catalytic hydrogenation (or Fe/Zn reduction) of the nitro group generates the aniline, which undergoes intramolecular reductive amination (condensation to cyclic imine/enamine followed by reduction) with the ketone to deliver the saturated benzoxazine. This is a well-established tandem reduction/reductive amination sequence. The product has a stereocenter at the 2-position (CH with ethyl), which will be formed as racemate unless asymmetric methods are used - acceptable for a racemic target. Selectivity is generally good. Reasonable transformation.

Williamson ether synthesis / O-alkylation of 2-nitrophenol with 1-bromobutan-2-one (CCC(=O)CBr). The phenol is deprotonated (K2CO3/Cs2CO3 in DMF or acetone) and the alkoxide displaces the alpha-bromoketone. The ortho-nitro group acidifies the phenol facilitating clean O-alkylation. Both starting materials are commercially available and inexpensive. Potential side reaction: the alpha-bromoketone could undergo competing self-condensation or Favorskii-type processes under strongly basic conditions, but with mild base this is well-precedented. Good step.

Formation of the ethoxymethylene malonate-type building block by condensation of the active methylene compound (ethyl 3-oxo-3-(thiazol-2-ylamino)propanoate, an amide-ester with an acidic CH2) with triethyl orthoformate (CCOC(OCC)OCC). This is a standard condensation, typically run with acetic anhydride at reflux, generating the ethoxymethylene derivative (CCOC=C...). Well-precedented in quinolone syntheses. Both starting materials are commercially available/accessible. The malonamide-ester substrate is reasonable. Good step.

This is the key disconnection of the tricyclic pyridoquinolone core. The forward reaction is a classic Gould-Jacobs-type cyclization. The 2,3-dihydro-1,4-benzoxazine (CCC1COc2ccccc2N1) condenses with the ethoxymethylene malonate-derived intermediate. The secondary amine of the benzoxazine displaces the ethoxy group of the enol ether to form an enamine, followed by intramolecular thermal cyclization (Conrad-Limpach/Gould-Jacobs) onto the aromatic ring to form the 4-oxo-quinolone ring. This builds both the new C-N enamine bond and the C-C bond to the arene. The disconnection is well-precedented for fluoroquinolone-type antibacterials (this scaffold resembles a levofloxacin-type ofloxacin core). One concern: regioselectivity of the cyclization onto the benzene ring is fixed by the oxazine, so it is fine. Overall a sound, convergent disconnection.

Reductive cyclization of the o-nitro aryl ether ketone (CCC(=O)COc1ccccc1[N+](=O)[O-]) to the 2-ethyl-3,4-dihydro-2H-benzoxazine. Reduction of the nitro group (e.g., H2/Pd-C, Fe/AcOH, or SnCl2) gives the aniline, which undergoes intramolecular reductive amination/condensation with the pendant ketone to form the cyclic amine. This tandem reduction/cyclization is well-precedented. The newly formed stereocenter at C2 would be racemic, which is acceptable if no enantiopurity is required. Mild reductants are preferred to avoid over-reduction. Generally feasible.

Williamson ether synthesis (O-alkylation) of 2-nitrophenol with 1-bromobutan-2-one (CCC(=O)CBr, an alpha-bromoketone). The phenol is deprotonated (K2CO3, Cs2CO3) and the phenolate displaces bromide. This is a standard, high-yielding transformation. Both starting materials are commercially available. Minor concern: alpha-haloketones can undergo competing O- vs C-alkylation or self-condensation, but with phenolate O-alkylation strongly dominates. Feasible.

Formation of the ethoxymethylenemalonate-type enol ether by condensation of the active methylene compound (ethyl 3-oxo-3-(thiazol-2-ylamino)propanoate, an amide-ester malonate equivalent) with triethyl orthoformate. This Knoevenagel-type condensation with triethyl orthoformate typically requires acetic anhydride and heat to give the ethoxymethylene derivative. Standard and well-precedented for building Gould-Jacobs precursors. Both reactants are accessible (the malonamide-ester is readily made from the thiazol-2-yl amine and a malonate half-ester/Meldrum's acid). Feasible.

This is an aza-Michael addition of an aromatic amine to acrylic acid, forming the secondary amine with a propanoic acid chain (NCCC(=O)O). The disconnection is sound and well-precedented. Aniline-type amines add to acrylic acid/acrylates under thermal or catalyzed conditions to give beta-amino acids. A few practical considerations: (1) The aniline here is an electron-rich (para-OMe) but the secondary amine product can undergo a second Michael addition to give the bis-adduct (di-substituted amine); controlling mono- vs bis-addition requires careful stoichiometry (excess amine or controlled acrylic acid) — a potential selectivity/over-addition concern. (2) The vinyl sulfone (/C=C/S(=O)(=O)) in the molecule is itself a Michael acceptor; the nucleophilic aniline could in principle react intramolecularly/intermolecularly with the styryl vinyl sulfone, though the aryl amine is a relatively poor nucleophile and the conjugated arylvinyl sulfone is sterically hindered by the trimethoxyphenyl group, so chemoselectivity should generally favor reaction with acrylic acid. (3) Using acrylic acid directly (free acid) is acceptable; sometimes the ester (methyl acrylate) followed by hydrolysis is cleaner, but the free acid route is viable. Overall this is a reasonable single-step disconnection to commercially available building blocks.

This step is an aza-Michael addition of the aniline nitrogen to acrylic acid (C=CC(=O)O) to form the β-amino acid product (NCCC(=O)O). This is a well-precedented transformation. Aniline nitrogens, though weakly nucleophilic, readily undergo conjugate addition to acrylic acid/acrylates, particularly under thermal conditions or with mild Lewis acid/base catalysis. The chemoselectivity is favorable: the aniline is the most nucleophilic site, and the existing vinyl sulfone (/C=C/S(=O)(=O)) Michael acceptor on the molecule should remain untouched because the free amine is the reactive partner toward acrylic acid rather than its own attached acceptor. One minor consideration: the aniline could in principle undergo a double addition (bis-alkylation) to give a tertiary amine with two propanoic acid arms, which is a common side reaction in aza-Michael additions with acrylates. Controlling stoichiometry (1 equiv acrylic acid) and reaction conditions is needed to favor mono-addition. Also, the free carboxylic acid product is fine since no protection is strictly necessary for this final step. Overall a clean, efficient final-step disconnection.

This is an aza-Michael addition of an aniline nitrogen to acrylic acid, forming the secondary amine with a 3-(arylamino)propanoic acid moiety. The disconnection is sound and well-precedented. Aryl amines are weak nucleophiles, but aza-Michael additions of anilines to acrylic acid/acrylate derivatives are known and proceed under thermal conditions or with mild catalysis. A few considerations: (1) Mono- vs. di-addition selectivity is a concern, as the aniline could undergo a second Michael addition to give the tertiary amine bis-adduct; using a controlled stoichiometry (1 equiv acrylic acid) helps, though aniline anilines being electron-rich (para-OMe) may push toward over-addition. (2) The free carboxylic acid of acrylic acid is fine here; using acrylic acid directly avoids ester hydrolysis steps. (3) The vinyl sulfone (electron-poor alkene) elsewhere in the molecule is itself a Michael acceptor, so there is a theoretical risk of intramolecular or intermolecular side reactions, but the aniline nitrogen is the intended nucleophile and the regiochemistry is controlled by proximity/electronics. Overall a reasonable single-step disconnection to commercially reasonable building blocks.

This step is an aza-Michael addition of an aniline nitrogen onto acrylic acid to install the -NHCH2CH2COOH moiety. The disconnection is sound and well-precedented: anilines add to acrylic acid/acrylates under thermal or mild Lewis/Bronsted acid/base catalysis to give β-amino acid/ester products. The aniline used here is moderately nucleophilic (electron-rich p-methoxy substituent activates it, though the ortho/para benzyl-sulfonyl substituent is mildly deactivating). One practical consideration: mono- vs bis-alkylation selectivity. With acrylic acid, the secondary amine product is generally less reactive than the primary aniline, so mono-addition predominates when stoichiometry is controlled (1 equiv acrylic acid). The vinyl sulfone (the /C=C/S(=O)(=O) styryl group) is also a Michael acceptor, so there is a theoretical risk the aniline could add intramolecularly/intermolecularly to that conjugated alkene; however the styryl vinyl sulfone is far less electrophilic toward weak aniline nucleophiles than acrylic acid and is remote, so chemoselectivity should favor the desired N-alkylation on acrylic acid. Recommend mild conditions (e.g., neat or in water/EtOH, with the acid, possibly catalytic) and 1 equiv acrylic acid to avoid bis-addition. Overall a reasonable, convergent final step.

This is a standard Suzuki-Miyaura cross-coupling between an aryl bromide and a pinacol boronate ester. The disconnection is appropriate and well-precedented. The bromide is selectively activated for coupling. One consideration: the secondary amine (piperazine NH) is present unprotected. While free piperazines are generally tolerated under Pd catalysis, they can occasionally coordinate to and poison the catalyst or slow the reaction. A free NH piperazine is usually acceptable, but if yields are low, Boc-protection of the piperazine nitrogen would be advisable. The primary aminopyridine (2-aminopyridine) is also tolerated. Overall a sound, convergent final step.

This Suzuki coupling installs the trimethoxyphenyl group onto an aminopyridine bearing both an iodide and a bromide (Nc1ncc(Br)cc1I). The strategy relies on chemoselective coupling at the C-I position over the C-Br position, leaving the bromide intact for the subsequent coupling (ca67b53b150b0603f13d1f0b6e6c1cdc827261df23c4eae2c09c89cbab0ef66a). Aryl iodides are indeed more reactive than aryl bromides in oxidative addition, so selectivity is achievable with careful control (mild conditions, controlled equivalents of boronic acid, low temperature). This is a reasonable and clever ordering of disconnections. However, mono-selectivity is not guaranteed and some bis-coupling/homo-coupling byproducts are likely, which may limit yield. The 2-amino group ortho to the iodide could also slow oxidative addition or promote protodehalogenation. The starting materials (3,4,5-trimethoxyphenylboronic acid and 5-bromo-3-iodopyridin-2-amine) are commercially available or readily accessible. Recommend mild Pd(PPh3)4 conditions with controlled stoichiometry to maximize chemoselectivity.

This is a Suzuki-Miyaura coupling between an aryl bromide and a pinacol boronate ester bearing a free piperazine NH. The disconnection at the biaryl bond is strategically sound and well-precedented. However, two concerns arise: (1) The free secondary amine (piperazine NH) can coordinate to Pd and may slow the coupling or require additional base/ligand optimization, though such couplings with unprotected piperazines are documented and generally tolerated. (2) The substrate already bears a free aminopyridine (NH2), which is generally compatible but can also coordinate Pd. The main selectivity consideration is that the coupling is performed on a monobromide so regioselectivity is not an issue here. Standard conditions (Pd(PPh3)4 or Pd(dppf)Cl2, K2CO3 or Cs2CO3, dioxane/water) should work. Consider whether protecting the piperazine NH (e.g., Boc) would improve reproducibility, but it is likely unnecessary. Overall feasible with modest optimization.

This step is a Suzuki coupling between 3,4,5-trimethoxyphenylboronic acid and 5-bromo-3-iodo-2-aminopyridine (Nc1ncc(Br)cc1I). The key strategic point is the desired chemoselectivity: the boronic acid should couple at the C-I position (more reactive in oxidative addition) while leaving the C-Br intact for the subsequent coupling (ca67b53b150b0603f13d1f0b6e6c1cdc827261df23c4eae2c09c89cbab0ef66a). This selectivity (Ar-I >> Ar-Br) is well-established and is an excellent and intelligent disconnection choice that exploits the differential reactivity of iodide vs bromide. With careful control (mild conditions, controlled temperature, ~1 equiv boronic acid, Pd(PPh3)4), high selectivity for the iodide is generally achievable. Minor risk of competing bromide coupling/diarylation exists but is manageable. The ortho-amino group adjacent to the iodide is sterically demanding but should still couple. Good disconnection overall.

This is a Suzuki-Miyaura coupling between an aryl boronic ester and an aryl bromide, which is a well-precedented transformation. The disconnection at the biaryl bond is strategic and sound. However, two concerns arise: (1) The free secondary amine (piperazine NH) on the boronic ester partner can coordinate Pd and potentially attenuate the reaction; while not prohibitive, protecting it (e.g., Boc) would be more robust. (2) The free primary aminopyridine (2-aminopyridine) is present and competing C-N coupling (Buchwald-Hartwig) of the secondary amine with the aryl bromide is conceivable under Pd catalysis, although Suzuki coupling is typically faster with boronic species present. Overall the transformation is feasible but the unprotected piperazine NH is a minor liability that affects selectivity/yield.

This Suzuki coupling disconnects the trimethoxyphenyl group from a 3-bromo-5-iodo-2-aminopyridine. The key strategic point is exploiting the differential reactivity of C-I vs C-Br: oxidative addition into the C-I bond is strongly favored, so selective coupling at the iodo position to leave the bromide intact for the subsequent step (ca67b53b150b0603f13d1f0b6e6c1cdc827261df23c4eae2c09c89cbab0ef66a) is reasonable and well-precedented. This is a sound sequential cross-coupling strategy. Main risks: (1) chemoselectivity between I and Br is generally good but not perfect, and some bis-coupling/homocoupling may erode yield; (2) the free 2-amino group is tolerated in Suzuki couplings. Using controlled stoichiometry (1 equiv boronic acid) and mild conditions should give the desired mono-coupled product. The starting materials (3,4,5-trimethoxyphenylboronic acid and 5-bromo-3-iodopyridin-2-amine) are commercially available.

This is a Suzuki-Miyaura cross-coupling between an aryl pinacol boronate bearing a free piperazine and an aryl bromide on a 2-aminopyridine core. The disconnection is sound and well-precedented. The free secondary amine of the piperazine is generally tolerated in Pd-catalyzed Suzuki couplings, though it may coordinate to Pd and could lower yield; if problematic, a Boc-protected piperazine boronate could be used and deprotected afterward. The 2-aminopyridine NH2 is also tolerated. Standard conditions (Pd(dppf)Cl2 or Pd(PPh3)4, aqueous base) should work. Chemoselectivity is fine since only one C-Br remains. Confidence high.

This is a Suzuki coupling between a 3,4,5-trimethoxyphenylboronic acid and 2-amino-3-iodo-5-bromopyridine (Nc1ncc(Br)cc1I). The strategy of installing the trimethoxyphenyl group selectively at the more reactive C-I position over the C-Br is reasonable, since oxidative addition into C-I is faster than C-Br. This sets up the subsequent coupling at C-Br (ca67b53b150b0603f13d1f0b6e6c1cdc827261df23c4eae2c09c89cbab0ef66a), which is a clever sequential differentiation strategy. The main concern is achieving high chemoselectivity between I and Br - using mild conditions (low temperature, Pd(PPh3)4) and controlling stoichiometry of boronic acid (1 equiv) is critical to avoid bis-coupling. Some bis-arylation byproduct is likely and will reduce yield. The free 2-amino group is compatible. Overall feasible but selectivity must be carefully managed. Both starting materials (3,4,5-trimethoxyphenylboronic acid and 2-amino-5-bromo-3-iodopyridine) are commercially available.

This disconnection proposes a Friedel-Crafts-type or Michael-type acylation/coupling between the 4-quinolone C-3 position and an unstable anhydride fragment 'O=C1C=C(O)C(=O)O1'. There are several major problems: (1) The product structure 'C(=O)C=C(O)C(=O)O' is an open-chain side chain bearing a ketone, an enol, and a free carboxylic acid, which does not arise cleanly from simple combination of the two stated fragments. The mass balance is incorrect: the anhydride O=C1C=C(O)C(=O)O1 (C3H2O4) plus the quinolone (C17H15NO2) does not straightforwardly map onto the product, requiring ring-opening of the anhydride concurrent with C-C bond formation, which is not a well-defined single step. (2) Direct C-3 functionalization of a 4-quinolone with such an electrophile would require enolization or metalation and lacks precedent for this exact bond construction. (3) The reactive maleic-anhydride-derived enol fragment is itself problematic (see 8ddf101907f751c9a79649b224be1483cac109da6390ab6ff25ae59722d9893f). Overall this is a poorly defined, low-precedent disconnection. A more rational approach would build the C-3 substituent via a Claisen/acylation on a preformed 4-quinolone-3-carbonyl system or via a 1,3-diketone/oxaloacetate-type condensation with defined reagents.

The transformation of 4-methoxy maleic anhydride (COC1=CC(=O)OC1=O, a methyl enol ether of oxaloacetic-type anhydride) to the free enol 'O=C1C=C(O)C(=O)O1' (hydroxymaleic anhydride / 2-hydroxymaleic anhydride) implies demethylation of an enol ether to the free enol while retaining the highly strained, reactive anhydride. This species is essentially the tautomer of oxaloacetic anhydride and is extremely unstable/reactive; isolation is impractical. Furthermore, simple O-demethylation reagents (BBr3, etc.) would also attack the anhydride. The product is not a viable, isolable intermediate. This step is chemically dubious.

N-alkylation of 4-quinolone (O=c1cc[nH]c2ccccc12) with 2-methoxybenzyl chloride (COc1ccccc1CCl) to give the N-benzyl quinolone is a reasonable and well-precedented transformation, typically using base (K2CO3, Cs2CO3) in DMF. The main caveat is the classic O- vs N-alkylation ambiguity of 4-quinolones/4-pyridones: alkylation can give significant O-alkylated (4-alkoxyquinoline) byproduct depending on base, solvent, and counterion. With appropriate conditions (e.g., Cs2CO3/DMF or Ag2O) N-selectivity is usually favored. Benzyl chloride is reactive enough; benzyl bromide would be a slightly better electrophile. Both starting materials are commercially available. Overall feasible with attention to regioselectivity.

This disconnection proposes a Friedel-Crafts/Michael-type coupling between the 4-quinolone (COc1ccccc1Cn1ccc(=O)c2ccccc21) and a reactive 2-hydroxymaleic anhydride fragment (O=C1C=C(O)C(=O)O1) to install the acyclic 1,3-dicarbonyl side chain (C(=O)C=C(O)C(=O)O). However, the product SMILES shows an open-chain diketo-acid, not an anhydride, so the ring-opening of the proposed anhydride electrophile must occur, AND a new C-C bond must form at the C3 position of the quinolone. The fragments do not balance: the product has an extra C(=O)C=C(O)C(=O)O moiety that cannot be derived from O=C1C=C(O)C(=O)O1 by a simple C–C bond formation without major reorganization. The regiochemistry, the unselective electrophilic substitution at C3 of an N-substituted 4-quinolone, and the lability/tautomerization of a 2-hydroxymaleic anhydride make this transformation highly implausible as a clean, predictable step. A more rational disconnection would involve a Claisen-type condensation of a 3-acetyl-4-quinolone with a diethyl oxalate equivalent, or acylation chemistry, rather than this anhydride pairing.

This step proposes converting methoxy-maleic anhydride (COC1=CC(=O)OC1=O) into 2-hydroxy-maleic anhydride/tetronic-type species (O=C1C=C(O)C(=O)O1) by demethylation of an enol ether. While O-demethylation of a vinyl methyl ether is conceivable (e.g., with BBr3 or TMSI), the resulting free enol within a strained, highly electrophilic maleic anhydride would be extremely unstable and prone to tautomerization, hydrolysis, and ring-opening. The product is essentially the enol tautomer of an oxaloacetic anhydride and is not a stable, isolable building block. This is not a reliable preparative transformation.

N-Alkylation of the 4-quinolone (O=c1cc[nH]c2ccccc12) with 2-methoxybenzyl chloride (COc1ccccc1CCl) is a well-precedented transformation. Deprotonation of the quinolone NH with a base such as K2CO3 or Cs2CO3 in DMF, followed by reaction with the benzylic chloride, gives N-benzylation cleanly. The main selectivity concern is N- vs O-alkylation (4-quinolones can alkylate on oxygen), which can be controlled by base/solvent choice; under typical conditions N-alkylation predominates. Both starting materials are commercially available. This step is sound.

This disconnection joins a 4-quinolone (unsubstituted at C-3) with the cyclic enol-anhydride O=C1C=C(O)C(=O)O1 to give an open-chain tricarbonyl product C(=O)C=C(O)C(=O)O at C-3. The atom mapping is inconsistent: a cyclic anhydride cannot simply ring-open and attach to the electron-rich C-3 of a vinylogous amide quinolone under any single well-defined transformation. There is no clear mechanistic pathway (acylation, Michael, etc.) that produces this exact connectivity and oxidation state. C-3 functionalization of 4-quinolones is feasible (e.g., via Friedel-Crafts acylation or directed metalation), but not with this reagent to give this product. The disconnection should be reconsidered, likely building the C-3 acyl chain via a Claisen-type acylation of a C-3 ester/ketone enolate.

N-alkylation of 4-quinolone (O=c1cc[nH]c2ccccc12, 4-hydroxyquinoline tautomer) with 2-methoxybenzyl chloride is well-precedented. Deprotonation of the quinolone N-H (e.g., with K2CO3 or Cs2CO3 in DMF) followed by alkylation gives the N-benzyl quinolone. Note potential O- vs N-alkylation selectivity (4-quinolones can give O-alkyl products), so base/solvent choice matters; under thermodynamic conditions N-alkylation typically dominates. Both starting materials are commercially available.

The transformation of methoxy maleic anhydride (COC1=CC(=O)OC1=O) to the hydroxy enol-anhydride O=C1C=C(O)C(=O)O1 is not a standard, clean reaction. Demethylation of a vinyl ether/enol ether to the enol within a sensitive maleic anhydride framework would face serious chemoselectivity and stability issues (anhydride hydrolysis, ring-opening). Moreover, the product fragment's role in the overall synthesis (per 8a7fa7d2013c3e9b704379bae98a43a31f996e185cf048f4bd1bf7dd2d328f54) is itself dubious. This step does not represent a reliable disconnection.

This disconnection is highly problematic. The product shows a 1,3-diketo acid side chain (C(=O)C=C(O)C(=O)O, an enol of a 1,3-dicarbonyl) attached at the 3-position of the 4-quinolone. The retrosynthesis proposes coupling the 4-quinolone (COc1ccccc1Cn1ccc(=O)c2ccccc21) with a cyclic anhydride/keto-lactone fragment (O=C1C=C(O)C(=O)O1). There is no straightforward, well-precedented reaction that takes the parent 4-quinolone (with an unsubstituted C-3) and a maleic-anhydride-type oxo-furanone and forms a C-C bond at C-3 to install this open-chain 2-oxo-glutaconate-type chain. A C-3 acylation (Friedel-Crafts-type or directed C-H functionalization) of the electron-rich enamine-like C-3 of the 4-quinolone might in principle occur, but the regiochemistry, ring-opening of the furanone to the open-chain product, and control of the enol tautomer make this implausible as drawn. The mass balance is also suspect since the furanone fragment would need to ring-open to give the C(=O)C=C(O)C(=O)O chain. This should be re-thought, e.g., as a Claisen-type acylation of the quinolone C-3 enolate or direct installation of a beta-ketoester followed by functionalization.

This step proposes converting methoxy-substituted glutaconic anhydride (COC1=CC(=O)OC1=O) into the hydroxy oxo-furanone (O=C1C=C(O)C(=O)O1) by demethylation. The product as drawn is a 5-membered ring (furan-2,3-dione type / a 4-hydroxy form) while the reactant COC1=CC(=O)OC1=O is a 5-membered maleic-anhydride-type ring with a methoxy group. The transformation as written (loss of the methyl to give the free enol/hydroxy) is essentially a demethylation of a vinyl ether on a highly reactive anhydride. Such a species (O=C1C=C(O)C(=O)O1) is an unstable, highly reactive tautomer and is unlikely to be a discrete isolable intermediate. The disconnection does not represent a sound, isolable transformation.

N-alkylation of the 4-quinolone NH (O=c1cc[nH]c2ccccc12) with 2-methoxybenzyl chloride (COc1ccccc1CCl) is a well-precedented transformation. Deprotonation of the quinolone NH with a base (K2CO3, Cs2CO3, NaH) followed by alkylation with the benzylic chloride proceeds smoothly. N- vs O-alkylation selectivity should be considered (4-quinolones can undergo O-alkylation), but under standard conditions (K2CO3/DMF) N-alkylation typically predominates. Both starting materials are commercially available. Minor caveat: chemoselectivity (N- vs O-) could lower yield but the disconnection is sound.

This step proposes the reduction of an amide carbonyl (C(=O)N of the piperazine amide) to a methylene (CH2) to install the aminomethyl tether. While amide-to-amine reduction is feasible (e.g., LiAlH4, BH3, or Red-Al), the substrate also contains an oxindole/2-indolinone lactam (C(=O)Nc2ccccc21). Selective reduction of the acyclic tertiary amide in the presence of the cyclic aromatic-fused amide (oxindole) would be extremely challenging. Both are amides and standard reducing agents (LiAlH4, BH3) would reduce or partially reduce the oxindole carbonyl as well, destroying the desired product. This represents a serious chemoselectivity problem. A better strategy would be to construct the C-N bond by reductive amination or alkylation of the piperazine with a pendant alkyl halide/aldehyde tether installed prior, rather than reducing one of two amides selectively.

This step proposes alkylation of the oxindole C3 quaternary center with ethyl bromide to set the quaternary carbon bearing both ethyl and the alkyl chain. The disconnection itself (C-alkylation at C3 of an oxindole to form a quaternary center) is a reasonable and well-precedented strategy using a strong base (e.g., NaH, LDA, KOtBu) to generate the stabilized C3 enolate, followed by alkylation with EtBr. However, the substrate already bears a C3-H mono-substituted oxindole with an existing alkyl chain (CCCC(=O)-piperazine). Deprotonation/alkylation should proceed, but there is concern about chemoselectivity: the substrate has an acidic N-H amide (oxindole NH) and a tertiary amide. The N-H would be deprotonated first by strong base, requiring 2 equivalents, and O- vs C-alkylation selectivity must be controlled. Also, base could deprotonate alpha to the tertiary amide carbonyl. With careful conditions (e.g., NaH then EtBr, or phase-transfer), the C3 quaternization is achievable. Reagent (EtBr) is appropriate and commercially available, as is the building block precursor. Confidence reflects the moderate selectivity risk.

This step proposes reduction of an amide carbonyl (the CCCC(=O)N piperazine amide) to a methylene (CH2-N), converting a tertiary amide to a tertiary amine, while leaving the oxindole lactam C(=O)N intact. This chemoselectivity is essentially impossible: standard amide-to-amine reductions (LiAlH4, BH3, etc.) would also reduce or significantly affect the oxindole amide carbonyl. The two amides are electronically similar enough that selective reduction of only the aliphatic amide cannot be reliably achieved. A better strategy would be to install the saturated aminobutyl chain via reductive amination or N-alkylation of the arylpiperazine with a pre-formed alkyl halide/aldehyde tethered to the oxindole, rather than reducing one of two amides selectively.

This step is the C-alkylation of the oxindole C3 position with ethyl bromide to form the quaternary center. Two major issues: (1) Chemoselectivity - the substrate contains an N-H oxindole (lactam N-H) which is more acidic and would be deprotonated/alkylated preferentially over the C3 position; N-alkylation competes strongly. (2) The C3 position already bears the long aminoalkyl-amide chain, so deprotonation at C3 with a strong base (e.g., NaH, LDA, KOtBu) followed by EtBr alkylation could in principle install the quaternary ethyl group, but the basic tertiary amine and amide functionalities present compatibility concerns. Practically, the quaternary C3 ethyl group is best installed early (e.g., on a 3-ethyloxindole) before chain elaboration, and N-protection of the oxindole nitrogen would be needed to ensure C- vs N-selectivity. As drawn, N-alkylation and over-alkylation are likely competing pathways.

This step proposes reduction of a tertiary amide carbonyl (C(=O)N-piperazine) to a methylene (CH2-N) to convert the amide into the corresponding aminoalkyl chain. While amide-to-amine reduction is feasible in principle (e.g., LiAlH4, borane, or related hydride reductants), the substrate also contains an oxindole (2-oxindole, lactam) carbonyl, which is far more reactive/comparably reactive toward hydride reducing agents. Selective reduction of the tertiary aliphatic amide in the presence of the anilide/oxindole lactam is highly unlikely. The oxindole C(=O) would be reduced or partially reduced as well, leading to a chemoselectivity failure. As written, this transformation would not cleanly deliver the target. A better strategy would build the aminoalkyl chain via reductive amination or N-alkylation of the piperazine with a halide/aldehyde bearing the preformed oxindole quaternary center, avoiding selective amide reduction altogether.

This step proposes C-alkylation of the oxindole C3 position with ethyl bromide to install the quaternary ethyl group, generating the 3,3-disubstituted oxindole. The disconnection of the quaternary center via enolate alkylation is strategically reasonable and well precedented for oxindoles (deprotonation at C3 with base such as NaH/LiHMDS, then alkylation with EtBr). However, the substrate as drawn (precursor before this alkylation) is a 3-monosubstituted oxindole bearing an acidic N-H and an acidic C3-H, plus a tertiary amide. Major selectivity issues: (1) competing N-alkylation of the oxindole nitrogen vs C-alkylation; the N-H must be addressed (often N-protection or use of conditions favoring C-alkylation); (2) the C3 already bears a long alkyl chain, so dialkylation/regiocontrol is the goal, but over-alkylation or O-alkylation can compete. Use of a suitable base and possibly N-protection (e.g., Boc) would improve selectivity. Reagent choice (EtBr) is reasonable. Overall feasible but requires careful control of N- vs C-selectivity.

This step proposes reduction of a tertiary amide carbonyl (the C(=O)-N of the piperazine amide) to a CH2 group, converting the amide into an amine while leaving the oxindole lactam (C(=O)-Nc2ccccc21) intact. This chemoselectivity is essentially impossible to achieve. Reducing agents capable of reducing a tertiary amide to an amine (e.g., LiAlH4, BH3, or Red-Al) would either also reduce the oxindole lactam carbonyl or interfere with it. There is no straightforward reagent that selectively reduces one amide in the presence of another secondary amide. Additionally, BH3 would reduce the more electron-rich (more nucleophilic nitrogen) amide preferentially, and the oxindole carbonyl is itself susceptible. A better strategy would be to construct the amine linkage via reductive amination or N-alkylation rather than amide reduction. As drawn, this is a severe chemoselectivity problem amounting to an unfeasible disconnection.

This step proposes alkylation with ethyl bromide (CCBr) to install the ethyl group on the quaternary carbon of the oxindole. The retrosynthetic logic implies deprotonation at the oxindole C3 position and C-alkylation with EtBr. However, the precursor drawn (COc1cccc(N2CCN(C(=O)CCCC3C(=O)Nc4ccccc43)CC2)c1) already bears a substituent (the butanoyl chain) at C3, so alkylation would form the quaternary center — this is plausible in principle. The bigger concern is regioselectivity and competing N-alkylation: the oxindole has both an acidic N-H and an acidic C3-H. Treatment with base and EtBr could give O-, N-, or C-alkylation. To favor C-alkylation, the lactam N-H typically needs protection or careful base/conditions (e.g., NaH then EtBr, or use of bulky bases). Also, deprotonation of the amide N-H competes. Without protecting the lactam nitrogen, selective C3-ethylation to form the quaternary center is challenging. The disconnection is reasonable but suffers from selectivity issues; a protecting group on the lactam N would improve it.

This is a classic amide bond formation (disconnection) between 4-aminoindole and a benzothiophene-2-carboxylic acid bearing a bromo substituent. The forward direction would be a standard amide coupling using reagents such as EDC/HOBt, HATU, T3P, or via acid chloride activation. The 4-aminoindole nucleophile is the aniline-type amine; the indole NH is far less nucleophilic and would not significantly compete under standard coupling conditions, so chemoselectivity favors acylation of the primary aromatic amine. The aryl bromide is fully compatible with amide coupling conditions. One minor consideration: the indole NH is unprotected, but in amide couplings the activated acid reacts preferentially with the more nucleophilic exocyclic amine; over-acylation of the indole nitrogen is generally not a major problem, especially with controlled stoichiometry. Both building blocks are reasonable: 4-aminoindole is commercially available, and 5-bromobenzothiophene-2-carboxylic acid (or close analogues) are commercially accessible or readily prepared. Overall a sound, single-step disconnection.

This is a classic amide bond formation between 4-aminoindole (Nc1cccc2[nH]ccc12) and a benzothiophene-2-carboxylic acid bearing a bromo substituent. The disconnection at the amide C-N bond is the most logical and well-precedented strategy. Standard coupling conditions (e.g., HATU, EDC/HOBt, T3P, or conversion to the acid chloride followed by reaction with the amine in the presence of a base) would deliver the target. Chemoselectivity is favorable: the indole NH is far less nucleophilic than the arylamine, so acylation should occur predominantly on the more nucleophilic aromatic amine, though a slight excess of acid/coupling agent and mild conditions are advisable to minimize any potential N-indole acylation. The aryl bromide is inert under these conditions and is preserved for potential downstream functionalization. Both building blocks are reasonable; 4-aminoindole is commercially available, and the brominated benzothiophene-2-carboxylic acid is either commercial or readily accessible. Main yield-limiting factors would be the modest nucleophilicity of the aniline (electron-rich but conjugated into the indole) and potential need to avoid over-acylation. Overall a robust, high-confidence transformation.

This is a classic amide bond formation between a carboxylic acid (5-bromobenzothiophene-2-carboxylic acid) and a primary aromatic amine (4-aminoindole). The disconnection at the amide C-N bond is the most logical and strategic choice. Standard coupling reagents such as HATU, EDC/HOBt, T3P, or conversion to the acid chloride (e.g., via oxalyl chloride or SOCl2) followed by reaction with the amine would all be viable. One consideration: the indole N-H is free and could in principle compete, but aniline-type amines are far more nucleophilic on the exocyclic NH2 than the indole N-H, and the indole N-H is a poor nucleophile under these conditions, so chemoselectivity should strongly favor the desired exocyclic amide. The 4-aminoindole is somewhat electron-rich, which actually enhances its nucleophilicity for the coupling. The aryl bromide is fully compatible with amide coupling conditions. Both starting materials are commercially available and listed as in stock. Mild bases (e.g., DIPEA, Et3N) and standard conditions should give good yields. Acid chloride route may require care due to the free indole N-H, so coupling-reagent-mediated conditions (HATU/DIPEA) are preferable.

This is a standard amide coupling between 4-aminoindole (Nc1cccc2[nH]ccc12) and a benzothiophene-2-carboxylic acid bearing a bromo substituent. The disconnection at the amide C-N bond is textbook retrosynthesis and well-precedented. The transformation can be accomplished with standard peptide/amide coupling reagents (e.g., HATU, EDC/HOBt, T3P, or via the acid chloride). Selectivity considerations: the indole N-H is far less nucleophilic than the aromatic amine, so chemoselective acylation at the exocyclic aryl amine is expected, though under acid chloride conditions some N1-acylation of the indole could compete and may require mild conditions or slight excess control. The aryl bromide is fully compatible with amide coupling conditions and is preserved for potential downstream functionalization. No protecting groups are needed. Both fragments are reasonable; the carboxylic acid may need to be synthesized but is plausibly accessible. Overall a clean, efficient disconnection.

This is a well-precedented hydantoin synthesis. The reaction between an α-amino ester (methyl 2-((4-bromophenyl)amino)-2-phenylacetate) and an aryl isocyanate (4-bromophenyl isocyanate) gives a urea intermediate, which then cyclizes with the ester via intramolecular cyclization (loss of methanol) to form the hydantoin (imidazolidine-2,4-dione) ring. The secondary amine adds to the isocyanate to form the urea, and subsequent base-mediated or thermal cyclization closes the 5-membered ring. The two aryl bromides are inert under these conditions and pose no chemoselectivity issues. This forms a 1,3,5-trisubstituted hydantoin matching the target. A minor consideration is the potential for epimerization at the benzylic stereocenter, but the product appears to be racemic/non-stereodefined so this is not a concern.

This is a straightforward SN2 amine alkylation/substitution. 4-Bromoaniline displaces the benzylic bromide of methyl 2-bromo-2-phenylacetate (methyl α-bromophenylacetate) to give the α-arylamino ester. The benzylic α-bromo ester is highly activated toward SN2 by both the ester and the adjacent phenyl, making this displacement facile. Both starting materials are commercially available and inexpensive. Possible side reactions include over-alkylation (dialkylation of the aniline) and competing O-alkylation/elimination, but these are typically minor; using excess aniline or controlled stoichiometry mitigates dialkylation. The aryl bromide on aniline is inert toward the soft benzylic electrophile under these conditions. Mild base (e.g., K2CO3, Et3N) and heating in a polar aprotic solvent would be appropriate.

This is the key ring-forming step constructing the hydantoin (imidazolidine-2,4-dione) core. The disconnection is sound: reacting an α-amino ester (COC(=O)C(Nc1ccc(Br)cc1)c1ccccc1) with an aryl isocyanate (O=C=Nc1ccc(Br)cc1) gives a urea intermediate that undergoes intramolecular cyclization with loss of methanol to form the hydantoin. This is a well-established hydantoin synthesis. One consideration: the secondary amine nitrogen is the nucleophile that attacks the isocyanate, forming the urea, and then the resulting urea N-H cyclizes onto the ester. The reaction typically requires mild base or heating to drive cyclization. A minor concern is that the new stereocenter at C5 is formed/retained as a racemate, but since the target appears to be racemic (no stereochemistry specified), this is acceptable. Overall a clean, convergent step with no protecting-group issues.

This is an SN2 N-alkylation of 4-bromoaniline with methyl α-bromophenylacetate (COC(=O)C(Br)c1ccccc1) to give the α-arylamino ester. The benzylic/α-ester bromide is activated toward substitution by both the adjacent ester carbonyl and the phenyl group, so displacement by the aniline nitrogen proceeds readily. A mild base (e.g., K2CO3, Et3N) is typically used to neutralize HBr. Potential side reactions: over-alkylation (dialkylation) of the aniline can be limited by using excess aniline; competing elimination is not relevant here (no β-hydrogens for E2 on this scaffold). The aryl-Br is untouched under these conditions. Both starting materials are commercially available and inexpensive. Note the product is formed as a racemate, consistent with the racemic target.

This is a well-precedented cyclization strategy to form a hydantoin (imidazolidine-2,4-dione) ring. The secondary amine of the amino ester adds to the isocyanate to form a urea intermediate, which then undergoes intramolecular cyclization with the methyl ester to close the five-membered ring and expel methanol. The reaction is typically promoted by base (e.g., Et3N) or thermal conditions. Both the urea formation and the subsequent lactamization are reliable transformations. The disconnection is strategically sound, building the hydantoin core from a secondary amine and an aryl isocyanate. One consideration: the secondary aniline nitrogen is somewhat hindered and electron-poor (attached to a 4-bromophenyl), which could slow urea formation, but this is well within normal operating conditions. The aryl bromides are inert under these conditions.

This is a straightforward N-alkylation (nucleophilic substitution) of 4-bromoaniline onto an activated benzylic bromide (methyl 2-bromo-2-phenylacetate). The benzylic position is highly activated toward SN2 by both the adjacent ester and aryl group, and aniline is a competent nucleophile. The reaction should proceed readily, often with a mild base to neutralize HBr. Potential concerns: (1) over-alkylation to form the tertiary amine, which can be mitigated by using excess aniline; (2) competing elimination is not relevant here as there is no beta-hydrogen suitable for E2 in a problematic way; (3) possible racemization is irrelevant since the product is used in a subsequent cyclization and stereochemistry at that center is not defined in the target. Both starting materials are commercially available. A good, robust step.

This is a classic hydantoin synthesis via reaction of an α-amino ester with an isocyanate. The amino nitrogen attacks the isocyanate to form a urea intermediate, which then undergoes intramolecular cyclization (the secondary amide nitrogen attacks the ester carbonyl) to release methanol and form the 5-membered hydantoin ring. The disconnection is sound and well-precedented. The 4-bromophenyl isocyanate is reactive and commercially available. One consideration: the cyclization requires base or heat to drive lactamization, and the existing aniline nitrogen (the one bearing the amino ester) is somewhat deactivated by the aryl group, but this is a standard and reliable route to 1,3,5-trisubstituted hydantoins. Regiochemistry of cyclization is well-controlled by the geometry. Minor competing side reaction could be over-reaction with a second equivalent of isocyanate, controllable by stoichiometry.

This step is an SN2 substitution of the benzylic α-bromo ester (methyl α-bromophenylacetate) by 4-bromoaniline to form the α-amino ester. Both starting materials are commercially available and inexpensive, making this an attractive disconnection. The benzylic α-bromo position is reasonably activated toward nucleophilic substitution. However, there are notable challenges: (1) Anilines are weak nucleophiles, and competing N,N-dialkylation can give bis-substituted products, requiring excess amine or careful stoichiometry. (2) The α-bromo ester is prone to elimination/Hofmann-type side reactions and the resulting product is racemic (which is acceptable here since the final hydantoin stereocenter is not specified). (3) Potential competing E2 or hydrolysis of the activated benzylic halide. The transformation will work but yields may be moderate; using a mild base and excess aniline or controlled conditions is advisable. Overall a reasonable and direct disconnection.

This step represents sulfamoylation of a secondary amine to install the sulfamoyl group (N-SO2NH2). The reaction of a secondary amine with sulfamoyl chloride (ClSO2NH2) is a well-established method to form sulfamides. While the retrosynthesis shows sulfamide (H2NSO2NH2) as the synthon, in practice the reagent would be sulfamoyl chloride or a related electrophilic sulfamoylating agent (e.g., generated in situ from chlorosulfonyl isocyanate followed by hydrolysis, or Burgess-type reagents). The secondary amine is the only nucleophilic site, so chemoselectivity is not a concern. The methoxy groups are inert under these conditions. Confidence is high, though the exact sulfamoylating reagent should be specified rather than free sulfamide.

This step proposes a tandem reduction/cyclization to form the tetrahydroisoquinoline core from an N-acyl phenethylamine (a Bischler-Napieralski / Pictet-Spengler-type approach). The amide C(=O) is reduced and a new C-C bond forms to the aromatic ring at the position ortho to one methoxy and meta to the other. Mechanistically, this resembles a Bischler-Napieralski cyclodehydration (POCl3, P2O5, or Tf2O) to form a 3,4-dihydroisoquinoline (cyclic imine bearing the cyclopentyl substituent), followed by reduction (NaBH4) to the tetrahydroisoquinoline. The electron-rich dimethoxyarene strongly activates the ring toward this electrophilic cyclization, and the regiochemistry shown (cyclization para to one OMe) is electronically favored, so the disconnection is sound. However: (1) the transformation as written combines two operations (cyclization + reduction) into one retrosynthetic step, which should be flagged; (2) the product bears a new stereocenter at the benzylic position which would be formed as a racemate with no stereocontrol; (3) the starting amide COc1ccc(CCNC(=O)C2CCCC2)cc1OC is plausibly accessible (from homoveratrylamine + cyclopentanecarbonyl chloride) and is reasonably available. Overall a viable but two-step transformation requiring careful regiochemical/conditions control.

The sulfamoylation of a secondary amine with sulfamide (NS(N)(=O)=O) or sulfamoyl chloride is a well-established transformation to install the N-sulfamoyl (NSO2NH2) group. Using sulfuryl-based reagents, the secondary tetrahydroisoquinoline-type amine should react chemoselectively. The use of sulfamide as the depicted reagent can work, though sulfamoyl chloride or N-protected sulfamoyl chlorides (e.g., from chlorosulfonyl isocyanate) are often more practical and higher-yielding. The amine is the most nucleophilic site, and the methoxy groups are inert, so chemoselectivity is good. Minor consideration: direct reaction with sulfamide typically requires forcing conditions (heating), so reagent optimization may be warranted.

This step constitutes a Bischler-Napieralski-type cyclization followed by reduction, or more directly a reductive Pictet-Spengler/intramolecular cyclization to build the tetrahydroisoquinoline core from the amide-tethered electron-rich arene. The amide COc1ccc(CCNC(=O)C2CCCC2)cc1OC can undergo Bischler-Napieralski cyclodehydration (POCl3, P2O5, or Tf2O) to form a 3,4-dihydroisoquinoline, which is then reduced (NaBH4) to give the tetrahydroisoquinoline. The electron-rich dimethoxyarene is well-suited to this electrophilic cyclization, and the regiochemistry (para/ortho to the methoxy groups) is favorable, leading to the observed substitution pattern. This is a classic and reliable disconnection. Note that the route compresses two operations (cyclization + reduction) into one retrosynthetic step, which is acceptable but should be recognized as two synthetic operations.

This is a sulfamoylation of a secondary amine to install the sulfamoyl group (-SO2NH2). The disconnection of the N-S bond to give the free secondary amine and sulfamide (NS(N)(=O)=O) is reasonable. In practice, sulfamoylation of secondary amines is typically achieved using sulfamoyl chloride (ClSO2NH2) or sulfuryl diamide-based reagents, or via in situ generated reagents (e.g., from chlorosulfonyl isocyanate). Using sulfamide directly is possible under forcing thermal conditions but often gives modest yields. The secondary amine here is sterically hindered (benzylic, adjacent to cyclopentyl), which may further reduce efficiency. The dimethoxy aromatic and cyclopentyl groups are compatible. A more optimal reagent would be sulfamoyl chloride or a Burgess-type/tert-butyl carbamate-protected sulfamoyl chloride followed by deprotection.

This step proposes construction of the tetrahydroisoquinoline core via a Bischler-Napieralski-type cyclization of the amide followed by reduction, or a direct intramolecular Friedel-Crafts/Pictet-Spengler-like cyclization. The amide COc1ccc(CCNC(=O)C2CCCC2)cc1OC would cyclize to a 3,4-dihydroisoquinoline (cyclic imine bearing the cyclopentyl substituent at C1), which upon reduction gives the target secondary amine. This is a well-precedented Bischler-Napieralski sequence (POCl3, P2O5, or Tf2O, then NaBH4 reduction). The main concern is regioselectivity of the electrophilic cyclization: with the 3,4-dimethoxy substitution pattern shown, cyclization can occur para or ortho to the activating methoxy groups, and the product drawn requires ring closure at the position between the two methoxy-bearing carbons / at the correct site. For 3,4-dimethoxyphenethylamine-derived substrates, cyclization is strongly favored at the 6-position (para to one OMe), which generally gives the desired 6,7-dimethoxytetrahydroisoquinoline regiochemistry consistent with the target. So regiochemistry is usually manageable, but it must be considered. Note the route shows a single-step conversion (amide directly to cyclic amine) which actually encompasses two operations (cyclodehydration + imine reduction). Overall feasible but should be drawn as two steps; this also explains the labeling as feasible with selectivity caveats.

This is a sulfamoylation of a secondary amine to install the sulfamoyl group (-SO2NH2). The reaction of a secondary amine with sulfamoyl chloride (H2N-SO2-Cl) or with sulfamide derivatives is a well-established method to form N-sulfamoyl amines. Note that the retrosynthesis shows sulfamide (NS(N)(=O)=O = H2N-SO2-NH2) as the partner; in practice, the more common reagent would be sulfamoyl chloride or activated sulfamides (e.g., from chlorosulfonyl isocyanate-derived chemistry, or Burgess-type reagents). Direct use of unsubstituted sulfamide would require forcing conditions and may suffer from selectivity issues, but the disconnection itself (C-N bond between amine nitrogen and sulfamoyl group) is sound. The methoxy groups and tetrahydroisoquinoline core are compatible. Minor concern over exact reagent choice.

This step represents a Bischler-Napieralski-type cyclization followed by reduction (or a reductive cyclization) to form the tetrahydroisoquinoline ring from the N-acyl phenethylamine precursor. The amide COc1ccc(CCNC(=O)C2CCCC2)cc1OC can undergo POCl3/P2O5-mediated cyclodehydration onto the electron-rich dimethoxyarene to give the 3,4-dihydroisoquinoline (with the cyclopentyl-bearing carbon as imine), followed by reduction (NaBH4) to the tetrahydroisoquinoline bearing the cyclopentyl substituent. The 6,7-dimethoxy substitution pattern strongly activates the ring para/ortho to direct cyclization to the correct position, which is classic for this reaction class. Regioselectivity is favorable due to the electron-donating methoxy groups. One caveat: the retrosynthesis collapses cyclization + reduction into a single step, but mechanistically this is a robust and highly precedented transformation. Starting material is commercially accessible or readily prepared.

This is a textbook amide coupling disconnection. The product is formed from a quinoline-4-carboxylic acid and N,N-dimethylethylenediamine. The reaction is well-established and would proceed readily using standard coupling reagents (e.g., HATU, EDC/HOBt, T3P) with a base such as DIPEA. Chemoselectivity is excellent: the primary amine is far more nucleophilic than the tertiary dimethylamino group, so coupling occurs cleanly at the primary nitrogen without need for protection. No competing functional groups (the aryl chloride and pyridine nitrogen are inert under these conditions). Both starting materials are simple and the carboxylic acid quinoline core is readily accessible. A slight excess of the diamine could lead to minor bis-acylation only if the acid were activated in excess, but standard stoichiometry avoids this. Overall a robust, high-yielding final step.

This is a standard amide coupling between a carboxylic acid (quinoline-4-carboxylic acid derivative) and a primary amine (N,N-dimethylethylenediamine). The disconnection at the amide C-N bond is textbook retrosynthesis. The reaction would proceed readily using standard coupling reagents (e.g., HATU, EDC/HOBt, T3P, or via acid chloride). Chemoselectivity is favorable: the primary amine of N,N-dimethylethylenediamine is far more nucleophilic than the tertiary dimethylamino group, so selective acylation at the primary amine is expected without protection. No competing functional groups (the aryl chloride and quinoline N are inert under amide coupling conditions). Both starting materials are reasonable building blocks; the quinoline-4-carboxylic acid bearing a 2-phenyl and 6-chloro substituent may need to be sourced or made (e.g., via Pfitzinger or Doebner-type chemistry), but it is plausibly commercially available or readily accessible.

This is a classic amide coupling disconnection between a primary amine (N,N-dimethylethylenediamine) and a quinoline-4-carboxylic acid. The disconnection is strategic and ideal as the final step. The amine partner CN(C)CCN is monofunctional (the tertiary dimethylamino group is non-nucleophilic enough to compete significantly with the primary amine, and even if it did, it cannot form a stable amide), so chemoselectivity strongly favors the primary amine. Standard coupling reagents (HATU, EDC/HOBt, T3P, or CDI) with a base such as DIPEA would deliver the desired amide cleanly. No protecting groups are needed. The aryl chloride and quinoline nitrogen are fully compatible. Both starting materials are commercially available. The only minor consideration is potential slight excess of acid or coupling reagent to avoid bis-acylation, but in practice this transformation is robust and high-yielding.

This is a classic amide coupling disconnection between a carboxylic acid (2-phenyl-6-chloroquinoline-4-carboxylic acid) and N,N-dimethylethylenediamine. The disconnection is appropriate and chemically sound. Standard coupling reagents such as HATU, EDC/HOBt, or T3P with a base (DIPEA or Et3N) would effect this transformation cleanly. Chemoselectivity is excellent: the primary amine of N,N-dimethylethylenediamine reacts preferentially over the tertiary dimethylamino group, so no protecting group is needed. The quinoline nitrogen and aryl chloride are inert under these conditions. Both starting materials are commercially available and inexpensive. Minor consideration: a slight excess of the diamine should be used to avoid bis-acylation, but selectivity strongly favors the primary amine.

This is a standard sulfamoylation of an aromatic amine using sulfamoyl chloride (NH2SO2Cl) to form the sulfamide (NHSO2NH2). The aniline nitrogen is the most nucleophilic site, and the reaction is well-precedented, typically run in the presence of a mild base (e.g., pyridine, Et3N, or NaH/DMA) to scavenge HCl. Chemoselectivity is good: the nitrile is unreactive toward sulfamoyl chloride under standard conditions, and the aniline is the clear nucleophile. One practical consideration is that sulfamoyl chloride is unstable and is often generated in situ or used freshly prepared; alternatives such as in-situ generated H2N-SO2-Cl from chlorosulfonyl isocyanate (CSI) followed by hydrolysis, or t-BuOC(O)NHSO2Cl (Burgess-type/Boc-protected sulfamoyl chloride) followed by deprotection, are commonly used to improve handling and yields. Mild over-reaction (bis-sulfamoylation) is unlikely given the deactivated, sterically encumbered aniline. Overall a clean, high-confidence final step.

This is a classic sulfamoylation of an aromatic primary amine using sulfamoyl chloride (NH2SO2Cl) to install the sulfamoyl group (-NHSO2NH2). The transformation is well-precedented and typically conducted in the presence of a base (e.g., pyridine, Et3N, or DBU) in an aprotic solvent (DCM, THF, or dioxane). Chemoselectivity is favorable: the aromatic amine is the only nucleophilic site, while the nitrile and aryl-CF3 groups are inert under these conditions. One practical consideration is that sulfamoyl chloride is unstable and reactive; it is often generated in situ or used freshly. The aniline here is somewhat electron-poor (ortho-nitrile, para-aryl), which slightly reduces nucleophilicity, but the reaction should still proceed in good yield. No protecting groups are required.

This is a sulfamoylation of a primary aniline using sulfamoyl chloride (NH2SO2Cl) to form the N-aryl sulfamide. The transformation is well-precedented; aniline nitrogen is nucleophilic and reacts with sulfamoyl chloride to give the desired N-(aryl)sulfamide. Typically performed with a base (e.g., pyridine, Et3N, or NaH) in an aprotic solvent (THF, DCM, MeCN), often at 0 °C to RT. Chemoselectivity is good: the nitrile is inert under these conditions, and the aniline is the only nucleophilic site. Minor concerns: sulfamoyl chloride is moisture-sensitive and can be unstable/decompose, so freshly prepared or in situ generated reagent may be preferable; also possible over-reaction or bis-sulfamoylation is unlikely given a single primary amine. The aniline here is somewhat electron-poor (ortho-nitrile, biaryl substitution), which may modestly reduce nucleophilicity, but the reaction should still proceed in good yield with appropriate base. Both starting materials are reasonable; the aminobiphenyl-nitrile precursor is the more advanced fragment but plausibly accessible via Suzuki coupling.

This is a sulfamoylation of an aromatic amine using sulfamoyl chloride (H2N-SO2-Cl) to form the sulfamide (Ar-NH-SO2-NH2). This is a well-established transformation, typically carried out in the presence of a base (e.g., pyridine, Et3N, or NaH) in an aprotic solvent (THF, DCM, or DMA). The aniline nitrogen is a good nucleophile and reacts cleanly with sulfamoyl chloride. Functional group compatibility is good: the nitrile and trifluoromethyl groups are both inert under these conditions. One minor consideration is the relatively low nucleophilicity of this aniline due to the ortho-nitrile (electron-withdrawing) and biaryl substitution, which may slow the reaction, but it should still proceed with appropriate base and possibly mild heating. The disconnection is logical and the aniline starting material is a reasonable precursor. Both starting materials are listed as in stock.

This step proposes bromination of the parent thiouracil-naphthol scaffold using NBS to install the para-bromo group on the pendant phenyl ring. This disconnection is highly problematic for multiple reasons: (1) Severe regioselectivity issues - NBS is an electrophilic brominating agent that would preferentially attack the most electron-rich aromatic positions. The naphthol ring (with its activating hydroxyl group) and the electron-rich positions ortho/para to OH would be far more reactive than the unactivated pendant phenyl ring. Bromination would occur on the naphthol, NOT selectively on the distal phenyl. (2) Chemoselectivity issues - the thiocarbonyl (C=S) of the thiouracil is highly nucleophilic and very susceptible to oxidation/reaction with NBS, which is a known reagent for desulfurization and oxidation of thiones/thioureas. The C=S would likely be consumed preferentially. (3) The active methylene/methine benzylic CH2 linker could also undergo radical bromination under NBS conditions. Installing the aryl bromide is far better achieved by starting from a pre-brominated 4-bromophenyl building block earlier in the synthesis (e.g., using 4-bromophenyl-containing precursors in the heterocycle assembly). This late-stage NBS bromination as drawn is not feasible.

This step proposes installing the para-bromo substituent on the phenyl ring via NBS (N-bromosuccinimide) bromination of the parent compound bearing an unsubstituted phenyl group. There are several serious problems: (1) Chemoselectivity/regioselectivity is a major concern. The substrate contains multiple electron-rich aromatic systems, most notably the naphthol (a highly activated, electron-rich arene). NBS would preferentially brominate the naphthol ring (ortho/para to the phenolic OH) rather than the relatively electron-poor pendant phenyl group. (2) The thiouracil/thiocarbonyl moiety (C=S) is highly susceptible to oxidation/bromination by NBS, which is commonly used to desulfurize thioamides/thioureas and oxidize C=S groups. This would lead to destruction of the thione functionality. (3) Even if directed at the phenyl ring, electrophilic aromatic bromination of an unactivated phenyl substituent is sluggish and would not be selective for the para position over the naphthol. A far better strategy would be to introduce the 4-bromophenyl group already brominated, i.e., construct the pyrimidinone ring using a 4-bromophenyl-bearing building block rather than attempting late-stage selective bromination. The disconnection of the C–Br bond at this stage is strategically poor. Confidence in the infeasibility is high.

This step proposes NBS bromination of the parent thiouracil/naphthol compound to install the aryl bromide on the pendant phenyl ring. This disconnection is highly problematic for several reasons. (1) NBS is an electrophilic brominating agent, and the molecule contains a highly activated electron-rich naphthol ring (free phenol) which would be brominated MUCH faster than the unactivated, electronically neutral pendant phenyl group. Electrophilic aromatic bromination would occur ortho/para to the naphthol OH, not on the distal phenyl. (2) The thiocarbonyl (C=S) of the thiouracil is extremely susceptible to oxidation/halogenation by NBS; N-bromosuccinimide readily reacts with thioamides/thioureas to give desulfurization or S-bromination products, so the C=S would likely be consumed. (3) NBS can also brominate the activated benzylic CH2 linker via radical pathways. (4) Even ignoring chemoselectivity, regioselective para-bromination of an unactivated phenyl ring by NBS does not occur efficiently. The retro-disconnection (installing aryl-Br last by direct C–H bromination of a simple phenyl ring) is not viable. A far better strategy would be to build the ring with the 4-bromophenyl group already in place (e.g., use a 4-bromophenyl-substituted building block in the ring-forming/condensation step) rather than late-stage bromination. Confidence is high that as written this step fails.

This step proposes a late-stage NBS bromination to install the para-bromine on the pendant phenyl ring of the thiouracil. There are several serious problems with this disconnection: (1) Chemoselectivity: The substrate contains a thiocarbonyl (C=S) group, which is extremely reactive toward NBS and electrophilic brominating agents. Thioureas/thiouracils readily undergo S-oxidation/desulfurization or alpha-halogenation at sulfur rather than aromatic bromination. NBS would preferentially attack the soft, nucleophilic sulfur. (2) Regioselectivity: Even if aromatic bromination occurred, NBS without a Lewis acid catalyst (or radical initiator) typically does not cleanly brominate an unactivated benzene ring; the electron-rich naphthol ring would be far more reactive toward electrophilic aromatic substitution than the pendant phenyl. The naphthol (activated by OH) would be brominated preferentially, not the desired para position of the phenyl. (3) The benzylic CH2 linker is also susceptible to radical bromination (Wohl-Ziegler conditions) if NBS is used under radical conditions. Overall, this NBS bromination would give a complex mixture and is not a viable disconnection. A much better strategy would be to introduce the 4-bromophenyl group earlier as a pre-functionalized building block (e.g., via a 4-bromophenyl-bearing precursor in the thiouracil ring formation), avoiding late-stage selectivity problems entirely.

This is a standard sulfonamide formation between methyl pipecolate (secondary amine) and an aryl sulfonyl chloride. The disconnection is sound and well-precedented. The reaction would typically proceed with a base (e.g., Et3N, pyridine, or DIPEA) in DCM or THF. The secondary amine nucleophile is appropriate, and the methyl ester is fully compatible. One consideration: the sulfonyl chloride bearing an amide (NHC=O) functionality could in principle compete, but the aniline-derived amide N-H is far less nucleophilic and the chemoselectivity for the piperidine N-H should be excellent. No protecting groups needed.

local_feedback: Problems with reaction type and functional group compatibility
local_feedback_text: This disconnection proposes amide coupling between the pyrazole carboxylic acid and the aniline (4-aminobenzenesulfonyl chloride) to form the anilide. The problem is that the reactant 4-aminobenzenesulfonyl chloride bears a free sulfonyl chloride, which is highly reactive and incompatible with typical amide coupling conditions. The aniline -NH2 and the sulfonyl chloride on the same molecule would lead to self-condensation/oligomerization, and any coupling reagent activation (or the acid chloride if formed) would also react with the sulfonyl chloride or be quenched. Furthermore, the aniline nitrogen could react intramolecularly/intermolecularly with sulfonyl chlorides. A better strategy would be to install the sulfonamide linkage first (couple the sulfonyl chloride with methyl pipecolate), then perform the amide coupling, OR to use a sulfonyl-protected/masked precursor (e.g., sulfonate or thioether oxidized late-stage). As drawn, chemoselectivity cannot be controlled. The acid and amide bond formation themselves are feasible, but the coexisting sulfonyl chloride makes this specific step problematic.

local_feedback: Problems with reaction type and functional group compatibility
local_feedback_text: This step proposes sulfonamide formation between methyl piperidine-2-carboxylate (a secondary amine) and an aryl sulfonyl chloride bearing a free anilide-linked sulfonyl chloride. The disconnection itself (sulfonamide bond) is reasonable. However, the sulfonyl chloride electrophile here coexists with a free anilide NH (the C(=O)NH-aryl). While the anilide NH is far less nucleophilic than the piperidine secondary amine, the bigger concern is selectivity: the molecule has only one sulfonyl chloride, so chemoselective reaction with the piperidine amine should proceed under standard conditions (base such as Et3N or pyridine, DCM, 0 °C to rt). The methyl ester is compatible. The main practical issue is that the sulfonyl chloride intermediate (f3c6eb5fe1a68e5f8755c045ce859f22a00e8f6dac1a7a36f6603e8d300af6b3 product) is itself unstable and bears both an electrophilic sulfonyl chloride and a nucleophilic amide - acceptable but requires careful control. Overall feasible; reverse the ester is fine. I flag minor compatibility concern but the transformation should work.

This step proposes that the pyrazole carboxylic acid is coupled to 4-aminobenzenesulfonyl chloride (sulfanilyl chloride) to form the anilide, while leaving the sulfonyl chloride intact. This is highly problematic: the starting material 4-aminobenzenesulfonyl chloride has both a nucleophilic aniline NH2 and an electrophilic sulfonyl chloride. Under amide coupling conditions (activation of the carboxylic acid as acid chloride, or with coupling reagents), the free aniline could react, but the sulfonyl chloride would not survive aqueous workup or many coupling conditions, and intermolecular self-condensation (aniline of one molecule attacking sulfonyl chloride of another) is a serious competing pathway. A far more practical route is to install the sulfonamide first (couple the amine to the piperidine), then perform the amide coupling, OR protect/keep the sulfonyl chloride as a late-stage handle. As written, performing the amide bond formation in the presence of a free ArSO2Cl is not chemoselective and would lead to oligomerization. Recommend reordering disconnections: form anilide first using a non-sulfonyl-chloride aniline, then chlorosulfonylate, or keep sulfonyl group masked.

This is a sulfonamide formation from a secondary amine (methyl pipecolate) and an arylsulfonyl chloride. The disconnection is sound and well-precedented. Standard conditions (base such as Et3N or pyridine, DCM, 0 °C to rt) would deliver the product. The main concern is chemoselectivity: the sulfonyl chloride must react with the secondary piperidine amine in preference to any other nucleophilic site, but in this case the only competing nucleophile is the anilide NH which is poorly nucleophilic (already acylated), so selectivity should be fine. The methyl ester is fully compatible. Note that the amine partner is a chiral pipecolate; if enantiopure material is required, the stereocenter should be preserved as sulfonylation does not racemize an sp3 carbon adjacent to nitrogen under these mild basic conditions.

This step proposes amide coupling between a pyrazole carboxylic acid and 4-aminobenzenesulfonyl chloride. The key problem is chemoselectivity: the aniline is presented as a free NH2 while the para position bears a sulfonyl chloride. Under standard amide coupling/acid-chloride conditions, the aniline NH2 and the highly electrophilic sulfonyl chloride on the same molecule are mutually incompatible — the free aniline can react intramolecularly/intermolecularly with the sulfonyl chloride to form oligomeric sulfonamides, and activation of the carboxylic acid (e.g., via acid chloride or coupling reagent) in the presence of an electrophilic ArSO2Cl is problematic. A better strategy is to perform the sulfonamide coupling (f9fc1ef34cff4c1c7280b9b86d4bc968a9ad9e22b4b9647fc2aa838fabee2821) first using a sulfonamide-stable aniline derivative, or to install the sulfonyl chloride later via chlorosulfonation. Practically, the order of operations in this route is questionable: carrying an intact sulfonyl chloride through an amide bond formation invites side reactions. Reconsider the sequence or use a protected/masked sulfonyl group (e.g., couple to sulfanilamide then derivatize).

This is a sulfonamide formation between methyl pipecolate (secondary amine) and an arylsulfonyl chloride. The disconnection is sound and well-precedented. The secondary amine reacts cleanly with the sulfonyl chloride in the presence of a base (e.g., Et3N, pyridine, or aqueous NaHCO3). The methyl ester is fully compatible. The main concern is chemoselectivity: the sulfonyl chloride bears both an amide (already formed) and the reactive sulfonyl chloride, but since the amide N-H is far less nucleophilic and the pipecolate amine is the only good nucleophile, selectivity should be excellent. Standard conditions (DCM, base, 0 °C to rt) should give good yields.

This step is an amide coupling between a pyrazole carboxylic acid and 4-aminobenzenesulfonyl chloride. The major problem is chemoselectivity/functional group compatibility: the aniline contains BOTH a free amine and a sulfonyl chloride on the same molecule. Activating the carboxylic acid (e.g., with a coupling agent or as the acid chloride) and reacting it with this aminobenzenesulfonyl chloride is highly problematic because (a) the aniline could self-condense intermolecularly with its own sulfonyl chloride to give oligomeric sulfonamides, and (b) sulfonyl chlorides are moisture-sensitive and incompatible with many amide-coupling conditions. A more robust strategy would be to perform the amide coupling first on a sulfonic acid or protected sulfonate, then convert to the sulfonyl chloride, OR to install the sulfonyl chloride via chlorosulfonation after the amide is formed on an aniline. As drawn, the simultaneous presence of free -NH2 and -SO2Cl makes this isolated intermediate unstable and prone to self-reaction. Reconsider the order of operations.

This is an N-alkylation of a primary amine (NCC(F)=C1CCCC1) with phenethyl bromide (BrCCc1ccccc1) to form the secondary amine. The disconnection itself is reasonable and well-precedented. However, the major concern is overalkylation: direct alkylation of a primary amine with an alkyl halide is notoriously difficult to control and typically yields a mixture of secondary and tertiary (and quaternary) amines. To favor the secondary amine, one would need a large excess of the amine or alternative strategies (e.g., reductive amination using phenylacetaldehyde, or a protection/Gabriel-type approach). Also note the vinyl fluoride and enol-ether-like alkene moiety should tolerate basic alkylation conditions, so chemoselectivity toward the amine nitrogen is fine, but the mono- vs poly-alkylation selectivity is the key liability. A reductive amination with PhCH2CHO would be a cleaner and more selective alternative giving the same bond disconnection.

This is an N-alkylation of a primary amine (NCC(F)=C1CCCC1) with phenethyl bromide (BrCCc1ccccc1) to form the secondary amine product. The disconnection itself is sound and very common. However, the major practical concern is overalkylation: direct alkylation of a primary amine with an alkyl bromide typically yields significant amounts of the tertiary (dialkylated) amine and even quaternary ammonium salt, leading to poor selectivity for the desired secondary amine. To improve this, a reductive amination strategy is strongly preferred (i.e., condense the primary amine with phenylacetaldehyde, then reduce with NaBH4/NaBH(OAc)3), which provides much cleaner mono-alkylation. Alternatively, using excess amine relative to the alkyl halide can partially mitigate overalkylation. Note also the allylic/vinylic fluoride bearing the exocyclic alkene is a sensitive motif but should be tolerated under mild basic alkylation conditions. Both starting materials are listed in stock; phenethyl bromide is commercially available and cheap, while the fluorinated amine building block is less common but plausible.

This is an N-alkylation of a primary amine (NCC(F)=C1CCCC1) with phenethyl bromide (BrCCc1ccccc1) to form the secondary amine product. The disconnection is chemically reasonable and both starting materials are simple. However, direct alkylation of primary amines with alkyl halides notoriously suffers from overalkylation, producing tertiary amines and quaternary ammonium salts as side products. To improve selectivity, one would typically use a large excess of the primary amine, or better, employ a reductive amination strategy (condensation of NCC(F)=C1CCCC1 with phenylacetaldehyde followed by NaBH(OAc)3/NaBH3CN reduction), which gives cleaner mono-alkylation. The allylic/vinylic fluoride and the strained fluoroalkylidene cyclopentane appear compatible with mild alkylation conditions, though the fluoroenamine-like motif (F on a vinylidene) is a potential concern under basic/nucleophilic conditions. Overall the disconnection is sound but the chosen reagent/method is non-optimal for selectivity.

This is an N-alkylation of a primary amine (NCC(F)=C1CCCC1) with phenethyl bromide (BrCCc1ccccc1) to form the secondary amine product. While the disconnection itself is reasonable and the bond formed (C-N) is sensible, direct alkylation of primary amines with alkyl halides is notoriously difficult to control: the secondary amine product is more nucleophilic than the starting primary amine, leading to overalkylation (tertiary amine and quaternary ammonium salt formation). This results in poor selectivity and mixtures. To improve this, consider reductive amination using phenylacetaldehyde with the primary amine (NaBH(OAc)3 or NaBH3CN), which provides much cleaner mono-N-alkylation. Both building blocks are simple and reasonable; phenethyl bromide is commercially available. The allylic/vinyl fluoride and the exocyclic alkene should be compatible with mild alkylation conditions. Overall the disconnection is acceptable but the specific reagent/method invites overalkylation.

This step proposes an SNAr/Williamson-type etherification between the primary alcohol of the bicyclic nitroimidazooxazine fragment and the 3-chloropyridazine.
