The disconnection itself is sound and reasonable: chloropyridazines are excellent electrophiles for SNAr with alkoxides (NaH or Cs2CO3 to deprotonate the primary alcohol). The key concern is chemoselectivity. The nitroimidazole scaffold contains a fused N,O-acetal/aminal (the OC...CC2 ring with an O-C-N motif), which is sensitive to strong base and to nucleophilic/basic conditions; deprotonation conditions could risk ring-opening or epimerization at the stereocenter. Additionally, the electron-poor nitroimidazole could itself undergo competing reactions. Using a mild base (Cs2CO3 in DMF/DMSO) is advisable. Note the pyridazine in the partner is now mono-chloro (only one leaving group after the biaryl is installed), so regiochemistry of SNAr is defined. The proposed alcohol fragment is marked in stock, which is convenient. Moderate confidence that this works with optimization, but chemoselectivity vs. the acid/base-sensitive bicyclic acetal is a genuine risk.

Standard Suzuki-Miyaura coupling between 3,6-dichloropyridazine and 4-(trifluoromethoxy)phenylboronic acid. Both building blocks are commercially available and inexpensive. With Pd(PPh3)4 or Pd(dppf)Cl2 and a base (K2CO3/K3PO4), mono-selective coupling at one of the two equivalent C-Cl positions is well-precedented; using ~1 equiv of boronic acid and controlled conditions gives good mono-arylation selectivity, leaving one chloride for the subsequent SNAr. The trifluoromethoxy group is fully compatible with Suzuki conditions. The main yield-limiting factor is over-arylation (bis-coupling), which can be controlled stoichiometrically. Disconnection is appropriate and reagents are well chosen.

This step forms the aryl ether linkage by an SNAr reaction between the primary alcohol (as alkoxide) of the bicyclic nitroimidazole-fused alcohol and the 6-chloropyridazine. SNAr displacement of chloride on pyridazines by alkoxides is well-precedented because the ring nitrogens activate the position. The disconnection is appropriate and the pyridazinyl chloride is a competent electrophile. However, there is a significant chemoselectivity concern: the substrate contains an aromatic nitro group and an electron-poor imidazo-fused bicyclic system. Under basic alkoxide-forming conditions (e.g., NaH, KOtBu, Cs2CO3), the deprotonation/etherification should target the primary OH selectively, but the strongly electrophilic positions on the nitroimidazole core could undergo competing nucleophilic attack or the base could promote ring degradation. Also note there is a stereocenter at the OC(CH2OH) carbon (oxetane/oxazine-like position); this is carried through unchanged. Overall feasible but mild base and controlled conditions are recommended to avoid side reactions on the nitroheteroaromatic core.

This is a classic Suzuki-Miyaura cross-coupling between 3,6-dichloropyridazine and 4-(trifluoromethoxy)phenylboronic acid. Both reagents are commercially available and inexpensive. The mono-arylation of 3,6-dichloropyridazine is well-precedented and can be controlled to selectively functionalize one chloride while leaving the second chloride intact for subsequent SNAr (as used in 1f5c34481bb634cf3e20e5d550203aaae6b43f74fc66526bd8f0125601426d94). Standard conditions (Pd(PPh3)4 or Pd(dppf)Cl2, K2CO3 or K3PO4, dioxane/water) would deliver this product. The main consideration is mono- vs bis-coupling selectivity; using ~1 equiv boronic acid and controlled temperature gives good mono-selectivity due to deactivation after the first coupling. This is a sound, high-confidence disconnection.

This step is an SNAr/O-arylation reaction between a primary alcohol and a 3-chloropyridazine activated toward nucleophilic aromatic substitution. The disconnection itself is reasonable—chloropyridazines bearing an electron-withdrawing aryl substituent are good electrophiles for SNAr with alkoxides (NaH or Cs2CO3 to deprotonate the alcohol). The major concern is chemoselectivity: the alcohol-bearing fragment contains a fused bicyclic imidazo-system with a nitro group and an aminal-type N-C-O (the OC of the ring is an aminal acetal/orthoamide-like center). Under basic conditions needed to generate the alkoxide, the existing nitroimidazole/triazole-type heterocycle and the strained O-CH center could be sensitive, and competitive deprotonation/elimination is possible. Nonetheless the primary alcohol is the most acidic/nucleophilic site, so O-arylation should predominate. Recommend mild base (Cs2CO3) and controlled temperature. Overall a feasible but somewhat delicate convergent coupling.

This is a Suzuki-Miyaura cross-coupling between 3,6-dichloropyridazine and 4-(trifluoromethoxy)phenylboronic acid. Both starting materials are commercially available and inexpensive. The mono-arylation of 3,6-dichloropyridazine via Suzuki coupling is well precedented; selectivity for mono-coupling can be achieved by controlling stoichiometry (1.0–1.1 equiv boronic acid) and temperature, leaving one C-Cl intact for the subsequent SNAr. Standard conditions (Pd(PPh3)4 or Pd(dppf)Cl2, K2CO3 or Na2CO3, dioxane/water) would work well. The trifluoromethoxy group is fully compatible with these conditions. The main risk is over-arylation (bis-coupling), but this is controllable.

This step is a nucleophilic aromatic substitution (SNAr) where the primary alcohol of the bicyclic nitroimidazole displaces the chloride on the pyridazine ring (forming an aryl ether). The disconnection itself is sound - chloropyridazines are good SNAr substrates and the aryl ether linkage is well-precedented. However, there are notable concerns: (1) The reaction requires a base (e.g., NaH, K2CO3, Cs2CO3) to deprotonate the primary alcohol. The substrate contains a nitro-substituted imidazole and a fused bicyclic O,N-acetal/aminal-type system (the OC...CC2 ring fused to the imidazole), which could be base- or nucleophile-sensitive. Chemoselectivity between alkoxide formation and potential side reactions on the electrophilic nitroimidazole must be considered. (2) The bicyclic core contains a stereocenter (the CH bearing the OCH2 group); under strongly basic SNAr conditions, epimerization could be a concern though unlikely. Overall the transformation is reasonable but would benefit from mild base and careful condition optimization. This corresponds closely to known PA-824/delamanid-type nitroimidazooxazine chemistry, which lends good precedent.

This is a standard Suzuki-Miyaura cross-coupling between 3,6-dichloropyridazine and 4-(trifluoromethoxy)phenylboronic acid. The mono-selectivity is well-precedented: 3,6-dichloropyridazine reacts preferentially at one position under controlled conditions (Pd catalyst, base, ~1 equiv boronic acid), leaving the second chloride for subsequent SNAr. The boronic acid and dichloropyridazine are both commercially available. Typical conditions (Pd(PPh3)4 or Pd(dppf)Cl2, Na2CO3/K2CO3, dioxane/water) would deliver the mono-arylated product. Minor concern is over-coupling to the bis-aryl product, controllable by stoichiometry and temperature. Excellent disconnection.

This is an O-alkylation of a 2-hydroxypyrimidine (which exists predominantly as the pyrimidinone tautomer) with 1-(3-chloropropyl)pyrrolidine under basic conditions (e.g., K2CO3/Cs2CO3, DMF). The major concern is the O- vs N-alkylation chemoselectivity. Pyrimidinones can alkylate on either oxygen or the ring nitrogen, and N-alkylation is frequently competitive or even dominant depending on conditions, counterion, and solvent. To bias toward O-alkylation, silver salts, harder counterions, or Mitsunobu conditions (with the corresponding alcohol) are often employed. As written with a chloride electrophile, expect significant N-alkylated byproduct. Additionally, the alkyl chloride is a relatively unreactive electrophile; NaI catalysis (Finkelstein) would help. The disconnection itself is reasonable and the building block (3-chloropropylpyrrolidine) is commercially available; only the selectivity/reagent choice is the issue.

This is a Suzuki-Miyaura coupling installing a cyclopropyl group via cyclopropylboronic acid onto a chloropyrimidine bearing a free hydroxyl. Cyclopropylboronic acid couplings are well-precedented (e.g., Pd(OAc)2/tricyclohexylphosphine with K3PO4, the classic Charette/Wallace conditions). The regiochemistry is defined by the C-Cl position. The free hydroxyl/pyrimidinone is generally tolerated in Suzuki couplings, though it may slow the reaction or require excess base; protection is not strictly necessary. The starting materials (cyclopropylboronic acid and 4-chloro-6-hydroxy-2-phenylpyrimidine) are commercially available or readily accessible. The main caveat is that the C-Cl on an electron-rich hydroxypyrimidine may be less reactive, requiring an active catalyst system, but the transformation is solid.

This step is a Williamson ether synthesis / O-alkylation of a pyrimidinol (2-aryl-6-cyclopropyl-pyrimidin-4-ol) with 1-(3-chloropropyl)pyrrolidine. The disconnection is reasonable, and the alkyl chloride coupling with the hydroxypyrimidine is a well-precedented way to install the aminopropoxy side chain. However, hydroxypyrimidines exist in an amide/lactam tautomeric equilibrium, so O- vs N-alkylation selectivity is a significant concern. Base-mediated alkylation (e.g., Cs2CO3, K2CO3 in DMF/MeCN) typically favors O-alkylation but mixtures are common. The primary alkyl chloride is also a sluggish leaving group; using the bromide/iodide or adding NaI (Finkelstein conditions) would improve the rate. The basic pyrrolidine nitrogen is tolerated. Overall feasible but selectivity and reagent activation are real issues.

This is a Suzuki-Miyaura coupling between cyclopropylboronic acid and a 4-chloro-2-phenyl-pyrimidin-6-ol to install the cyclopropyl group. Cyclopropylboronic acid couplings with heteroaryl chlorides are well established (e.g., Pd(OAc)2/P(Cy)3, K3PO4, toluene/water, conditions per Charette/Wallace). The chloride on the electron-poor pyrimidine ring is activated and is the expected site of oxidative addition. The free hydroxyl/lactam tautomer is generally tolerated under these conditions, though it may require extra base equivalents. Regioselectivity is unambiguous since only one C-Cl bond is present. Both starting materials are commercially available. A minor caveat is potential protodeboronation of cyclopropylboronic acid, but optimized conditions exist.

This is an O-alkylation of a hydroxypyrimidine with 3-chloropropyl-pyrrolidine (Williamson-type ether synthesis), forming the C-O bond. The major concern is the well-known O/N ambident nucleophilicity of 2-hydroxypyrimidines (which exist predominantly as the pyrimidinone tautomer). Alkylation can occur at nitrogen (giving N-alkyl pyrimidinone) rather than oxygen (giving the desired aryl ether). To favor O-alkylation, one would use Ag2O, or a silver salt, or convert to a silver/cesium alkoxide; alternatively a Mitsunobu approach with the corresponding alcohol (HOCCCN-pyrrolidine) would give cleaner O-selectivity. The disconnection itself is reasonable and the alkyl chloride building block is commercially available, but reagent/conditions selection and the O vs N selectivity must be carefully managed. The product structure shown is the O-alkylated ether, which is the harder regiochemical outcome to achieve.

This is a Suzuki-Miyaura cross-coupling between a chloropyrimidine and cyclopropylboronic acid to install the cyclopropyl group at the activated 4-position of the pyrimidine. Heteroaryl chlorides flanked by ring nitrogens are sufficiently activated for Pd-catalyzed coupling, and cyclopropylboronic acid couplings are well precedented (e.g., Pd(OAc)2/PCy3, K3PO4). Chemoselectivity is favorable: the C-Cl is far more reactive than the free hydroxyl/pyrimidinone OH, which simply needs base. The free OH is tolerated. Both building blocks (cyclopropylboronic acid and the chloro-hydroxy-phenylpyrimidine) are commercially available. A minor note is potential competing protodehalogenation or coupling efficiency with the free OH present, but overall this is a sound, feasible step.

This step proposes O-alkylation of a 2-hydroxypyrimidine (which exists predominantly in its pyrimidinone tautomer) with a 3-chloropropyl pyrrolidine under Williamson-type conditions. The major concern is O- vs N-alkylation selectivity: pyrimidinones strongly favor N-alkylation under basic conditions, which would lead to the undesired N-alkylated product as a significant or even major byproduct. To favor O-alkylation, silver salts (Ag2CO3, Ag2O), Mitsunobu conditions (DIAD/PPh3 with the alcohol instead of the chloride), or hard bases/conditions favoring the O-anion are recommended. Additionally, the primary alkyl chloride is a relatively poor leaving group; the iodide or a Mitsunobu approach would improve efficiency. The basic pyrrolidine nitrogen is compatible. Overall the disconnection is sensible (forms the C-O ether bond to the side chain), but reagent/conditions need optimization to control chemoselectivity.

This is a Suzuki-Miyaura cross-coupling installing a cyclopropyl group at the chloropyrimidine position using cyclopropylboronic acid. Cyclopropylboronic acid is a well-established coupling partner (Pd catalyst, e.g., Pd(OAc)2/PCy3 with K3PO4, per Charette's conditions). The chemoselectivity is favorable: oxidative addition occurs at the more reactive C-Cl of the chloropyrimidine while the free hydroxyl/pyrimidinone is tolerated. The starting materials (cyclopropylboronic acid and 4-chloro-6-hydroxy-2-phenylpyrimidine) are commercially available or readily accessible. One minor consideration is that the free OH may slightly diminish yield or require excess base, but this is a robust and precedented transformation.

The amide coupling between 3-(trifluoromethoxy)benzoyl chloride and the aniline is a well-established transformation and would proceed readily under standard conditions (e.g., base such as Et3N/pyridine, DCM or THF). However, the chemoselectivity is a concern: the substrate contains two N-H sites on the cyclic urea (the [nH]c(=O)[nH] pyrimidinone/urea moiety) plus the aniline NH2. An acyl chloride is a reactive electrophile and could acylate the urea nitrogens (which, while less nucleophilic than the aniline, are still reactive toward acyl chlorides). The aniline is the most nucleophilic site, so selective N-acylation of the aniline should be achievable with careful stoichiometry (1 equiv acyl chloride, controlled addition, mild base), but competing O/N-acylation of the urea is a real risk. The disconnection itself is sound and the building block (3-(trifluoromethoxy)benzoyl chloride) is commercially available. Recommend confirming chemoselectivity or considering temporary protection of the urea, though in practice the aniline usually reacts preferentially.

This step proposes an SNAr (or Smiles-type) etherification of 4-amino-2-methylphenol with 8-chloro (4-chloro) substituted pyridopyrimidinedione. The chloride on the electron-poor pyridopyrimidinone ring is activated toward SNAr by the ring nitrogen and adjacent carbonyl, so O-arylation to form the diaryl ether is chemically reasonable (base such as K2CO3/Cs2CO3, DMF/DMSO, heat). However, there are two selectivity concerns: (1) chemoselectivity between the phenol O-H and the aniline N-H2 of the aminophenol. The free amine is also nucleophilic and could undergo competing N-arylation; deprotonation of the phenol (more acidic) with a mild base to generate the phenolate favors O-arylation, but selectivity is not guaranteed and N-arylation/diarylation could occur. (2) The urea N-H groups on the heterocycle may also interfere. A protecting-group strategy on the aniline (e.g., performing the SNAr before introducing/unmasking the amine, or using the nitro precursor and reducing afterward) would improve selectivity. The chloro-pyridopyrimidinedione building block and the aminocresol are plausible commercial/accessible materials. The disconnection is strategically reasonable but selectivity should be addressed.

This is a standard amide bond formation (Schotten-Baumann type) between an aromatic amine and an aroyl chloride. The disconnection at the amide C-N bond is logical and well-precedented. The acyl chloride 3-(trifluoromethoxy)benzoyl chloride is commercially available. One consideration: the urea N-H groups of the deazapurine/pteridinone-type heterocycle and the aniline N-H are both nucleophilic, so there is a potential chemoselectivity issue. However, aniline amines are far more nucleophilic than the conjugated cyclic urea N-H groups, and under controlled conditions (1 equiv acyl chloride, mild base such as pyridine or Et3N, low temperature), the aniline will react selectively. A slight excess of acyl chloride could cause over-acylation on the urea nitrogens, but this is manageable. Overall a high-yielding, robust transformation.

This step is an SNAr displacement of the chloride on the chloro-deazapurine/pteridinone heterocycle by the phenol of the aminophenol building block, forming the diaryl ether. The disconnection is sound and SNAr on an activated chloro-azine is feasible. However, there are notable selectivity concerns: (1) The aminophenol contains both a free aromatic NH2 and a phenol OH. The amine is more nucleophilic than the phenol, so without protection the aniline nitrogen could compete or preferentially attack the C-Cl, giving the undesired C-N rather than the desired C-O linkage. To favor O-arylation, the phenol should be deprotonated to the phenolate (e.g., with a base such as Cs2CO3 or K2CO3), which enhances O-selectivity, but amine competition remains a real risk. A protecting group on the aniline (e.g., Boc or acetyl) would improve chemoselectivity and is advisable. (2) The heterocyclic substrate bears two acidic N-H (urea) groups which could be deprotonated and interfere. (3) Regioselectivity of SNAr should be acceptable since the 4-chloro position is the activated site. Recommend amine protection or careful base/solvent control. Both building blocks (4-amino-2-methylphenol and the chloro-heterocycle) are reasonable; the chloro-deazapurinone is the more specialized reagent but plausibly accessible.

This is a standard amide coupling between an aryl amine and an aroyl chloride (Schotten-Baumann type). The disconnection is well-precedented and reliable. The aryl amine is the most nucleophilic site, and the acid chloride will react cleanly with it. One consideration: the urea (cyclic, the [nH]c(=O)[nH] moiety) contains NH groups that are potential competing nucleophiles, but these are far less nucleophilic than the aniline nitrogen (amide-type NH within a hydrogen-bonded urea), so chemoselectivity strongly favors the aniline. Use of a mild base (e.g., pyridine, Et3N, or NaHCO3 in a biphasic system) and controlled stoichiometry (1.0-1.1 equiv acid chloride) should give clean monoacylation. Both starting materials are reasonable; the acid chloride is commercially available.

This is an SNAr reaction forming a diaryl ether by displacement of the C-Cl on the deazapurine/pyridopyrimidinone core by the phenol. The disconnection is reasonable: the chloride is activated toward SNAr by the adjacent ring nitrogen, and aryloxide displacement of activated heteroaryl chlorides is well-precedented. However, there are significant selectivity/chemoselectivity concerns. (1) The aminophenol substrate (Cc1ccc(N)cc1O) contains both a free aniline (-NH2) and a phenol (-OH). Under basic SNAr conditions, the more nucleophilic aniline nitrogen could compete with the phenoxide for the chloride, leading to C-N rather than the desired C-O product. To ensure O-selectivity the amine should ideally be protected, or conditions favoring phenoxide (deprotonation of the more acidic OH with a base like K2CO3/Cs2CO3) must be carefully chosen. (2) The bis-urea NH groups in the heterocycle are acidic and could be deprotonated, but should not interfere with the ether formation. (3) Possible competing reactions involving the urea carbonyl are minor. Recommend protecting the aniline (or accepting reduced yield/selectivity), and using Cs2CO3 in DMF/NMP at elevated temperature. Reagent choice and the free amine make this the weakest step.

This is a standard amide bond formation between an aroyl chloride (3-(trifluoromethoxy)benzoyl chloride, commercially available) and an aniline. The disconnection itself is sound and well-precedented. However, there is a significant chemoselectivity concern: the aminophenol-derived intermediate contains a cyclic urea (the imidazolone/pyrimidinone N-H groups) with two relatively nucleophilic/acidic N-H sites. Treatment with a reactive acyl chloride could lead to competing N-acylation of the urea nitrogens. To ensure selective acylation of the aniline nitrogen over the urea N-H groups, mild conditions (e.g., controlled stoichiometry, low temperature, aqueous Schotten-Baumann or use of base such as pyridine/Et3N) should be employed. The aniline is the most nucleophilic site, so selective monoacylation is achievable, but careful control is needed. Overall feasible with attention to selectivity.

This step proposes an SNAr reaction between 4-amino-2-methylphenol and 4-chloro-1,3-dihydro-2H-imidazo[4,5-b]pyridin-2-one (both listed in stock). The chloride on the electron-deficient azine ring is indeed activated toward SNAr by the ring nitrogen, and the phenol (as phenoxide) can serve as the nucleophile. However, there is a clear chemoselectivity problem: the starting aminophenol contains BOTH a free aniline (-NH2) and a phenol (-OH). Under basic SNAr conditions, the more nucleophilic aniline nitrogen could compete with the phenol oxygen for displacement of the chloride, leading to a C-N rather than the desired C-O bond. To achieve O-selectivity, the aniline likely needs protection, OR conditions must be carefully tuned (phenoxide is a good nucleophile, but aniline is also reactive). Additionally, the free urea N-H groups on the heteroarene could interfere. A protecting-group strategy for the aniline would substantially improve the reliability of this disconnection. As drawn (using the unprotected aminophenol directly), regio/chemoselectivity is questionable.

This step proposes oxime formation from a ketone (the alpha-keto amide) using hydroxylamine. The major chemoselectivity problem is that the molecule contains a free primary aliphatic amine (NCCCO-) which is far more nucleophilic and would react readily/competitively with any electrophilic centers, and the alpha-keto amide presents TWO carbonyls (the ketone and the amide). Hydroxylamine would preferentially condense with the more electrophilic alpha-keto carbonyl, but the presence of the free primary amine creates serious selectivity and side-reaction concerns (intramolecular condensation/imine formation, salt formation). The free amine should be protected during this step. Additionally, oxime formation gives E/Z isomer mixtures which is not addressed. The disconnection itself (oxime <- ketone + NH2OH) is reasonable in principle but requires amine protection.

local_feedback_text: This step is Boc deprotection (acidic, typically TFA or HCl) to reveal the free primary amine. While Boc removal itself is feasible, removing the protecting group at this early stage exposes a free amine that then must survive subsequent ester hydrolysis (8ef1a458b1dcc01df49fe56050f790a04a48da1d7c3dece3448e54e2c736a0dd), amide coupling (513a4b23e5e9afb2b052c448edf052c4862e75b012f262c6cb20532ce47e5354), and oxime formation (a9e0cac978720ec363ddf6a9193ce7352a6f55f141bd19f49476cc6d22dea6f6) — all of which involve reactive carbonyls (alpha-keto ester/acid/amide) that the free amine could attack intramolecularly or competitively. The Boc group should be retained until after the amide coupling and oxime formation, then removed as the final step. As ordered, the protecting group strategy is non-optimal and creates downstream selectivity/compatibility problems.

This is a Williamson ether synthesis (O-alkylation of the phenol with Boc-protected 3-bromopropylamine). The disconnection is sound and well-precedented. The phenol is the most acidic/nucleophilic site and will be selectively alkylated under basic conditions (K2CO3, Cs2CO3 in DMF/acetonitrile). The Boc-protected bromide is commercially available and stable to these conditions. The alpha-keto ester is reasonably compatible, though strong base should be avoided to prevent ester transesterification or aldol-type side reactions; mild base is appropriate. Overall a reliable transformation.

This step proposes forming the benzylic alpha-keto ester (ArCH2-C(=O)-C(=O)OEt) from diethyl oxalate and the cresol (Cc1cc(Cl)cc(Cl)c1O, a 2,4-dichloro-6-methylphenol). This disconnection is not chemically sensible as drawn: it implies a benzylic C-H of the toluene-type methyl group attacking diethyl oxalate to form a C-C bond. A free benzylic methyl group on an electron-poor arene is not nucleophilic and cannot perform a Claisen-type condensation with diethyl oxalate without first generating a benzylic anion (which would require very strong base and is impractical with an unprotected phenol and dichloroarene present). The mapping connects the ArCH2 to the oxalate carbonyl, which is not a feasible direct transformation. A proper route would use an arylacetic acid/ester enolate or an active methylene partner, not a benzylic methyl arene. This disconnection should be revised.

This step proposes oxime formation from a 1,2-dicarbonyl (ketoamide) by condensation with hydroxylamine (NH2OH). The chemistry of converting a ketone to an oxime is well-established. However, there are significant selectivity concerns: (1) The substrate is an α-ketoamide, and hydroxylamine could potentially attack either the ketone OR the amide carbonyl, though the ketone is far more electrophilic and would be favored. (2) Critically, the molecule contains a free primary amine (NCCCO-), which is more nucleophilic than hydroxylamine and could undergo intramolecular or intermolecular condensation with the ketone, leading to enamine/imine side products or cyclization. The free amine should be protected during this transformation. (3) E/Z selectivity of the oxime is not addressed. Overall the oxime formation is feasible but the unprotected primary amine creates a major chemoselectivity problem.

This step represents the hydrolysis of an ethyl ester to a carboxylic acid (and the Boc has already been removed). Ester saponification under basic conditions (LiOH/NaOH) is well-precedented. The α-ketoester to α-ketoacid hydrolysis is feasible, though one must use mild conditions to avoid decarboxylation/decarbonylation of the sensitive α-ketoacid. The free amine is compatible. Reasonable transformation, but note the lability of α-keto acids.
This is a standard Boc deprotection (TFA or HCl) to reveal the primary amine. Well-established and high-yielding. The α-ketoester is compatible with acidic Boc removal conditions. No major concerns.

This is a Williamson ether synthesis: O-alkylation of the phenol with N-Boc-3-bromopropylamine to install the aminopropyl ether side chain. This is a well-precedented transformation using base (K2CO3/Cs2CO3) in DMF/acetone. The Boc-protected bromide is commercially available. Potential competing O- vs C-alkylation is minimal as the phenol oxygen is the favored nucleophile. The α-ketoester is base-sensitive (enolizable, possible retro-Claisen), so mild base and controlled conditions are advised. Overall feasible.

This step proposes forming the α-ketoester by reaction of diethyl oxalate with the benzylic position of 2,4-dichloro-6-methylphenol (the methyl group). This implies a Claisen-type condensation of a benzylic methyl with diethyl oxalate. However, a simple aryl-CH3 is not acidic enough to be deprotonated and undergo Claisen condensation with diethyl oxalate under normal conditions; the benzylic methyl has no activating group. This disconnection as drawn (deprotonation of ArCH3 then acylation) is unlikely without strong activation. A more realistic precursor would be an arylacetic acid/ester or an aryl acetonitrile, or use of a benzyl anion equivalent. Additionally, the free phenol would interfere. The intended bond disconnection (Ar-CH2-C(=O)-CO2Et) is reasonable retrosynthetically but the exact reagents/substrate are non-optimal; an arylacetate + oxalate Claisen, or an aryl Grignard/organometallic addition to diethyl oxalate would be needed.

This step proposes oxime formation from an alpha-ketoamide (1,2-dicarbonyl) by condensation of hydroxylamine with the ketone, selective over the amide. While oxime formation on the ketone of an alpha-ketoamide is chemically reasonable and the amide is unreactive toward NH2OH, the major issue is that the molecule contains a free primary amine (the aminopropyl chain). This primary amine would compete with hydroxylamine and could form an intramolecular or intermolecular imine/enamine with the reactive 1,2-diketone-type carbonyl, leading to side products. The free amine should be protected during this condensation. Additionally, oxime geometry (E/Z) would not be controlled. The disconnection itself (oxime from ketone) is sound, but selectivity/compatibility with the free amine is a concern.

This step proposes constructing the alpha-ketoester benzylic CH2 linkage from diethyl oxalate and a 2-methylphenol (4,6-dichloro-o-cresol). A more sensible route to the ArCH2C(=O)CO2Et fragment would start from an arylacetic acid/ester or aryl acetonitrile, or from an ortho-methyl benzyl halide. The bond disconnection (benzylic C–C(=O) acylation with oxalate) has precedent only for activated/benzylic anions stabilized appropriately. The free phenol would also interfere. Reagent/substrate choice is non-optimal; an analogous transformation requires a substantially more acidic/activated benzylic precursor.

Also, oxime geometry (E/Z) would be uncontrolled. Forward reaction (oxime from ketone + NH2OH) is well precedented, but chemoselectivity in the presence of the free amine is questionable.

Selective ester hydrolysis while retaining Boc would be preferable so the amine stays protected for the subsequent amide coupling (513a4b23e5e9afb2b052c448edf052c4862e75b012f262c6cb20532ce47e5354). Removing the Boc here exposes the amine that then interferes with the downstream coupling. Ester saponification under basic conditions (LiOH) would retain the Boc and is the better choice; the route's choice to deprotect simultaneously is non-optimal. Additionally, the alpha-keto ester hydrolysis could be complicated by the reactive ketone.

Boc deprotection of the carbamate to reveal the free primary amine using acid (e.g., TFA or HCl) is well established and reliable. The ethyl ester and aryl chlorides are compatible with these conditions. Standard transformation. Note: in the context of the overall route, exposing this amine before the downstream coupling is problematic, but the deprotection chemistry itself is sound.

O-Alkylation (Williamson ether synthesis) of the phenol with N-Boc-3-bromopropylamine. The phenol is alkylated under basic conditions (K2CO3, Cs2CO3) with the alkyl bromide. This is a well-precedented transformation. Chemoselectivity favors O-alkylation of the phenol. The alpha-keto ester and aryl chlorides are compatible. Good disconnection using a commercially available building block.

This step proposes forming the arylacetyl alpha-keto ester (ArCH2-C(=O)-C(=O)OEt) from diethyl oxalate and 2,4-dichloro-6-methylphenol (Cc1cc(Cl)cc(Cl)c1O). The disconnection implies a benzylic C-C bond formation between the aryl methyl group and the oxalate carbonyl. A simple phenol + diethyl oxalate combination will NOT effect deprotonation of the benzylic methyl and Claisen-type acylation; benzylic methyl groups on simple arenes are not acidic enough to be deprotonated and condensed with oxalate under normal conditions. The benzylic position would need to be activated (e.g., a benzyl halide/organometallic) for such a Claisen condensation with diethyl oxalate. As drawn (using the methylphenol directly), this transformation is not feasible. A redesign using ArCH2MgX/ArCH2-metal or an arylacetate enolate condensing with diethyl oxalate is needed.

This is a thioether formation via S-alkylation of the thiol O=C(CCCS)NO onto the alkyl chloride O=C(NC(CCl)C(=O)NCc1ccccc1)c1cccc2ccccc12. The disconnection is reasonable in principle (C-S bond formation), but there are significant chemoselectivity concerns. The hydroxamic acid (CONHOH) in the thiol partner contains both N-H and O-H nucleophilic sites that could compete with the thiol for alkylation, although the thiolate is the softest/most nucleophilic species and would likely react preferentially under mild base. A more serious issue is the alpha-chloro position adjacent to an amide-bearing stereocenter: SN2 displacement at this benzylic/alpha-amido position could cause epimerization or elimination. The hydroxamic acid should ideally be protected (e.g., O-benzyl as in the parallel branch) during this alkylation to avoid side reactions, then deprotected. As written, using the free hydroxamic acid risks competing O-alkylation.

Hydrogenolytic removal of the O-benzyl group from the O-benzyl hydroxamate to give the free hydroxamic acid is a well-established transformation (e.g., H2/Pd-C). However, note that the thiol present in the molecule (O=C(CCCS)NO) is a known catalyst poison for Pd and may interfere with hydrogenolysis. An alternative deprotection (e.g., BCl3 or transfer hydrogenation conditions) may be needed. The disconnection itself is sound and the O-benzyl is a standard hydroxamic acid protecting group.

local_feedback_text: This step forms the O-benzylhydroxamate from 4-mercaptobutanoic acid (O=C(O)CCCS) and O-benzylhydroxylamine (NOCc1ccccc1) via amide coupling. The disconnection is reasonable, but a free thiol is present in the carboxylic acid partner, which is incompatible with most standard amide coupling reagents (e.g., the thiol can react with activated esters/acyl species, or with carbodiimides). The thiol should be protected (e.g., trityl, acetyl) during the coupling, or chemoselective conditions used. Both starting materials are commercially available. With thiol protection this becomes a straightforward EDC/HOBt or similar coupling.

Amide bond formation between benzylamine and the acid chloride O=C(NC(CCl)C(=O)Cl)c1cccc2ccccc12 is a standard, high-yielding transformation. Chemoselectivity is acceptable since the acid chloride is far more reactive than the pre-existing naphthamide. One caveat: benzylamine could also displace the alpha-chloride, but acylation of the acid chloride is much faster; using one equivalent and low temperature should give clean amide formation. Good disconnection.

Conversion of carboxylic acid to acid chloride using thionyl chloride (SOCl2) is standard. The substrate already contains an alkyl chloride and an amide, which are tolerated. One concern: SOCl2 with an alpha-amido carboxylic acid bearing an adjacent C-Cl could risk side reactions, but the transformation is generally feasible. Oxalyl chloride/cat. DMF would be a milder alternative.

Acylation of the amine of 3-chloroalanine (NC(CCl)C(=O)O) with 1-naphthoyl chloride to give the naphthamide is feasible and standard (Schotten-Baumann conditions). Chemoselective N-acylation of the amine over the carboxylic acid is straightforward. Both starting materials are commercially available. Note 3-chloroalanine is the masked dehydroalanine/cysteine surrogate used here for later thioether formation - a sensible strategy.

This is a thioether formation via S-alkylation of the thiol (O=C(CCCS)NO) onto the alkyl chloride partner. The disconnection itself is sound and well-precedented (thiol + alkyl halide under basic conditions). However, there are significant chemoselectivity concerns: the thiol-bearing fragment contains a free hydroxamic acid (-C(=O)NHOH), which is both nucleophilic (N and O) and acidic. Under the basic conditions needed to deprotonate the thiol for SN2 displacement, the hydroxamate could compete as a nucleophile or be deprotonated, leading to side reactions. Additionally, the alkyl chloride is alpha to two carbonyl-bearing carbons and is a secondary/activated center, raising risk of elimination or epimerization at the adjacent stereocenter. A cleaner approach would protect the hydroxamic acid (consistent with 96494abc6b8beed8342711ea93806a0debd04df86cad718e1e75adf70c8aa0c6) before the alkylation. Reaction is feasible but selectivity must be managed carefully; a thiolate alkylation should be selective for sulfur over the harder hydroxamate oxygen/nitrogen if the thiol is selectively deprotonated (pKa thiol ~10 vs hydroxamic acid ~9), so partial competition is likely.

Amide bond formation between benzylamine and the acid chloride (O=C(NC(CCl)C(=O)Cl)...). Coupling of an acid chloride with a primary amine to form an amide is highly reliable. One caution: the substrate also contains an alpha-chloro group adjacent to the carbonyl and the amide N-H; the benzylamine could in principle displace the alkyl chloride (intramolecular or intermolecular alkylation) or cause elimination, but acylation of the amine by the much more reactive acid chloride will dominate kinetically, especially at low temperature with controlled stoichiometry. Use of a mild base (e.g., Et3N) and low temperature recommended.

Conversion of a carboxylic acid to the acid chloride using thionyl chloride (SOCl2). This is a standard, well-established transformation. The substrate contains an amide (the naphthamide) and an alkyl chloride which are both compatible with SOCl2. Minor caution: prolonged exposure or excess SOCl2 could affect the secondary amide, but under standard conditions this is a robust step. The activated acid chloride is then carried directly into the amide coupling (44f3eb9ad4c0aff382412c1131bf1a8e61f61df883c7fa296fac7c07729bb88d).

Amide formation coupling 1-naphthoyl chloride with 3-chloro-2-aminopropanoic acid (beta-chloroalanine, NC(CCl)C(=O)O). The acylation of the free amine with the acyl chloride is feasible. However, there is chemoselectivity concern: with a free carboxylic acid present, the acyl chloride could also react with the carboxylate, and the free amine of beta-chloroalanine can undergo intramolecular cyclization (aziridine formation via displacement of the beta-chloride by the amine) — this is a known facile reaction for beta-haloamines under basic conditions. Schotten-Baumann conditions with careful pH control would be needed. The starting materials are commercially available. Stereochemistry at the alpha carbon should be considered if enantiopure material is required.

This is a thioether formation via S-alkylation of the thiol (O=C(CCCS)NO) with the alkyl chloride partner. The bond disconnection (C-S) is reasonable. However, there is a major chemoselectivity issue: the thiol-bearing fragment is a hydroxamic acid (-C(=O)NHOH), which contains a nucleophilic N-OH and an acidic N-H. Under the basic conditions typically required to generate the thiolate for SN2 displacement, the hydroxamate nitrogen/oxygen could compete as nucleophiles, and the free hydroxamic acid is prone to side reactions (Lossen rearrangement, O- vs N-alkylation). Use of the free hydroxamic acid here is risky; it would be far better to perform the thioether coupling BEFORE unmasking the hydroxamic acid (i.e., keep the O-benzyl protected hydroxamate and deprotect at the very end). The chloride is also a relatively poor leaving group; an iodide or activation may improve the SN2. Additionally, the alpha-chloride is alpha to an amide and adjacent to a stereocenter — risk of epimerization/elimination.

Overall a reasonable, well-precedented disconnection.

Amide bond formation between benzylamine (NCc1ccccc1) and the acid chloride O=C(NC(CCl)C(=O)Cl). Coupling an amine with an acyl chloride is straightforward and high-yielding with a base (e.g., Et3N). Use stoichiometric control and low temperature.

Amide coupling between benzylamine and the acid chloride to form the benzylamide is a standard, robust transformation. Benzylamine is commercially available and inexpensive. The acid chloride is reactive and selective toward the amine. Good disconnection.

local_feedback_text: Conversion of the carboxylic acid to the acid chloride with SOCl2 is standard. However, the substrate contains a beta-chloro alpha-amido carbonyl. Acid chloride formation generates a reactive species that, together with the adjacent amide, could cyclize (e.g., to an oxazolone/azlactone) or the alpha-stereocenter could epimerize. Also the existing alkyl chloride is benign to SOCl2. The main concern is selectivity/epimerization at the alpha center and possible intramolecular side reactions. Use of oxalyl chloride with catalytic DMF under mild conditions would be preferable.

Acylation of 3-chloroalanine (NC(CCl)C(=O)O) with 1-naphthoyl chloride to form the amide is feasible (Schotten-Baumann conditions). Both starting materials are commercially available. Note the use of the free amino acid; chemoselectivity for N-acylation over O-acylation is generally achievable under aqueous basic conditions. Mild epimerization risk exists but the disconnection is sound.

This is an amide coupling between the carboxylic acid and the benzylamine of an unprotected benzamidine. The disconnection is sound, but the free amidine (-C(=N)NH2) is a strong nucleophile and competes with the benzylic primary amine during the coupling. Standard coupling reagents (HATU, EDC, T3P) would acylate the amidine nitrogen preferentially or give mixtures. To improve selectivity, the amidine should be protected (e.g., Boc) or introduced late from a nitrile precursor, OR the coupling should be performed with the amidine present as a salt to attenuate its nucleophilicity. As written, chemoselectivity is a real concern.

Acidic cleavage of a tert-butyl ester (TFA or HCl) to reveal the carboxylic acid is a robust, well-precedented transformation. The remaining functionality (aryl chloride, CF3, secondary amine, pyrimidinone) is fully compatible with TFA conditions. No issues.

SNAr displacement of one of the two ring chlorides by phenethylamine on the dichloropyrimidinone is reasonable. The amine selectively substitutes the position activated by the adjacent ring nitrogen/carbonyl. Regioselectivity between the two remaining chlorines (the one ortho to aryl vs. the one used) should be considered, but the position para to the carbonyl/ortho to N is typically the most electrophilic, giving the desired product. Mild heating with the amine and a base would suffice.

N-alkylation of the pyrimidinone NH with tert-butyl bromoacetate under basic conditions (K2CO3/Cs2CO3, DMF) is a standard transformation. The N-H of the 2-pyridinone/pyrimidinone is the most acidic and nucleophilic site, so N- vs O-alkylation selectivity is the main concern; ambident reactivity can give some O-alkylated byproduct, but N-alkylation typically predominates with these conditions and soft electrophiles. Reasonable step.

Suzuki coupling of the arylboronic acid onto the trichloropyrimidinone is the key disconnection. The problem is regioselectivity: the substrate has three C-Cl bonds of differing reactivity, and achieving selective mono-arylation at the desired position requires careful control (the most electrophilic/least hindered C-Cl typically reacts first). Also, the free N-H pyrimidinone and the presence of multiple oxidative-addition-prone C-Cl sites may give polyarylation or wrong-regiochemistry products. Conditions (Pd catalyst, ligand, base, stoichiometry control to 1 equiv boronic acid) must be carefully optimized. Mono-selectivity is plausible but not guaranteed.

This proposes ring chlorination of a dichloropyrimidinone at a ring C-H using N-chlorosuccinimide (NCS) to install the third chlorine. Electrophilic C-H chlorination of an electron-poor (already dichlorinated) pyrimidinone ring with NCS is sluggish and the regiochemistry/feasibility is questionable on such a deactivated ring. More commonly, 2,3,5-trichloro/halogenated pyrimidinones or the fully chlorinated heterocycle (e.g., from POCl3 chemistry on a polyhydroxy precursor) would be used. The disconnection direction is plausible but the exact reagent/conditions are non-optimal; consider starting from a commercially available trichloropyrimidinone instead.

local_feedback_text: The final amide coupling between the carboxylic acid and the benzylamine-containing benzamidine is a sound disconnection. However, the use of an unprotected benzamidine in an amide coupling step is problematic: the highly nucleophilic/basic amidine group can interfere with standard coupling reagents (e.g., HATU, EDC, T3P) by competing for activation of the carboxylic acid, leading to acyl-amidine adducts and reduced yields. Chemoselectivity for the primary benzylic amine over the amidine N-H is not guaranteed. A better approach would be to couple at a stage where the amidine is masked (e.g., as a Boc-protected amidine or installed from a nitrile late-stage via Pinner/amidoxime route). The disconnection itself is reasonable; the concern is selectivity/compatibility.

Cleavage of the tert-butyl ester to reveal the free carboxylic acid (TFA or HCl in dioxane) is a standard, robust transformation. The aryl chloride, trifluoromethyl, and secondary amine functionalities are all stable to acidic Boc/tBu deprotection conditions. Straightforward and well-precedented.

This is an SNAr displacement of one of two chlorines on the pyrazinone/pyrimidinone ring by phenethylamine. The disconnection is chemically reasonable since the ring has two distinct C-Cl positions (one adjacent to the ring N, one vinylic chloride). However, regioselectivity between the two chlorides must be addressed - the desired product retains the C-Cl adjacent to the aryl group while displacing the one para/positioned to the carbonyl. Achieving clean monosubstitution at the correct position requires careful control (temperature, stoichiometry); over-substitution and wrong-regiochemistry products are plausible. The amine nucleophile and conditions are compatible with the ester and CF3 groups.

N-alkylation of the pyrimidinone/pyrazinone N-H with tert-butyl bromoacetate under basic conditions (K2CO3, Cs2CO3, NaH) is well-precedented. The ambident N vs O nucleophile issue exists (N- vs O-alkylation), so some O-alkylation could compete, but N-alkylation typically predominates with appropriate base/solvent (DMF, Cs2CO3). The bromoacetate electrophile is a standard reagent. Minor selectivity caveat noted, but overall feasible.

A Suzuki-Miyaura coupling installing the 3-(trifluoromethyl)phenyl group onto the polychlorinated pyrimidinone. The disconnection is sound, but the substrate has three chlorine atoms in distinct electronic environments, and achieving mono-arylation at the specific desired position with regiocontrol is challenging. Differentiation of the three C-Cl bonds toward oxidative addition is non-trivial; competing di-/tri-coupling and wrong-site coupling are real risks. Careful catalyst/ligand choice and stoichiometry control are required. The free N-H lactam may also require attention. Boronic acid coupling partner is commercially available.

This step proposes chlorination of a dichlorinated pyrimidinone with N-chlorosuccinimide (NCS) to introduce the third chlorine at the vacant ring carbon. Direct C-H chlorination of an electron-poor, already di-chlorinated heteroarene by NCS is questionable in terms of reactivity - electrophilic chlorination on such an electron-deficient ring is sluggish. While NCS can chlorinate activated positions, this dichloro-pyrimidinone is deactivated. More likely, the trichloro-pyrimidinone (or its precursor) would be accessed via POCl3-type chlorination of the corresponding polyhydroxy/oxo precursor, or the trichloro building block may be directly purchasable. The disconnection direction (which atoms become which) is also chemically awkward. Reagent/strategy non-optimal.

The final step is an amide coupling between a benzamidine-bearing benzylamine and a carboxylic acid. The disconnection itself is sound and very common (e.g., HATU/EDC, DIPEA). However, the strongly nucleophilic/basic benzamidine group will compete with the benzylamine for the activated acid, potentially leading to acylation on the amidine nitrogen. In practice the amidine is often introduced last or protected (e.g., as Boc-amidine or installed via nitrile/Pinner sequence) to ensure chemoselective amide formation on the benzylamine. As written there is risk of poor selectivity and reduced yield. Consider using the benzonitrile precursor and converting to amidine after the coupling.

Simple Boc/tert-butyl ester deprotection of the glycine ester with TFA or HCl to reveal the free carboxylic acid. Well-precedented and chemoselective. The aryl chloride, trifluoromethyl, secondary aniline amine, and pyrimidinone are stable to acidic deprotection conditions. Note that the secondary amine (NHCH2CH2Ph) is unprotected and will be protonated under acidic conditions, which is fine.

SNAr displacement of one of the two chlorines on the pyrimidinone by phenethylamine. The regioselectivity of substitution between the chlorine alpha to the carbonyl (C-Cl adjacent to ring N) vs. the other positions must be controlled. The dichloropyrimidinone has two electrophilic chlorines (the one being displaced and the vinyl/ring chloride retained); achieving mono-substitution at the desired position with the correct regiochemistry is non-trivial and may give mixtures. Temperature control and stoichiometry (1 equiv amine) would be needed. Plausible but selectivity is the key concern.

N-alkylation of the pyrimidinone NH with tert-butyl bromoacetate. Standard N-alkylation using a base (K2CO3, Cs2CO3, or NaH) in DMF/MeCN. The ambident pyrimidinone could in principle give O- vs N-alkylation, but N-alkylation is typically favored under these conditions for such 2-pyridone/pyrimidinone systems. Generally reliable.

Suzuki-Miyaura coupling to install the 3-(trifluoromethyl)phenyl group onto the trichloropyrimidinone. The substrate bears three chlorines plus an NH; achieving selective mono-arylation at one specific position is a major challenge. Polyhalogenated pyrimidinones show position-dependent reactivity, but predicting/controlling selective C-arylation of the desired carbon over the others requires careful optimization and may give regioisomeric mixtures. Also, a free pyrimidinone NH can interfere with Pd catalysis. Feasible in principle but significant selectivity risk.

Chlorination of the dichloropyrimidinone at the remaining ring CH using N-chlorosuccinimide. Electrophilic aromatic/ring chlorination of an electron-poor pyrimidinone with NCS is plausible but may be sluggish given the electron-deficient ring; harsher chlorinating conditions (e.g., Cl2, SO2Cl2, or POCl3-based chemistry) might be required. The disconnection (adding the third chlorine last) is reasonable but reagent efficacy on this deactivated heterocycle is uncertain.

This is an amide coupling between a carboxylic acid and a benzylamine bearing a free, unprotected benzamidine group. The amidine (N=C(N)NH) is highly nucleophilic and will compete with the benzylic primary amine for the activated acid (e.g., HATU/EDC ester), leading to acylation of the amidine nitrogen as a major side reaction. While the disconnection (amide bond) is strategically sound, the free amidine should ideally be introduced later or protected (e.g., as Boc-amidine or installed via a nitrile that is converted to amidine post-coupling). As written, chemoselectivity will be poor. Consider coupling with the 4-(aminomethyl)benzonitrile and then converting the nitrile to the amidine (Pinner or LiHMDS/NH addition) as a cleaner endgame.

Simple acid-mediated cleavage of a tert-butyl ester to reveal the carboxylic acid (TFA or HCl). This is well precedented and high-yielding. The aryl chloride, trifluoromethyl, secondary amine, and pyrimidinone are all stable under these conditions. No issues.

SNAr displacement of one of two chlorines on the dichloropyrimidinone by phenethylamine. The disconnection is reasonable since amines readily displace activated halides on such heteroaromatic systems. However, there is a regioselectivity concern: the substrate has two distinct ring chlorines (the C adjacent to carbonyl/N vs. the other position), and selective mono-substitution at the desired (4-amino) position must be confirmed. The chlorine alpha to the carbonyl is typically less activated than the one para/positioned to ring nitrogen. Controlled stoichiometry (1 equiv amine) and mild temperature would be needed to avoid bis-amination and to control regiochemistry. Generally feasible but selectivity must be verified.

N-alkylation of the pyrimidinone NH with tert-butyl bromoacetate. This is a standard alkylation (base such as K2CO3 or Cs2CO3 in DMF). The ambident N/O nucleophile could in principle give O-alkylation, but N-alkylation is typically favored for pyrimidinones under these conditions. Minor O-alkylation side product is the main concern. Overall feasible and well precedented.

Suzuki-Miyaura coupling of the arylboronic acid with the trichloropyrimidinone to install the aryl group. The strategic disconnection is sound, but the substrate bears three chlorines of differing reactivity, and achieving mono-arylation regioselectively at the desired position is non-trivial. Selectivity is governed by the relative oxidative-addition rates at each C-Cl; careful catalyst/ligand and stoichiometry control are required. Competing bis/tris-arylation and protodeboronation of the electron-poor CF3-arylboronic acid are realistic concerns. Feasible but requires optimization for regioselectivity.

Electrophilic chlorination of a dichloropyrimidinone with NCS to give the trichloro compound. Ring C-H chlorination on an electron-poor pyrimidinone with NCS is sluggish and may require forcing conditions or a different chlorinating agent. Regioselectivity for the single remaining C-H position should be acceptable since only one CH is available, but the reactivity/feasibility of direct NCS C-H chlorination on this deactivated ring is questionable. A pre-halogenated building block (commercially available 2,5,6-trichloropyrimidin-4(3H)-one or analogous) would be more reliable.

This step proposes forming a methyl ester from a carboxylic acid using carbonic acid (O=C(O)O) as a reagent. Carbonic acid cannot esterify a carboxylic acid to a methyl ester. The retrosynthetic logic is broken: a methyl ester is conventionally made from the acid plus methanol (Fischer esterification), or via diazomethane/TMS-diazomethane, or methyl iodide with a base. The disconnection shown is chemically nonsensical. Replace with COC->methanol-based esterification.

This step converts a carboxylic acid to an ethyl ester (then later the ethyl ester is hydrolyzed back to the acid in 69fb4cb668241de49b02e83496c56ab91f64da2bc10942eafd0f553ca07cfc42). Interconverting methyl/ethyl/acid esters across multiple steps adds no synthetic value. The whole sequence of ester swaps (methyl->acid->ethyl->acid->methyl) is highly redundant. A single, consistent ester protecting strategy should be chosen. These shuffling steps should be eliminated.

Removal of the trifluoroacetyl (TFA) protecting group from the secondary amine to reveal the free aniline/amine is a well-established transformation, typically accomplished with mild base (K2CO3/MeOH) or NaOH. The TFA amide is base-labile and cleaves cleanly. Functional groups (nitro, ester, alkyl chloride) are compatible, though strongly basic/nucleophilic conditions could risk displacing the primary alkyl chloride - mild K2CO3/MeOH conditions are recommended to avoid this. Feasible as a deprotection.

Esterification of the carboxylic acid to the ethyl ester. As with 62e03488a97c257b6052c13bf18efa7e2e28e539dbea936c6f6c8cd21d098674, this is part of a redundant ester interconversion cycle. The ethyl ester is created here only to be carried forward and is inconsistent with the methyl ester appearing elsewhere in the route. The repeated changing of ester identity is non-strategic and should be removed in favor of a single protecting/masking choice.

Hydrolysis of the methyl ester to the free carboxylic acid. This is the inverse of an esterification appearing elsewhere; combined with 62e03488a97c257b6052c13bf18efa7e2e28e539dbea936c6f6c8cd21d098674/69fb4cb668241de49b02e83496c56ab91f64da2bc10942eafd0f553ca07cfc42 it creates a pointless acid<->ester loop. Selective hydrolysis would also need to avoid cleaving the TFA amide and displacing the alkyl chloride, adding chemoselectivity concerns. The step is unnecessary in the context of the overall route.

This step proposes converting a primary alcohol (CH2OH) to a primary alkyl chloride (CH2Cl) using dichloromethane (ClCCl) as the chlorinating reagent. DCM is a solvent, not a chlorinating agent; it will not convert an alcohol to a chloride. The appropriate reagents for this Appel/halogenation-type transformation are SOCl2, PCl3, (COCl)2/cat., or Appel conditions (CBr4/PPh3 analog with CCl4 or PPh3/NCS). As written the disconnection/reagent is invalid - replace ClCCl with a genuine chlorinating reagent (e.g., SOCl2 or MsCl then LiCl).

This step proposes forming a methyl ester from a carboxylic acid using 'carbonic acid' (O=C(O)O) as the methylating/coupling partner. This is chemically nonsensical - carbonic acid cannot serve as a methyl source for ester formation. To make the methyl ester from the carboxylic acid, one would use MeOH/acid catalysis, TMS-diazomethane, or MeI/base. The disconnection itself (acid to methyl ester) is reasonable, but the proposed reagent is impossible. Additionally, the benzylic chloride (CCl) would be highly reactive under many esterification conditions, risking side reactions.

This step interconverts an ethyl ester to a carboxylic acid (or vice versa in synthetic direction, acid to ethyl ester). The retrosynthetic logic here is deeply flawed and redundant: the target already has a methyl ester (764fbad847b09d52ed8b07bad5a95f653589e6caaeec453aa83ddc104f27d9f9), then this converts to a free acid, which then becomes an ethyl ester (62e03488a97c257b6052c13bf18efa7e2e28e539dbea936c6f6c8cd21d098674). Carrying an acid through to an ethyl ester only to later need a methyl ester represents circular, inefficient logic. The transformation acid→ethyl ester is feasible chemically (Fischer esterification), but the strategic placement makes no sense and introduces an ester-swap that serves no purpose.

This step is the removal of a trifluoroacetyl (TFA) protecting group from the secondary amine (the dihydropyrrole/indoline-type nitrogen). TFA amide deprotection under mild basic conditions (K2CO3/MeOH or NaOH) is well-precedented. The trifluoroacetamide is a reasonable amine protecting group. However, note that basic hydrolysis conditions could also hydrolyze the ethyl ester present in the molecule, creating a chemoselectivity concern. The benzylic chloride could also be vulnerable. Overall the disconnection (N-deprotection) is sound.

This proposes forming an ethyl ester from a carboxylic acid using ethanol (EtOH). The disconnection (Fischer esterification, acid + EtOH) is chemically feasible. However, this step combined with 62e03488a97c257b6052c13bf18efa7e2e28e539dbea936c6f6c8cd21d098674 and 44c059ad64b23e8f60ea445a89a998d454cfcb4cbe33342de9c0709a2e7763da reveals a pointless ester-juggling sequence: methyl ester → acid → methyl ester → acid → ethyl ester → acid → methyl ester. This is highly redundant. Also, acidic Fischer esterification conditions risk solvolysis of the reactive benzylic chloride.

This step converts a carboxylic acid to a methyl ester but the reagent/mechanism is not specified and the overall logic creates a redundant ester interconversion loop. The molecule already contains a methyl ester that gets converted to acid then back to methyl ester then to ethyl ester elsewhere in the tree - this is strategically incoherent. As a standalone acid→methyl ester transformation it is feasible (with proper reagents like TMSCHN2), but the lack of a sensible reagent and the redundancy are major problems.

This step converts a primary alcohol (CH2OH) to a benzylic-type chloride (CH2Cl) using DCM (ClCCl, dichloromethane) as the apparent chlorine source. Dichloromethane is NOT a chlorinating reagent for alcohol-to-chloride conversion; it is a solvent. The correct reagents would be SOCl2, (COCl)2, PPh3/CCl4 (Appel), or MsCl followed by chloride displacement. The disconnection (alcohol→chloride) is reasonable and useful, but the reagent is wrong. The neopentyl-like primary alcohol on the cyclopentane-fused ring should chlorinate cleanly with proper reagents. Note: the TFA amide and nitro groups are compatible with SOCl2.

This step proposes that the methyl ester (COC(=O)) of the target is formed from the corresponding carboxylic acid plus carbonic acid (O=C(O)O). This makes no chemical sense as a methyl esterification. Carbonic acid is not a methylating agent and cannot deliver a methyl group. To form a methyl ester from a carboxylic acid, one would use MeOH/acid catalysis, TMS-diazomethane, or MeI/base. The disconnection to carbonic acid is spurious and chemically impossible as written. Additionally, the secondary amine (NH of the indoline/tetrahydro ring) would also be reactive under typical esterification conditions, raising chemoselectivity concerns.

This step converts a carboxylic acid (target product, free NH) into an ETHYL ester intermediate, then in the forward sense the ethyl ester is hydrolyzed to the acid. But the overall route makes no sense: the final product is a METHYL ester (764fbad847b09d52ed8b07bad5a95f653589e6caaeec453aa83ddc104f27d9f9), yet here the carboxylic acid is being elaborated to an ETHYL ester. Switching from ethyl to methyl ester adds no value. More critically, this is an interconversion that does nothing productive — esterification of a free acid bearing a free secondary amine and a primary alkyl chloride raises serious chemoselectivity problems (the amine could be acylated/alkylated, and the chloride could undergo intramolecular cyclization with the amine). The disconnection is redundant and ill-conceived.

local_feedback: Protecting group strategy is wrong / non-optimal
local_feedback_text: This step removes a trifluoroacetamide (TFA) protecting group from the ring nitrogen to reveal the free secondary amine, on the ethyl ester. The chemistry of TFA deprotection (mild base, K2CO3/MeOH) is feasible. However, in the context of the whole route, the protecting group strategy is poorly organized: the TFA group is installed and removed without clear necessity given that the parallel late-stage steps (ethyl/methyl ester juggling) are redundant. Also a serious concern: the free secondary amine and the pendant primary alkyl chloride (CC3CCl) are 1,4/1,5-disposed and would readily cyclize intramolecularly upon deprotection. Liberating the amine in the presence of the alkyl chloride is a significant chemoselectivity/stability liability.

This step proposes forming an ethyl ester from a carboxylic acid plus ethanol. Fischer esterification (EtOH, acid catalyst) is in principle feasible. However, the substrate bears a primary alkyl chloride and a TFA-protected amine; strongly acidic esterification conditions risk TFA cleavage and side reactions. More fundamentally, the route then immediately converts the carboxylic acid (44c059ad64b23e8f60ea445a89a998d454cfcb4cbe33342de9c0709a2e7763da) into the ethyl ester (this step) and later back to acid/methyl ester — a redundant ester shuffle. As a discrete transformation the bond disconnection is reasonable, but the reagent (EtOH) producing an ethyl ester that is never needed makes the step strategically pointless. Mark as non-optimal/redundant.

This proposes converting a methyl ester (product) into a carboxylic acid (reactant), i.e. in forward direction ester hydrolysis of the methyl ester to the acid. Saponification of the methyl ester is feasible, BUT the substrate carries a primary alkyl chloride and a TFA amide. Basic hydrolysis conditions would also cleave the TFA group and could hydrolyze/displace the alkyl chloride. This is a chemoselectivity disaster. Moreover, the route already manipulates methyl vs ethyl esters redundantly; converting methyl ester→acid→ethyl ester→acid→methyl ester across the route is nonsensical and wasteful.

This step proposes forming a primary alkyl chloride (CC3CCl) from the corresponding primary alcohol (CC3CO) with dichloromethane (ClCCl) shown as the chlorine source. DCM is NOT a chlorinating reagent for converting alcohols to alkyl chlorides; it is only a solvent. The correct reagents would be SOCl2, (COCl)2/cat. DMF, MsCl then chloride, or Appel conditions (PPh3/CCl4 or PPh3/NCS). The bond disconnection (alcohol→chloride) is sound and well-precedented, but the reagent shown is wrong. Additionally, chemoselectivity must be considered: the TFA amide protects the nitrogen (good), but the activated benzylic-type position and the nitroarene must tolerate the chlorination conditions, which they generally would.

This step proposes forming the methyl ester from the corresponding carboxylic acid using carbonic acid (O=C(O)O) as the reagent. This is chemically nonsensical - carbonic acid cannot serve as a methylating agent to convert a carboxylic acid into a methyl ester. A proper methyl ester formation would require a methylating agent (e.g., MeI/base, TMS-diazomethane, or MeOH under Fischer conditions). The proposed disconnection is invalid as written.

This step converts a carboxylic acid directly to an ETHYL ester. While esterification is feasible in principle, the strategic problem is that the target molecule is a METHYL ester, yet the route detours through an ethyl ester. This is internally inconsistent and pointless. Additionally, no esterifying reagent/conditions are specified, and a free secondary amine (indoline NH) is present which would compete under acidic Fischer conditions or coupling conditions. The disconnection is non-productive within the route.

local_feedback: Protecting group strategy is wrong / non-optimal
local_feedback_text: This step removes the trifluoroacetyl (TFA) protecting group from the indoline nitrogen to reveal the free amine. While TFA removal (typically with K2CO3/MeOH or NaOH) is feasible, the overall protecting group logic is flawed: the route installs the amine protection and carries it through multiple ester interconversions only to remove it at the end without clear necessity. The reactive primary alkyl chloride (CH2Cl) present in the molecule is a major liability - basic conditions for TFA removal could promote intramolecular N-alkylation/cyclization once the amine is freed. This is a significant chemoselectivity concern.

This step proposes esterification of a carboxylic acid with ethanol to form an ethyl ester. Setting aside that an ethyl ester is the wrong target (methyl ester is needed), the deeper issue is the route's redundancy: it goes acid -> ethyl ester -> (later) methyl ester with no rationale. No coupling/activation reagent is provided. Under Fischer conditions, the acid-sensitive functionality and the alkyl chloride raise compatibility concerns. The disconnection is unproductive.

This step claims conversion of a methyl ester to a carboxylic acid (ester hydrolysis), but it is written as a single-reactant -> single-reactant transformation that simply swaps OMe for OH. While ester hydrolysis itself is feasible (LiOH/NaOH), placing it here creates a wasteful cycle: methyl ester -> acid -> ethyl ester -> ... -> methyl ester. This circular ester manipulation adds no value and is strategically incorrect. The route should retain a single ester throughout if one is needed.

This step converts a primary alcohol (CH2OH) to a primary chloride (CH2Cl), with dichloromethane (ClCCl) listed as the chlorine source. DCM is not a chlorinating reagent for alcohols. The correct reagents would be SOCl2, (COCl)2, MsCl then chloride, or Appel conditions (PPh3/CCl4 or NCS). The bond disconnection (alcohol -> chloride) is reasonable and well-precedented, but the specific reagent shown is incorrect; close analogues exist. Note the nitro group and TFA amide are compatible with SOCl2/Appel conditions.

This is a Williamson ether synthesis forming the O-CH2CH2CH2-O linkage by coupling the indole-4-ol phenol with the alkyl chloride. The disconnection is reasonable in principle. However, two issues: (1) The nucleophile fragment 'O=C(O)Cn1ccc2c(O)cccc21' bears a free carboxylic acid, which is incompatible with the basic conditions (K2CO3/Cs2CO3) needed for O-alkylation - the carboxylate would compete as a nucleophile, and chemoselective phenol O-alkylation over carboxylate O-alkylation is problematic. The carboxylic acid should be protected (e.g., as an ester) until after this coupling, then hydrolyzed. (2) A primary alkyl chloride is a sluggish electrophile; the corresponding bromide/iodide or addition of NaI (Finkelstein) would be preferable. Recommend reordering steps so the ester is hydrolyzed last.

Saponification/hydrolysis of an ethyl ester to the corresponding carboxylic acid (LiOH or NaOH, aqueous THF/MeOH) is a standard, robust transformation. The free phenol is compatible. This step is well-precedented and high-yielding. Note however its placement in the route is questionable - hydrolyzing to the free acid before the subsequent O-alkylation coupling (8b98ceaa34b21f70c71c1553aa0dcb61cb074984a0c889cb690b81f874f241ab) creates the selectivity problem noted there; the acid should ideally be liberated as the final step.

Debenzylation of a benzyl-protected phenol to reveal the free phenol (H2/Pd-C, or BCl3/transfer hydrogenation) is well-established. The ethyl ester and indole N-CH2CO2Et are compatible with hydrogenolytic debenzylation. The indole ring is generally stable under mild Pd/C hydrogenation though over-reduction conditions should be controlled. Reasonable choice of protecting group strategy for a phenol.

Friedel-Crafts acylation of the naphthalene with benzoyl chloride (AlCl3). The disconnection is sound and FC acylation on an electron-rich alkoxynaphthalene is feasible, but regioselectivity of acylation on a substituted naphthalene bearing an alkoxy group and a propyl group is a real concern - multiple positions are activated and predicting the desired 6-position acylation is uncertain. Additionally, the substrate contains an alkyl chloride ether chain (OCCCCl); under strong Lewis acid (AlCl3) conditions, the ether linkage and the primary chloride may be susceptible to cleavage/side reactions. Better to install the benzoyl group before constructing the full ether chain, or use milder acylation conditions.

Williamson ether synthesis between the naphthol and 1-bromo-3-chloropropane (base such as K2CO3/Cs2CO3). The differential reactivity of the more reactive bromide vs. the chloride allows chemoselective alkylation of the phenol with the bromide terminus, leaving the chloride intact for downstream coupling. This is a well-precedented strategy. Some bis-alkylation/polymerization is possible but controllable with excess dihalide.

This is a Williamson ether synthesis (O-alkylation) coupling the indole-7-ol nucleophile with an alkyl chloride to form the propyloxy linker. The disconnection is strategically sound and convergent. However, there are two concerns: (1) The carboxylic acid (CH2COOH) on the indole N is unprotected and could compete as a nucleophile (forming an ester) or require deprotonation conditions that affect chemoselectivity. The phenol O-alkylation is generally favored under mild base (K2CO3), but the free acid may need to be considered. (2) The alkyl chloride is a relatively unreactive leaving group for SN2 etherification; iodide or bromide analogues would react more efficiently (Finkelstein conditions could help). Overall a reasonable convergent disconnection but the free acid should ideally be protected during this alkylation.

Ester hydrolysis (saponification) of the ethyl ester to the free carboxylic acid. This is a very well-established transformation, readily achieved with LiOH or NaOH in aqueous THF/MeOH. The free phenol and indole are compatible. No selectivity issues expected. Straightforward and high-yielding.

Debenzylation of the benzyl-protected phenol to reveal the free phenol. Hydrogenolysis (H2, Pd/C) is the standard method and proceeds cleanly. The indole and ethyl ester are compatible with these conditions. One minor caution: hydrogenation conditions could potentially reduce the indole C2-C3 double bond, but indoles are generally resistant to standard Pd/C hydrogenolysis at ambient pressure. Alternatively, transfer hydrogenation or Lewis acid conditions could be used. The benzyl protecting group choice is appropriate for masking the phenol.

Friedel-Crafts acylation of the naphthalene with benzoyl chloride (AlCl3 or similar Lewis acid). The disconnection is reasonable, but regioselectivity is a significant concern: the substituted naphthalene bears a propyl group and an alkoxy substituent, and electrophilic acylation could occur at multiple positions. The product shown places the benzoyl group at a specific position on the distal ring, but achieving this regioselectivity may be challenging without careful control. Additionally, the alkyl chloride (OCCCCl) tether could potentially undergo side reactions under strong Lewis acid conditions, though primary alkyl chlorides are relatively stable. The electron-rich alkoxy-activated ring is the most likely site of acylation, which may compete with the desired distal acylation. Regiochemical control is the main risk.

Williamson ether synthesis between the naphthol and 1-bromo-3-chloropropane (ClCCCBr). The bromide is selectively displaced over the chloride due to its better leaving group ability, giving the chloropropyl ether. This chemoselectivity is well-precedented for 1-bromo-3-chloropropane reactions with phenols/naphthols under K2CO3 conditions. Both starting materials are commercially available. Straightforward and reliable.

This is a Williamson ether synthesis coupling the indole-7-ol (phenolic OH) with the alkyl chloride bearing chain. The disconnection itself is reasonable (O-alkylation of phenol with a primary chloride under basic conditions, e.g., K2CO3/Cs2CO3, KI catalysis). However, there is a serious chemoselectivity problem: the nucleophilic partner 'O=C(O)Cn1ccc2c(O)cccc21' contains a free carboxylic acid in addition to the phenol. Under basic alkylation conditions both the carboxylate and the phenolate can be alkylated, leading to ester formation and O-alkylation competition. The carboxylic acid should be protected (as an ester) during this etherification and deprotected afterward, or the sequence should be reordered. As drawn, this step will suffer poor selectivity. A primary alkyl chloride is also a sluggish electrophile; the bromide analogue or in situ Finkelstein (NaI) would be preferable.

Ester hydrolysis (saponification) of the ethyl ester to the carboxylic acid using e.g. LiOH or NaOH in aqueous THF/MeOH is a well-established, robust transformation. The phenol and indole are stable under these mild basic conditions. No selectivity concerns. Standard final-stage deprotection.

Debenzylation of the O-benzyl ether to reveal the phenol. Hydrogenolysis (H2, Pd/C) is the standard method and is fully compatible with the ethyl ester and indole core. One caveat: indoles can occasionally be sensitive to hydrogenation conditions, but benzyl ether cleavage typically proceeds selectively at low pressure/short time. Alternatively, Lewis-acid (BCl3) or transfer hydrogenation could be used. Overall a sound, standard deprotection.

Friedel-Crafts acylation of the naphthalene with benzoyl chloride under Lewis acid catalysis (AlCl3) to install the benzophenone. The disconnection is logical and well-precedented for electron-rich naphthalenes. Regioselectivity is a consideration: acylation should occur at the 6-position as drawn, directed by the alkoxy substituent, but mixtures of regioisomers on the naphthalene are possible and may require separation. The alkyl chloride side chain is generally stable to AlCl3, though prolonged exposure could risk some interference. Selecting the position is the main risk; overall feasible.

Williamson ether synthesis between the naphthol and 1-bromo-3-chloropropane. Selective reaction at the more reactive bromide over the chloride under mild base (K2CO3) is well-precedented and gives the chloro-terminated ether cleanly. Both starting materials are commercially available and inexpensive. Standard, reliable transformation.

This step is a Williamson ether synthesis coupling the indole-4-ol (as nucleophile via its phenol oxygen) with the alkyl chloride to form the ether linkage. The disconnection is reasonable. However, there is a significant chemoselectivity concern: the phenolic fragment contains a free carboxylic acid (CH2COOH on the indole nitrogen), which would compete with the phenol for alkylation under basic conditions (e.g., K2CO3), potentially leading to ester (O-alkylation of carboxylate) formation. Selective O-alkylation of the phenol in the presence of a free carboxylic acid is problematic. A better strategy would carry the carboxylic acid as its ester (as is done earlier in the route) and perform the ether coupling before final saponification. Additionally, primary alkyl chlorides are sluggish; an iodide or use of NaI (Finkelstein) would be advisable.

Friedel-Crafts acylation of the naphthalene with benzoyl chloride/AlCl3 to install the aroyl group. The disconnection is sound, but regioselectivity is a major concern. The substituted naphthalene has multiple available positions; controlling acylation to give exactly the 6-position (as drawn) over other electron-rich positions (e.g., other ring positions activated by the alkoxy substituent) is non-trivial and would likely give regioisomeric mixtures. The propyl and alkoxy substituents direct electrophilic substitution, and the product regiochemistry should be carefully justified. Also, AlCl3 may cleave or complex with the alkyl ether and the chloride chain is a potential side-reaction site, though primary alkyl chlorides are reasonably stable under FC conditions.

Williamson ether synthesis between the naphthol (3-propyl-2-naphthol type) and 1-bromo-3-chloropropane. Use of a base such as K2CO3 with the dihalide allows selective reaction of the more reactive bromide, leaving the chloride intact for subsequent etherification. This is a well-precedented and chemoselective transformation. Slight excess of the dihalide is advisable to avoid bis-alkylation.

Ester hydrolysis (saponification) of the ethyl ester to the carboxylic acid using LiOH or NaOH. This is a routine, high-yielding transformation. The indole and free phenol are compatible. Standard step.

Debenzylation of the benzyl-protected phenol to reveal the free phenol, typically via catalytic hydrogenation (H2/Pd-C). The ethyl ester and the indole are compatible, though care must be taken that the indole C2-C3 double bond is not reduced (indoles are generally stable to mild hydrogenation). Hydrogenolysis of O-benzyl is clean and well-precedented. Alternatively, BCl3 or Lewis-acid mediated debenzylation could be used if hydrogenation is problematic.

This is a nitro reduction to give the corresponding aniline. The transformation is well-established.
