As a transformation, hydrodebromination is feasible (e.g., Pd/H2, or Bu3SnH), but strategically this is an unnecessary detour.

This step is the mesylation (N-SO2Me installation) of the indole nitrogen using MsCl. Reaction of indole NH with MsCl/base is feasible. However, the substrate also contains a secondary aliphatic amine within the ring system... wait, here the nitrogen is part of a tertiary amine in the polycyclic framework, so chemoselectivity of N-sulfonylation should favor the indole NH only if the tertiary amine cannot react. The tertiary amine could be quaternized/sulfonylated competitively or the sulfonyl chloride could react with it. Careful base/conditions selection needed. Regioselectivity for the indole N over the only NH present is fine since the other amine is tertiary. Main concern is potential competing reaction at the tertiary amine. Overall feasible with attention to conditions.

This step corresponds to intramolecular cyclization/C-N bond formation where a benzylic chloride and a secondary amine combine to close the azepine/tetracyclic ring (the chloro-amine precursor cyclizes to form the new C-N bond, displacing chloride). Intramolecular N-alkylation of a benzylic/secondary chloride by a secondary amine is a well-precedented ring-closing reaction. The benzylic chloride is activated and the geometry favors macrocyclization/medium-ring formation. Reasonable transformation, though ring size and conformational constraints should be considered. Note the Br is retained here.

local_feedback: Problems with reaction type and functional group compatibility
local_feedback_text: This step proposes removal of the trifluoroacetyl (TFA) protecting group from the amine concurrent with revealing the free secondary amine that then would cyclize. The precursor contains a benzylic chloride alpha to the indole. Standard TFA amide cleavage requires basic (K2CO3/MeOH, NaOH) or reductive conditions, which are likely incompatible with the highly reactive benzylic/doubly-benzylic chloride present — the chloride would undergo solvolysis, elimination, or premature intramolecular alkylation. There is significant risk of side reactions. The deprotection chemoselectivity in the presence of this labile chloride is questionable. Conditions must be carefully chosen, and the order of operations (deprotect then cyclize) may not be cleanly separable.

This is an aromatic bromination using NBS on an indole-containing substrate, intended to install Br on the carbocyclic ring of the indole. NBS on indoles typically brominates the electron-rich C3 (or C2) position of the pyrrole ring preferentially rather than the benzenoid ring. Achieving selective bromination at the specified aromatic position (para to the indole, ring carbon) over the inherently more reactive indole C3 is challenging, especially since here C3 is substituted but C2 may still be reactive. Additionally NBS could brominate the benzylic C-H position or react with the existing benzylic chloride center. Significant chemo/regioselectivity concerns. Moreover, since the Br is later removed (2dcdfaba0b39f9811e955fc9641ba0a3dda980699559ea7f1c9bb06355596713), the entire bromination is strategically unnecessary.

This step shows the preparation of methanesulfonyl chloride from methanesulfonic acid and oxalyl chloride. While chemically feasible (oxalyl chloride converts sulfonic acids to sulfonyl chlorides), MsCl is a cheap, ubiquitous commercial reagent and does not need to be synthesized. This step is unnecessary and should be removed; MsCl should be sourced directly.

This step removes the mesyl (Ms) protecting group from the indole nitrogen to reveal the free N-H indole product. Methanesulfonyl groups on indole nitrogens are readily cleaved under basic hydrolytic conditions (e.g., NaOH/MeOH, K2CO3, or TBAF). The transformation is chemoselective and well-precedented. No issues with the other functional groups (the basic tertiary amine is unaffected). Reasonable final deprotection step.

This step represents a hydrodebromination (removal of the aryl bromide to give the parent arene). In the synthetic direction, the bromide present on the product was used as a regiochemical handle/blocking group and is then removed (e.g., via Pd-catalyzed hydrogenolysis or reduction). This is a plausible transformation. However, one should note that introduction of the Br in an earlier step followed by its removal here adds steps; its purpose would be to direct regiochemistry of the mesylation/functionalization. Feasible but consider step economy.

This step installs the methanesulfonyl group on the indole nitrogen using MsCl. N-sulfonylation of indoles is well-established (MsCl, base such as NaH or Et3N/DMAP). The transformation is feasible. The main concern is chemoselectivity: the substrate contains a basic tertiary amine in the polycyclic system, which could compete with the indole N-H for sulfonylation. Since the indole N-H is the only N-H present and the tertiary amine cannot be sulfonylated (no N-H), selectivity should be acceptable, though over-reaction/quaternization of the tertiary amine by MsCl is a possible side reaction. Use of mild base and controlled stoichiometry recommended.

This disconnection corresponds to an intramolecular cyclization/ring closure where the benzylic chloride and the secondary amine combine to form the new C-N bond of the azepane/piperidine ring with concomitant loss of HCl. Intramolecular N-alkylation of a benzylic chloride by a secondary amine is a feasible ring-forming step. Geometric feasibility of forming the macro/medium ring should be carefully considered, but the disconnection is reasonable. Potential for elimination side reactions at the benzylic position.

This step represents removal of the trifluoroacetyl (TFA) protecting group from the secondary amine to reveal the free amine, which then undergoes cyclization (see 0c0133d4363ed3173585481fe732bb7e22309cc99da30ceadc713bbdcb9f2ee4). TFA amide cleavage is standard (K2CO3/MeOH, NaOH, or NH3). Feasible deprotection. The benzylic chloride and indole should survive mild basic hydrolysis, though competing intramolecular cyclization (which is in fact the desired downstream reaction) and possible solvolysis of the benzylic chloride are concerns under the deprotection conditions.

This step is an electrophilic aromatic bromination of the indole-containing arene using NBS to install the aryl bromide regioselectively at the position para/ortho to the ring fusion. NBS bromination of electron-rich indole systems is feasible, but indoles are inherently most reactive at C3 (here substituted) and C2; ring bromination on the benzenoid portion at the desired position requires careful control. There is significant risk of bromination at undesired positions (e.g., indole C2 if free, or other electron-rich sites). Additionally, a benzylic chloride is present in the molecule, which could be susceptible to radical side reactions under NBS conditions. Regioselectivity and chemoselectivity need to be controlled.

This step shows the preparation of methanesulfonyl chloride from methanesulfonic acid and oxalyl chloride. While chemically valid, MsCl is an inexpensive, ubiquitous commercial reagent and need not be synthesized in the route. This is an unnecessary disconnection cluttering the tree.

This step represents the removal of the N-methanesulfonyl (mesyl) protecting group from the indole nitrogen. Cleavage of an N-Ms indole using basic hydrolysis (e.g., NaOH/MeOH, TBAF, or K2CO3) is well-established and chemoselective. The other functional groups (tertiary amine, aromatic rings) are compatible. A reasonable final deprotection step.

This is a reductive dehalogenation (removal of the aryl bromide) of the N-Ms protected intermediate. Hydrogenolysis (H2/Pd) or other dehalogenation methods are well-precedented. The bromine was presumably installed earlier for regiochemical control, then removed. While feasible, this raises step-economy concerns: introducing then removing a bromine adds two steps. Chemoselective removal of ArBr in presence of the sulfonamide and benzylic positions is achievable but could risk over-reduction.

N-sulfonylation of the indole NH with methanesulfonyl chloride (CS(O2)Cl) under basic conditions (NaH, then MsCl) is a standard, robust transformation. The reactant has a free indole NH and the tertiary amine; selectivity for indole N over the tertiary amine (which is already substituted) is fine. The reaction is chemically sound. The strategic question is whether the Ms group is needed at all at this stage.

This step proposes the in-situ generation of methanesulfonyl chloride from methanesulfonic acid and oxalyl chloride. While chemically feasible, methanesulfonyl chloride is an inexpensive, commercially available bulk reagent and is listed as in_stock elsewhere conceptually. There is no need to synthesize it; this transformation adds unnecessary complexity to a retrosynthetic analysis.

This step constructs the central C-N ring via intramolecular reductive amination/cyclization. The precursor has a benzylic chloride (ClC...) and a secondary amine that can cyclize to form the tetracyclic core, with concomitant displacement/aromatization. The disconnection of the polycyclic C-ring is reasonable, though the actual mechanism (intramolecular N-alkylation of benzylic chloride by the secondary amine) is plausible. Stereochemistry at the benzylic stereocenter and competing elimination are concerns. Moderate confidence given the complexity.

This step corresponds to TFA (trifluoroacetamide) removal/deprotection of the amine, generating the free secondary amine that then participates in cyclization. Removal of a trifluoroacetyl protecting group is straightforward (K2CO3/MeOH or NaOH). The chemistry is sound; the benzylic chloride must survive the basic deprotection conditions, which could be problematic (intramolecular alkylation or hydrolysis may occur prematurely). This actually couples nicely with 0c0133d4363ed3173585481fe732bb7e22309cc99da30ceadc713bbdcb9f2ee4 but raises chemoselectivity concerns regarding the benzylic chloride under basic conditions.

This step proposes bromination of an indole-containing substrate with NBS (N-bromosuccinimide). The intended outcome is regioselective aromatic bromination on the benzenoid ring of the indole (at the position para to the alkyl chain). However, NBS on indoles preferentially brominates the electron-rich C3/C2 positions of the pyrrole ring, not the carbocyclic ring. Here C3 is substituted (fused), but C2 (shown as the c[nH] position) is open and would be the kinetically favored site. Additionally, the benzylic C-Cl and benzylic positions are susceptible to radical bromination with NBS. Significant regio- and chemoselectivity issues are expected; a directed metalation or directed C-H functionalization approach would be more reliable for the desired carbocyclic bromination.

This step removes a methanesulfonyl (mesyl) protecting group from the indole nitrogen to reveal the free NH indole. Removal of N-sulfonyl groups from indoles is well-precedented under basic conditions (NaOH/MeOH, K2CO3, or TBAF/Mg-MeOH). The transformation is chemically sound. However, one should note that the target retains the free indole NH while the protecting group was carried through the bromination/cross-coupling sequence - this ordering is logical. No selectivity concerns since this is a deprotection.

This step proposes a reductive dehalogenation (removal of the aryl bromide to give the des-bromo arene). The disconnection itself (hydrodebromination) is feasible via catalytic hydrogenation or other reductive methods. However, the key concern is WHY the bromine was introduced at all - in this retrosynthetic direction, the forward step removes a Br that appears to serve no constructive purpose, since it is simply removed later. This suggests the bromine was used as a regiochemical blocking/directing element or the route is inefficient. If the bromine plays no role in C-C bond formation, this is a wasteful protect-deprotect-like sequence. Reductive debromination conditions must also be chemoselective in the presence of the N-mesyl indole. See route-level comment.

This step installs the N-mesyl group on the indole nitrogen (sulfonylation with MsCl). N-sulfonylation of indole NH with MsCl/base (e.g., NaH, then MsCl) is standard and feasible. The bond disconnection is appropriate as a protection step. The main consideration is chemoselectivity: the secondary aliphatic amine in the polycyclic framework would compete for sulfonylation. Wait - examining the structure, the basic amine has already been incorporated into the ring (tertiary amine), so it is not nucleophilic enough to interfere significantly under controlled conditions. Sulfonylation should favor the indole NH after deprotonation. Reagent choice (MsCl) is appropriate.

This step proposes synthesizing methanesulfonyl chloride from methanesulfonic acid and oxalyl chloride. While this transformation is chemically valid (oxalyl chloride converts sulfonic acids to sulfonyl chlorides), MsCl is an inexpensive, ubiquitous commercial reagent. There is no need to include its synthesis in a retrosynthetic tree - it should be treated as a building block. This adds unnecessary complexity.

This step constructs the central polycyclic ring system via intramolecular cyclization, where a benzylic chloride (ClC-) is displaced by the secondary amine to form a new C-N bond closing the azacycle and simultaneously the indole NH is freed/aromatized. The Friedel-Crafts-type or N-alkylation cyclization forming the bridged ring is plausible. The benzylic chloride is well-positioned for intramolecular amine alkylation to form the tertiary amine ring. Conditions (base, heat) should drive cyclization. Some concern over competing elimination of the benzylic chloride, but cyclization is generally favorable for forming such rings.

This step removes a trifluoroacetyl (TFA) protecting group from the amide nitrogen to reveal the secondary amine, which then cyclizes (in the preceding/following step). TFA amide removal under mild basic conditions (K2CO3/MeOH or NaOH) is well-established. The disconnection is reasonable. Chemoselectivity is fine since the benzylic chloride could be sensitive to strongly nucleophilic/basic conditions - mild conditions should be used to avoid premature reaction of the chloride. Functional group compatibility of the benzylic chloride during TFA removal is a minor concern.

This step is an aromatic bromination using NBS on a substrate containing both an electron-rich indole and an electron-rich benzene ring, plus a sensitive benzylic chloride. NBS bromination of indole-containing substrates is notorious for occurring at the electron-rich indole C3 position (which here is substituted) or other ring positions rather than cleanly at the desired carbocyclic position shown. Achieving regioselective bromination at the specific aryl position (peri to the indole) over competing indole-ring bromination is highly questionable. Additionally, NBS can promote benzylic bromination/radical pathways given the benzylic C-Cl present. Significant selectivity concerns - this is the weakest step. Directed metalation or use of a pre-functionalized building block would be more reliable.

Methyl ester hydrolysis to the free acrylic acid is a standard final-step deprotection. Basic hydrolysis (LiOH or NaOH) should cleanly afford the cinnamic acid. The free phenol and the benzylic C-F are compatible. Mild conditions are advised to avoid E/Z isomerization of the acrylate; LiOH/THF-H2O at low temperature is recommended.

This is a Suzuki-Miyaura coupling between the 3-bromothiophene (vinyl/aryl bromide on the benzothiophene core) and the ortho-substituted aryl pinacol boronate. The disconnection is sound and well-precedented. However, two concerns: (1) the free phenol on the benzothiophene should tolerate Pd coupling but may benefit from protection to avoid catalyst inhibition; (2) the ortho-substituted boronate bearing a benzylic C-F is sterically demanding, and protodeboronation/competing reactions could lower yield. Choice of bulky ligand (SPhos/XPhos) is advisable. Overall feasible but with potential yield-limiting selectivity/sterics.

Miyaura borylation of the aryl bromide with bis(pinacolato)diboron (B2pin2), Pd catalyst and base (KOAc) is a textbook transformation. The ortho benzylic C-F is inert under these conditions. Standard and reliable.

This step depicts conversion of the aniline (CC(F)c1ccccc1N) to the aryl bromide (CC(F)c1ccccc1Br) using HBr. A direct aniline-to-aryl-bromide substitution does not proceed this way; it requires a Sandmeyer-type sequence (diazotization with NaNO2/HBr then CuBr). As written with simple 'Br' it is not a valid one-step transformation. Recommend representing the full diazotization/Sandmeyer sequence or sourcing the bromide directly.

Reduction of the nitroarene to the aniline is a standard transformation (H2/Pd-C, Fe/AcOH, or SnCl2). The benzylic C-F should be stable under mild reduction conditions, though hydrogenolysis of benzylic C-F could be a minor concern; non-hydrogenative conditions (Fe/NH4Cl or SnCl2) are preferred to preserve the fluoride.

Deoxyfluorination of the benzylic alcohol with DAST (Et2NSF3) to install the secondary benzylic fluoride is well-established. Possible side reactions include elimination to styrene and competing nitro-group involvement is minimal. Use of Deoxo-Fluor or low-temperature DAST conditions recommended to suppress elimination. Starting materials commercially available.

Demethylation of the aryl methyl ether to the free phenol (BBr3, or other Lewis acid). Concern: BBr3 can also cleave the diaryl ether linkage and may react with the acrylate ester/vinyl bromide. Milder demethylation (e.g., LiCl/DMF, or thiolate) may be preferred to chemoselectively unmask the phenol without affecting the diaryl ether or ester. Feasible with careful reagent choice.

Regioselective bromination of the benzothiophene at the 3-position (alpha to the existing aryloxy substituent) using NBS. Benzothiophenes brominate readily at C-3/C-2 positions; here the open position is selectively brominated. The acrylate, methyl ether, and diaryl ether are compatible with NBS. Radical vs ionic conditions should be controlled to avoid allylic bromination of the cinnamate.

This is a Heck reaction between methyl acrylate and the aryl bromide. The disconnection is appropriate and Heck couplings reliably give E-cinnamates. However, the substrate 'COc1ccc2c(Oc3ccc(Br)cc3)csc2c1' contains both an aryl bromide on the pendant phenyl ring AND the C-2 position of the benzothiophene is unsubstituted. The Heck must occur selectively at the para-aryl bromide, which it will (only one C-Br present). The labeling as 'in_stock' for this rather elaborate benzothiophenyl aryl ether is questionable - this is a complex intermediate unlikely to be commercially available. Heck itself is feasible and E-selective.

Methyl ester hydrolysis to the free acrylic acid is a standard final-step transformation. Basic hydrolysis (LiOH/NaOH) should be chemoselective and tolerate the free phenol, aryl thiophene, and benzylic fluoride. Mild conditions are advised to preserve the acid-sensitive benzylic C-F and the acrylate geometry. Straightforward and well-precedented.

Suzuki-Miyaura coupling between the 2-bromothiophene fragment and the aryl pinacol boronate to form the biaryl C-C bond. This is a sound disconnection. The free phenol and the acrylate ester are tolerated under standard Pd-catalyzed Suzuki conditions. One concern: the benzylic C-F (a secondary benzylic fluoride) could be sensitive under basic conditions, but typical Suzuki bases (K2CO3, K3PO4) at moderate temperature should be acceptable. Coupling at a 2-thienyl bromide is well-precedented. Possible homocoupling/protodeboronation are minor risks but manageable.

Miyaura borylation of the aryl bromide with bis(pinacolato)diboron (B2pin2) under Pd catalysis is a standard, reliable transformation to install the pinacol boronate. The benzylic fluoride should tolerate these conditions. Good disconnection providing the coupling partner for the subsequent Suzuki step.

This step proposes converting an aniline (CC(F)c1ccccc1N) directly to an aryl bromide using HBr. A direct ArNH2 + HBr -> ArBr substitution does not occur; aromatic amines are converted to aryl halides via diazotization (NaNO2/HBr) followed by a Sandmeyer-type reaction (CuBr), not by simple treatment with HBr. As written this is mechanistically incorrect. The reagent set is incomplete/misleading. Recommend explicit diazotization/Sandmeyer conditions, or better, source 2-(1-fluoroethyl)bromobenzene differently. Also note the benzylic fluoride may not survive aqueous acidic diazotization conditions (risk of solvolysis to benzylic alcohol/cation).

Reduction of the nitroarene to the aniline is straightforward (e.g., H2/Pd-C, Fe/AcOH, SnCl2). Chemoselective reduction of the nitro group in the presence of a benzylic fluoride is achievable, though strongly acidic conditions (Fe/AcOH, SnCl2) risk solvolysis of the secondary benzylic C-F. Catalytic hydrogenation under neutral conditions is preferred. Note also potential hydrogenolysis of the benzylic C-F over Pd — milder/selective conditions or transfer hydrogenation may be needed.

Deoxyfluorination of the benzylic secondary alcohol with DAST is chemically reasonable to install the benzylic C-F. However, benzylic alcohols are prone to elimination (forming styrene) and SN1 cation chemistry under DAST conditions, which can compete and erode yield. The ortho-nitro group is electron-withdrawing and may suppress carbocation formation somewhat, improving the SN2-like pathway, but elimination remains a concern. Deoxofluor or XtalFluor may give cleaner results. Acceptable disconnection but watch for elimination/rearrangement byproducts.

local_feedback: Protecting group strategy is wrong / non-optimal
local_feedback_text: This step is the demethylation of an aryl methyl ether to reveal the phenol. While O-demethylation (BBr3, etc.) is feasible, BBr3 conditions are harsh and would likely cleave/affect the aryl-O-aryl diaryl ether, the acrylate ester, and could be problematic with the thiophene. More importantly, in the context of the whole route the methyl protecting group is introduced and removed when a more orthogonal phenol protection (or carrying the free phenol through Suzuki, which is tolerated) would be more efficient. The PG strategy adds steps; consider avoiding methyl protection altogether since the free phenol is tolerated in subsequent steps.

NBS bromination at the 3-position of the benzothiophene to install the bromide for the later Suzuki coupling. Regioselectivity is a concern: the substrate already bears substituents on the thiophene ring (the 2-aryloxy group), and electrophilic bromination must occur cleanly at the desired position. There is also a risk of bromination of the electron-rich methoxy-bearing benzene ring or the acrylate-bearing aryl ring. Radical vs electrophilic conditions need to be chosen carefully. Workable but selectivity must be controlled.

Heck reaction between the aryl bromide (COc1ccc2c(Oc3ccc(Br)cc3)csc2c1) and methyl acrylate to install the E-cinnamate is a standard, well-precedented Pd-catalyzed transformation giving high E-selectivity. Good disconnection. The selected aryl bromide partner is reasonable and reportedly in stock. Note the bromide must be the para-position on the pendant phenoxy ring as drawn — selectivity is fine since it is the only aryl bromide.

Ester hydrolysis of a methyl cinnamate to the free acrylic acid is well-precedented. Use mild conditions (LiOH/THF/H2O) to avoid isomerization of the (E)-alkene and to tolerate the free phenol. The benzylic C-F bond is stable to these conditions. Straightforward final deprotection step.

Suzuki–Miyaura coupling between the 2-bromothiophene (aryl bromide on the benzothiophene C2) and the ortho-substituted aryl pinacol boronate. The disconnection is reasonable and well-precedented for constructing the biaryl C-C bond. However, the free phenol (4-OH on the benzothiophene) is unprotected during the coupling; while phenols are generally tolerated in Suzuki couplings, basic conditions could complicate the reaction. More importantly, the boronate bears an ortho-CH(F)CH3 group adjacent to a heavily substituted thiophene — significant steric hindrance at this hindered biaryl junction may lower yield. Use Pd with bulky electron-rich ligands (SPhos/XPhos) and consider protecting the phenol. Overall feasible but selectivity/steric concerns warrant attention.

Miyaura borylation of the aryl bromide with bis(pinacolato)diboron (B2pin2), Pd catalyst and base (KOAc) is a standard, robust transformation. The benzylic C-F is compatible. Good disconnection to set up the subsequent Suzuki coupling.

This represents a Sandmeyer-type conversion of an aniline to an aryl bromide, but the reagents shown are simply 'Br' (HBr) and the aniline, which is not a complete/correct reagent set. A proper Sandmeyer requires diazotization (NaNO2/HBr or t-BuONO) followed by CuBr. The disconnection (ArNH2 -> ArBr) is valid, but the reagents as written are incomplete and would not effect the transformation. Note also the benzylic C-F is stable to diazotization conditions.

Reduction of an aromatic nitro group to the aniline is a standard transformation (H2/Pd-C, Fe/AcOH, SnCl2). Caution: H2/Pd-C could risk hydrogenolysis of the benzylic C-F bond; use chemoselective conditions (Fe/NH4Cl or SnCl2) to preserve the C-F. Disconnection is fine.

Deoxofluorination of a benzylic secondary alcohol with DAST (Et2NSF3) to give the benzylic fluoride is well-established. Some risk of elimination to styrene byproduct and possible carbocation rearrangement, but for a simple benzylic alcohol this proceeds reasonably. Both reagents commercially available. Consider Deoxo-Fluor for improved safety/selectivity.

Demethylation of an aryl methyl ether to the free phenol. Standard reagents (BBr3, or milder conditions). Caution: BBr3 may cleave the diaryl ether and could affect the vinyl bromide/Michael acceptor; the benzylic C-F should be monitored. Milder demethylation (e.g., LiCl/DMF, or thiolate) may be preferable to preserve the aryl-aryl ether and methyl ester. Disconnection is sound.

Bromination of the benzothiophene C2/C3 position with NBS. The disconnection installs the bromide needed for subsequent Suzuki coupling. Regioselectivity for the electron-rich position of the benzothiophene must be controlled; NBS bromination of benzothiophenes typically favors C3, but here C3 is occupied by the aryloxy group, directing to C2. Feasible with attention to regiocontrol. Note potential competing bromination of the electron-rich anisole ring.

Heck reaction between methyl acrylate and an aryl bromide to form the (E)-cinnamate. The disconnection is reasonable and Heck typically gives high (E)-selectivity. However, the substrate contains TWO aryl bromides equivalents in the building block sense? Here the building block 'COc1ccc2c(Oc3ccc(Br)cc3)csc2c1' has an aryl bromide on the pendant phenoxy ring — Heck would occur there to install the acrylate, which is correct. Good regio/stereo outcome expected with Pd(OAc)2/phosphine. Feasible; flagged only for ensuring chemoselectivity if other halides/reactive positions exist.

This is the final ester hydrolysis (methyl ester to carboxylic acid). Saponification with LiOH or NaOH in THF/MeOH/water is a standard, robust transformation. The free phenol and biaryl-thiophene system are compatible. The E-geometry of the acrylate is retained. A reasonable end-game disconnection.

Suzuki-Miyaura coupling between the 3-bromobenzothiophene and the aryl pinacol boronate to install the biaryl bond. This is a well-precedented disconnection. Note that the free phenol on the benzothiophene is present; while phenols are generally tolerated under Suzuki conditions (Pd(PPh3)4 or SPhos/Pd, K2CO3 or K3PO4), the unprotected phenol might warrant attention. The hindered ortho-substituted aryl boronate (with the CH(CH3)F group ortho) introduces some steric demand, but Suzuki couplings of ortho-substituted boronates are feasible with appropriate ligands (SPhos, XPhos). The Michael acceptor (acrylate) is generally compatible. Sound disconnection.

Miyaura borylation of the aryl bromide with bis(pinacolato)diboron (B2pin2) under Pd catalysis (PdCl2(dppf), KOAc) to give the pinacol boronate. Standard transformation. The benzylic C-F (CH(CH3)F) group is compatible with these conditions. Well-precedented.

This represents a Sandmeyer-type conversion of an aniline to an aryl bromide. The disconnection shows ArNH2 + HBr giving ArBr, but a true Sandmeyer requires diazotization (NaNO2/HBr) followed by CuBr. The simple representation with just 'Br' is mechanistically incomplete; the correct reagents are NaNO2/HBr/CuBr. The benzylic fluoride should survive these conditions. The disconnection itself (aniline to aryl bromide) is valid, but the reagent depiction is non-optimal/incomplete.

Reduction of the aromatic nitro group to the aniline. Standard transformation (H2/Pd-C, Fe/AcOH, SnCl2, or Zn). Caution: with H2/Pd-C, hydrogenolysis of the benzylic C-F could be a concern, so milder conditions (Fe/NH4Cl or SnCl2) would be preferable to preserve the CH(CH3)F group. Otherwise a feasible step.

Deoxyfluorination of the benzylic secondary alcohol using DAST (Et2NSF3) to convert CH(OH)CH3 to CH(F)CH3. This is a standard DAST transformation on a benzylic/secondary alcohol. Possible side reactions include elimination to the styrene and racemization/E1-type pathways given the benzylic cation stabilization, which could lower yield. Both starting materials are commercially available. Overall feasible.

Demethylation of the aryl methyl ether to reveal the phenol (BBr3, or other Lewis acid). This is standard. However, in the context of the route, BBr3 demethylation could be incompatible with the acrylate ester (transesterification/cleavage risk) and the aryl ether linkage. Milder conditions (e.g., NaSEt, LiCl/DMF, or BCl3) may be needed for chemoselectivity. The diaryl ether should be stable. Feasible but requires careful condition selection.

NBS bromination at the 3-position of the benzothiophene (C adjacent to the C-O ether). Electrophilic bromination of benzothiophenes typically favors the 3-position, which is consistent here. However, with an electron-rich methoxy arene and the activated acrylate-bearing aryloxy substituent already present, there is potential for competing ring bromination on the electron-rich aromatic rings. Regioselectivity should be confirmed; radical vs ionic conditions matter. Possible but selectivity is a genuine concern.

local_feedback: Problems with reaction type and functional group compatibility
local_feedback_text: This step proposes a Heck reaction between methyl acrylate and an aryl bromide (COc1ccc2c(Oc3ccc(Br)cc3)csc2c1) to install the E-cinnamate. The disconnection is reasonable (Heck of methyl acrylate with aryl bromide, Pd cat., base, gives E-acrylate selectively). However, the substrate contains TWO potentially reactive aryl halide/C-O sites and the benzothiophene C3-H; the aryl bromide is on the pendant phenoxy ring, which is the intended site and should undergo Heck cleanly. The main concern: the labeled in-stock starting material COc1ccc2c(Oc3ccc(Br)cc3)csc2c1 is unlikely to be genuinely commercially available — this is a complex 3-aryloxy benzothiophene. The Heck itself is feasible, but the building block availability is questionable.

This step represents global deprotection of phosphonate/phosphate isopropyl esters to give the free phosphonic acid/phosphate. The disconnection (removing two isopropyl groups) is reasonable, but the stated product retains one P-OH while the reactant has two isopropyl esters on one phosphorus and one isopropyl ester (plus an O-P-OH) on the other - the bookkeeping of how many esters are cleaved is inconsistent. Typically isopropyl phosphonate esters are cleaved with TMSBr (McKenna procedure) or strong acid. The chloroacrylamide/uracil core, allylic system, and pyrophosphate linkage are acid-sensitive; a pyrophosphate (P-O-P) bond may not survive harsh acidic global deprotection. TMSBr is the preferred mild reagent. Confidence moderate due to ambiguity in the exact esters being removed.

This is the selective demethylation of a methyl phosphonate ester to give the free P-OH while retaining the two isopropyl esters. Selective mono-demethylation in the presence of isopropyl esters is difficult to control - methyl esters are indeed more labile (e.g., to thiolate nucleophiles like PhSH/Et3N or LiBr), so chemoselective methyl cleavage over isopropyl is plausible. However, controlling stoichiometry to cleave exactly one methyl group without touching the pyrophosphate linkage or causing over-deprotection is challenging. A thiolate-mediated SN2 demethylation (LiBr in acetone or NaSEt) would be the reagent of choice. Mark as non-optimal pending clearer reagent specification.

This is the key N-alkylation of the chlorouracil with an allylic bromide. The major concern is N1 vs N3 regioselectivity: 5-chlorouracil has two N-H sites. N1-alkylation is generally favored (and is the desired site here, matching the product), but achieving clean regiocontrol typically requires protection of N3 or careful conditions (e.g., persilylation/Vorbrüggen-type conditions, or mild base such as K2CO3/DMF with the silver or cesium salt). O-alkylation is also a competing pathway with allylic halides on ambident uracil anions. Additionally, the allylic bromide could undergo SN2' isomerization affecting the E-alkene geometry. The phosphonate/phosphate esters are compatible. Overall feasible but selectivity must be addressed - likely requires N3 protection.

This step proposes forming the isopropyl phosphoester (P-OC(C)C) from isopropanol and a phosphoryl chloride (P-Cl). The transformation itself (alcohol + P-Cl -> P-OR) is standard esterification. However, the reactant P-Cl coexists with an allylic bromide; under the basic conditions normally needed to drive P-Cl alcoholysis, the allylic bromide is highly reactive and prone to side reactions (elimination, ether formation with isopropanol, quaternization). More importantly, sequencing is poor: installing the labile allylic bromide before the phosphoester esterification is strategically backwards. The disconnection logic is questionable. Better to esterify before introducing the allylic bromide.

local_feedback_text: This is an Appel-type bromination (CBr4, presumably with PPh3) converting an allylic alcohol to an allylic bromide. The Appel reaction on an allylic alcohol is feasible, but the substrate still bears a reactive P-Cl (phosphorochloridate) which is highly moisture/nucleophile-sensitive and would not survive co-existence with the alcohol substrate (intramolecular/intermolecular reaction) or Appel conditions. Having a free P-Cl and a free alcohol in the same molecule is chemically problematic - they would react with each other. Also note CBr4 alone is shown without PPh3; the standard Appel requires a phosphine. Reagent/intermediate design is flawed.

This step represents global deprotection of the isopropyl phosphonate/phosphate esters to reveal the free phosphonic acid/diphosphate. The transformation is chemically reasonable - isopropyl phosphate esters can be cleaved with TMSBr/TMSI followed by hydrolysis, which is a standard McKenna-type deprotection. However, the depicted product still bears one isopropyl group on the reactant while the product is fully deprotected, and the chemoselectivity (cleaving all three esters cleanly without degrading the vinyl chloride uracil or the allylic system) is plausible with TMSBr. The disconnection itself is sound; the reagent/conditions should be specified clearly. Note also the product is a pyrophosphate-analogue (phosphonate-phosphate anhydride), which is hydrolytically labile and may complicate isolation.

This step proposes selective demethylation of one methyl phosphonate ester while leaving the two isopropyl esters intact, generating a free P-OH. Achieving chemoselective cleavage of a single methyl ester in the presence of isopropyl esters is difficult; standard conditions (e.g., TMSBr, thiolate nucleophiles, or LiOH) would not cleanly differentiate to give exactly one free acid without over-deprotection. This selectivity issue makes the step questionable as written. A better strategy would be to use orthogonal protecting groups from the outset rather than relying on differential alkyl ester cleavage.

This is an N-alkylation of 5-chlorouracil with an allylic bromide bearing the phosphonate-phosphate tether. The disconnection is reasonable (N1-alkylation of uracil). However, the major concern is regioselectivity: 5-chlorouracil has two nitrogen atoms (N1 and N3) and O-alkylation is also possible. Selective N1-alkylation typically requires controlled conditions (e.g., silylation/Vorbruggen-type or careful base selection such as K2CO3/DMF or use of a protected uracil). As drawn (free unprotected uracil + allylic bromide), N1 vs N3 vs O-alkylation selectivity is a real issue. Also, the allylic bromide could undergo SN2' rearrangement scrambling the alkene geometry. Recommend protecting/activating the uracil or using metal templating to ensure N1 selectivity.

This step proposes converting a P-Cl (phosphorochloridate) to a P-O-iPr ester by reaction with isopropanol. Mechanistically this esterification is fine, BUT the retrosynthetic logic is inconsistent with the rest of the route: the product retains a methyl ester on the phosphonate and gains a second iPr ester. The use of a phosphorochloridate intermediate carrying a free allylic bromide is problematic because the alcohol nucleophile (iPrOH) and the reactive P-Cl could give mixtures, and the allylic bromide is also electrophilic. Moreover, generating a fully alkylated mixed phosphonate-phosphate diester with two different alkyl groups (Me and two iPr) is a fragile, low-value intermediate. The disconnection is awkward and the mixed ester strategy is poorly conceived.

local_feedback_text: This step is an Appel-type bromination (CBr4, presumably with PPh3) of an allylic alcohol to give the allylic bromide. The Appel reaction on a primary allylic alcohol is feasible. However, the substrate contains a reactive P-Cl (phosphorochloridate) which is highly moisture-sensitive and electrophilic; it would not survive Appel conditions cleanly and could react with PPh3 or with liberated nucleophiles. Additionally, allylic bromides can suffer from allylic rearrangement (SN2') affecting E/Z geometry. The presence of the labile P-Cl alongside the free alcohol makes chemoselectivity for clean Appel bromination doubtful. The CBr4 reagent is shown without PPh3, which is incomplete.

This step proposes the global deprotection of a triisopropyl phosphonate-phosphate ester to reveal the free phosphonate-phosphate diphosphate analogue. The disconnection (deprotection of isopropyl esters on P) is reasonable in principle, as isopropyl phosphate esters can be cleaved with TMSBr/TMSI followed by hydrolysis. However, the reactant shown still has three isopropyl groups while the product has all free OH groups, requiring removal of all three esters in one operation. The chlorinated uracil and the allylic phosphonate linkage are sensitive; harsh acidic conditions risk hydrolyzing the labile P-O-P anhydride bridge. A milder, stepwise TMSBr deprotection is preferred. The bond disconnection class is valid but reagent/conditions need careful optimization to preserve the pyrophosphate-mimic linkage.

This step converts a methyl phosphonate ester (P-OMe) to a free P-OH while retaining the two isopropyl esters on the adjacent phosphorus. Selective demethylation of one phosphorus ester in the presence of two isopropyl esters on a neighboring phosphorus is challenging. Methyl esters are indeed more labile than isopropyl esters (e.g., toward thiolate nucleophiles or TMSBr at controlled stoichiometry), so chemoselectivity is feasible but not trivial. There is significant risk of over-deprotection affecting the isopropyl groups or cleavage of the P-O-P linkage. Careful control of reagent equivalents (e.g., NaI/thiophenol, or limited TMSBr) would be required.

This is an N-alkylation of 5-chlorouracil with an allylic bromide to install the N1-substituent. The disconnection is sound and N-alkylation of uracils with allylic halides is well precedented (typically with a base such as K2CO3, Cs2CO3, or DBU in DMF). However, two key selectivity concerns: (1) N1 vs N3 regioselectivity of uracil alkylation - mono-N1 selectivity is achievable but mixtures with N3 and N1,N3-dialkylation are common and require careful optimization; (2) the allylic bromide could undergo SN2 vs SN2' competition, though the E-allylic geometry and primary position favor direct SN2. Overall feasible but regioselectivity at the uracil nitrogen needs control.

This step proposes installation of an isopropyl ester onto a phosphoryl chloride (P-Cl) using isopropanol to give the fully esterified product. The transformation P-Cl + iPrOH -> P-OiPr is chemically straightforward (esterification of a phosphorochloridate, typically with a base such as pyridine or Et3N). However, the reactant contains a reactive allylic bromide (C/C=C/CBr) that would compete: under basic esterification conditions the allylic bromide could be attacked by isopropoxide/isopropanol, or the alkoxide could cause elimination. Chemoselectivity for the P-Cl over the allylic C-Br is questionable without careful conditions. The disconnection itself (P-O bond formation) is reasonable, but functional group compatibility is the concern.

This step is an Appel-type bromination of an allylic alcohol to the allylic bromide using CBr4. The Appel reaction normally requires a phosphine (PPh3) in addition to CBr4; only CBr4 is shown as the reagent. Furthermore, the substrate contains a phosphoryl chloride (P-Cl) which is highly moisture/nucleophile sensitive and would be incompatible with Appel conditions and the free alcohol that has somehow not already reacted with the P-Cl intramolecularly/intermolecularly. The ordering is problematic - having a P-Cl and a free OH in the same molecule is inherently unstable. The bromination disconnection is fine but the reagent set is incomplete (missing PPh3) and the FG context is poor.

This step represents the global deprotection of the isopropyl phosphonate/phosphate esters to reveal the free phosphonic acid diphosphate. The disconnection itself is reasonable (final deprotection to liberate the acidic phosphonate). However, the parent molecule retains one free P-OH while three isopropyl groups remain protected, which is chemically inconsistent for a 'protecting group removal' step - typically all esters would be cleaved together (e.g., with TMSBr/McKenna conditions) to give the fully deprotected product in one operation. The presence of the chlorouracil and the allylic system are compatible with TMSBr cleavage. The non-symmetric protection state across steps is awkward; a uniform deprotection strategy is preferred. Confidence is moderate because the transformation is feasible but the reagent/state mismatch is non-optimal.

This step shows selective conversion of one methyl phosphonate ester (COP) to a free P-OH while leaving the two isopropyl esters intact. Achieving selective mono-demethylation of a methyl ester in the presence of isopropyl esters is challenging and not cleanly selective; methyl esters of phosphonates are typically cleaved with TMSBr or thiolate nucleophiles (e.g., LiBr, NaI, or PhSH/base) but these conditions can also affect other P-O esters. The mixed methyl/isopropyl protecting group scheme creates unnecessary differentiation problems. A unified protecting group choice would simplify and improve selectivity. Feasible in principle but reagent choice and selectivity are suboptimal.

This is the key N-alkylation of 5-chlorouracil with the allylic bromide bearing the phosphonate-phosphate scaffold. The intended N1-alkylation is reasonable and well-precedented for uracil chemistry, but 5-chlorouracil has two nitrogen sites (N1 and N3) and the regioselectivity of alkylation requires careful control (typically N1 is favored, often via silylation/Vorbrüggen-type conditions or controlled base). Without protection of N3 or selective base conditions, mixtures of N1/N3 alkylation and possibly O-alkylation can occur. Also the allylic bromide can undergo SN2 vs SN2' competition, potentially scrambling the alkene position. The disconnection is strategically sound but selectivity must be addressed (e.g., use of a silylated uracil or controlled stoichiometry/base). E-geometry of the allylic system should be preserved under mild SN2 conditions.

This step proposes formation of the P-O-C(isopropyl) bond by reacting isopropanol with a phosphorochloridate (P-Cl). That esterification (alcohol + P-Cl → P-OR + HCl) is chemically reasonable in itself and usually requires a base (e.g., pyridine, Et3N). However, the depicted reactant already contains an allylic bromide AND a methyl phosphonate ester; under the basic conditions needed for alcoholysis of P-Cl, the allylic bromide is highly susceptible to side reactions (elimination, substitution by alkoxide/isopropoxide), making this poorly chemoselective. The disconnection as drawn (installing isopropyl ester late, after bromide is present) is order-of-operations flawed. Better to install all esters before introducing the labile allylic bromide. Marked as problematic due to functional group incompatibility and poor sequencing.

Appel-type conversion of the allylic alcohol to the allylic bromide using CBr4 (typically with PPh3, which is not shown). The transformation of a primary allylic alcohol to allylic bromide is feasible, but the reactant still bears a phosphorochloridate (P-Cl), which is highly moisture/nucleophile sensitive and incompatible with Appel conditions (PPh3/CBr4 and the byproducts). The P-Cl would likely react or hydrolyze under these conditions. Also, PPh3 co-reagent is missing from the equation. Reagent/condition selection is non-optimal and the P-Cl functionality should not be present at this stage. Allylic bromination can also give allylic rearrangement (SN2' type) products.

This is a Suzuki-Miyaura coupling between a boronic acid and bromobenzene to form the biaryl. The disconnection is reasonable, but there is a strategic issue: the molecule contains a free secondary amine (the methoxyethylamino group) which can coordinate/poison Pd catalysts and interfere with the coupling. Additionally, coupling aryl boronic acids with aryl bromides under standard Suzuki conditions is feasible, but using the bromide as the electrophile and the more elaborate boronic acid partner is counterintuitive - it would be more efficient and convergent to use phenylboronic acid (commercial, cheap) and keep the bromide on the complex fragment. The current direction requires installation of a boronic acid on the complex molecule (step f4fc4a0fba70e73ab342cefccee7ab16c476414be4d2ce6a4c6bb3c525a34be9), which adds steps. Recommend reversing the polarity of the coupling.

local_feedback: Problems with reaction type and functional group compatibility
local_feedback_text: This step proposes Miyaura borylation of the aryl bromide using triisopropyl borate to generate the boronic acid. The standard Miyaura borylation uses bis(pinacolato)diboron with Pd catalysis, or lithium-halogen exchange followed by trapping with a borate ester. The lithiation route (with iPrO-borate) is incompatible with the free secondary amine, the amide/lactam C=O, the thiophene, and the pyrimidinone present. Pd-catalyzed borylation with B2pin2 would be more appropriate but still risks issues with the free amine. More importantly, this entire borylation step is unnecessary if the Suzuki coupling polarity is reversed (use phenylboronic acid + the aryl bromide directly). This step adds complexity.

Reductive amination between the primary amine and methoxyacetaldehyde (COCC=O) to install the methoxyethyl group on the secondary amine. This is a well-precedented transformation using NaBH(OAc)3 or NaBH3CN. The aryl bromide, lactam, and heteroaromatic systems are compatible. Chemoselectivity favors reductive amination of the primary aliphatic amine. Good step.

Boc deprotection to reveal the primary amine. Standard transformation using TFA or HCl. The aryl bromide, lactam, thiophene, and pyrimidinone are all stable to acidic Boc removal conditions. Straightforward and appropriate as a precursor to the reductive amination.

N-alkylation of the pyrimidinone NH with 1,3-bis(bromomethyl)... wait, it is 3-bromobenzyl bromide (BrCc1cccc(Br)c1). The benzylic bromide is selectively more reactive than the aryl bromide, so chemoselective N-alkylation at the lactam/pyrimidinone nitrogen is feasible with a base (K2CO3, Cs2CO3). However, N- vs O-alkylation selectivity for the amide/pyrimidinone system can be an issue (ambident nucleophile), potentially giving O-alkylated byproducts. Regioselectivity of N-alkylation should be controllable but warrants attention. Overall feasible with care.

This step constructs the pyrimidinone ring from a 2-aminothiophene-3-carboxylic ester via cyclization with formamide (NC=O). This is a classic Niementowski-type/formamide cyclization to build fused pyrimidin-4(3H)-one rings from ortho-amino esters. Heating the aminoester with formamide is well-precedented. The Boc group should survive moderate heating, though prolonged high temperatures (>150 °C typical for formamide cyclizations) may risk Boc decomposition - this is a potential concern. The starting aminothiophene ester is a reasonable building block accessible via Gewald chemistry. Good disconnection.

This is a Suzuki-Miyaura coupling between bromobenzene and the arylboronic acid to form the biaryl. The disconnection itself is sound and well-precedented. However, the coupling partner choice is suboptimal: bromobenzene as the electrophile coupling with the more elaborate boronic acid is fine, but the reverse (using PhB(OH)2 with the aryl bromide intermediate) would be more convergent and avoid carrying the boronic acid through. There is also a chemoselectivity concern: the secondary amine (NH) and the methoxyethyl group are tolerated by Pd catalysis, but protodeboronation of the benzylic-substituted arylboronic acid is a real risk. Overall feasible but the route should be reordered (see general feedback).

Miyaura borylation of the aryl bromide. Note that the reagent shown is triisopropyl borate (CC(C)OB(OC(C)C)OC(C)C), which is typically used with an organolithium/Grignard, not directly with an aryl bromide under Pd catalysis (which would use bis(pinacolato)diboron, B2pin2). Direct lithium-halogen exchange in the presence of the free secondary amine, the thienopyrimidinone, and the carbonyl is problematic. For Pd-catalyzed borylation with B2pin2 the transformation is feasible. As drawn with the borate ester it is non-optimal but the disconnection is correct. The strategy of installing boron then coupling, instead of coupling PhB(OH)2 directly, adds unnecessary steps.

Reductive amination between the primary amine and methoxyacetaldehyde (COCC=O) to give the secondary amine. This is a standard, robust transformation (NaBH(OAc)3 or NaBH3CN). The free primary amine on the cyclohexane ring is the only nucleophile, so chemoselectivity is good. The aryl bromide and thienopyrimidinone are compatible. Well-precedented and reliable.

Boc deprotection of the carbamate to reveal the primary amine. Standard acidic conditions (TFA or HCl). The thienopyrimidinone, benzylic C-Br, and aryl ring are all stable under these conditions. Straightforward and reliable.

N-alkylation of the pyrimidinone NH with 3-bromobenzyl bromide. The disconnection is reasonable, but two selectivity issues arise: (1) the ambident nucleophile (N vs O alkylation of the amide/pyrimidinone) can give O-alkylated byproducts, though N-alkylation is usually favored with benzylic halides and a base like K2CO3/Cs2CO3; (2) using a benzyl bromide that also bears an aryl bromide is fine since the aryl C-Br is much less reactive toward SN2, so chemoselective benzylic alkylation should dominate. Overall feasible with attention to N/O selectivity.

Construction of the pyrimidinone ring from the 2-aminothiophene-3-carboxylate (ethyl ester) by cyclization with formamide (NC=O). This is the classic Niementowski-type/formamide cyclization to build the fused pyrimidin-4(3H)-one. The Boc carbamate may be partially labile under the harsh thermal conditions (typically >150 °C) used for formamide cyclizations, which is a concern, but the disconnection itself is well-established. Consider whether Boc survives the cyclization conditions; an alternative would be to cyclize first and protect later.

Suzuki coupling of bromobenzene with the arylboronic acid to form the biaryl bond is a well-precedented transformation. Pd(PPh3)4 or Pd(dppf)Cl2 with base would work. The unprotected secondary amine and the heterocyclic system are generally tolerated under Suzuki conditions. This step is feasible.

local_feedback_text: This is a Miyaura-type borylation converting the aryl bromide to a boronic acid using triisopropyl borate (the SMILES shows isopropyl borate as a metalation/borylation reagent). Direct conversion of ArBr to ArB(OH)2 with B(OiPr)3 normally requires generation of an aryllithium or Grignard, which is completely incompatible with the free secondary amine (would need protection), the lactam N-H equivalent, and especially the thienopyrimidinone carbonyl. A Pd-catalyzed Miyaura borylation with B2pin2 would be more appropriate, giving a pinacol boronate rather than free boronic acid. As written with B(OiPr)3 implying organometallic borylation, this step has serious compatibility problems. Recommend Pd-catalyzed Miyaura borylation conditions.

Reductive amination between methoxyacetaldehyde and the primary amine to install the COCCNH- group is a sound, well-precedented disconnection. NaBH(OAc)3 or NaBH3CN in DCE/MeOH would deliver the secondary amine cleanly. Chemoselectivity is good as the only reactive electrophile is the aldehyde and the only nucleophilic amine is the primary amine. Feasible.

Boc deprotection of the carbamate to reveal the primary amine using TFA or HCl is standard and reliable. The aryl bromide, thienopyrimidinone, and benzyl groups are stable under acidic deprotection conditions. Feasible.

N-alkylation of the pyrimidinone N-H with 3-bromobenzyl bromide is a sound disconnection. However, selectivity is a concern: the ambident nucleophilic lactam/amidine system (N vs O alkylation) could give O-alkylation byproducts, and regioselectivity between the available nitrogen atoms must be controlled. With a suitable base (K2CO3 or Cs2CO3 in DMF), N-alkylation typically predominates. Additionally, the use of the dibromide BrCc1cccc(Br)c1 risks bis-alkylation, but the benzylic bromide is far more reactive than the aryl bromide so chemoselectivity should be acceptable. Feasible with attention to N/O selectivity.

This is the construction of the pyrimidinone ring from an ortho-aminothiophene ester via cyclization with formamide (Niementowski-type synthesis of fused pyrimidinones). Heating the 2-aminothiophene-3-carboxylic ester with formamide is a classic, well-precedented method to form the fused 4-oxo-pyrimidine ring. The Boc group should survive moderate heating but prolonged high temperatures with formamide could risk Boc cleavage; this should be monitored. Overall a feasible and standard transformation.

Miyaura borylation of an aryl bromide to install the boronic acid (here drawn from triisopropyl borate). Conversion of ArBr to ArB(OH)2 via lithiation/borate quench or Pd-catalyzed borylation is well-precedented. Using triisopropyl borate typically proceeds via organolithium/Grignard formation, which would be incompatible with the free NH amine, the lactam, and the aminothiophene. A Pd-catalyzed Miyaura borylation with B2pin2 would be much more compatible here. The disconnection is correct but reagent choice is non-optimal given functionality; still, the bond formation is valid.

This step proposes forming the arylboronic acid from the aryl bromide using triisopropyl borate. As noted, the classical lithiation/borate route is incompatible with the secondary amine, lactam NH-free positions, and other heteroatoms in this densely functionalized substrate. A Pd-catalyzed Miyaura borylation (Pd(dppf)Cl2, B2pin2, KOAc) followed by hydrolysis would be the optimal choice and tolerate the functionality. Same disconnection, better reagent needed.

Reductive amination between the primary amine and methoxyacetaldehyde (COCC=O) to install the 2-methoxyethyl group on the cyclohexane-fused amine. This is a standard reductive amination (NaBH(OAc)3 or NaBH3CN). The aminothiophene-fused lactam scaffold should tolerate these conditions. Chemoselectivity favors the aliphatic primary amine over the ring nitrogens. Feasible and appropriate.

Boc deprotection to reveal the free primary amine. Standard TFA or HCl treatment. The aryl bromide, thienopyrimidinone, and benzyl groups are all stable under acidic Boc removal. Straightforward and necessary to allow the subsequent reductive amination.

N-alkylation of the lactam/pyrimidinone NH with 3-bromobenzyl bromide. Selective N-alkylation at the ring nitrogen with a benzyl bromide using a base (K2CO3, Cs2CO3) is well-precedented. Possible competing O-alkylation of the amide could occur, but N-alkylation typically predominates with these conditions. The aryl bromide on the benzyl group survives. Good disconnection for assembling the N-benzyl handle.

Construction of the thienopyrimidinone ring from a 2-aminothiophene-3-carboxylate via condensation with formamide (Niementowski-type/pyrimidinone annulation). Heating the 2-amino-3-ester thiophene with formamide is a classic method to build the fused 4-oxo-pyrimidine ring. The Boc group could be partially labile under the high temperatures usually required for formamide cyclization (150-200 C), which is a concern. Otherwise the disconnection is sound and well-precedented.

This is a proposed Buchwald-Hartwig type C–N coupling (or SNAr) between a 2-bromopyrimidinone and a primary amine. While the aryl bromide on the activated pyrimidinone ring is plausible for amination, there are serious chemoselectivity concerns: the molecule contains a free, highly nucleophilic aminoguanidine/N-aminoxyguanidine moiety (NOC(=N)N) and an amide, both of which could compete with the desired secondary amine product or coordinate/poison Pd catalysts. Performing this coupling without protecting the guanidine is risky. The disconnection itself (amine + halopyrimidinone) is reasonable as the final convergent step, but selectivity and FG compatibility issues are significant. Consider doing the amination earlier, before installing the sensitive aminoxyguanidine.

Bromination with NBS at the pyrimidinone C-position. Electrophilic bromination here is conceivable on an electron-rich aminopyridinone/pyrimidinone ring, but regioselectivity is a concern given the existing methyl substituent and ring nitrogens. More critically, the substrate carries a free guanidine/aminoxyguanidine and an amide N–H; NBS is an electrophilic brominating agent that can brominate or oxidize amines, guanidines, and other nucleophilic sites, leading to poor chemoselectivity. This step would be far cleaner if performed before installation of the aminoxyguanidine fragment, or with protection. Regiochemistry of the C–H bromination on this heterocycle also needs verification.

local_feedback_text: Amide bond formation between the carboxylic acid (Cc1cncc(=O)n1CC(=O)O) and the primary amine of N=C(N)NOCCN. The disconnection is sound (standard amide coupling, e.g., EDC/HOBt, HATU). However, the coupling partner bears a free aminoxyguanidine that contains multiple nucleophilic N–H sites; selective acylation of the desired primary amine over the guanidine nitrogens is non-trivial and could give regiochemical mixtures or guanidine acylation. A protecting group strategy on the guanidine (e.g., Boc-protected guanidine carried through) would substantially improve selectivity. As drawn with the free guanidine, chemoselectivity is questionable.

This step claims N=C(N)NOCCN (an amine) derives from N#CCONC(=N)N (a nitrile). Reduction of a nitrile (RCH2C#N) to a primary amine (RCH2CH2NH2) requires adding two carbons-worth... actually the carbon count: N#C-CH2-O... reduction of the nitrile gives H2N-CH2-CH2-O..., which matches. So this is a nitrile reduction to primary amine. That transformation (LiAlH4, or H2/catalyst, or borane) is feasible in principle BUT the substrate also contains a free guanidine (C(=N)N) which is base/reductant sensitive and an N-O bond (aminoxy) that is readily cleaved under hydrogenation conditions. Selective nitrile reduction without cleaving the weak N–O bond or reducing the guanidine is highly problematic. This disconnection/transformation as drawn is unlikely to succeed cleanly.

local_feedback_text: This step proposes converting a bis-Boc protected aminoxyguanidine-nitrile to the free guanidine-nitrile (N#CCONC(=N)N), i.e., Boc deprotection. Boc removal (TFA or HCl) is standard. However the free aminoxyguanidine product is reactive, and carrying it forward into subsequent steps (nitrile reduction, amide coupling, NBS bromination, Pd amination) creates the cascade of selectivity problems noted in later/earlier steps. The deprotection chemistry itself is feasible; the strategy of unmasking the guanidine this early is non-optimal.

Boc protection of a guanidine nitrogen using Boc2O to give the bis-Boc protected guanidine. This is a standard, well-precedented transformation. Boc2O is commercially available and cheap. The mono-Boc guanidine starting material is reasonable. No major issues; selectivity for the second Boc installation is generally controllable with stoichiometry/base.

N-alkylation of the pyridinone/pyrimidinone N–H (Cc1cncc(=O)[nH]1) with tert-butyl bromoacetate. This is a classic N-alkylation of an amide/lactam nitrogen with an alkyl halide under basic conditions (K2CO3, Cs2CO3, NaH). Both starting materials are commercially available. Minor concern: O- vs N-alkylation ambiguity for the ambident pyridinone, but N-alkylation typically predominates with these conditions. Good step.

Acidic cleavage of the tert-butyl ester to reveal the carboxylic acid (TFA or HCl). Straightforward and well-precedented. No competing functionality at this stage (the heterocyclic core only). Feasible as written.

This is a Buchwald-Hartwig type C-N coupling (or SNAr) between an aryl/heteroaryl bromide and a primary amine. However, the substrate contains a highly nucleophilic guanidine/aminooxy-guanidine moiety (NOC(=N)N) and a free amide N-H, which would compete with the desired phenethylamine for coupling or interfere with Pd catalysis. The guanidine is a strong ligand/poison for Pd and would likely chelate the metal. A SNAr pathway is plausible given the electron-poor pyridinone ring, but chemoselectivity for the primary amine over the guanidine nitrogens is questionable. Late-stage installation of an unprotected guanidine is generally a poor strategy. Recommend installing the phenethylamine earlier and carrying the guanidine in a protected (Boc) form or installing it last.

local_feedback_text: NBS bromination at the position alpha to the ring nitrogen of a 2-pyridinone is a reasonable electrophilic halogenation. However, performing NBS bromination on a substrate bearing a free guanidine/aminooxyguanidine and an amide is problematic: NBS can oxidize/brominate the electron-rich guanidine and aminooxy functionality, and N-H bonds are susceptible. This step should be performed before installation of the sensitive guanidine moiety. Chemoselectivity is a serious concern.

local_feedback_text: This amide coupling between the carboxylic acid (Cc1cncc(=O)n1CC(=O)O) and the amine of the aminooxyguanidine (N=C(N)NOCCN) is in principle feasible. However, the free guanidine is more nucleophilic/basic than the primary amine and competitive acylation on the guanidine nitrogens is likely, leading to selectivity problems. Standard practice is to couple with a Boc-protected guanidine to ensure chemoselective amide formation on the primary amine. Recommend using the Boc2-protected aminooxyguanidine for this coupling, then deprotect.

This step proposes converting a nitrile (N#CCONC(=N)N) into a primary amine-terminated aminooxyguanidine (N=C(N)NOCCN), i.e. nitrile reduction to primary amine. While nitrile-to-amine reduction is well known, doing so selectively in the presence of a free guanidine and an N-O bond is problematic: catalytic hydrogenation would cleave the N-O bond and could reduce the guanidine; LiAlH4 would be incompatible with the guanidine. Moreover the retrosynthetic logic of carrying an unprotected guanidine through these steps is flawed. This transformation as drawn is unlikely to proceed cleanly.

This step indicates the bis-Boc guanidine (CC(C)(C)OC(=O)N=C(NOCC#N)NC(=O)OC(C)(C)C) is the precursor to the free guanidine nitrile (N#CCONC(=N)N), i.e. Boc removal. Boc deprotection (TFA) is feasible chemically. However, the disconnection direction/labeling here is confusing and the overall sequence to free guanidine before further functionalization is strategically poor. As a simple Boc deprotection it would work, but it is mislabeled relative to the product shown.

Boc protection of a mono-Boc guanidine with Boc2O to give the bis-Boc guanidine is a standard, well-precedented transformation. Boc2O is commercially available. The nitrile is compatible. This step is reasonable.
Acidic (TFA) cleavage of a tert-butyl ester to reveal the carboxylic acid is a robust, standard transformation. Fully compatible with the pyridinone substrate. Feasible.

N-alkylation of the pyridinone N-H with tert-butyl bromoacetate under basic conditions (K2CO3/Cs2CO3, DMF) is a well-established reaction. Both starting materials are commercially available. Possible competing O-alkylation of the ambident pyridinone is a minor concern but N-alkylation typically predominates under these conditions. Good step.

This is a proposed C–N coupling (Buchwald-Hartwig-type amination or SNAr) between a 2-bromopyrimidinone and a primary alkylamine. While such couplings on 2-halo pyrimidinones are precedented, there is a serious chemoselectivity concern: the substrate contains a free aminoguanidine/N-hydroxyguanidine moiety (NOC(=N)N) which is highly nucleophilic and would compete with the desired alkylamine for the coupling. Additionally, the amide N-H and other heteroatoms could interfere with Pd catalysis. A protecting group strategy on the guanidine would be essential. Without protection, multiple competing reactions are expected. Doing this coupling at an earlier stage (before installing the sensitive guanidine functionality) would be far better.

NBS bromination of the pyrimidinone ring to install the 2-bromo substituent is problematic. NBS is more commonly used for benzylic/allylic radical bromination or for bromination of electron-rich (hetero)aromatics at C-H positions, not for installing a halide at the ring nitrogen-adjacent carbon shown. The desired regiochemistry (bromination at the specific ring carbon) is questionable, and the benzylic-like methyl group and the activated guanidine/amide are at risk of competing bromination. Furthermore, the free N-hydroxyguanidine is readily oxidized and would likely react with NBS. This disconnection is poorly conceived; a directed metalation/halogenation or use of a pre-halogenated pyrimidinone building block would be preferable.

local_feedback: Problems with reaction type and functional group compatibility
local_feedback_text: This is an amide coupling between the carboxylic acid (Cc1cncc(=O)n1CC(=O)O) and the amine of an aminoxy-guanidine (N=C(N)NOCCN). The disconnection itself is reasonable (standard amide bond formation). However, the free, unprotected N-hydroxyguanidine is both a competing nucleophile and prone to side reactions under typical coupling conditions (EDC/HATU). Chemoselective acylation of the primary amine over the guanidine N-H functions is not guaranteed. A protecting group strategy (e.g., Boc on the guanidine, as used elsewhere in this route) should be retained through this step rather than carrying a fully deprotected guanidine.

This step proposes that the aminoxy-amine N=C(N)NOCCN derives from the nitrile N#CCONC(=N)N. Converting a nitrile (-CH2-C#N) to a primary amine (-CH2-CH2-NH2) requires reduction (e.g., LiAlH4, catalytic hydrogenation). However, such reducing conditions would also reduce/destroy the N-hydroxyguanidine (N-O bond cleavage with LiAlH4 or hydrogenolysis) and potentially the guanidine itself. The chemoselectivity is essentially unachievable. This disconnection should be reconsidered—reduction of the nitrile must precede installation of the sensitive N-O-guanidine.

This step claims the free guanidine N#CCONC(=N)N is obtained from the bis-Boc protected precursor. The product of Boc removal should be the free guanidine — that direction is logical (TFA deprotection). However, the SMILES mapping shows the bis-Boc compound being formed/cleaved inconsistently and the connectivity of the guanidine is questionable. As written, the simple di-Boc to mono/free guanidine transformation is plausible chemically (acidolysis), but the way the disconnection is structured is unclear. The deprotection itself (TFA) is feasible; rated lower confidence due to ambiguous representation.

Boc protection of a guanidine using Boc2O (di-tert-butyl dicarbonate) to give the bis-Boc protected guanidine is a well-established transformation. The mono-Boc guanidine reacting with another equivalent of Boc2O to give the di-Boc species is standard. Conditions (Boc2O, base such as DMAP/Et3N) are routine. This step is feasible.

Cleavage of a tert-butyl ester to the free carboxylic acid using TFA (or HCl) is a standard, high-yielding deprotection. The pyrimidinone and methyl substituents are stable under these acidic conditions. This step is feasible and well-precedented.

N-alkylation of the pyrimidinone NH (Cc1cncc(=O)[nH]1) with tert-butyl bromoacetate is a straightforward SN2 alkylation, typically performed with a base (K2CO3, Cs2CO3) in DMF/MeCN. N- vs O-alkylation selectivity could be a minor concern for ambident pyrimidinone anions, but N-alkylation generally predominates with these conditions. Both starting materials are commercially available. Feasible.

This is a Buchwald-Hartwig (or SNAr) amination of an aryl/heteroaryl bromide with a primary amine. The disconnection itself is reasonable for installing the secondary amine on the pyrimidinone ring. However, there are serious chemoselectivity concerns: the substrate contains a highly nucleophilic, unprotected aminooxy-guanidine moiety (NCCONC(=N)N) and a free amide NH. Under Pd-catalyzed amination or SNAr conditions, the guanidine and aminooxy groups are far more nucleophilic than the desired arylethylamine and would compete/poison the catalyst. A protecting group strategy for the guanidine would be essential. As written, selectivity for the intended amine is very poor.

local_feedback: Problems with reaction type and functional group compatibility
local_feedback_text: Bromination with NBS at the C-position of the pyridinone ring on a substrate bearing an unprotected guanidine, aminooxy group, and electron-rich amide is highly problematic. NBS is an electrophilic brominating/oxidizing agent that would react preferentially with the electron-rich guanidine/aminooxy functionality and the amide N-H, leading to N-bromination, oxidation, and decomposition rather than clean ring bromination. The regiochemistry of ring bromination also needs control. This step should be performed much earlier on a simpler, protected substrate. As proposed on this advanced intermediate, it is not viable.

local_feedback: Problems with reaction type and functional group compatibility
local_feedback_text: This is an amide coupling between the carboxylic acid (Cc1cncc(=O)n1CC(=O)O) and the aminooxy-guanidine amine (N=C(N)NOCCN). The disconnection is logical. However, the free guanidine is a strongly basic/nucleophilic group that competes with the desired primary amine during amide coupling (activation by EDC/HATU etc.), leading to possible acylation at the guanidine nitrogen and poor chemoselectivity. A Boc-protected guanidine would be far preferable here, then global deprotection at the end. As written with the free guanidine, selectivity and yield are concerns.

This step proposes that the amino-aminooxy-guanidine (N=C(N)NOCCN) derives from a nitrile (N#CCONC(=N)N) by, presumably, nitrile reduction to a primary amine. While nitrile reduction to a primary aminoethyl group is feasible (e.g., catalytic hydrogenation/LiAlH4), doing so in the presence of a free guanidine and an N-O (aminooxy) bond is problematic: hydrogenation conditions cleave N-O bonds and the guanidine/imine would be reduced or interfere. The retrosynthetic mapping (CH2CN -> CH2CH2NH2) is sound in principle but the specific substrate functionality makes this disconnection unlikely to succeed without protection and reagent re-selection.

This step implies conversion of bis-Boc-protected guanidine-nitrile (CC(C)(C)OC(=O)N=C(NOCC#N)NC(=O)OC(C)(C)C) to the free guanidine-nitrile (N#CCONC(=N)N) by removal of both Boc groups. That deprotection (TFA) is feasible. However, as a retrosynthetic disconnection the direction here is odd — it removes protecting groups going forward but then the route later does an amide coupling and bromination on the unprotected guanidine, which contradicts the value of having protected it. The chemistry of Boc removal itself is fine, but its placement renders it strategically wasteful. The bond logic is acceptable; the route context is flawed.

Boc protection of a guanidine with Boc2O to give the bis-Boc protected guanidine is a well-established transformation. Conditions (Boc2O, base such as DMAP/Et3N) reliably install Boc groups on guanidines. This step is chemically sound.
Acidic (TFA) cleavage of a tert-butyl ester to the free carboxylic acid is a standard, high-yielding transformation fully compatible with the pyridinone substrate. No issues.

N-alkylation of the pyridinone NH with tert-butyl bromoacetate is a standard alkylation (base such as K2CO3/Cs2CO3, DMF). N- vs O-alkylation selectivity of ambident pyridinone systems should be considered, but N-alkylation is generally favored under these conditions. Both starting materials are commercially available. Reasonable step.

This is the key Gould-Jacobs-type cyclization/annulation. The disconnection of the tricyclic pyrano-quinolone into the benzoxazine (CCC1COc2ccccc2N1) plus the ethoxymethylene malonate-type enol ether bearing the thiazole amide is a classic strategy for quinolone antibacterials. The secondary amine of the dihydrobenzoxazine performs a Michael addition/condensation with the ethoxymethylene malonate (displacing EtOH), and subsequent thermal/base-mediated intramolecular Dieckmann-type cyclization (Gould-Jacobs) forms the 4-oxo-quinolone ring closing onto the aromatic ring. One concern: the cyclization requires an unsubstituted aromatic position ortho to the nitrogen, which is available here. The regiochemistry of the cyclization (onto C-3 vs C-5 of the benzene ring relative to oxygen) should be checked, but the connectivity drawn is consistent with established quinolone chemistry. The thiazolyl amide should survive these conditions.

Reductive cyclization of the nitro-aryl ketone (CCC(=O)COc1ccccc1[N+](=O)[O-]) to the 3-substituted-3,4-dihydro-2H-1,4-benzoxazine (CCC1COc2ccccc2N1). Under reduction conditions (e.g., H2/Pd-C, Fe/AcOH, or SnCl2), the nitro group is reduced to the aniline, which then undergoes intramolecular reductive amination/condensation with the adjacent ketone to give the cyclic amine. This is a well-precedented route to dihydrobenzoxazines. Note the product is a racemate (one stereocenter at C-3) - if a single enantiomer is needed this is not addressed. Over-reduction or incomplete cyclization to the imine could be minor issues, but overall feasible.

O-alkylation of 2-nitrophenol with 1-bromo-2-butanone (CCC(=O)CBr) under basic conditions (K2CO3, DMF or acetone) to give the aryl ether. This Williamson ether synthesis is straightforward. The phenol is acidic enough (ortho-nitro lowers pKa) to be deprotonated readily, and the alpha-bromoketone is a good electrophile. Potential side reaction: the alpha-bromoketone can be prone to self-condensation or hydrolysis, and there is a minor risk of C- vs O-alkylation, but O-alkylation strongly predominates with phenoxides. Both starting materials are commercially available. Good step.

Condensation of the thiazol-2-yl beta-ketoamide ester (CCOC(=O)CC(=O)Nc1nccs1) with triethyl orthoformate (CCOC(OCC)OCC) to form the ethoxymethylene derivative. This is a standard transformation (typically with Ac2O as co-solvent/dehydrating agent, reflux) widely used in quinolone synthesis to install the ethoxymethylenemalonate-type Michael acceptor. The active methylene flanked by ester and amide carbonyls condenses readily with the orthoester. Both starting materials are commercially available or easily accessible. The product is drawn as a single geometric isomer but E/Z mixtures are typical and inconsequential for the downstream condensation. Feasible and well-precedented.

This is the key Gould-Jacobs-type cyclization/annulation forming the tricyclic quinolone core. The secondary amine of the benzomorpholine (CCC1COc2ccccc2N1) condenses with the ethoxymethylene malonate-type intermediate (CCOC=C(C(=O)Nc1nccs1)C(=O)OCC) via enamine formation (displacement of ethoxy), followed by thermal intramolecular Friedel-Crafts-type acylation onto the aromatic ring to build the 4-oxo-quinolone fused ring. This is well-precedented in fluoroquinolone synthesis (analogous to levofloxacin). The regiochemistry of cyclization onto the aromatic ring ortho to the oxygen is favored electronically. Note: in levofloxacin chemistry the cyclization is typically done on the diester then amide coupling at the end; here the thiazole amide is already installed, which is plausible but the harsh cyclization conditions (PPA, polyphosphate ester, or thermal in Dowtherm at ~250 °C) might risk the amide. Still, the disconnection itself is sound and convergent.

Reductive cyclization of the o-nitro aryloxy ketone (CCC(=O)COc1ccccc1[N+](=O)[O-]) to the 2-ethyl-3,4-dihydro-2H-benzo[1,4]oxazine. Reduction of the nitro group (e.g., H2/Pd-C, Fe/AcOH, or SnCl2) generates the aniline, which undergoes intramolecular reductive amination/condensation with the pendant ketone to form the cyclic amine. This is a standard route to 2-substituted dihydrobenzoxazines and gives the correct ring with the ethyl substituent at C2. Reasonable and well-precedented.

Williamson-type O-alkylation of 2-nitrophenol with 1-bromobutan-2-one (CCC(=O)CBr) under basic conditions (K2CO3, DMF/acetone). The phenol is acidified by the ortho-nitro group, making O-alkylation facile and chemoselective. The alpha-bromoketone is a good electrophile. Minor concern: potential O- vs competing side reactions and over-alkylation are not significant here. Both starting materials are commercially available and cheap. Good step.
