Condensation of the beta-ketoamide (ethyl 3-oxo-3-(thiazol-2-ylamino)propanoate, CCOC(=O)CC(=O)Nc1nccs1) with triethyl orthoformate to generate the ethoxymethylene derivative (the enol ether of the active methylene). This is a classic transformation, typically run with triethyl orthoformate and acetic anhydride at reflux. Well-precedented and high-yielding. The active methylene flanked by ester and amide carbonyls condenses readily. Starting materials are accessible (the ketoamide from ethyl malonyl chloride or diketene chemistry + 2-aminothiazole). Good step.

This is the key disconnection forming the tricyclic 4-oxo-quinolizine (pyrido-fused benzoxazine) core. The forward reaction is a classic Gould-Jacobs type annulation: condensation of the secondary amine of the 3,4-dihydro-2H-benzoxazine (CCC1COc2ccccc2N1) with the ethoxymethylene malonate-type electrophile (CCOC=C(C(=O)Nc1nccs1)C(=O)OCC), with displacement of ethanol to give the enamine, followed by thermal (or Eaton's reagent/POCl3-mediated) intramolecular Friedel-Crafts cyclization onto the aromatic ring to form the pyridone ring. This is a well-precedented route for quinolone/quinolizinone antibacterials and similar scaffolds. One regiochemical caveat: the cyclization must occur on the ring carbon ortho to the oxygen-bearing position to deliver the observed fused tricyclic product; the substitution pattern (OC at position bridging) is consistent with this. Overall a sound and standard disconnection.

Condensation of the active-methylene amide (ethyl malonate mono-amide of 2-aminothiazole, CCOC(=O)CC(=O)Nc1nccs1) with triethyl orthoformate (CCOC(OCC)OCC) to give the ethoxymethylene derivative is a textbook transformation, typically run with acetic anhydride at reflux. This generates the EtO-CH= activated alkene needed for the subsequent enamine formation/annulation. The reagents are commercially available and inexpensive. Geometry (E/Z) of the resulting enol ether is not critical since it reacts further. Standard and reliable.

This step proposes reductive cyclization of 1-(2-nitrophenoxy)butan-2-one (CCC(=O)COc1ccccc1[N+](=O)[O-]) to the 2-ethyl-3,4-dihydro-2H-1,4-benzoxazine. Catalytic hydrogenation (or Fe/AcOH, SnCl2) reduces the nitro to the amine, which undergoes intramolecular reductive amination/condensation with the adjacent ketone to give the cyclic amine after reduction of the intermediate imine. This is a well-established tandem reduction–reductive amination to form dihydrobenzoxazines. The product bears the 2-ethyl substituent consistent with the ketone chain. Feasible with appropriate conditions (H2/Pd-C, or Zn/AcOH then NaBH4). Minor caution regarding over-reduction or incomplete cyclization, but generally reliable.

Williamson-type O-alkylation of 2-nitrophenol (O=[N+]([O-])c1ccccc1O) with 1-bromobutan-2-one (CCC(=O)CBr) under basic conditions (K2CO3, acetone or DMF) cleanly gives the aryl ether 1-(2-nitrophenoxy)butan-2-one. The phenol is acidified by the ortho-nitro group, facilitating O-alkylation. The alpha-bromoketone is a reactive electrophile; both starting materials are commercially available. Possible competing self-condensation of the alpha-haloketone or O- vs C-alkylation is minor; phenoxide O-alkylation dominates. Good, standard step.

This is the key Gould-Jacobs-type cyclization/quinolone formation step. The benzoxazine secondary amine (CCC1COc2ccccc2N1) reacts with the diethyl ethoxymethylenemalonate-derived enamine bearing the thiazole amide (CCOC=C(C(=O)Nc1nccs1)C(=O)OCC). The aniline nitrogen displaces the ethoxy group to form an enamine, followed by thermal Gould-Jacobs cyclization onto the aromatic ring to build the 4-oxo-quinolone (pyridobenzoxazinone) core. This is a well-precedented strategy in fluoroquinolone-type chemistry. One concern: typically the amide to the aminothiazole is installed AFTER quinolone ring formation (via the carboxylic acid/ester) rather than being carried through the cyclization, since the second ester is usually the one cyclizing. Carrying the thiazole amide through the high-temperature cyclization may risk side reactions, but the disconnection logic is sound. The chiral center (ethyl-bearing carbon) defines stereochemistry of the final tricyclic compound.

Reductive amination/cyclization: the o-nitrophenyl ether ketone (CCC(=O)COc1ccccc1[N+](=O)[O-]) undergoes nitro reduction to the aniline, which then condenses intramolecularly with the ketone to form a cyclic imine, followed by reduction to give the 3-ethyl-3,4-dihydro-2H-benzoxazine (CCC1COc2ccccc2N1). This is a standard reductive cyclization (e.g., H2/Pd or Fe/AcOH then NaBH4 or one-pot reductive amination). The transformation is feasible and commonly used to access 2,3-dihydrobenzoxazines. Note that this generates a stereocenter as a racemate unless asymmetric conditions are used, which is relevant given the chiral center in the final product.

Williamson-type O-alkylation of 2-nitrophenol with 1-bromobutan-2-one (CCC(=O)CBr) to give the aryl ether. Both starting materials are commercially available and inexpensive. The phenol is deprotonated (K2CO3) and alkylates the alpha-bromoketone. This is a robust, high-yielding reaction. Minor concern: alpha-bromoketones can undergo competing O- vs C-alkylation or self-condensation, but with the phenoxide nucleophile O-alkylation strongly dominates. Good disconnection.

Knoevenager-type condensation of the malonamide-ester (CCOC(=O)CC(=O)Nc1nccs1, ethyl 3-oxo-3-(thiazol-2-ylamino)propanoate / the malonic acid mono-amide ester) with triethyl orthoformate (CCOC(OCC)OCC) to form the ethoxymethylene (enol ether) derivative. This is a classic preparation of ethoxymethylenemalonate analogues, typically run with Ac2O catalysis at reflux. The active methylene between the ester and amide carbonyls is sufficiently acidic to react. Feasible and well-precedented. The geometry (E/Z) of the resulting vinyl ether is set thermodynamically and is typically inconsequential for the subsequent cyclization.

This is an aza-Michael addition of an aniline nitrogen to acrylic acid, forming the β-amino acid (NCCC(=O)O) linkage. This is a well-precedented transformation. The aniline (an electron-rich aromatic amine due to para-OMe) is a competent nucleophile, and acrylic acid is a standard Michael acceptor. The reaction typically proceeds under mild thermal conditions (neat or in water/alcohol, sometimes with mild Lewis acid catalysis). Key considerations: (1) Mono- vs di-addition selectivity - anilines can add twice to acrylates, giving the bis-adduct; controlling stoichiometry (slight excess of acrylic acid, but not large) is important to favor mono-addition. (2) The vinyl sulfone moiety (/C=C/S(=O)(=O)) present in the substrate is itself a potent Michael acceptor; there is a risk of competing intramolecular or intermolecular nucleophilic addition of the aniline (or the acrylic acid carboxylate/water) to the vinyl sulfone. However, since the aniline and vinyl sulfone are on separate aromatic rings and the aniline preferentially reacts intermolecularly with the more accessible acrylic acid, the desired chemoselectivity is plausible but not guaranteed. Overall a reasonable, simple disconnection.

This step is an aza-Michael addition of an aniline nitrogen to acrylic acid (C=CC(=O)O), forming the secondary amine with a pendant propanoic acid. This is a well-precedented transformation; aromatic amines add to acrylic acid/acrylates under thermal or Lewis acid catalysis to give beta-amino acids/esters. The disconnection is logical and the aniline is the most nucleophilic site, providing good chemoselectivity. A few considerations: (1) Anilines are relatively weak nucleophiles, so the aza-Michael may require elevated temperature, prolonged reaction time, or a catalyst (e.g., water/microwave conditions, or Lewis acid). (2) Mono- vs bis-addition selectivity is a concern — primary anilines can undergo double Michael addition to give the bis(propanoic acid) tertiary amine. Use of a slight excess (1.0-1.1 equiv) of acrylic acid and controlled conditions favors mono-addition, but over-alkylation is a realistic side reaction reducing yield. (3) The free carboxylic acid product is compatible with all other functional groups present (vinyl sulfone, methyl ethers). (4) The electron-rich aniline (para-OMe is actually ortho/meta to the amine here) is somewhat activated, which helps. Overall a sound, efficient final-step disconnection. The aniline precursor is listed as in-stock and acrylic acid is a cheap commodity chemical.

This is an aza-Michael addition of an aromatic amine to acrylic acid, forming the β-amino acid (3-(arylamino)propanoic acid). The disconnection is logical and the forward reaction is well-precedented. Anilines, although weakly nucleophilic, readily undergo conjugate addition to acrylic acid/acrylates, often under thermal or mild Lewis acid/base catalysis. Considerations: (1) Mono- vs. bis-addition – with an excess of acrylic acid, double addition to give the tertiary amine N(CH2CH2CO2H)2 is a real competing pathway; controlling stoichiometry (slight excess of amine or one equivalent of acrylic acid) is required for selective mono-addition. (2) The free carboxylic acid is fine, but using methyl acrylate followed by hydrolysis would give cleaner conversion and easier purification. (3) Chemoselectivity is good – the electron-poor vinyl sulfone present in the molecule will not react preferentially with the aniline because intramolecular geometry is unfavorable and the aniline is the intended nucleophile; however, in principle the aniline could also add intermolecularly to the vinyl sulfone of another molecule, so the acrylic acid should be the more reactive/controlled electrophile. Overall a reasonable, single-step disconnection to commercially available building blocks.

This is an aza-Michael addition of an aniline nitrogen onto acrylic acid (C=CC(=O)O), forming the secondary amine with a propanoic acid chain. The disconnection is chemically sound and well-precedented. Aniline nitrogens are good nucleophiles for conjugate addition to acrylates/acrylic acid. A few considerations: (1) The aniline used here is electron-rich (ortho/para-methoxy substituents activate the ring and increase nitrogen nucleophilicity), which favors the aza-Michael addition. (2) However, the molecule contains an electrophilic vinyl sulfone (/C=C/S(=O)(=O)) which is itself a strong Michael acceptor. There is a real chemoselectivity concern that the aniline nitrogen could add intramolecularly or intermolecularly to the vinyl sulfone Michael acceptor rather than (or in addition to) reacting with acrylic acid. (3) Acrylic acid (with a free carboxylic acid) is a weaker Michael acceptor than the corresponding ester; using a protected acrylate (e.g., tert-butyl or methyl acrylate) followed by hydrolysis might improve control, though mono- vs bis-addition selectivity (over-addition to give the tertiary amine) is also a concern with anilines and acrylic acid derivatives. Overall the transformation is feasible but selectivity (mono-addition and chemoselectivity vs. the vinyl sulfone) should be carefully controlled, e.g., by stoichiometry and mild conditions.

This is a Suzuki-Miyaura coupling between an aryl bromide and an aryl pinacol boronate bearing a free piperazine NH. The disconnection itself is sound and well-precedented for biaryl bond formation. However, two practical concerns: (1) The free secondary amine (piperazine NH) can coordinate to the Pd catalyst and may reduce efficiency or require excess catalyst, though such couplings are well-documented to proceed. (2) The substrate also contains a free 2-aminopyridine (NH2), which is generally tolerated. The main risk is competitive chemoselectivity issues and potential need for the piperazine to be Boc-protected to ensure clean coupling. Overall feasible but a protecting group on the piperazine would improve robustness. The boronate and bromide are correctly positioned for selective single coupling since only one halide remains.

This Suzuki coupling between 2-amino-5-bromo-3-iodopyridine and 3,4,5-trimethoxyphenylboronic acid exploits the well-known reactivity difference between C–I and C–Br bonds. Oxidative addition occurs preferentially at the more reactive C–I site, giving excellent regioselectivity for coupling at the position ortho to the amino group while leaving the bromide intact for the subsequent coupling (ca67b53b150b0603f13d1f0b6e6c1cdc827261df23c4eae2c09c89cbab0ef66a). Both starting materials are commercially available and reasonably priced. The free 2-aminopyridine is tolerated in Suzuki conditions. This is an excellent, well-precedented chemoselective disconnection. Minor consideration: steric hindrance from the ortho-amino group is manageable; standard Pd(PPh3)4 or SPhos-based conditions would work well.

This is a Suzuki-Miyaura coupling between an aryl bromide and a pinacol boronate ester, which is a well-established transformation. The disconnection at the biaryl bond is strategically sound. However, the boronate partner contains a free secondary amine (piperazine N-H), which can coordinate to palladium and potentially slow the catalysis or require slight excess of ligand/base; this is usually tolerable but a Boc-protected piperazine would be cleaner. The major concern is chemoselectivity: the pyridine ring bears a free primary amine (2-aminopyridine) ortho to the coupling site, which can also coordinate Pd, but Suzuki couplings on such aminopyridyl bromides are generally feasible. The free amine functionalities can reduce yields but the reaction should proceed with appropriate catalyst (e.g., Pd(dppf)Cl2 or SPhos/XPhos systems) and base (K2CO3, Cs2CO3). Overall feasible but optimization needed.

This is a Suzuki coupling between 3,4,5-trimethoxyphenylboronic acid and a dihalopyridine (Nc1ncc(Br)cc1I) bearing both a bromide and an iodide. The strategy relies on chemoselective coupling at the more reactive C-I bond over the C-Br bond, which is well-precedented for Pd-catalyzed cross-couplings (oxidative addition is faster at C-I). This selectivity is generally achievable under mild conditions (e.g., Pd(PPh3)4, low temperature, controlled stoichiometry of boronic acid). The free 2-amino group is tolerated in most cases. The main risk is competing coupling at the C-Br site or double coupling if conditions are too forcing or excess boronic acid is used. The starting materials are commercially reasonable. With careful control of conditions, this selective mono-coupling is feasible and represents a good strategic choice to install the trimethoxyphenyl group first while retaining the bromide for the subsequent coupling.

This is a Suzuki-Miyaura cross-coupling between an aryl bromide and an arylboronic acid pinacol ester. The disconnection is logically sound and the boronate partner (4-piperazinyl-phenyl pinacol boronate) is commercially available. However, two concerns: (1) The pinacol boronate bears a free secondary amine (piperazine N-H), which can coordinate to Pd and slow the reaction, though such couplings are well-documented and usually proceed without protection. (2) More importantly, the aryl bromide substrate also contains a free primary aminopyridine (2-aminopyridine NH2). Free anilines/aminopyridines are generally tolerated in Suzuki couplings, so this is acceptable. The chemoselectivity is fine since there is only one C-Br. Overall the step is feasible; the free piperazine and free amine make it slightly less clean but no protection is strictly required.

This Suzuki coupling uses a dihalopyridine (Nc1ncc(Br)cc1I) where the goal is to couple selectively at the C-I position (ortho to the amino group) with the trimethoxyphenylboronic acid, leaving the C-Br intact for the subsequent coupling (ca67b53b150b0603f13d1f0b6e6c1cdc827261df23c4eae2c09c89cbab0ef66a). Oxidative addition is intrinsically faster at C-I than C-Br, so chemoselective coupling at iodine is reasonable and is a classic strategy for orthogonal sequential functionalization. However, selectivity is not guaranteed to be perfect — some bis-coupling or competing reaction at the bromide can occur, requiring careful control of stoichiometry (limiting boronic acid, mild Pd/ligand, controlled temperature). The starting materials (3,4,5-trimethoxyphenylboronic acid and the 2-amino-5-bromo-3-iodopyridine) are both reasonable building blocks; the trimethoxyphenylboronic acid is commercially available. Overall feasible with attention to mono-selectivity.

This is a Suzuki-Miyaura coupling between an aryl bromide and a pinacol boronate ester bearing a free piperazine (secondary amine). The disconnection at the biaryl bond is strategically sound and well-precedented. However, two concerns arise: (1) The boronic ester partner contains a free, unprotected piperazine NH. While secondary amines are generally tolerated under Pd catalysis, they can coordinate to Pd and potentially slow the catalytic cycle or cause issues; for robust yields, Boc-protection of the piperazine would be advisable. (2) The aryl bromide substrate also contains a free primary aminopyridine (2-aminopyridine motif), which can coordinate Pd. Despite these issues, such couplings with free amines do work in practice, often requiring careful ligand choice (e.g., SPhos, XPhos) and base. Chemoselectivity for the C-Br over the other positions is fine since only one halide remains. Overall feasible but optimization of protecting groups and catalyst is recommended.

This Suzuki coupling forms the first biaryl bond between 3,4,5-trimethoxyphenylboronic acid and a dihalogenated aminopyridine (Nc1ncc(Br)cc1I). The key strategic point is the desired chemoselectivity: oxidative addition of Pd should occur preferentially at the C-I bond over the C-Br bond, which is well-established (C-I >> C-Br in oxidative addition rates). This allows selective installation of the trimethoxyphenyl group at the iodide position, leaving the bromide intact for the subsequent coupling (ca67b53b150b0603f13d1f0b6e6c1cdc827261df23c4eae2c09c89cbab0ef66a). This is a sensible and well-designed sequential cross-coupling strategy. The free 2-aminopyridine is tolerated under standard conditions. Both starting materials are commercially available. Main risk is some loss of selectivity if conditions are too forcing (potential bis-coupling or homocoupling), but with controlled stoichiometry (1 equiv boronic acid) and mild conditions, selectivity at the iodide is achievable. The regiochemistry of the final product is consistent with iodide-selective coupling.

This step proposes converting methoxymaleic anhydride (COC1=CC(=O)OC1=O) into a 4-hydroxy-furan-2,3-dione type species (O=C1C=C(O)C(=O)O1) by demethylation. While methoxy-to-enol (vinylogous acid) tautomerization is conceivable, the implied transformation of a maleic anhydride into a furan-2,3(?)-dione/tetronic-acid-like ring is not a clean, precedented single step and the regiochemistry/oxidation state mapping is inconsistent. The product structure itself is a strained, highly reactive species of questionable stability. This disconnection is not realistic as drawn.

N-alkylation of 4-quinolone (O=c1cc[nH]c2ccccc12) with 2-methoxybenzyl chloride is a sound disconnection and well precedented. The key caveat is the classic O- vs N-alkylation ambiguity of 4-quinolones/4-hydroxyquinoline tautomers. Use of a base such as K2CO3/Cs2CO3 in DMF generally favors N-alkylation, but O-alkylation is a common competing pathway. Both starting materials are commercially available. The methoxybenzyl chloride is a good electrophile. Overall feasible with attention to conditions to enforce N-selectivity.

This disconnects the C-3 substituent of the quinolone into an electrophilic furanone/anhydride-derived fragment plus the parent 1-(2-methoxybenzyl)-4-quinolone. Mechanistically, this implies a Friedel-Crafts-type C-acylation/Michael coupling at C-3 of the quinolone using the cyclic species O=C1C=C(O)C(=O)O1, with concomitant ring-opening to the open-chain product (C(=O)C=C(O)C(=O)O). The atom mapping does not balance cleanly (the cyclic fragment must ring-open to a free carboxylic acid plus a new C-C bond), and the position/regiochemistry of attack on the unsymmetrical reactive heterocycle is uncertain. While C-3 of 4-quinolones is nucleophilic and can undergo electrophilic functionalization, coupling with this particular fragment to give exactly this connectivity is not a well-precedented transformation and would suffer from competing reactions and poor selectivity.

This disconnection is chemically problematic. The forward reaction implies a C-C bond formation between the C3 position of the 4-quinolone and the carbonyl of the cyclic anhydride/furanone fragment (O=C1C=C(O)C(=O)O1), generating a complex acyclic 2,4-dioxo acid/enol product (C(=O)C=C(O)C(=O)O). The retron product shows a ring-opened tetronic-acid-derived chain attached via a ketone. The combination of two separate species into the depicted open-chain 1,3-dicarbonyl with a free carboxylic acid and enol is not a clean single-step transformation. A Friedel-Crafts-type acylation at C3 of the quinolone with the furanone would not give the depicted ring-opened product, and regioselectivity/oxidation state mismatch make this unlikely. The proposed product SMILES does not correspond to a recognizable simple coupling of the two fragments.

This step proposes converting methoxy-maleic anhydride (COC1=CC(=O)OC1=O) into the hydroxy-furanone/anhydride (O=C1C=C(O)C(=O)O1) by demethylation of the enol ether to the free enol. While O-demethylation of vinylogous esters to give tetronic-acid-like enols is feasible in principle (e.g., with BBr3 or HBr), the product as drawn (O=C1C=C(O)C(=O)O1) is an unusual 5-membered ring oxidation state that may tautomerize or be unstable. Moreover this fragment (hydroxymaleic anhydride / hydroxyfuranedione) is itself essentially a known commercial/accessible compound, so the demethylation step adds little value. The disconnection is questionable as drawn.

This is an N-alkylation of 4-quinolone (O=c1cc[nH]c2ccccc12) with 2-methoxybenzyl chloride (COc1ccccc1CCl). The disconnection itself is reasonable and well-precedented for N-functionalization of 4-quinolones. However, 4-quinolones are ambident nucleophiles and can undergo competing O-alkylation versus N-alkylation; selectivity depends strongly on base, solvent, and counterion. With a benzyl halide and a suitable base (e.g., K2CO3 in DMF), N-alkylation is generally favored, so the step is feasible but selectivity should be controlled. Starting materials are commercially available and inexpensive. Overall a good, practical step with manageable selectivity considerations.

This disconnection proposes a C-C bond formation between the C3 position of the 4-quinolone and a fragment 'O=C1C=C(O)C(=O)O1' (a cyclic anhydride/furanone). The product is drawn as an open-chain triketo-acid 'C(=O)C=C(O)C(=O)O' attached at C3 of the quinolone. The mechanistic correspondence between the cyclic furanedione fragment and the open-chain product is incorrect: the forward reaction (acylation at C3 of the 4-quinolone) would not simply give this ring-opened product without a defined nucleophile/electrophile pairing. A 4-quinolone C3 is nucleophilic (enaminone-like, vinylogous amide) and can undergo Friedel-Crafts-type or Mannich acylations, but reaction with this anhydride would not cleanly produce the depicted open-chain enol-keto-acid. The regiochemistry, the requirement for the C3 H to be displaced, and the ring-opening/tautomer assignment make this a poorly defined and unlikely transformation as drawn. A more sensible disconnection would be a Claisen-type acylation of the C3 position with a dedicated activated acyl donor.

This step proposes converting methoxy-maleic anhydride 'COC1=CC(=O)OC1=O' to the hydroxy furanedione 'O=C1C=C(O)C(=O)O1' (i.e., demethylation of the enol ether to the free enol/hydroxy). While O-demethylation of a vinylogous methyl enol ether to the corresponding enol is conceivable (e.g., with BBr3 or acid), the product is a tautomeric hydroxyfuranone whose stability and clean isolation are questionable, and the overall purpose given the problematic 8a7fa7d2013c3e9b704379bae98a43a31f996e185cf048f4bd1bf7dd2d328f54 step is unclear. The transformation as a single clean retrosynthetic step lacks precedent and reagent specification. If the intent is simply demethylation, the reagent and selectivity need to be defined; otherwise this is a non-productive disconnection.

This is an N-alkylation of 4-quinolone (4-hydroxyquinoline tautomer, 'O=c1cc[nH]c2ccccc12') with 2-methoxybenzyl chloride. The disconnection is reasonable and N-alkylation of 4-quinolones is well precedented. However, 4-quinolones are ambident nucleophiles and notoriously give mixtures of N-alkylation and O-alkylation products. To favor N-alkylation, appropriate base (e.g., K2CO3 in DMF) and conditions should be specified. Both starting materials are simple and commercially available. With proper conditions this step is feasible but the O- vs N-selectivity is a genuine concern that must be controlled.

This disconnection proposes joining a 4-quinolone (COc1ccccc1Cn1ccc(=O)c2ccccc21) with a hydroxy-furanone/anhydride fragment (O=C1C=C(O)C(=O)O1) to form the target C(=O)C=C(O)C(=O)O side chain at C-3 of the quinolone. As written this is highly problematic. First, the SMILES of the fragment 'O=C1C=C(O)C(=O)O1' is a cyclic species (a 4-hydroxy-2-furanone / tetronic-acid-like ring) whereas the product side chain is an open-chain 2,4-dioxo acid enol (an aroylpyruvate-type unit). The atom mapping does not balance: the product side chain contains an additional C=C-C(=O)O unit that does not cleanly arise from acylation by this fragment. A realistic forward synthesis to install a 3-(2,4-dioxobutanoate) chain on a 4-quinolone proceeds via Claisen-type acylation of the C-3 active methylene/methine or via condensation of the 3-acetyl quinolone with a diethyl oxalate (Claisen condensation) to give the 2,4-dioxoester. The proposed single-step coupling with this cyclic fragment is not a recognized transformation and the regiochemistry of C-3 functionalization of an unsubstituted 4-quinolone is also questionable (C-3 is not inherently nucleophilic without prior activation). This disconnection is not chemically sound as drawn.

This step proposes converting methoxymaleic anhydride (COC1=CC(=O)OC1=O) into 4-hydroxy-furan-2(5H)-one-type species (O=C1C=C(O)C(=O)O1) by demethylation of an enol ether. While O-demethylation of a vinylogous ester to the corresponding enol/tautomer is conceivable in principle, the two structures shown are not simple tautomers/demethylation partners - the connectivity and ring oxidation states differ. Moreover, the product fragment itself is of dubious relevance (see 8a7fa7d2013c3e9b704379bae98a43a31f996e185cf048f4bd1bf7dd2d328f54). The transformation as drawn lacks clear precedent and the product would likely be unstable. Both starting and product molecules are small and odd; the disconnection adds confusion rather than simplifying toward a building block.

N-alkylation of 4-quinolone (O=c1cc[nH]c2ccccc12) with 2-methoxybenzyl chloride (COc1ccccc1CCl) is a reasonable and well-precedented transformation to give the N-(2-methoxybenzyl)quinolin-4-one. Both building blocks are commercially available. The principal concern is the classic O- vs N-alkylation ambiguity of 4-quinolones (ambident nucleophile): alkylation can occur at the ring oxygen to give the 4-alkoxyquinoline instead of the desired N-alkyl-4-quinolone. N-selectivity is favored under appropriate conditions (e.g., basic conditions with K2CO3/Cs2CO3 in DMF), so the step is feasible but selectivity should be addressed. Benzyl chloride reactivity is adequate (benzyl iodide or addition of NaI may help).

This step proposes reduction of the amide carbonyl (C(=O)N to CH2-N) of the piperazine amide to give the tertiary amine, while leaving the oxindole amide (C(=O)Nc2ccccc21, a secondary lactam) intact. There is no chemoselective reagent that would reduce the tertiary aliphatic amide to an amine without also reducing the more reactive (or at least equally reactive) oxindole lactam carbonyl. LiAlH4, BH3, or similar reagents would attack both amide functionalities. Furthermore, the quaternary all-carbon center alpha to the oxindole would not protect that lactam from reduction. This selectivity is not achievable as written. A better strategy would be to perform a reductive amination or N-alkylation to install the C-N bond directly: disconnect at the N-CH2 bond using a 4-halobutyl or aldehyde precursor reacting with the arylpiperazine. As drawn, the amide-to-amine reduction with retained lactam is not feasible chemoselectively.

This step is an N-alkylation/C-alkylation issue. The product CCC1(...)C(=O)Nc2ccccc21 shows ethylation at the quaternary C3 carbon of the oxindole using EtBr. However, the proposed precursor COc1cccc(N2CCN(C(=O)CCCC3C(=O)Nc4ccccc43)CC2)c1 contains both an acidic C-H at the oxindole C3 (the carbon to be alkylated) and an N-H lactam. Deprotonation/alkylation at C3 requires a base (e.g., NaH, LDA), but the lactam N-H is also acidic and competing N-alkylation can occur. While C-alkylation of oxindoles at C3 is well precedented and often favored under appropriate conditions, chemoselectivity (C vs N) must be controlled, and the basic conditions are also compatible with the existing tertiary amide. The disconnection of the C3-ethyl bond is reasonable, but selectivity and ensuring mono-C-alkylation (avoiding over-alkylation or O/N alkylation) are concerns. Use of a controlled base/temperature is advised.

This step proposes reduction of a tertiary amide carbonyl (the C(=O)-N of the piperazine amide) to a methylene (CH2), converting an amide into an amine while NOT touching the oxindole secondary amide (C(=O)Nc2ccccc21). Such chemoselectivity is essentially impossible. Amide-to-amine reductions require strong reducing agents (LiAlH4, BH3, or similar). These reagents would reduce or compete strongly with the oxindole lactam carbonyl as well, leading to loss of chemoselectivity. The oxindole carbonyl is actually quite susceptible to reduction. A better strategy would be to introduce the aminoalkyl chain via reductive amination or N-alkylation of the piperazine with a haloalkyl/aldehyde tether AFTER constructing the oxindole core, rather than selectively reducing one amide in the presence of another. As drawn, this selective reduction is not feasible.

This step is the C-alkylation of a 3-substituted oxindole at the quaternary C3 position using ethyl bromide. While alkylation alpha to the oxindole carbonyl is well-precedented (deprotonation with a base such as NaH, LDA, or KOtBu, then alkylation), there are significant selectivity concerns: (1) The oxindole has both an acidic N-H (lactam) and the C3-H; the N-H (pKa ~18) would compete and could lead to N-alkylation rather than the desired C-alkylation. Typically N-protection or careful base/conditions (e.g., use of 2+ equiv base to deprotonate both, with C-alkylation favored) is required. (2) The molecule also contains a tertiary amide and a tethered chain with an existing stereocenter/CH at C3. Using a simple alkyl bromide on a substrate already bearing a long aminoacyl chain at C3 would create the quaternary center; this is feasible but requires that the C3 already bears the chain (it does). The competing O-alkylation/N-alkylation and the need to form a quaternary carbon make this moderately challenging but achievable with proper conditions (e.g., NaH/excess base, polar aprotic solvent). Recommend N-protection of the oxindole nitrogen to ensure clean C-alkylation.

This step proposes reduction of an amide carbonyl (C(=O)N piperazine) to a methylene (CH2-N) to convert the tertiary amide into a tertiary amine, while leaving the oxindole lactam (C(=O)Nc2ccccc21) intact. This is a major chemoselectivity problem: any amide-reducing reagent (LiAlH4, BH3, etc.) strong enough to reduce the tertiary acyl-piperazine amide to the amine would also reduce the oxindole lactam carbonyl. There is no practical way to achieve this selective reduction. A far better forward strategy would be a reductive amination or N-alkylation of the piperazine with a halide/aldehyde tether, avoiding the need to selectively reduce one amide in the presence of another. This disconnection as drawn is not feasible.

This step is an N-ethylation/C-ethylation disconnection using ethyl bromide. The intended transformation forms the quaternary C-ethyl center at the oxindole C3 position (the product has CCC1(...)C(=O)N...). However, the precursor shown (COc1cccc(N2CCN(C(=O)CCCC3C(=O)Nc4ccccc43)CC2)c1) bears both an acidic oxindole C3-H and an acidic amide N-H (lactam N-H). Deprotonation/alkylation with EtBr would face serious chemoselectivity issues: the lactam N-H (pKa ~18-20) and the C3-H both can be deprotonated. To achieve clean C-alkylation at C3, the oxindole nitrogen typically needs protection, or careful use of 2 equivalents of base and controlled conditions to enforce C-alkylation. As written, competing N-alkylation and O-alkylation, plus possible dialkylation, are significant concerns. The disconnection (C-ethyl from EtBr) is reasonable in principle but needs a protecting group on the lactam N and a strong base (e.g., NaH/LDA). Reagents are commercially available.

This step proposes reduction of an amide carbonyl (the tertiary amide on the piperazine nitrogen) to a methylene (CH2) to give the tertiary amine, while leaving the oxindole lactam (secondary amide, C(=O)Nc) intact. There is no chemoselective reagent that would reduce one amide carbonyl to a CH2 while preserving the more reactive (or comparably reactive) oxindole lactam. Borane or LiAlH4 would reduce both amides, and there is no good way to differentiate them. As written, this is an unfeasible chemoselective transformation. A better strategy would be to construct the amine linkage directly via reductive amination or N-alkylation of the arylpiperazine with a halide/aldehyde tether, avoiding the need to selectively reduce one of two amides.

This step proposes C-alkylation at the quaternary carbon of the oxindole using ethyl bromide on a precursor bearing a free oxindole N-H and a free C-H at the 3-position. While 3,3-disubstituted oxindoles can be made by base-mediated C-alkylation at C3, several issues arise: (1) the oxindole N-H is acidic and would be deprotonated/alkylated competitively, so N-protection (e.g., Boc or Bn) or careful use of excess base with the more acidic C-H is typically required; (2) regioselectivity between the benzylic C3 position and the N-H is a real concern; (3) installing the second alkyl group at an already substituted (the molecule shows C3 already bearing the long chain) quaternary center is sterically demanding but feasible with strong base (e.g., NaH, LDA, or KOtBu) and EtBr. The disconnection itself is reasonable for forming the 3,3-disubstituted oxindole, but selectivity (N vs C) and the tertiary amide compatibility need attention. Consider protecting the lactam nitrogen.

This is a straightforward amide bond formation between 4-aminoindole (7-aminoindole regiochemistry shown: amino at position adjacent to the benzo ring) and 6-bromobenzothiophene-2-carboxylic acid. The disconnection at the amide C-N bond is the most logical and highest-priority disconnection for this target. The transformation is well-precedented using standard coupling reagents (e.g., HATU, EDC/HOBt, T3P, or via the acid chloride). Functional group compatibility is good: the aryl bromide is inert under amide coupling conditions, and the indole NH should not significantly compete with the more nucleophilic aniline amine, though there is a minor chemoselectivity consideration. The aromatic amine is somewhat deactivated (aniline-type), so a more activated coupling protocol (acid chloride or T3P with base) may give the best yields. The carboxylic acid coupling partner is the 2-carboxy regiochemistry on the benzothiophene, which is readily accessible. Both building blocks (the aminoindole and the brominated benzothiophene-2-carboxylic acid) are commercially available or readily synthesized. Minor caution: heating with strongly acidic activation could risk indole reactions, but standard conditions avoid this.

This is a standard amide bond formation between a carboxylic acid (5-bromobenzothiophene-2-carboxylic acid) and a primary aromatic amine (4-aminoindole). The disconnection is logical and high-yielding methods exist (e.g., EDC/HOBt, HATU, T3P, or acid chloride formation followed by coupling). The free indole N-H is compatible with standard amide coupling conditions, as the aniline-type amino group is far more nucleophilic than the indole nitrogen; minor N-acylation at the indole nitrogen could occur but is generally suppressed. No protecting group is strictly necessary, though for cleaner selectivity one could consider mild coupling reagents. Both starting materials are reasonable and commercially accessible or readily prepared. Chemoselectivity favors the more nucleophilic arylamine, so the desired product should dominate.

This is a classic amide bond formation between 4-aminoindole (a free NH-indole bearing an aromatic amine) and 5-bromobenzothiophene-2-carboxylic acid. The disconnection at the amide C-N bond is the most logical and reliable strategy. Standard coupling reagents (HATU, EDC/HOBt, T3P, or via acid chloride) would effect this transformation. Key considerations: (1) Chemoselectivity - the aromatic amine (more nucleophilic) will react preferentially over the indole NH, so no protection of the indole nitrogen is strictly required, though some N-acylation of the indole could occur as a minor side reaction with very active acylating agents (e.g., acid chloride). Use of milder coupling conditions (e.g., HATU/DIPEA or T3P) favors selective amide formation on the arylamine. (2) The aryl bromide is fully compatible with amide coupling conditions. (3) No stereocenters are involved. Both starting materials are reasonable - 4-aminoindole is commercially available, and 5-bromobenzo[b]thiophene-2-carboxylic acid is also commercially available or readily accessible. Overall a high-quality, single-step disconnection.

This is a classic amide bond formation between 4-aminoindole (a 7-amino indole, specifically the smiles depicts an aminoindole with NH free) and a benzothiophene-2-carboxylic acid bearing a bromide. The disconnection at the amide C–N bond is the most logical and strategic choice. Standard coupling reagents (HATU, EDC/HOBt, T3P, or conversion to the acid chloride) would readily effect this transformation. Considerations: (1) The indole N–H is present and could in principle compete, but aromatic indole N–H is far less nucleophilic than the aryl amine, so chemoselective acylation of the primary aromatic amine is expected; minor N-acylation on the indole nitrogen is possible with very aggressive acylating agents but easily controlled with mild coupling conditions. (2) The aryl bromide is fully compatible with amide coupling conditions and provides a useful handle for further functionalization. (3) The aromatic amine is somewhat deactivated/electron-poor relative to aliphatic amines, so an activated acyl species (acid chloride or active ester) may give superior yields. No protecting groups are needed. Both building blocks are reasonable in complexity and likely commercially available or readily prepared.

This step constructs the hydantoin ring via reaction of the secondary amine ester (methyl 2-(4-bromophenylamino)-2-phenylacetate) with an aryl isocyanate (4-bromophenyl isocyanate). The amine attacks the isocyanate to form a urea, which then undergoes intramolecular cyclization (the resulting urea nitrogen displaces methoxide from the ester) to close the 5-membered hydantoin ring. This is a well-precedented hydantoin synthesis. The disconnection is sound and chemoselective: the only nucleophile is the secondary amine, and cyclization onto the ester is favorable. A mild base may be needed to promote the final cyclization, but overall the step is reliable. The two aryl bromides are inert under these conditions.

This SN2 amination of methyl 2-bromo-2-phenylacetate (a benzylic, activated alpha-bromo ester) by 4-bromoaniline is chemically feasible and well-precedented. However, two concerns: (1) Chemoselectivity—the aniline nitrogen could in principle also attack the ester carbonyl, but N-alkylation at the activated benzylic alpha-carbon is strongly favored, so this is minor. (2) Over-alkylation: the resulting secondary aniline is still nucleophilic and could undergo a second alkylation to give a tertiary amine; using excess aniline (or controlled stoichiometry) mitigates this. The alpha-bromo ester is also prone to elimination/racemization, but since the product center is destined for the hydantoin (and stereochemistry is not specified in the target), racemization is not an issue here. A base such as K2CO3 or Et3N and excess aniline would optimize the reaction. Both starting materials are commercially available.

This is a well-precedented hydantoin synthesis. The reaction of an isocyanate (4-bromophenyl isocyanate) with an α-amino ester (methyl 2-(4-bromophenylamino)-2-phenylacetate) gives an intermediate urea, which then cyclizes intramolecularly via attack of the urea nitrogen on the ester carbonyl to form the hydantoin (imidazolidine-2,4-dione) ring with loss of methanol. This forward synthesis is reliable and commonly used for the construction of 1,3,5-trisubstituted hydantoins. The disconnection is sensible. One minor concern: the secondary amine nitrogen reacting with the isocyanate is sterically and electronically reasonable; cyclization typically requires mild base or heating, but the transformation is robust. The C5 stereocenter will be racemic, but the target appears to be drawn without defined stereochemistry, so this is acceptable.

This is a straightforward N-alkylation (SN2) of 4-bromoaniline with methyl α-bromophenylacetate (methyl 2-bromo-2-phenylacetate) to form the secondary amine α-amino ester. Both starting materials are commercially available and inexpensive. The benzylic α-bromo ester is highly activated toward nucleophilic substitution. Potential concerns: over-alkylation (dialkylation) of the aniline, but this can be controlled by using excess aniline or stoichiometric base. The aryl bromide is inert under these conditions. The reaction may benefit from a mild base (e.g., K2CO3, Et3N) to neutralize HBr. Overall a reliable and efficient disconnection.

This is a classic hydantoin synthesis. The reaction of an α-amino ester (methyl 2-(4-bromophenylamino)-2-phenylacetate) with an aryl isocyanate (4-bromophenyl isocyanate) forms a urea intermediate, which then cyclizes intramolecularly: the secondary amide/urea nitrogen attacks the ester carbonyl, displacing methanol to close the 5-membered imidazolidine-2,4-dione (hydantoin) ring. This is a well-precedented and reliable route to 1,3,5-trisubstituted hydantoins. The reaction typically proceeds under mild base or thermal conditions. The disconnection is appropriate and chemoselective; the aryl bromides are inert under these conditions. One minor consideration is potential racemization at the benzylic stereocenter, but for a target with a single stereocenter this is generally not an issue (likely racemic target anyway).

This is an SN2 amination of an α-bromo ester (methyl α-bromophenylacetate) with 4-bromoaniline to form the α-arylamino ester. The benzylic/α-carbonyl bromide is highly activated toward nucleophilic substitution, and anilines are competent nucleophiles. The transformation is well-precedented. Potential issues: (1) over-alkylation to give the tertiary amine is possible but can be controlled by stoichiometry (excess aniline) and the steric bulk of the secondary product; (2) competing elimination is unlikely given the lack of β-hydrogens suitable for E2 (the α-carbon bears aryl and ester). A mild base (e.g., K2CO3, Et3N) to scavenge HBr is recommended. Both starting materials are commercially available and inexpensive.

This is a well-precedented hydantoin synthesis. The reaction of an α-amino ester with an isocyanate forms a urea intermediate, which then cyclizes intramolecularly (the secondary amine nitrogen, now part of the urea, attacks the methyl ester) to form the 5-membered imidazolidine-2,4-dione (hydantoin) ring with loss of methanol. The disconnection is chemically sound. The secondary amine of the amino ester adds to the electrophilic isocyanate carbon to give a urea, and base-promoted (or thermal) cyclization closes the ring. One minor consideration: regiochemistry of cyclization is well-defined here since the only nucleophilic group capable of cyclizing onto the ester is the newly formed urea NH bearing the aryl group. The product correctly shows both N-aryl(4-bromophenyl) substituents and the C5 phenyl group. No significant selectivity or compatibility concerns; the aryl bromides are inert under these conditions.

This is an SN2 amination of an α-bromo ester (methyl 2-bromo-2-phenylacetate) with 4-bromoaniline to give the α-arylamino ester. The disconnection is reasonable and the transformation is precedented for amination of activated (benzylic, α-to-carbonyl) halides. However, several practical concerns exist: (1) Chemoselectivity - the aniline nitrogen could potentially over-alkylate to give the dialkylated tertiary amine, though steric bulk of the benzylic position mitigates this. (2) Competing elimination/hydrolysis - the activated benzylic α-bromo ester is prone to hydrolysis and elimination is not possible here (no β-H on a suitable carbon), but solvolysis is a real competing pathway. (3) The aryl-Br on the aniline is inert under thermal SN2, so no cross-reactivity there. Use of mild base (e.g., excess aniline as base, or K2CO3) in a polar aprotic solvent would be advisable. Overall feasible but yields may be modest due to competing N-overalkylation and racemization at the benzylic center (the product is formed as a racemate, which is fine if the final hydantoin C5 stereocenter is not controlled).

This step represents the sulfamoylation of a secondary amine to form a sulfamide (N-S(=O)2-NH2). Treatment of the secondary amine with sulfamoyl chloride (H2N-SO2-Cl) is the standard approach, rather than sulfamide (NS(N)(=O)=O = H2N-SO2-NH2) itself, which is shown as the building block. The retrosynthetic disconnection is sound and the bond formed (N-S) is well-precedented. In the forward direction, the secondary amine would be reacted with sulfamoyl chloride or in-situ generated reagents (e.g., from chlorosulfonyl isocyanate followed by hydrolysis, or Burgess-type reagents). The methoxy groups and tetrahydroisoquinoline core are fully compatible. Minor note: the depicted building block sulfamide is not the actual acylating agent; sulfamoyl chloride is the practical reagent. Chemoselectivity is good since the only nucleophilic site is the secondary amine.

This step proposes a Bischler-Napieralski-type cyclization combined with reduction to form the 1-substituted tetrahydroisoquinoline directly from an amide (COc1ccc(CCNC(=O)C2CCCC2)cc1OC). Mechanistically this involves: (1) Bischler-Napieralski cyclodehydration (e.g., POCl3, P2O5, or Tf2O) to give the 3,4-dihydroisoquinoline (cyclic imine bearing the cyclopentyl group at C1), followed by (2) reduction (NaBH4) to the tetrahydroisoquinoline. This is a well-precedented sequence and the electron-rich dimethoxy arene strongly activates the ring toward electrophilic cyclization. The major concern is REGIOSELECTIVITY of cyclization: with a 3,4-dimethoxyphenethylamine, cyclization can occur para to one methoxy group, and the substitution pattern of the product must match the desired regiochemistry — for 3,4-dimethoxy substrates, cyclization typically occurs at the position para to the 4-methoxy (giving 6,7-dimethoxy THIQ), which appears consistent with the product. A secondary issue is that the product C1 stereocenter is formed with no stereocontrol (racemic), which is acceptable if a racemate is targeted. Combining two operations (cyclodehydration + reduction) into a single retrosynthetic step is reasonable but should be recognized as two physical steps. Overall feasible but flag regiochemical verification.

This is a sulfamoylation of a secondary amine to install the sulfamoyl group (N-SO2-NH2). Reaction of a secondary amine with sulfamoyl chloride (H2NSO2Cl) is a well-established method to form sulfamides. The disconnection to sulfamide (NS(N)(=O)=O, written as sulfamide) and the secondary amine is chemically reasonable. In practice, sulfamoyl chloride or sulfamide/activated reagents like in-situ generated chlorosulfonyl isocyanate-derived reagents would be used. The free amine is the only nucleophile, so chemoselectivity is good. The two aryl methyl ethers are inert. Minor caveat: the reagent listed is sulfamide (H2NSO2NH2) rather than sulfamoyl chloride; using sulfamide directly often requires harsh conditions, so a more activated reagent may be preferable, but the disconnection itself is sound.

This step is a Bischler-Napieralski-type cyclization/reduction forming the tetrahydroisoquinoline core. The amide COc1ccc(CCNC(=O)C2CCCC2)cc1OC undergoes intramolecular electrophilic cyclization (e.g., POCl3, P2O5, or Tf2O) onto the electron-rich dimethoxyaryl ring to give a 3,4-dihydroisoquinoline (cyclic imine), which is then reduced (NaBH4) to give the 1-substituted tetrahydroisoquinoline. The electron-rich veratrole-type ring strongly favors cyclization and the regiochemistry is directed para/ortho to the methoxy groups, giving the desired 6,7-dimethoxy substitution pattern. This is a classic and reliable transformation. The retrosynthesis here combines cyclization and reduction into one reported step, which is acceptable. Starting amide is readily prepared from the corresponding amine (3,4-dimethoxyphenethylamine) and cyclopentanecarbonyl chloride, both commercially available.

This is a sulfamoylation of a secondary amine to install the sulfamoyl group (-N-SO2NH2). Reaction of the secondary tetrahydroisoquinoline amine with sulfamoyl chloride (ClSO2NH2) or sulfamide (NH2SO2NH2) under appropriate conditions is well-precedented. Sulfamoyl chloride in the presence of a base (e.g., Et3N, DMA) is the most common reagent. Using free sulfamide (NS(N)(=O)=O) as drawn is less efficient and often requires forcing conditions, but the disconnection itself is sound. The aromatic methoxy groups and cyclopentyl group are inert under these conditions. Chemoselectivity for the secondary amine is good as there are no other competing nucleophiles. Recommend specifying sulfamoyl chloride as the actual acylating agent rather than sulfamide.

This step represents a Bischler-Napieralski-type cyclodehydration followed by reduction, or more precisely a reductive cyclization, forming the tetrahydroisoquinoline core from an N-acyl phenethylamine. The amide COc1ccc(CCNC(=O)C2CCCC2)cc1OC undergoes Bischler-Napieralski cyclization (POCl3, P2O5, or Tf2O) to give the 3,4-dihydroisoquinoline (cyclic imine), which is then reduced (NaBH4) to the tetrahydroisoquinoline bearing the cyclopentyl substituent at C1. The electron-rich dimethoxy arene strongly activates the ring toward cyclization at the desired (para to one OMe) position, giving good regioselectivity. Note that the single-step retrosynthesis drawn collapses two operations (cyclodehydration + reduction) into one transformation; this is acceptable for retrosynthetic planning. The newly formed C1 stereocenter would be racemic. The disconnection is strategically strong and the starting amide is readily accessible.

This step represents sulfamoylation of a secondary amine to install the sulfamide (N-SO2-NH2) group. Reaction of a secondary amine with sulfamoyl chloride (ClSO2NH2) is a well-established method to form N-sulfamides. The disconnection of the N-S bond to a free secondary amine and sulfamide/sulfamoyl chloride equivalent is sound. The amine here is the only nucleophilic site, so chemoselectivity is fine; the methoxy aromatic groups are unreactive. Note: the reactant shown is sulfamide (NS(N)(=O)=O) which is a less reactive reagent than sulfamoyl chloride; in practice sulfamoyl chloride or in-situ generated reagents (e.g., from chlorosulfonyl isocyanate) are typically used for higher yields. Overall a feasible, standard transformation.

This step proposes a Bischler-Napieralski-type cyclization / reductive ring closure to form the tetrahydroisoquinoline core from an arylethyl amide (N-(2-arylethyl)cyclopentanecarboxamide). The disconnection is conceptually reasonable: Bischler-Napieralski cyclodehydration (POCl3, P2O5, or Tf2O) of the amide would give a 3,4-dihydroisoquinoline (cyclic imine bearing the cyclopentyl substituent at C1), which then requires reduction (e.g., NaBH4) to the secondary amine. However, two concerns: (1) the route compresses cyclization AND reduction into a single retrosynthetic step, when mechanistically these are two distinct operations — this should be drawn as two steps. (2) Regioselectivity of the cyclization: with a 3,4-dimethoxy (veratrole) substrate, Bischler-Napieralski typically proceeds para to one methoxy and is generally favorable; the electron-rich ring activates cyclization well, so regiochemistry should be acceptable. The main flaw is the omission of the explicit reduction step and the conflation of two transformations. Recommend splitting into amide->dihydroisoquinoline (B-N) and imine->amine (reduction).

This is a standard amide coupling disconnection between a quinoline-4-carboxylic acid and N,N-dimethylethylenediamine. The disconnection at the amide C-N bond is the most logical and well-precedented strategy. Both starting materials are commercially available. The reaction can be carried out with standard coupling reagents (e.g., HATU, EDC/HOBt, T3P) in the presence of a base such as DIPEA. One selectivity consideration: N,N-dimethylethylenediamine has two nitrogen atoms, but the primary amine is far more nucleophilic than the tertiary dimethylamino group, so chemoselective acylation at the primary amine will dominate with no significant issue. The aryl chloride, quinoline nitrogen, and biaryl moiety are all fully compatible with amide coupling conditions. No protecting groups are needed. Overall an efficient, clean, and high-yielding step.

This is a textbook amide coupling disconnection between a carboxylic acid (6-chloro-2-phenylquinoline-4-carboxylic acid) and a primary amine (N,N-dimethylethylenediamine). The disconnection is strategically sound and represents the most logical late-stage bond formation. The terminal primary amine is significantly more nucleophilic than the tertiary dimethylamino group, so chemoselective acylation at the primary amine is expected with standard coupling reagents (HATU, EDC/HOBt, T3P, or via the acid chloride). No protecting groups are needed. Both building blocks are commercially available and inexpensive. The only minor consideration is ensuring excess of the diamine or controlled stoichiometry to avoid bis-acylation, but this is routinely managed. Overall a high-confidence, robust final step.

This is a classic amide bond formation via coupling of a carboxylic acid (2-phenyl-6-chloroquinoline-4-carboxylic acid) with a primary amine (N,N-dimethylethylenediamine). The disconnection at the amide C-N bond is textbook retrosynthesis. Using standard peptide coupling reagents (e.g., HATU, EDC/HOBt, or via the acid chloride), this transformation should proceed cleanly. The tertiary dimethylamino group is non-nucleophilic enough relative to the primary amine that chemoselective acylation at the primary amine is expected without protection. Both starting materials are simple and commercially available. The quinoline nitrogen and aryl chloride are fully compatible with amide coupling conditions. No significant side reactions anticipated; only minor concern is potential over-activation or epimerization, which is irrelevant here as there are no stereocenters.

This is a classic amide coupling disconnection between a quinoline-4-carboxylic acid and N,N-dimethylethylenediamine. The disconnection is strategically sound, cleaving the amide C-N bond to give two commercially available or readily accessible fragments. The reaction is well-precedented using standard coupling reagents (e.g., HATU, EDC/HOBt, T3P, or via acid chloride). Chemoselectivity is excellent here: the primary amine of the diamine is far more nucleophilic than the tertiary dimethylamino group, so selective acylation at the primary amine is expected without protecting group requirements. No interfering functional groups are present (the aryl chloride and quinoline nitrogen are inert under coupling conditions). Both building blocks are reasonable: N,N-dimethylethylenediamine is cheap and commercial, and the 2-phenyl-6-chloroquinoline-4-carboxylic acid is a known scaffold (Pfitzinger-type or Doebner chemistry derived). Overall a high-confidence, efficient final step.

This is a sulfamoylation of an aromatic primary amine using sulfamoyl chloride (NH2SO2Cl) to form a sulfamide (ArNH-SO2-NH2). This is a well-established transformation. The reaction typically proceeds in the presence of a base (e.g., pyridine, Et3N, or NaH) at low temperature. The aniline nitrogen is the most nucleophilic site, so chemoselectivity is good - the nitrile and CF3 groups are inert under these conditions. One minor consideration: sulfamoyl chloride is unstable and must be freshly prepared or handled carefully; alternatives such as in situ generation from chlorosulfonyl isocyanate (CSI) followed by hydrolysis are common. The electron-poor aniline (bearing an ortho-nitrile) is somewhat deactivated, which may reduce reaction rate, but the transformation remains feasible. Both starting materials are reasonable; the aniline precursor is depicted as in_stock.

This is a standard sulfamoylation of an aromatic amine using sulfamoyl chloride (NH2SO2Cl) to form the corresponding sulfamide (ArNH-SO2-NH2). The transformation is well-precedented and proceeds via nucleophilic attack of the aniline nitrogen on the electrophilic sulfur. A base (e.g., pyridine, Et3N, or aqueous NaOH/Na2CO3) is typically required to scavenge HCl. Chemoselectivity is favorable: the aniline is the most nucleophilic site, and the nitrile and aryl-CF3 groups are inert under these conditions. One minor caveat: the aniline is somewhat electron-poor due to the ortho-nitrile, which may slow the reaction, but sulfamoyl chloride is sufficiently reactive that this should still proceed in good yield. Sulfamoyl chloride itself is moisture-sensitive and should be freshly prepared or handled carefully, but it is commercially available/accessible. The aniline starting material (N#Cc1cc(-c2ccc(C(F)(F)F)cc2)ccc1N) is listed as in stock, which is plausible given biaryl coupling chemistry would readily provide it.

This is a sulfamoylation of an aromatic amine using sulfamoyl chloride (NH2SO2Cl) to form the sulfamide (NHSO2NH2). The disconnection is logical and well-precedented; primary aromatic amines react with sulfamoyl chloride in the presence of a base (e.g., pyridine, Et3N, or NaH) to give N-aryl sulfamides. Chemoselectivity favors N-sulfamoylation of the more nucleophilic amine. The nitrile and trifluoromethyl groups are fully compatible with these conditions. One practical note: sulfamoyl chloride is unstable and is often generated in situ or used as a freshly prepared reagent; alternatively, chlorosulfonyl isocyanate (CSI) followed by hydrolysis or sulfamide-transfer reagents (e.g., Burgess-type or t-Bu carbamate-protected sulfamoyl chlorides) are sometimes preferred to improve yields. The aniline starting material containing both a biaryl CF3 group and an ortho-nitrile is a reasonable building block accessible via Suzuki coupling. Overall a clean, feasible final step.

This is a sulfamoylation of an aromatic amine using sulfamoyl chloride (NH2SO2Cl) to form the sulfamide (N-arylsulfamide). The disconnection is logical and well-precedented. Aniline derivatives react with sulfamoyl chloride, typically in the presence of a base (e.g., pyridine, Et3N) to afford N-aryl sulfamides. Considerations: (1) Chemoselectivity favors N-sulfamoylation of the amine; the nitrile and aryl-CF3 groups are inert under these conditions. (2) Sulfamoyl chloride is somewhat unstable/reactive and is often generated in situ or used with care, but the transformation is robust. (3) The arylamine here is somewhat electron-poor (ortho to a nitrile), which may reduce nucleophilicity and require slightly forcing conditions or longer reaction times, but the reaction should still proceed. No protecting groups required. Minor competing reaction: bis-sulfamoylation or hydrolysis of sulfamoyl chloride, mitigated by controlled stoichiometry. Both starting materials are reported as in stock.

This step proposes electrophilic aromatic bromination of the phenyl ring using NBS (N-bromosuccinimide) to install the para-bromo substituent on the pendant phenyl group. There are several serious problems with this disconnection. First, the molecule contains a highly electron-rich naphthol moiety and an extremely nucleophilic thiouracil/dihydropyrimidine-2-thione core. The thiocarbonyl (C=S) sulfur is far more nucleophilic than any aromatic ring and would be the preferred site of attack by NBS, leading to S-bromination/oxidative desulfurization rather than aryl bromination. Second, even if ring bromination occurred, the naphthol ring (activated, electron-rich) would be brominated preferentially over the unactivated, neutral phenyl group. NBS would not selectively target the para position of the comparatively electron-poor phenyl ring. Third, the free phenol is highly susceptible to oxidation by NBS. The proposed late-stage, non-selective bromination is therefore highly unlikely to deliver the desired product. A better strategy would be to introduce the 4-bromophenyl group at an earlier stage using a pre-functionalized building block (e.g., a 4-bromophenyl-bearing chalcone or aldehyde used in the Biginelli-type construction of the thiouracil ring), avoiding selectivity problems entirely.

This disconnection proposes installation of the aryl bromide via electrophilic bromination of the phenyl ring using NBS (N-bromosuccinimide) as the final step. This is highly problematic for several reasons. (1) Regioselectivity: NBS bromination of an unactivated/weakly activated phenyl group would not selectively install bromine at the para position cleanly. More critically, the substrate contains far more electron-rich and reactive sites for electrophilic bromination, namely the naphthol (the activated naphthalene ring bearing a free OH) and the thiouracil/2-thioxopyrimidinone core. The free hydroxynaphthalene is strongly activated and would be brominated preferentially over the pendant phenyl ring. (2) Chemoselectivity: NBS is known to oxidize or brominate thiocarbonyl (C=S) groups; the 2-thiouracil moiety would likely react with NBS (S-bromination/desulfurization or oxidation), destroying the thione functionality. (3) The active methylene/benzylic CH2 linker could also undergo radical benzylic bromination under NBS conditions. Overall, attempting selective aryl C-H bromination of the para-phenyl position in the presence of a naphthol, an active CH2, and a thione is not feasible. A better strategy would be to introduce the 4-bromophenyl group already brominated at the ring-construction stage (e.g., use a 4-bromophenyl building block in the pyrimidinone/thiouracil assembly) rather than late-stage C-H bromination. The disconnection is therefore non-optimal and would fail on selectivity grounds.

The proposed step uses NBS (N-bromosuccinimide) to brominate the para-position of a pendant phenyl ring to install the aryl bromide. This disconnection has multiple serious problems. First, electrophilic aromatic bromination with NBS on an unactivated benzene ring (the phenyl substituent) is sluggish and non-selective; NBS strongly prefers benzylic/allylic radical bromination or bromination of electron-rich aromatics. Second, and most critically, the molecule contains a highly activated, electron-rich naphthol (the 2-naphthol-type moiety) and a thiourea/thiouracil (C=S) system. NBS would preferentially brominate the electron-rich naphthol ring and/or oxidize the thiocarbonyl (C=S) sulfur, leading to chemoselectivity disasters. The benzylic CH2 linker is also a prime site for radical bromination. Achieving clean para-bromination of the unactivated pendant phenyl in the presence of all these reactive groups is unrealistic. A far better strategy would be to introduce the 4-bromophenyl group earlier from a pre-brominated building block (e.g., a 4-bromophenyl-bearing precursor) rather than attempting late-stage selective bromination.

This step proposes installing the aryl bromide via NBS bromination of a phenyl-substituted precursor. There are several serious problems: (1) The molecule contains an electron-rich naphthol moiety which is FAR more activated toward electrophilic aromatic bromination than the pendant unactivated phenyl ring. NBS would preferentially brominate the naphthol (ortho/para to the OH) rather than the desired para position of the phenyl substituent. (2) The thiourea/thione (C=S) functionality is highly susceptible to oxidation/bromination by NBS, which would lead to desulfurization or S-bromination side reactions. (3) Even setting aside chemoselectivity, achieving clean para-selectivity on an unactivated monosubstituted benzene ring with NBS is not feasible without a strong Lewis acid catalyst, and even then the unactivated phenyl would not compete with the naphthol. The retrosynthetic disconnection of the C-Br bond is reasonable in principle, but it should be installed before assembling the electron-rich and sulfur-containing framework, ideally starting from a pre-brominated aryl building block (e.g., 4-bromobenzaldehyde or 4-bromophenyl precursor) in the ring-forming step.

This is a sulfonamide-forming reaction between methyl piperidine-2-carboxylate (a secondary amine) and an aryl sulfonyl chloride. The disconnection is sound and well-precedented. The reaction is typically run with a base (Et3N, pyridine, or aqueous NaHCO3) in DCM or THF. The main concern is chemoselectivity: the sulfonyl chloride must react with the secondary amine of the pipecolate rather than competing with the existing amide N-H, but amide nitrogens are very poor nucleophiles and the secondary amine will react preferentially. The methyl ester is inert under these conditions. No issues anticipated.

This step proposes amide bond formation between a pyrazole carboxylic acid and 4-aminobenzenesulfonyl chloride, where the aniline nitrogen is acylated. The major chemoselectivity concern is that the sulfonyl chloride is highly electrophilic and the free aniline NH2 in the same molecule could react intramolecularly/intermolecularly, or the activated carboxylic acid (after coupling reagent activation) could react with water/the sulfonyl chloride could hydrolyze. Coupling a carboxylic acid onto an aniline while a sulfonyl chloride is present in the SAME coupling partner is problematic - the aniline and sulfonyl chloride could self-condense or the coupling conditions (which often involve bases/nucleophilic activators) would degrade the sulfonyl chloride. A better strategy would be to install the sulfonamide (couple with the pipecolate) BEFORE or after forming the amide, or to use the sulfonic acid/protected form. Reversing the order of operations (form sulfonamide first, then amide) would be cleaner. Consider doing the amide coupling on a precursor where the sulfonyl is already capped or is a sulfonic acid that is later chlorinated.

This is a sulfonamide formation between the secondary amine (methyl pipecolate) and an aryl sulfonyl chloride. This is a well-established transformation, typically performed with a base (Et3N, pyridine, or aqueous Na2CO3) in DCM or THF. The secondary amine is nucleophilic and the sulfonyl chloride reactive. Chemoselectivity is excellent here: the only competing nucleophile (the aryl amide NH) is much less nucleophilic and already acylated, so it will not react. The methyl ester is inert under these conditions. No protecting groups needed. Good convergent disconnection.

This step proposes amide coupling between the pyrazole carboxylic acid and 4-aminobenzenesulfonyl chloride bearing a free sulfonyl chloride. The major concern is chemoselectivity: the substrate 4-aminobenzenesulfonyl chloride contains both a nucleophilic aromatic amine AND an electrophilic sulfonyl chloride. Under standard amide coupling conditions (activation of carboxylic acid via acid chloride, EDC/HOBt, T3P, etc.), the aniline NH2 is the intended nucleophile, but the coexistence of a free sulfonyl chloride in the same molecule is highly problematic — it can lead to self-condensation/oligomerization (the aniline of one molecule attacking the sulfonyl chloride of another), forming polymeric sulfonamides. Additionally, if the acid is activated as an acyl chloride, no issue arises with the SO2Cl itself, but the aniline+SO2Cl pairing within the same molecule is intrinsically unstable. A better strategy would be to form the amide first on a precursor where the sulfonyl group is masked (e.g., as a thioether or sulfonamide), then introduce/unmask the sulfonyl chloride, OR reorder the synthesis so the sulfonyl chloride is installed/coupled with the amine last (as in step f9fc1ef34cff4c1c7280b9b86d4bc968a9ad9e22b4b9647fc2aa838fabee2821) before the amide is formed. As written, the intermediate Cn1nc(C(F)(F)F)cc1C(=O)Nc1ccc(S(=O)(=O)Cl)cc1 is difficult to isolate cleanly. Consider chlorosulfonation of the pre-formed acetanilide-type amide as an alternative route to this sulfonyl chloride intermediate.

This is a sulfonamide bond formation between methyl pipecolate (a secondary amine) and an aryl sulfonyl chloride. The disconnection is sound and well-precedented. Standard conditions (base such as Et3N, pyridine, or aqueous NaHCO3 in DCM or THF) would deliver the product. The secondary amine of methyl pipecolate is the only nucleophile, and the ester is stable under these conditions. One minor consideration: the substrate already bears an amide N-H (the anilide), but anilide N-H is far less nucleophilic than the aliphatic secondary amine, so chemoselectivity favors the desired sulfonamidation. No significant competing reactions expected.

This step proposes amide coupling between a pyrazole carboxylic acid and 4-aminobenzenesulfonyl chloride. The key problem is chemoselectivity: the aniline starting material bears both a free amine (-NH2) and a highly electrophilic sulfonyl chloride. Under typical amide coupling conditions (activation of the acid as acid chloride, anhydride, or via coupling reagents), the free aniline could self-condense with the sulfonyl chloride of another molecule, or the activated acid could react with the amine while the sulfonyl chloride simultaneously undergoes hydrolysis/side reactions. The sulfonyl chloride is moisture/base sensitive and is generally incompatible with the conditions needed to form the anilide. A better strategy would introduce the sulfonyl chloride functionality LATE (e.g., via chlorosulfonation of an acetanilide-type precursor after amide formation) or use a protected sulfonate. As drawn, the simultaneous presence of free -NH2 and -SO2Cl in the product/reactant is problematic and would require careful order-of-operations. Consider performing the amide coupling first on an aniline lacking the SO2Cl, then introducing the sulfonyl chloride.

This step forms the sulfonamide bond by reacting methyl pipecolate (piperidine-2-carboxylic acid methyl ester) with the aryl sulfonyl chloride. Sulfonylation of a secondary amine with a sulfonyl chloride is a well-established, high-yielding transformation (typically with a base like Et3N, pyridine, or aqueous NaHCO3/DCM). The methyl ester is compatible. The pre-existing amide linkage on the aryl ring is inert under these conditions. The main concern is chemoselectivity: the sulfonyl chloride intermediate also bears a carboxamide N-H, but secondary amide N-H is far less nucleophilic than the piperidine secondary amine, so selective S-N bond formation at the amine is expected. Good disconnection at the sulfonamide.

This step proposes amide coupling between the pyrazole carboxylic acid and 4-aminobenzenesulfonyl chloride to form the anilide while RETAINING the free sulfonyl chloride. This is highly problematic. Sulfonyl chlorides are far more electrophilic than carboxylic acids, and the aniline nitrogen is nucleophilic. Standard amide coupling reagents (EDC, HATU, T3P, acid chloride formation) would either react preferentially at the sulfonyl chloride or, more likely, the aniline would self-condense with the sulfonyl chloride (intermolecular sulfonamide formation/oligomerization). It is essentially impossible to selectively acylate the aniline N-H while leaving an intramolecular/intermolecular reactive -SO2Cl untouched. Furthermore, activation of the carboxylic acid (e.g., to acid chloride) is incompatible with a free sulfonyl chloride and aniline coexisting. A better strategy would reverse the order: install the sulfonamide FIRST (couple sulfanilamide-derived chloride with the amine, OR use a sulfonamide rather than sulfonyl chloride), then perform the amide coupling on the aniline. As written, retaining a free -SO2Cl through an amide coupling is not viable.

This is an N-alkylation of a primary amine (NCC(F)=C1CCCC1) with phenethyl bromide (BrCCc1ccccc1) to give the secondary amine product. The disconnection itself is reasonable and represents a classic SN2 alkylation. However, the principal concern is overalkylation: primary amines react readily with alkyl halides to give a mixture of secondary and tertiary (and quaternary) amines. Achieving selective monoalkylation to the secondary amine is difficult and typically gives modest yields unless a large excess of the amine is employed or alternative strategies are used. A superior approach would be reductive amination (e.g., condensation of the primary amine with phenylacetaldehyde followed by NaBH(OAc)3 or NaBH3CN reduction), which cleanly affords the monoalkylated secondary amine and avoids overalkylation. The vinyl fluoride (fluoroalkene) functionality should be compatible with mild alkylation/reductive amination conditions. Both building blocks are simple; phenethyl bromide is commercial, and the fluoroallylic amine is plausibly accessible.

This is an N-alkylation of a primary amine (NCC(F)=C1CCCC1) with phenethyl bromide (BrCCc1ccccc1) to form the secondary amine product. While the disconnection itself is logical and the bond formed (C-N) is appropriate, direct alkylation of a primary amine with an alkyl halide is notoriously poor for selectivity. The secondary amine product is more nucleophilic than the starting primary amine, leading to over-alkylation (tertiary amine and even quaternary ammonium salts). To improve selectivity, one would typically use a large excess of the primary amine, or better yet, employ reductive amination using phenylacetaldehyde and the primary amine with NaBH(OAc)3 or NaBH3CN, which cleanly delivers the secondary amine and avoids over-alkylation. Both proposed building blocks are reasonable: phenethyl bromide is commercially available and cheap. The fluoroalkene-containing primary amine (NCC(F)=C1CCCC1) is less common but plausible as a building block. Note also potential chemoselectivity concerns regarding the vinyl fluoride, though it should be inert under alkylation conditions.

This step proposes N-alkylation of a primary amine (NCC(F)=C1CCCC1) with (2-bromoethyl)benzene to form the secondary amine product. The disconnection at the C-N bond is reasonable and well-precedented in principle. However, the major issue is overalkylation: primary amines react with alkyl halides to give mixtures of secondary and tertiary amines (and quaternary salts), so monoalkylation selectivity is poor without an excess of the amine or alternative strategy. A reductive amination approach (using phenylacetaldehyde with the primary amine and NaBH(OAc)3 or NaBH3CN) would be far more selective and is the preferred method for installing this secondary amine motif. Additionally, the fluorinated allylic/vinyl amine starting material (NCC(F)=C1CCCC1) bears an allylic C-F that is generally robust but the primary allylamine is somewhat nucleophilic and could undergo competing reactions; nonetheless the main concern remains chemoselective monoalkylation. Recommend switching to reductive amination with phenylacetaldehyde for improved selectivity and yield.

This is an N-alkylation of a primary amine (NCC(F)=C1CCCC1) with phenethyl bromide to form the secondary amine product. While the disconnection is reasonable and both starting materials appear commercially available, direct alkylation of primary amines with alkyl halides is notoriously poorly selective. The secondary amine product is more nucleophilic than the starting primary amine, leading to overalkylation and formation of tertiary amine and quaternary ammonium salt byproducts. To improve selectivity, consider: (1) using a large excess of the primary amine, (2) reductive amination using phenylacetaldehyde and the primary amine with NaBH(OAc)3 or NaBH3CN, which is much cleaner and more selective for monoalkylation, or (3) protecting/staged approaches. The fluoroalkene (vinyl fluoride) moiety should be stable under these conditions. The reductive amination route would be strongly preferred for this disconnection.

This is an SNAr etherification forming the alkyl aryl ether by displacement of the chloride on the activated pyridazine with the primary alkoxide. Pyridazines bearing a leaving group adjacent to ring nitrogen are good SNAr substrates, and alkoxide displacement of 3-chloropyridazines is well precedented (typically NaH or K2CO3/Cs2CO3 with the alcohol in DMF or THF). The disconnection is sensible and convergent. Two cautions: (1) The nitroimidazole-fused bicyclic alcohol contains an acidic/electrophilic heteroaromatic nitro system; strong bases (NaH) could promote side reactions, so a milder base (Cs2CO3) or controlled deprotonation is advisable. (2) Chemoselectivity of O- vs potential competing reactions is generally fine since the only nucleophilic site is the primary OH. Overall a robust, well-precedented late-stage coupling.

This is a Suzuki–Miyaura cross-coupling between 3,6-dichloropyridazine and 4-(trifluoromethoxy)phenylboronic acid. The transformation itself is well precedented (Pd(PPh3)4 or Pd(dppf)Cl2, base such as K2CO3/Na2CO3). The principal concern is mono- vs bis-arylation selectivity: the substrate is symmetric 3,6-dichloropyridazine, so achieving clean mono-coupling to retain one chloride for the subsequent SNAr requires careful stoichiometry control (typically ~1.0 equiv boronic acid, controlled temperature) and will inevitably give some bis-coupled byproduct plus unreacted starting material, lowering yield and complicating purification. Both starting materials (3,6-dichloropyridazine and 4-(trifluoromethoxy)phenylboronic acid) are commercially available. The disconnection is reasonable but the mono-selectivity issue is the key limiting factor.

This is an SNAr-type etherification (Williamson/nucleophilic aromatic substitution) between a primary alcohol and a 3-chloropyridazine bearing an aryl group.
