The proposed forward step is a late-stage electrophilic bromination of the phenyl substituent using N-bromosuccinimide to give the para-bromophenyl analogue. While NBS can brominate sufficiently activated aromatic rings under appropriate conditions, this substrate presents severe chemoselectivity and regioselectivity problems. The intended phenyl ring is only weakly activated or possibly deactivated by conjugation to the electron-poor thiobarbiturate/uracil-like heterocycle, whereas the molecule contains a free phenolic naphthalene unit, which is far more electron-rich and would be expected to undergo bromination preferentially. Bromination ortho/para to the phenol on the naphthalene ring is a major competing pathway. In addition, the thiourea/thioamide functionality may be susceptible to halogenation or oxidation by NBS, and the heterocyclic enolizable/conjugated system may also participate in side reactions. Therefore, selective monobromination of the pendant phenyl ring at the para position in the presence of an unprotected phenolic naphthalene and thione is unlikely to be reliable. A better strategy would be to introduce the p-bromophenyl group earlier, for example by using a p-bromobenzaldehyde or p-bromophenyl-containing building block in the condensation that constructs the heterocyclic core, rather than attempting late-stage arene bromination. If late-stage bromination were unavoidable, protection of the phenol and extensive condition screening would be required, but even then the desired ring is probably not the most reactive site.

The proposed forward step is late-stage bromination of a complex thiobarbiturate/dihydropyrimidinone-like scaffold using N-bromosuccinimide to convert an unsubstituted phenyl group into the para-bromophenyl analogue. This is a high-risk transformation. The desired phenyl ring is not obviously the most activated arene in the molecule; the molecule also contains a phenolic naphthol unit, which is much more electron-rich and would be expected to brominate preferentially under electrophilic bromination conditions. In addition, NBS can react with the thiocarbonyl/thioamide functionality by S-bromination or oxidative side processes, and the two imide/thiourea-like NH groups may undergo N-bromination. Benzylic/allylic bromination at the methylene linking the heterocycle to the naphthol unit is also a possible competing pathway under radical conditions. Regioselective para-bromination of the pendant phenyl ring in the presence of these more reactive sites is therefore unlikely. Even if aryl bromination occurred, mixtures of ortho/para bromination and polybromination could be problematic. A better strategy would be to introduce the bromine substituent earlier, for example by constructing the heterocyclic core from a commercially available p-bromobenzaldehyde or another prefunctionalized p-bromophenyl precursor, rather than attempting nonselective late-stage bromination.

The proposed forward transformation is direct bromination of a phenyl-substituted thioxopyrimidinone using N-bromosuccinimide to give the para-bromophenyl analogue. While electrophilic aromatic bromination with NBS can be feasible on simple arenes, this substrate presents major selectivity and compatibility concerns. The intended phenyl ring is only weakly activated and bromination would be expected to give ortho/para mixtures unless steric effects are highly controlling. More importantly, the molecule contains a phenolic naphthyl/aryl system that is substantially more electron-rich and would likely brominate preferentially. The thioamide/thione-containing heterocycle may also undergo N-bromination, S-bromination/oxidation, or other decomposition under brominating conditions. Benzylic bromination at the methylene linker is also a potential competing pathway depending on conditions. Therefore, selective para-bromination of only the phenyl substituent is unlikely to be clean. A better strategy would be to introduce the bromine substituent earlier by using a prefunctionalized aryl building block, e.g. a p-bromobenzaldehyde, p-bromobenzoyl precursor, or other p-bromophenyl synthon in the construction of the pyrimidinone/thioxopyrimidinone core, rather than performing late-stage electrophilic bromination on such a multifunctional molecule.

The proposed forward step appears to be direct bromination of the phenyl analogue using N-bromosuccinimide to give the para-bromophenyl product. This is not a reliable or selective transformation in this substrate. The phenyl ring to be brominated is attached to an electron-poor heterocyclic barbiturate/thiobarbiturate-like core and is likely less activated than the free phenolic naphthyl unit. The phenolic naphthalene ring is much more electron-rich and would be expected to undergo electrophilic bromination preferentially, especially at positions ortho/para to the phenol. In addition, the thiocarbonyl/thiourea motif and multiple NH groups may react with electrophilic bromine sources, leading to sulfur bromination/oxidation, N-bromination, or decomposition. Therefore, late-stage selective para-bromination of only the pendant phenyl ring is highly unlikely to be clean. A better strategy would be to introduce the p-bromophenyl group earlier using a commercially available p-brominated aryl precursor, for example through the corresponding p-bromobenzaldehyde or p-bromophenyl-substituted heterocycle intermediate, rather than attempting late-stage aromatic bromination. If late-stage halogenation were unavoidable, the phenol would likely require protection and the thioamide motif may still be problematic; even then regioselectivity on the deactivated phenyl ring would remain questionable.

Forward reaction is N-sulfonylation of methyl pipecolinate with an arylsulfonyl chloride. This is a standard and chemically reasonable transformation. The secondary amine should be substantially more nucleophilic than the anilide NH present in the sulfonyl chloride partner, so chemoselectivity should favor formation of the desired sulfonamide. Mild anhydrous conditions using a hindered base such as DIPEA or triethylamine in DCM, MeCN, or THF should be appropriate. If methyl pipecolinate is used as an HCl salt, extra base will be required. Potential issues include hydrolysis of the sulfonyl chloride, slower reaction due to steric hindrance around the pipecolinate nitrogen, and possible epimerization at the alpha-ester stereocenter under strongly basic conditions. These are manageable with mild base and controlled temperature. The lack of stereochemical specification in the SMILES should be clarified if a single enantiomer is required.

Formation of the sulfonamide from methyl piperidine-2-carboxylate and the arylsulfonyl chloride is a well-precedented and chemically sound disconnection. The secondary amine should react readily with the sulfonyl chloride under standard basic conditions, e.g. Et3N, DIPEA, pyridine, or aqueous bicarbonate biphasic conditions. The methyl ester should be compatible provided strongly basic or aqueous prolonged conditions are avoided to minimize ester hydrolysis or epimerization at the alpha-carbon if an enantioenriched pipecolate is intended. The pyrazole amide and trifluoromethyl group should be inert. The main practical considerations are use of the free-base amine rather than an HCl salt, control of HCl generated during the reaction, and avoiding excess amine/base conditions that could promote hydrolysis of the sulfonyl chloride or ester. Overall this is a logical late-stage sulfonylation and should be high-yielding after optimization.

local_feedback: Problems with reaction type and functional group compatibility
local_feedback_text: The proposed coupling of 4-aminobenzenesulfonyl chloride with the pyrazole carboxylic acid to give the corresponding anilide while retaining the sulfonyl chloride is chemically problematic. 4-Aminobenzenesulfonyl chloride contains two mutually reactive functionalities: a nucleophilic aniline and an electrophilic sulfonyl chloride. The free aniline can react intermolecularly with the sulfonyl chloride, leading to oligomeric or self-sulfonylated byproducts. In addition, standard amide coupling conditions require base and/or nucleophilic additives, which are often poorly compatible with sulfonyl chlorides because hydrolysis, sulfonate formation, or reaction with coupling additives can occur. Chemoselective acylation of the aniline in the presence of an unprotected sulfonyl chloride is therefore unreliable. A better route would change the order of operations: install the sulfonamide first using a nitro-substituted arylsulfonyl chloride, e.g. 4-nitrobenzenesulfonyl chloride plus methyl pipecolate, then reduce the nitro group to the aniline and finally couple with the pyrazole carboxylic acid. Alternatively, use a protected aniline/sulfonyl chloride equivalent, but the proposed unprotected aminobenzenesulfonyl chloride is not an optimal intermediate.

Forward reaction is a standard sulfonylation of a secondary amine, methyl piperidine-2-carboxylate, with an arylsulfonyl chloride. This disconnection is appropriate and should form the N-sulfonyl piperidine cleanly under typical conditions such as DIPEA, triethylamine, pyridine, or carbonate base in an aprotic solvent. The methyl ester should be compatible if strongly aqueous or strongly basic conditions are avoided. The amide NH present on the arylsulfonyl chloride fragment is much less nucleophilic than the piperidine nitrogen, so chemoselectivity should favor sulfonylation of the piperidine. However, the amide NH can be acidic and may consume base or, under forcing conditions, undergo minor competing sulfonylation/deprotonation. Use of dry conditions and slight excess amine or base would be advisable. If stereochemistry at the pipecolate center matters, the route does not specify whether racemic or enantiopure methyl piperidine-2-carboxylate is used.

Formation of the N-sulfonyl piperidine from methyl pipecolinate and the arylsulfonyl chloride is a well-precedented and chemically sound transformation. The secondary amine should selectively attack the sulfonyl chloride in the presence of a mild non-nucleophilic base such as DIPEA, triethylamine, or pyridine, typically in DCM, MeCN, or THF. The methyl ester should be compatible under these conditions, although prolonged exposure to strong base or water should be avoided to minimize ester hydrolysis. The pre-existing pyrazole carboxamide is unlikely to compete as a nucleophile. Key practical concerns are hydrolysis of the sulfonyl chloride and possible use of methyl pipecolinate as an HCl salt, which would require sufficient base. If stereochemistry at the pipecolinate center matters, racemization is unlikely under mild sulfonylation conditions, but the route as drawn does not specify enantiopurity.

local_feedback: Problems with reaction type and functional group compatibility
local_feedback_text: The proposed amide coupling between the pyrazole carboxylic acid and 4-aminobenzenesulfonyl chloride is the problematic step. Free 4-aminobenzenesulfonyl chloride is a highly challenging bifunctional reagent: the aniline is nucleophilic/basic while the sulfonyl chloride is strongly electrophilic, leading to potential self-condensation/polymerization, hydrolysis, and reaction with bases or coupling-reagent additives. Commercial material, when available, is often handled as a hydrochloride or is unstable; if protonated, the aniline will be poorly reactive toward amide coupling, while liberating the free base increases risk of intermolecular sulfonamide formation. Additionally, the para-sulfonyl chloride strongly deactivates the aniline, so direct coupling to a heteroaryl carboxylic acid may require forcing activation conditions that are not very compatible with an unprotected sulfonyl chloride. A more robust approach would be to reverse the order: install the sulfonamide first using 4-nitrobenzenesulfonyl chloride or 4-acetamidobenzenesulfonyl chloride with methyl pipecolinate, then reduce/deprotect to the aniline, followed by amide coupling with the pyrazole carboxylic acid using HATU, T3P, EDCI/HOAt, or conversion of the acid to an acid chloride if compatible. This avoids carrying a free arylsulfonyl chloride through an aniline acylation step.

This step is a straightforward N-alkylation of a primary amine, NCC(F)=C1CCCC1, with 2-phenethyl bromide to give the secondary amine. The bond disconnection is chemically reasonable and the desired SN2 reaction at the primary bromide should be feasible. However, the main concern is chemoselectivity/overalkylation: the initially formed secondary amine will generally be more nucleophilic than the starting primary amine and can undergo further alkylation to the tertiary amine or even quaternary ammonium salt, especially if phenethyl bromide is used in excess or the reaction is run too long. Use of a large excess of the primary amine, slow addition of phenethyl bromide, careful stoichiometric control, and a mild base such as K2CO3 or DIPEA would be advisable. Phenethyl bromide can also undergo some elimination to styrene under strongly basic or high-temperature conditions, so mild conditions are preferred. The fluoroalkene motif should be reasonably compatible with neutral/mildly basic N-alkylation conditions, although strongly basic conditions should be avoided. An alternative potentially cleaner approach would be reductive amination of the primary amine with phenylacetaldehyde, which may reduce overalkylation issues.

This is a chemically reasonable SN2 N-alkylation of a primary amine, NCC(F)=C1CCCC1, with a primary phenethyl bromide electrophile. The desired C-N bond formation should be feasible under standard conditions such as K2CO3, DIPEA, or Et3N in MeCN, DMF, or ethanol. However, the main concern is chemoselectivity: alkylation of a primary amine can readily proceed beyond the desired secondary amine to give tertiary amine and potentially quaternary ammonium byproducts, especially if phenethyl bromide is used in excess or the reaction is heated. This can likely be managed by using excess amine, slow addition of phenethyl bromide, careful stoichiometry, or purification of the secondary amine salt. The fluoroalkene motif should generally tolerate these mild basic/nucleophilic conditions, although strong base should be avoided to minimize alkene isomerization or elimination of phenethyl bromide to styrene. A potentially cleaner alternative would be reductive amination of the primary amine with phenylacetaldehyde, although phenylacetaldehyde can be less convenient due to instability. Overall, the disconnection is standard and feasible, but monoalkylation selectivity may limit yield.

The proposed final step is an N-alkylation of the primary amine NCC(F)=C1CCCC1 with phenethyl bromide to give the secondary amine target. The basic disconnection is chemically reasonable: phenethyl bromide is a competent primary alkyl bromide for SN2 substitution, and the fluorinated alkene motif should generally be compatible with mild amine alkylation conditions. However, the main concern is chemoselectivity/overalkylation. Primary amines reacting with alkyl bromides often give mixtures of secondary amine, tertiary amine, and sometimes quaternary ammonium salts because the initially formed secondary amine can remain nucleophilic. This could be controlled by using an excess of the fluorinated primary amine, slow addition of phenethyl bromide, and a mild base such as K2CO3, DIPEA, or NaHCO3 in MeCN/DMF, but purification may still be needed. A potentially cleaner alternative would be reductive amination of the primary amine with phenylacetaldehyde, which would avoid alkyl bromide overalkylation and may be more selective. Phenethyl bromide can also undergo minor elimination to styrene under strongly basic conditions, so strongly basic or high-temperature conditions should be avoided. Overall, the transformation is feasible but requires careful control of monoalkylation.

This is a plausible direct N-alkylation of the primary amine NCC(F)=C1CCCC1 with phenethyl bromide to form the target secondary amine. The C–N bond disconnection is appropriate and chemically well precedented: phenethyl bromide is a competent primary alkyl bromide for SN2 substitution, and the aminofluoroalkene should generally tolerate mild basic alkylation conditions. The main issue is chemoselectivity/overalkylation. The product is a secondary amine and may undergo further alkylation with phenethyl bromide to give the tertiary bis-phenethylated amine or even quaternary ammonium salts if excess alkyl halide or forcing conditions are used. This can be mitigated by using excess starting primary amine, slow addition of phenethyl bromide, mild inorganic base such as K2CO3 or NaHCO3, or hindered organic base such as DIPEA in MeCN/DMF, followed by careful stoichiometric control. Alternatively, reductive amination of the aminofluoroalkene-derived amine with phenylacetaldehyde could be considered if overalkylation is problematic. The fluoroalkene motif should be compatible with neutral to mildly basic conditions, though strong base should be avoided to minimize alkene isomerization or decomposition. Overall, the reaction is feasible but requires optimization to suppress overalkylation.

This disconnection corresponds to formation of the aryl ether by nucleophilic aromatic substitution of an activated chloropyridazine with the primary alcohol side chain of the nitroimidazo-oxazine fragment. Electron-deficient chloropyridazines, especially chlorides adjacent to ring nitrogens, are good SNAr electrophiles, and displacement by an alkoxide is a well-precedented strategy. The primary alcohol should be converted to the corresponding alkoxide using a base such as NaH, KHMDS, Cs2CO3, or KOtBu depending on substrate stability. The main practical concern is compatibility of the nitroimidazole/oxazine fragment with strong base and polar aprotic conditions; nitroheterocycles can be sensitive to prolonged exposure to strong base or high temperature. However, if the alcohol fragment is indeed a known stable intermediate, this transformation is chemically plausible. Chemoselectivity should be favorable because the alcohol is the only obvious nucleophile, and the chloropyridazine is activated toward SNAr. Potential side reactions include hydrolysis of the chloropyridazine, decomposition or ring opening of the nitroimidazo-oxazine under strongly basic conditions, and incomplete conversion if the alkoxide is insufficiently nucleophilic. Mild SNAr conditions using Cs2CO3 or K2CO3 in DMF/DMSO, or careful NaH-mediated alkoxide formation at low temperature followed by addition of the heteroaryl chloride, would be reasonable optimizations.

This step is a Suzuki coupling between a dichloropyridazine and 4-trifluoromethoxyphenylboronic acid to give the monoarylated chloropyridazine electrophile. Electron-deficient chloropyridazines are suitable electrophiles for Pd-catalyzed cross-coupling, and arylboronic acids bearing para-OCF3 substituents are commonly used in Suzuki chemistry. The remaining chloro substituent is required for the subsequent SNAr step, so control of mono- versus bis-coupling is the key issue. If the starting dichloropyridazine is symmetrical, regioselectivity is not a problem, but overcoupling to the diarylated pyridazine may occur. This can usually be controlled by using limiting boronic acid, excess dichloropyridazine, lower catalyst loading, and careful monitoring. The trifluoromethoxy group should be stable under standard Suzuki conditions. Potential yield-limiting issues include protodeboronation of the arylboronic acid, hydrolysis or decomposition of the chloropyridazine under strongly basic aqueous conditions, and formation of bis-coupled product. Suitable conditions could include Pd(PPh3)4, Pd(dppf)Cl2, or a Buchwald precatalyst with K2CO3, Cs2CO3, or K3PO4 in dioxane/water, toluene/water, or THF/water.

This is a plausible SNAr etherification between the primary alcohol-containing nitroimidazo-oxazine fragment and an electron-deficient chloropyridazine. Chloropyridazines are generally good SNAr electrophiles because the ring nitrogens activate the C-Cl bond, and the alcohol fragment has no obvious competing N-H or strongly nucleophilic heteroatom. The fused nitroimidazole/oxazine system and nitro group should tolerate relatively mild basic conditions, although strongly basic or high-temperature conditions could cause decomposition or epimerization/degradation of the sensitive nitroheterocycle. The preferred forward conditions would likely use a mild inorganic base such as Cs2CO3 or K2CO3 in DMF/DMSO, or carefully controlled NaH if needed, with exclusion of water to avoid hydrolysis of the chloropyridazine. Main risks are incomplete conversion, hydrolysis of the heteroaryl chloride, or decomposition of the nitroimidazo-oxazine under harsh base. Overall, the disconnection is chemically sound and efficient.

The proposed Suzuki coupling of dichloropyridazine with 4-trifluoromethoxyphenylboronic acid is feasible, and arylation of chloropyridazines under Pd catalysis is well precedented. The main issue is chemoselective monoarylation versus diarylation. If the starting material is 3,6-dichloropyridazine, the two chlorides are symmetry-equivalent initially, so regioselectivity is not a concern, but once monoarylation occurs the remaining chloride can still undergo a second Suzuki coupling. Control would likely require using excess dichloropyridazine, limiting boronic acid, short reaction times, and an appropriate catalyst/base system. The trifluoromethoxyphenylboronic acid is a reasonable partner but may undergo some protodeboronation depending on conditions. Suggested conditions would include Pd(PPh3)4, Pd(dppf)Cl2, or a more active biarylphosphine Pd catalyst with K2CO3, Cs2CO3, or K3PO4 in dioxane/water or toluene/water. Purification may need to separate mono- and bis-arylated pyridazine products. Overall feasible, but selectivity/yield optimization is important.

This disconnection corresponds to formation of a primary alkyl heteroaryl ether by nucleophilic aromatic substitution of an activated chloropyridazine with the alcohol-derived alkoxide. Chloropyridazines are sufficiently electron-poor to undergo SNAr with alcohol nucleophiles, and the retained biaryl/trifluoromethoxy aryl unit should be compatible with typical basic conditions. The nitroimidazooxazine alcohol contains a primary alcohol appended to a stereogenic center; substitution occurs at oxygen and should not directly disturb the stereocenter, although strong base or prolonged heating could risk degradation or epimerization/decomposition of the nitro heterocycle. Mild inorganic bases such as K2CO3 or Cs2CO3 in DMF/DMSO, or carefully controlled NaH conditions, would be reasonable. Potential side reactions include hydrolysis of the chloropyridazine, decomposition of the nitroimidazooxazine under strongly basic conditions, and incomplete conversion if the alcohol is insufficiently deprotonated. Overall, this is a well-precedented and appropriate final etherification strategy.

This step is a Suzuki coupling between a dichloropyridazine and 4-trifluoromethoxyphenylboronic acid to give a monoarylated chloropyridazine. Electron-poor heteroaryl chlorides such as chloropyridazines are competent electrophiles under Pd-catalyzed Suzuki conditions, especially with ligands such as dppf, XPhos/SPhos, or related electron-rich phosphines. The 4-trifluoromethoxyphenylboronic acid is a plausible commercial reagent and should tolerate standard aqueous carbonate/phosphate bases. The main issue is control of monoarylation versus bis-arylation, since the remaining chloropyridazine C-Cl bond can also undergo Suzuki coupling. This can usually be managed by stoichiometry, catalyst loading, temperature, and monitoring conversion; the second chloride may be somewhat deactivated after the first arylation but is not inert. Protodeboronation of the arylboronic acid and dechlorination are possible minor side reactions. The transformation is otherwise chemically sound.

This disconnection corresponds to formation of an aryl/heteroaryl ether by SNAr of the primary alcohol-derived alkoxide onto a chloro-pyridazine. This is a chemically reasonable and well-precedented transformation because chloropyridazines are activated toward nucleophilic aromatic substitution by the adjacent ring nitrogens. The primary alcohol on the nitro-fused heterocycle should be the dominant nucleophile after deprotonation, and the stereocenter in the cyclic nitroimidazo/oxazine fragment should be retained because the reacting center is the pendant alcohol, not the stereogenic carbon. Functional group compatibility is generally acceptable, but the nitro-heteroaryl fragment may be base- and heat-sensitive, so strongly basic or very high-temperature conditions should be avoided if possible. Mild inorganic base conditions such as Cs2CO3 or K2CO3 in DMF, DMAc, MeCN, or DMSO, or carefully controlled NaH conditions, would likely be suitable. Potential side reactions include decomposition of the nitroheterocycle under harsh base, competitive reaction of trace water, and possible slow SNAr if the chloropyridazine is insufficiently activated by substitution. Overall, this is an appropriate late-stage convergent etherification.

This step is a Suzuki coupling between dichloropyridazine and a para-trifluoromethoxyphenylboronic acid to give a monoarylated chloropyridazine. The transformation is feasible: chloropyridazines are competent electrophiles in Pd-catalyzed cross-coupling, and the arylboronic acid is a reasonable coupling partner. However, the key issue is chemoselective mono-coupling versus bis-coupling. The dichloropyridazine starting material contains two reactive C-Cl bonds; depending on the exact isomer, they may be electronically similar or equivalent, so over-arylation to the diaryl pyridazine can be a significant competing pathway. This can often be controlled by using an excess of dichloropyridazine, limiting arylboronic acid, lower catalyst loading, shorter reaction time, and careful monitoring. Heteroaryl chlorides can also coordinate to palladium and slow catalysis, so catalyst/ligand selection may be important; Pd(dppf)Cl2, Pd(PPh3)4, or more active bulky phosphine systems could be screened. The trifluoromethoxy-substituted arylboronic acid is generally compatible, though protodeboronation can occur under strongly basic aqueous conditions. Overall, the step is plausible but requires optimization for mono-selectivity and isolation of the desired chlorinated product.

This step is proposed as alkylation of a hydroxypyrimidine/pyrimidinone-type heterocycle with 1-(3-chloropropyl)pyrrolidine to form the O-alkylated ether. The disconnection is reasonable and commonly used for installing aminoalkoxy side chains, but the substrate is ambident: the hydroxy-pyrimidine can exist as a lactam/lactim tautomer and may undergo competing O- versus N-alkylation. Formation of the desired O-alkyl product is plausible under carefully chosen conditions, but selectivity should not be assumed. Mild inorganic base such as K2CO3 or Cs2CO3 in DMF/MeCN, or NaH under controlled conditions, may favor O-alkylation, but screening would likely be needed. The alkylating agent is a relatively unreactive primary chloride and contains a tertiary amine; it may be used as a free base or salt depending on availability, but if heated strongly it can undergo intramolecular quaternization or side reactions. A better electrophile may be the corresponding bromide, iodide, mesylate, or tosylate, or use KI/TBAI as an additive. The tertiary amine may also complicate purification and salt formation. Overall the transformation is feasible, but O/N alkylation selectivity and the choice of leaving group are important risks.

This step is a Suzuki-type cross-coupling of an electron-poor chloropyrimidine derivative with cyclopropylboronic acid. The disconnection is appropriate: heteroaryl chlorides, especially chloropyrimidines, are generally competent Suzuki electrophiles under Pd catalysis because the ring is electron deficient. The free hydroxy/lactam functionality should be tolerated under basic aqueous Suzuki conditions, although it may influence solubility and coordination to palladium. Cyclopropylboronic acid is a known coupling partner, but it can suffer from protodeboronation and sometimes gives variable yields; using optimized catalysts such as Pd(dppf)Cl2, Pd(PPh3)4, or more active biaryl phosphine systems, and bases such as K3PO4, Cs2CO3, or Na2CO3, would be advisable. Cyclopropyl potassium trifluoroborate or MIDA boronate could be alternatives if protodeboronation is problematic. There is little regiochemical ambiguity since only one chloride is present. Overall this is a well-precedented and likely feasible transformation.

The proposed alkylation of the hydroxypyrimidine/enolic pyrimidinol with 1-(3-chloropropyl)pyrrolidine is chemically plausible, but this is an ambident heteroaryl hydroxy system and O- versus N-alkylation could be a significant issue. Pyrimidinols can exist as lactam/lactim tautomers, and alkylation may occur at oxygen or at ring nitrogen depending on base, solvent, counterion, and electrophile. The desired product is the O-alkylated pyrimidine ether, so conditions should be optimized toward O-alkylation, e.g. K2CO3 or Cs2CO3 in DMF/MeCN, or possibly NaH with careful control. The alkyl chloride is a relatively poor electrophile; the corresponding bromide, iodide, mesylate, or tosylate would likely improve conversion. The tertiary amine may also be supplied as an HCl salt, which would consume base and complicate reaction setup. Intramolecular quaternization or formation of ammonium salts from the chloroalkyl tertiary amine is a possible competing process under some conditions. Overall, this step is feasible but will likely require optimization and careful analytical confirmation of O- versus N-alkylated regioisomers.

The Suzuki coupling of an activated chloropyrimidine derivative with cyclopropylboronic acid is a reasonable and precedented transformation. The heteroaryl chloride is electronically activated by the pyrimidine nitrogens, and cyclopropylboronic acid is a common coupling partner. The free hydroxypyrimidine/enolic OH should generally be tolerated under Suzuki conditions, although it may bind metal or be deprotonated under basic conditions; ligand/base screening may be needed. Suitable conditions could include Pd(dppf)Cl2, Pd(PPh3)4, or a more active biarylphosphine Pd catalyst with K3PO4, K2CO3, or Cs2CO3 in dioxane/water, toluene/water, or related mixed solvents. Potential side reactions include protodeboronation of cyclopropylboronic acid, homocoupling, dehalogenation, or poor conversion if the hydroxypyrimidine tautomer coordinates strongly to palladium. However, with only one halide and a commercially available boronic acid partner, the disconnection is appropriate and likely practical.

Formation of the O-alkylated pyrimidine ether from the hydroxypyrimidine and 1-(3-chloropropyl)pyrrolidine is chemically plausible, but this is an ambident heteroaryl alcohol/lactam system. Hydroxypyrimidines can exist as hydroxy/lactam tautomers and may undergo competing O- versus N-alkylation depending on base, solvent, temperature, and electrophile. The desired O-alkylation is likely favored under phenoxide-forming conditions, but selectivity should not be assumed. The alkyl chloride electrophile is also relatively sluggish for SN2 displacement, especially in the presence of a tertiary amine that can complicate salt formation and purification. A better approach would be to use the corresponding bromide, iodide, mesylate, or tosylate, or to perform the reaction with NaH, K2CO3/Cs2CO3, or another carefully chosen base in DMF/MeCN with monitoring for N-alkylated byproducts. Alternatively, converting the hydroxypyrimidine to a more defined O-nucleophile or using Mitsunobu-type etherification with the corresponding alcohol could be explored, though heteroaryl lactam tautomerism would still need attention.

Suzuki coupling of an activated chloropyrimidine with cyclopropylboronic acid is a reasonable and precedented disconnection. The heteroaryl chloride is electronically activated by the pyrimidine nitrogens, so oxidative addition should be feasible with standard Pd catalysts. The free hydroxypyrimidine could coordinate to palladium or be deprotonated under the basic coupling conditions, potentially lowering yield, but it is not necessarily incompatible. Cyclopropylboronic acid can suffer from protodeboronation or homocoupling, so optimization may be needed. More robust cyclopropyl nucleophile variants such as potassium cyclopropyltrifluoroborate, cyclopropylboronate esters, or MIDA boronates may improve reproducibility. Overall, the bond construction is appropriate and likely workable with Pd(dppf)Cl2, Pd(PPh3)4, or modern bulky phosphine catalysts and a mild inorganic base such as K3PO4 or Cs2CO3.

The proposed final O-alkylation of the hydroxypyrimidine/pyrimidinone precursor with N-(3-chloropropyl)pyrrolidine is chemically plausible, but it is the main risk point in the route. Hydroxypyrimidines are ambident nucleophiles and often exist significantly as pyrimidinone/lactam tautomers; therefore N-alkylation of the heterocycle can compete with the desired O-alkylation. The product drawn is the O-alkylated ether, but depending on base, solvent, counterion, and temperature, mixtures of O- and N-alkylated products may be obtained. Cs2CO3 or K2CO3 in DMF/MeCN, possibly with KI/TBAI, may favor O-alkylation, but this would need empirical optimization. NaH can work but may increase side reactions and N-alkylation. The electrophile ClCCCN1CCCC1 is commercially available, but as a tertiary amine bearing a primary chloride it can undergo competing quaternization/cyclization or salt formation, especially under prolonged heating. Use of the corresponding bromide/iodide, mesylate/tosylate, or the HCl salt carefully neutralized in situ may improve conversion but could also increase side reactions. A potentially more robust alternative would be to prepare the corresponding 4-chloropyrimidine and displace it with 3-(pyrrolidin-1-yl)propanol under SNAr conditions, which often gives cleaner aryl ether formation for electron-poor pyrimidines.

The Suzuki coupling of the chloro-hydroxypyrimidine derivative with cyclopropylboronic acid is a reasonable and precedented transformation. The aryl/heteroaryl chloride is electron-deficient and should be activated toward oxidative addition, particularly with modern Pd catalysts such as Pd(dppf)Cl2, Pd(PPh3)4, XPhos/SPhos-based systems, or related precatalysts. Cyclopropylboronic acid is commercially available and commonly used in Suzuki couplings, although protodeboronation and homocoupling can reduce yield. The free hydroxypyrimidine/pyrimidinone functionality may coordinate to palladium or exist as a lactam, which can affect catalyst performance, but it is not inherently incompatible. Basic aqueous conditions should be selected carefully to avoid decomposition or dehalogenation; K3PO4, Cs2CO3, or carbonate bases in dioxane/water, toluene/water, or similar mixed solvents would be typical. Competing dechlorination and protodeboronation are likely the main side reactions. Overall this is a sensible disconnection and likely feasible with catalyst/base optimization.

Forward reaction is acylation of an electron-rich aniline with 3-(trifluoromethoxy)benzoyl chloride to form the target benzamide. This is a standard and chemically reasonable transformation. The aryl amine should be substantially more nucleophilic than the lactam/urea-like NH groups on the pyridopyrimidinone core, so selective anilide formation is likely under controlled conditions. However, the substrate contains two heterocyclic NH groups that could in principle undergo N-acylation or O-acylation under forcing conditions or with excess acid chloride, so reagent stoichiometry and base choice matter. Recommended conditions would include slow addition of the acid chloride, mild organic base such as DIPEA or triethylamine, or pyridine/DMAP only cautiously, in a dry aprotic solvent. Hydrolysis of the acid chloride and formation of HCl salts may also reduce yield. Overall, this is a feasible final-stage amidation using a commercially available acid chloride.

Forward reaction is intended as SNAr coupling of 4-amino-m-cresol-type phenol with an activated chloro-pyridopyrimidinone to give the aryl ether. The heteroaryl chloride is plausibly activated toward nucleophilic aromatic substitution by the adjacent ring nitrogens, so the C-O bond formation is chemically plausible. The main concern is chemoselectivity: the aminophenol contains both a phenol and a free aniline. Under basic SNAr conditions, phenoxide formation should favor O-arylation, but the free aniline can also act as a nucleophile toward activated heteroaryl chlorides, potentially giving C-N arylated side product. In addition, the heterocyclic lactam NH groups are acidic and may be deprotonated, causing solubility issues, salt formation, or reduced electrophilicity. Strong base or high temperature may also promote hydrolysis/dechlorination. This step would likely require careful optimization, e.g. K2CO3 or Cs2CO3 in DMF/DMSO, controlled temperature, and possibly use of excess phenol. A more robust strategy would be to acylate/protect the aniline first, converting the aminophenol into the corresponding benzamide phenol, then perform O-arylation; this would suppress competitive N-arylation.

Forward reaction is acylation of an aniline with 3-(trifluoromethoxy)benzoyl chloride to form the target benzamide. This is a standard and chemically sound disconnection. The aniline should be the most nucleophilic site, and the acid chloride is an appropriate activated acyl donor. However, the substrate contains two heterocyclic lactam/urea-like N-H groups and a pyridine-like nitrogen, so over-acylation or transient N-acylation of the heterocycle is a possible side reaction, especially with excess acid chloride or strongly activating additives. Conditions should use approximately stoichiometric acid chloride, a non-nucleophilic base such as DIPEA or triethylamine, low-to-moderate temperature, and dry solvent. Avoiding excess DMAP may be beneficial if heterocycle N-acylation is observed. Overall, the step is likely to work with routine optimization.

Forward reaction is an SNAr-type O-arylation of an aminocresol phenoxide onto an activated chloro-fused heteroarene. The disconnection is plausible because the heteroaryl chloride is activated by adjacent ring nitrogens and carbonyl functionality, and aryl ether formation under K2CO3, Cs2CO3, NaH, or similar base in DMF/DMSO/NMP is reasonable. The main concern is chemoselectivity: the aminophenol contains both phenol and aniline nucleophiles, so competing C-N bond formation at the activated heteroaryl chloride is possible. The heterocyclic N-H groups may also be deprotonated under basic conditions, affecting solubility and electrophilicity. The overall strategy is sound: build the stilbene core via a Heck coupling, install the ether-tethered fluoroethyl group via SNAr on a nitro-activated aryl fluoride, then reduce the nitro group to the aniline. With these modifications—chiefly reordering the 18F introduction to the end and choosing a selective reductant—the route is feasible and convergent.

With reordering of the 18F introduction to the final step and appropriate protecting-group/selectivity considerations, the route could work.

A redesigned sequence—protect the exocyclic amines, install the hydroxyethyl chain regioselectively on N1, alkylate the alcohol with TsOCH2P(O)(OEt)2, then deprotect amines and cleave the phosphonate with TMSBr—would convert this into a viable, literature-supported route. As drawn, the core disconnections are right but the execution requires substantial revision.

With these modifications the route could deliver the target.

(4) The ether-forming coupling (9e24c72895f0821d6adb41aa64966ff40bd4c0312620fd2d9eaf6cb3a598fa02) as drawn is not the conventional approach; the standard method alkylates the side-chain alkoxide with a (tosyloxymethyl)phosphonate or uses Mitsunobu/alkoxide chemistry. The final phosphonate deprotection (a22fd8283408cd0c44ae089956f0060a291d0d47224337c11511215b86a42516) is sound. Recommended modifications: introduce the hydroxyethyl chain with a proper protecting group (e.g., acetate/THP/silyl), protect the exocyclic amines, convert OH to a leaving group, then alkylate with diethyl (tosyloxymethyl)phosphonate (or use the alkoxide + phosphonate electrophile), and finish with TMSBr deprotection. The starting materials (diaminopyrimidinone, halomethyl/hydroxymethyl phosphonate ethers) are largely accessible. The core strategy has merit but requires substantial revision to be practical.

Recommend: move the Suzuki coupling earlier (before installing the sensitive sulfonate ester), reduce the nitro before installing the alkene/triflate, replace hydrogenolytic OBn removal with Lewis-acid debenzylation, and provide a disconnection for the oxabicyclic core.

As written, the route does not reach commercially available building blocks for the core, so the synthesis is incomplete. The peripheral functionalization chemistry is fine but the central scaffold construction is the real problem and must be designed. I recommend: remove unnecessary phenol protection, address chemoselectivity in acylation, and most importantly provide a disconnection for the oxabicyclic core (e.g., via a Diels-Alder/oxa-bridge or cycloaddition strategy).

The amide-coupling and protecting-group steps are well-precedented and scalable, but the route requires both the selectivity fix and completion to commercial building blocks.

The overall strategy targets a 4-substituted N-(cyclohexylmethyl)piperidine bearing an O-methyl oxime on an aminochloro-methoxyarene. Strengths: the use of THP protection for the alcohol, nitro as a masked aniline, and late-stage mesylate displacement are all reasonable individual tactics, and most building blocks (cyclohexylmethylamine, DHP, MsOH/oxalyl chloride) are commercial. However, there are major problems: (1) The final piperidine-forming step (8c5ea146d998b718ad21ff505929cccc1f2ba099797f1dad4e2856aa02f560c9) does not map structurally onto the proposed acyclic amino-mesylate precursor—a single mesylate plus a pre-formed secondary amine cannot close a 4-substituted piperidine ring with correct connectivity; the ring-construction logic is flawed. (2) Severe chemoselectivity issues plague the amine alkylation (1b3e857ca542ad75bd317d42279d6866d6d62efa22dcbb0731bf2e0c2ec21d71), where a primary amine confronts BOTH a bromide and a mesylate simultaneously, guaranteeing over-alkylation/polymerization. (3) The mesylation (ccd64bdf697e16f51b5a1a89c79d1e9abd1605f0b6705917939eb7ce82bade0e) and nitro reduction (67342e89cf256506f2f86201d3cd378491660d19c746fa237fb6baf0a7df808c) are run in the presence of an unprotected aniline and a labile alkyl bromide/oxime, requiring careful reagent control and likely aniline protection. (4) 33cef9e576b26567d1395c55155c567aaf291958528c8f85868335ba05c72671 (synthesis of MsCl) is an unnecessary step. Recommendations: rethink the piperidine ring construction (e.g., build the piperidine ring first via a 4-substituted piperidinone or reductive amination/double alkylation with a proper bis-electrophile, then install the cyclohexylmethyl group by reductive amination of cyclohexanecarboxaldehyde); protect the aniline (or carry the nitro through) during mesylation; and use only one leaving group at a time to avoid chemoselectivity chaos. As drawn, the core disconnection strategy for the ring is not sound, so significant modifications are needed.

The overall strategy is sound and short (3 steps from an in-stock ester building block). The key disconnection at the amide bond between the indoline nitrogen and the acetic acid side chain of the pyrimidinone is logical and convergent, using a commercially available 7-(trifluoromethyl)indoline. The ester hydrolysis is trivial. The main weakness is the isolation of the acyl chloride via oxalyl chloride (640c5d262fa9f2126b8718f81693e177edd03ec5df48d9ac2cc863111902b811): the substrate bears a hydroxypyrimidinone/lactam that is sensitive to chlorinating reagents and could undergo ring chlorination or O-/N-acylation side reactions. A more robust approach would couple the carboxylic acid directly with the indoline using a peptide coupling reagent (HATU, T3P, EDC/HOBt) under mild conditions, bypassing the acyl chloride. Additionally, chemoselectivity in the amide coupling must be controlled to avoid acylation of the pyrimidinone NH. With these modifications (replacing the acyl chloride route with direct coupling), the route should be quite practical and scalable. Starting materials are accessible.

The overall strategy is logical and concise: build the final amide bond between an indoline (commercially available 4-trifluoromethylindoline) and an arylacetic acid derivative, which in turn derives from a commercially available ethyl ester via saponification. The retrosynthesis reaches reasonable building blocks and is only 3 steps. The main weakness is the choice to route through an isolated acid chloride (640c5d262fa9f2126b8718f81693e177edd03ec5df48d9ac2cc863111902b811) which then undergoes amidation (92ed09f3254cae63270b66407728138bedd7b4a162d57dc16329c71a9a2f10ab). Given the multifunctional, NH-bearing, tautomerizable pyrimidinone scaffold and the basic morpholine, the acid chloride is a poor intermediate prone to side reactions and chemoselectivity problems (acylation of the lactam NH, possible chlorination of the hydroxypyrimidine). The route would be significantly improved by collapsing 640c5d262fa9f2126b8718f81693e177edd03ec5df48d9ac2cc863111902b811 and 92ed09f3254cae63270b66407728138bedd7b4a162d57dc16329c71a9a2f10ab into a single direct amide coupling (HATU, T3P, or EDCI/HOBt with a base) from the carboxylic acid to the indoline. This removes a sensitive intermediate, improves chemoselectivity, and shortens the route. Starting materials (oxalyl chloride, 4-CF3-indoline, the ethyl ester) appear accessible. With this consolidation the route should be quite practical and scalable.

The overall strategy is sound and reasonably short: hydrolyze a commercially available ethyl ester to the acid, then couple to 2-(trifluoromethyl)indoline (which appears to be a 7-CF3 indoline, commercially accessible) to form the target amide. The key weakness is the choice to proceed through the acid chloride via oxalyl chloride (640c5d262fa9f2126b8718f81693e177edd03ec5df48d9ac2cc863111902b811) and then acylate the indoline (92ed09f3254cae63270b66407728138bedd7b4a162d57dc16329c71a9a2f10ab). The pyrimidinone substrate has an unprotected N-H and a ring carbonyl (hydroxypyrimidine tautomer) that are incompatible with oxalyl chloride (risk of ring chlorination) and may compete during acylation. The recommended modification is to delete the acid chloride step and perform a direct amide coupling of the free acid with the indoline using a peptide coupling reagent (HATU, T3P, or EDCI/HOBt) with a base such as DIPEA. This collapses two problematic steps into one robust transformation, improves chemoselectivity, and avoids handling an unstable, multifunctional acid chloride. Starting materials (oxalyl chloride, the ethyl ester, and the trifluoromethyl indoline) are commercially available. With this single strategic change, the route should be quite practical and scalable.

The overall strategy is sound and short: it disconnects the target at the amide bond into a commercially available trifluoromethyl indoline and a heteroaryl acetic acid derivative, which itself derives from a commercially available ethyl ester via simple hydrolysis. Strengths: convergent amide disconnection, readily available building blocks, minimal steps. Main weakness: the route channels through an acid chloride (640c5d262fa9f2126b8718f81693e177edd03ec5df48d9ac2cc863111902b811) that is generated from a substrate bearing an unprotected, acidic pyrimidinone NH and a tautomerizable hydroxy/oxo heterocycle. Oxalyl chloride risks ring chlorination and the acid chloride risks self-acylation at the ring N/O. The recommended modification is to delete the acid chloride step and couple the free carboxylic acid directly with the indoline using a peptide-type coupling reagent (HATU/EDC/T3P) with a base such as DIPEA. This shortens the route by one step, avoids an unstable intermediate, and improves chemoselectivity. With that single change, the route is robust and scalable. No protecting group is strictly needed for the pyrimidinone NH if a direct coupling is used, though slight excess of acid/reagent may be required to account for the acidic NH.

The overall strategy is fundamentally flawed for several reasons. (1) The core target is a 2-imino-thiazolidinone/rhodanine bearing a conjugated arylidene — the most logical and well-precedented disconnection is a Knoevenagel condensation between an aryl aldehyde (ideally 4-(dimethylamino)benzaldehyde, commercially available) and a 2-imino-rhodanine derived from the appropriate aniline (here a 5-amino-2-hydroxyanisole/aminoguaiacol). The proposed route ignores this clean convergent disconnection. (2) The benzyl protection/deprotection of the phenol (356b098873bd6273f08913a9ceb7287b8d612269694b081ff24072045d83f2d0/af133b73429531ef163e26c846288b4a37171cf02acaf98271375715d1ec3de6) is unnecessary AND uses an SNAr that will not proceed on an electron-rich (methoxy-substituted) arene lacking activating EWGs. The debenzylation (H2/Pd) would also reduce the conjugated alkenes. (3) The late-stage para-bromination (fb4550d4deebd5e915c35d7bfacdbc7b78faf7967ad2573d71669dab2ac32fea) with NBS is non-selective and would attack the electron-rich exocyclic alkene rather than the aromatic ring. (4) The dimethylamino group is installed by Pd-amination of an aryl bromide late in the sequence (3c217b1efcd131c22be5cc2f32f8d9123a8faf524094bc18cabf1a734ff87376), risking catalyst poisoning by the rhodanine sulfur/N-H, when it should simply come from commercial 4-(dimethylamino)benzaldehyde. (5) The synthesis of dimethylamine from N-methylformamide (5cbb3547d0fb1159754d900e0754ba4c314989c8323b407391521d61f83dcd9d) is gratuitous since HNMe2 is a bulk commodity. RECOMMENDATION: Redesign as a convergent Knoevenagel: condense 4-(dimethylamino)benzaldehyde with a 2-(arylimino)-thiazolidin-4-one (built from the hydroxy-methoxy aniline + a rhodanine/thiazolidinedione precursor). This eliminates all the protecting-group and late-stage functionalization problems and uses entirely commercial building blocks.

This is a 4-arylidene-rhodanine-type scaffold (with an imino-substituted thiazolone). The proposed route has multiple fundamental problems: (1) The key disconnections ignore the most logical and well-precedented retrosynthesis: the exocyclic C=C should be disconnected via a Knoevenagel condensation between a rhodanine/thiazolone core and 4-(dimethylamino)benzaldehyde, immediately providing both partners in a convergent fashion. (2) The route instead introduces the dimethylamino and aryl substituents via late-stage NBS bromination of an unactivated arene followed by Buchwald amination (fb4550d4deebd5e915c35d7bfacdbc7b78faf7967ad2573d71669dab2ac32fea/3c217b1efcd131c22be5cc2f32f8d9123a8faf524094bc18cabf1a734ff87376) - the bromination step is non-selective and the rhodanine alkene would be the more reactive site. (3) The phenol is installed by SNAr displacement of an unactivated aryl fluoride with benzyl alcohol (af133b73429531ef163e26c846288b4a37171cf02acaf98271375715d1ec3de6), which will not proceed; this should instead come from a protected catechol/guaiacol building block. (4) The final debenzylation (356b098873bd6273f08913a9ceb7287b8d612269694b081ff24072045d83f2d0) by hydrogenolysis would reduce the Michael-acceptor alkene (chemoselectivity failure); a Lewis-acid deprotection would be needed. (5) Generating dimethylamine from DMF (5cbb3547d0fb1159754d900e0754ba4c314989c8323b407391521d61f83dcd9d) is an unnecessary, impractical step. Overall the strategy is linear, non-convergent, and relies on several unfeasible disconnections. A redesign using a Knoevenagel approach with appropriately substituted aldehyde and a pre-functionalized phenolic/methoxy aryl-imino thiazolone core is strongly recommended.

The overall strategy is poorly conceived. The target is an arylidene rhodanine bearing a 4-(dimethylamino)phenyl group and a catechol-monomethyl-ether-derived aniline as the N-substituent (imine). The most efficient and well-precedented disconnection is a Knoevenagel condensation between a rhodanine and 4-(dimethylamino)benzaldehyde (a cheap commercial reagent), with the aryl-imine/N-aryl portion derived from an appropriately substituted aniline (e.g., 4-amino-2-methoxyphenol or its monomethyl ether). Instead, this route makes a series of strategically backward and chemically dubious choices: (1) late-stage SNAr to install a benzyl ether on a non-activated ring (will not work); (2) late-stage Buchwald-type amination to install NMe2 on a highly sensitive polyfunctional scaffold (poor chemoselectivity); (3) NBS bromination to install an aryl-Br para to a vinyl group on a neutral ring (non-selective); (4) needless 'synthesis' of dimethylamine from N-methylformamide. The route also never reaches the rhodanine/aldehyde building blocks and so is incomplete. The free phenol and dimethylamino groups should be carried in from commercially available aldehyde and aniline building blocks via a final Knoevenagel condensation, avoiding the unnecessary fluoride/benzyl protecting-group gymnastics. This route should be redesigned from scratch.

The target is a rhodanine-type scaffold: a 2-(arylimino)-4-oxo-thiazolidine bearing an exocyclic 4-(dimethylamino)benzylidene group and a catechol-derived (3-methoxy-4-hydroxyphenyl)imino substituent. The most efficient and well-precedented synthesis would assemble the rhodanine/iminothiazolidinone core and then perform a single Knoevenagel condensation with 4-(dimethylamino)benzaldehyde, with the aryl imine formed from the appropriate aniline. The proposed route instead introduces unnecessary and chemically problematic steps: (1) late-stage benzyl protection/deprotection of the phenol via hydrogenolysis or SNAr that is incompatible with the redox-sensitive, sulfur-rich Michael acceptor; (2) installation of the NMe2 group by NBS aromatic bromination (poor regioselectivity, competing alkene/heterocycle bromination) followed by amination (potential Pd poisoning by sulfur); (3) a needless reduction to make commercially available dimethylamine; (4) an SNAr benzylation of an unactivated aryl fluoride. A far superior strategy is the convergent, two-component approach: condense a preformed 2-(3-methoxy-4-hydroxyphenylimino)-4-thiazolidinone (or 3-substituted rhodanine) with 4-(dimethylamino)benzaldehyde under Knoevenagel conditions (piperidine/AcOH). The phenol generally does not require protection, and if it does, a simpler acetate would suffice. Overall, the disconnection logic is inefficient and chemically flawed.

The overall strategy assembles a 4-isopropylcyclohexylamine-piperidine-indole scaffold with a pendant aminoethanol. The final reductive amination (2e15ae198e7b513f06ac6d13f66ed259f16027ad9de83e90f2b1a55b577136a0) and the ketone reduction (d9755b89141acd5d649d1f4ff0122597b719fa7d80579949a6324cab0b52de17) are sound. However, several middle steps are problematic: (601842f1002468c2da235792afad2ea20f299b79d946cede5d2832302d48135b) the formic acid 'reduction' of nitrile to aldehyde as written is not a valid transformation - DIBAL-H should be used, and the indole-3-carbaldehyde is more directly accessed by Vilsmeier formylation, making the nitrile intermediate unnecessary; (5321f60960b107cca6a51ed519a27e5b6ab21411e7d53e0b2b149cf6374f5e8d) the N-coupling of the 4-piperidinol with the cyano-indole NH via dehydration is non-trivial and faces selectivity/feasibility issues - an N-alkylation with a proper leaving group or Mitsunobu is needed, and the C3-substitution timing should be reconsidered; (5cdc1c357d7e2be674ac982449cf2d840985758a4ceec020f6126e011a60880e) uses an unusual quaternary ammonium piperidinone reagent that is non-optimal for assembling the N-cyclohexyl piperidinone. The route does reach commercially available building blocks (ethanolamine, 3-cyanoindole, 4-isopropylcyclohexylamine), so it is solved to building blocks, but requires reagent/step revisions. A cleaner route would: (1) couple 4-isopropylcyclohexylamine with N-Boc-4-piperidone by reductive amination, (2) convert piperidinol/use Mitsunobu or N-alkylation to attach indole, (3) install C3 substituent by Vilsmeier formylation directly, (4) reductive amination with ethanolamine. Core strategy has merit but needs substantial reagent and sequence changes.

The overall target is a complex polysubstituted indole bearing a 4-(4-isopropylcyclohexylamino)piperidine motif and a 3-(aminomethyl) substituent functionalized with ethanolamine. The final reductive amination (2e15ae198e7b513f06ac6d13f66ed259f16027ad9de83e90f2b1a55b577136a0) and the ketone reduction (d9755b89141acd5d649d1f4ff0122597b719fa7d80579949a6324cab0b52de17) are sound. However, several key disconnections are flawed: (1) The nitrile-to-aldehyde step (99d015f8e33deb408f795114fa265b8ce5af6c63133f4c240ea5f49cb6adf2ef) using formic acid is mechanistically incorrect—DIBAL-H reduction or direct Vilsmeier formylation should be used. (2) The N1-indole alkylation by a free secondary alcohol (601842f1002468c2da235792afad2ea20f299b79d946cede5d2832302d48135b/5321f60960b107cca6a51ed519a27e5b6ab21411e7d53e0b2b149cf6374f5e8d) is not feasible without activation; a Mitsunobu with an activated partner or, better, building the N-substituent via SN2 on a mesylate/halide, or using N-arylation/N-alkylation strategy is needed. (3) The piperidinone-forming step (5cdc1c357d7e2be674ac982449cf2d840985758a4ceec020f6126e011a60880e) employs an implausible quaternary ammonium reagent; a reductive amination between 4-isopropylcyclohexylamine and an N-protected 4-piperidone is the standard, reliable approach. The strategic order (build amine-piperidine core, install indole on N, then elaborate C3) is reasonable, but the specific reagents and the indole N-alkylation method must be substantially revised. Starting materials (ethanolamine, 4-isopropylcyclohexylamine, 3-cyanoindole, formic acid) are commercially available, but the quaternary salt building block is unusual. Overall the core strategy has merit but requires substantial reagent and method changes.

The overall strategy builds a 3-substituted indole bearing an N-piperidinyl group, with a final reductive amination to install the aminoethanol side chain. Strengths: the final reductive amination (2e15ae198e7b513f06ac6d13f66ed259f16027ad9de83e90f2b1a55b577136a0) and ketone reduction (d9755b89141acd5d649d1f4ff0122597b719fa7d80579949a6324cab0b52de17) are robust and well-precedented; starting materials such as ethanolamine, 4-isopropylcyclohexylamine, and 3-cyanoindole are commercially available. Weaknesses: (1) The nitrile-to-aldehyde step (99d015f8e33deb408f795114fa265b8ce5af6c63133f4c240ea5f49cb6adf2ef) uses formic acid, which is not an appropriate reagent; DIBAL-H partial reduction would be needed and selectivity is a concern. (2) The N-piperidinyl-indole coupling (601842f1002468c2da235792afad2ea20f299b79d946cede5d2832302d48135b/5321f60960b107cca6a51ed519a27e5b6ab21411e7d53e0b2b149cf6374f5e8d) via a secondary 4-hydroxypiperidine requires Mitsunobu or alcohol activation, which is moderate yielding and risks elimination, complicated by the basic tertiary amine. (3) The initial piperidinone construction (5cdc1c357d7e2be674ac982449cf2d840985758a4ceec020f6126e011a60880e) uses an illogical quaternary ammonium salt reagent; this should be redesigned, e.g., reductive amination of 4-isopropylcyclohexylamine with a mono-protected 4-oxopiperidine equivalent or double alkylation with a bis-electrophile bearing a masked ketone. The route is linear (non-convergent) and could be made more efficient. Core strategy has merit but several steps need substantial rework, particularly 99d015f8e33deb408f795114fa265b8ce5af6c63133f4c240ea5f49cb6adf2ef and 5cdc1c357d7e2be674ac982449cf2d840985758a4ceec020f6126e011a60880e.

The overall strategy is reasonable in broad outline: build a 4-substituted piperidine bearing the isopropylcyclohexyl group, attach the indole, install the C3 substituent, and finish with reductive amination to append the aminoethanol side chain. The final reductive amination (2e15ae198e7b513f06ac6d13f66ed259f16027ad9de83e90f2b1a55b577136a0) and the ketone reduction (d9755b89141acd5d649d1f4ff0122597b719fa7d80579949a6324cab0b52de17) are sound. However, there are two critical problems. First, 601842f1002468c2da235792afad2ea20f299b79d946cede5d2832302d48135b (nitrile to aldehyde using formic acid) is chemically incorrect — the conversion requires a partial reduction (DIBAL-H) or use of indole-3-carbaldehyde directly. Second, 5321f60960b107cca6a51ed519a27e5b6ab21411e7d53e0b2b149cf6374f5e8d (coupling the secondary piperidinol to the indole N-H) faces serious selectivity/efficiency issues; N-alkylation of indole with a hindered secondary alcohol is problematic (elimination, low yield). It would be better to introduce the piperidine onto the indole nitrogen via an N-alkylation with a 4-oxo/4-substituted piperidine bearing a proper leaving group early on, or to assemble the C3 aldehyde via a Vilsmeier formylation of the preformed N-piperidinyl indole. The 5cdc1c357d7e2be674ac982449cf2d840985758a4ceec020f6126e011a60880e transamination using a quaternary ammonium salt is also non-optimal. Stereochemistry of the trans-4-isopropylcyclohexylamine moiety must also be carefully controlled. Reordering the sequence (e.g., Vilsmeier formylation to install C3-CHO directly, replacing the nitrile route) and revising the N-piperidinyl indole formation would substantially improve feasibility.

The overall route is logical, reasonably convergent, and terminates in commercially available building blocks (3-bromo-4-fluoroaniline, 3-(trifluoromethyl)benzoyl chloride, N-methylpyrazole-5-Bpin, and 2-(pyrrolidin-1-yl)ethanol). The strategy proceeds sensibly: amide formation, then chemoselective Suzuki on the bromide (retaining the fluoride), then SNAr to install the aminoethanol side chain. Strengths: clean disconnections, good FG compatibility, late-stage diversification potential. The principal weak point is the final SNAr (0dd4697dda085f2257f748b647019a3e7bc891535873098d0c602dd2563481f2): the aryl fluoride is only modestly activated (ortho-pyrazole but no strong EWG para/ortho to F), so this step may require forcing conditions or could fail/give low yield. A recommended modification is to switch the order or use a transition-metal-catalyzed C-O coupling (Cu/Pd) on a bromide or triflate at that position, or to perform the O-alkylation before the Suzuki step on a more activated halide. Protodeboronation of the pyrazole boronate is a secondary concern to optimize. With these adjustments the route should deliver the target efficiently.

This is a well-conceived, linear four-component assembly toward the target. The strategy is logical: (1) amide formation from cheap commercial aniline and acid chloride, (2) Suzuki coupling installing the pyrazole with good chemoselectivity (Br reacts, F retained), and (3) final SNAr to install the pyrrolidinylethoxy side chain via fluoride displacement. All building blocks (3-bromo-4-fluoroaniline, 3-(trifluoromethyl)benzoyl chloride, N-methylpyrazole-5-Bpin, 2-(pyrrolidin-1-yl)ethanol) are commercially available. The main risk lies in the final SNAr step (0dd4697dda085f2257f748b647019a3e7bc891535873098d0c602dd2563481f2): the aryl fluoride is only weakly activated, so this displacement may be sluggish and require forcing conditions or may give incomplete conversion. A Cu/Pd-catalyzed C-O coupling alternative, or repositioning the alkoxy installation earlier when stronger activation could be engineered, should be considered as a backup. The amide N-H tolerance under strongly basic SNAr conditions should be checked (deprotonation but should not interfere). Overall the route is short, convergent at the boronate stage, and scalable. Recommend the route as feasible with attention to the final SNAr conditions.

This is a well-conceived, logical linear synthesis of a 4-step (3 reaction) route to the target. The strategy is sound: (1) amide coupling of a commercial aniline with an acid chloride, (2) Suzuki coupling to install the pyrazole biaryl unit with excellent chemoselectivity for Br over F, and (3) final SNAr to install the pyrrolidinylethoxy side chain by displacing the retained fluoride. The orthogonal use of Br (for Suzuki) vs F (for SNAr) is elegant and exploits the differential reactivity well. All building blocks are commercially available and in stock. Strengths: short, convergent at the Suzuki step, no protecting groups needed, cheap starting materials. Main weakness: the final SNAr step relies on an aryl fluoride that is only modestly activated (ortho to pyrazole, but lacks a strong para/ortho EWG), so this step may require forcing conditions or could give modest yields - this is the riskiest step. An alternative would be to introduce the alkoxy group earlier or use a Cu/Pd-catalyzed C-O coupling (Ullmann/Buchwald) on the fluoride/triflate/bromide instead. Overall the route is feasible with good scalability; only minor optimization of the SNAr conditions is advised.

This is a concise, logical 3-step linear route to the target. Strengths: (1) robust amide coupling from commercial building blocks; (2) well-chosen Suzuki coupling installing the N-methylpyrazole with clear chemoselectivity (Br over F); (3) all key building blocks (3-bromo-4-fluoroaniline, 3-(CF3)benzoyl chloride, N-methylpyrazole boronate, 2-(pyrrolidin-1-yl)ethanol) are commercially available. The main concern is the final SNAr etherification (0dd4697dda085f2257f748b647019a3e7bc891535873098d0c602dd2563481f2): the aryl fluoride is not strongly activated by a powerful EWG ortho/para to it (the amide is electron-donating at the para position via N), so this SNAr may be sluggish or low-yielding and could require forcing conditions. A more reliable alternative would be to retain an aryl bromide/iodide at that position and use a Cu- or Pd-catalyzed C-O (Ullmann/Buchwald-type) etherification, or perform the etherification earlier on a more activated substrate. Additionally, the order of operations is reasonable, but consider whether the free amide N-H might interfere in the alkoxide-mediated SNAr (competing deprotonation); this is manageable. Overall a sound strategy needing only minor refinement of the etherification step.

The overall strategy builds a thieno-fused naphthalimide (a chromophore/intercalator-type scaffold) from a readily available bromonaphthalene dicarboxylic anhydride. The first (last forward) step - imide formation with N,N-dimethylethylenediamine (29a410863c73d6bf98f49edf9fbad1c65c6e1646db1504bd939196a0975dc766) - is excellent and well-precedented. The thiophene annulation using methyl thioglycolate (7d31c21b999e01f42998a1c53f4e52b3b0db26052414635bee9b8df363a0c8d1) is a sound, classical strategy for fusing the thiophene ring. However, two steps are problematic. (1) The formylation step (421b589ea194594931cbefa148b9b7aff5d569e0011c5c3591038429153bfc95) to install the aldehyde ortho to the retained bromide suffers from both regioselectivity and chemoselectivity issues: organometallic formylation routes (DMF quench) are incompatible with the imide carbonyls and would consume the bromide, while electrophilic formylation (Vilsmeier/Duff) is disfavored on the electron-poor naphthalimide and lacks regiocontrol. A better approach might install the ortho-CHO before imide/bromination or use a designed ortho-halo aldehyde building block. (2) The final decarboxylation (eda7f8c0f0096284eff6ff9ceaadbf6b1c1504bb9a8060d6290f4435299ff50f) that removes the thiophene ester is chemically awkward as written (direct ester-to-CH) and synthetically wasteful - it requires saponification then protodecarboxylation under harsh conditions that may degrade the polycyclic system. Consider whether the target truly needs an unsubstituted thiophene, in which case a thiophene annulation reagent that does not leave a residual ester (or a route that retains the ester for the C-S bond formation but allows easier decarboxylation) would be preferable. The route reaches commercial building blocks (methyl thioglycolate, DMAEDA-type amine, bromoanhydride, DMF) and is convergent in the thiophene-forming step. With reworking of the formylation regiochemistry and the terminal decarboxylation strategy, the route is viable.

The overall strategy builds a thieno-fused naphthalimide. The first disconnection to the bromo-anhydride + diamine (29a410863c73d6bf98f49edf9fbad1c65c6e1646db1504bd939196a0975dc766) is excellent and reliable. The thiophene annulation (7d31c21b999e01f42998a1c53f4e52b3b0db26052414635bee9b8df363a0c8d1) from an ortho-bromo aldehyde and methyl thioglycolate is a sound, well-precedented strategy. However, two steps are problematic: (1) The Vilsmeier formylation (421b589ea194594931cbefa148b9b7aff5d569e0011c5c3591038429153bfc95) to install the aldehyde will not work on the strongly electron-deficient naphthalimide core - an alternative aldehyde installation (directed metalation/DMF quench, or starting from a pre-functionalized aldehyde-bearing anhydride) is needed. (2) The final step (eda7f8c0f0096284eff6ff9ceaadbf6b1c1504bb9a8060d6290f4435299ff50f) removing the thiophene ester via protodecarboxylation of a methyl ester is non-trivial and adds no synthetic value unless the ester is needed as an activating/directing group; a cleaner approach would be to use an annulation reagent that does not leave a residual ester (e.g., using an appropriate two-carbon unit) or to retain the ester if it is part of the target. The free tertiary amine carried through multiple steps could also interfere with some conditions (e.g., Vilsmeier, strong base). Overall the convergent logic and the bookend disconnections are sound, but the aldehyde installation and the terminal decarboxylation require substantial rethinking.

The overall strategy builds a thieno-fused naphthalimide. The core logic is sound: (1) form the naphthalimide from a bromonaphthalic anhydride and the diamine (29a410863c73d6bf98f49edf9fbad1c65c6e1646db1504bd939196a0975dc766, solid), then (2) annulate a thiophene ring using methyl thioglycolate (7d31c21b999e01f42998a1c53f4e52b3b0db26052414635bee9b8df363a0c8d1, well-precedented). However, two steps are problematic. The Vilsmeier-type formylation (421b589ea194594931cbefa148b9b7aff5d569e0011c5c3591038429153bfc95) on a strongly electron-deficient naphthalimide is unlikely to succeed via EAS chemistry, and the regiochemistry would not be controlled — this step needs a different formylation strategy or a substrate already bearing the aldehyde (e.g., start from a haloformyl-substituted naphthalic anhydride). The final 'demethoxycarbonylation' (eda7f8c0f0096284eff6ff9ceaadbf6b1c1504bb9a8060d6290f4435299ff50f) to remove the ester is mechanistically implausible as a single transformation; it should be hydrolysis followed by thermal/Cu-mediated decarboxylation, or better, the ester could be retained or be the desired feature. Step economy is reasonable and the route does reach commercial building blocks (methyl thioglycolate, DMF, dimethylethylenediamine, bromonaphthalic anhydride). With re-engineering of 421b589ea194594931cbefa148b9b7aff5d569e0011c5c3591038429153bfc95 (proper formylation/metalation) and clarification of eda7f8c0f0096284eff6ff9ceaadbf6b1c1504bb9a8060d6290f4435299ff50f (two-step decarboxylation), the route could become viable.

The overall strategy is sound conceptually: build the naphthalimide first (robust imidization from a commercial bromoanhydride + diamine), then annulate a thiophene ring onto the aromatic core, then remove the residual ester. Strengths: starting materials (bromonaphthalic anhydride, dimethylaminoethylamine, methyl thioglycolate) are commercial/cheap; the imidization (29a410863c73d6bf98f49edf9fbad1c65c6e1646db1504bd939196a0975dc766) and thiophene annulation (7d31c21b999e01f42998a1c53f4e52b3b0db26052414635bee9b8df363a0c8d1) are well-precedented and convergent enough. Key weaknesses: (1) The formylation step (421b589ea194594931cbefa148b9b7aff5d569e0011c5c3591038429153bfc95) is the critical liability — electrophilic (Vilsmeier) formylation will fail on the very electron-poor naphthalimide, and metalation strategies clash with the imide carbonyls and tertiary amine. The aldehyde should likely be installed earlier on a more electron-rich, less functionalized precursor, or via a different group (e.g., pre-installed CHO or a masked aldehyde on the anhydride). (2) The final demethoxycarbonylation (eda7f8c0f0096284eff6ff9ceaadbf6b1c1504bb9a8060d6290f4435299ff50f) should be shown as a two-step saponification/Cu-mediated protodecarboxylation rather than direct ester removal, and one should question whether retaining the ester (a useful functional handle) is even necessary. (3) Order-of-operations: performing the harsh annulation/formylation chemistry after installing the base-sensitive dimethylaminoethyl imide may cause side reactions; consider installing the side chain last. With reworking of the formylation strategy and clarification of the decarboxylation, the core disconnections (imide formation + thioglycolate annulation) are viable.

The overall strategy is sound and converges on commercially available building blocks: 2,4-dichloro-5,6,7,8-tetrahydroquinazoline-type fused dichloropyrimidine, 1-naphthaleneboronic acid, and bis(4-methoxybenzyl)amine. The logic—(1) regioselective Suzuki to install the naphthyl, (2) SNAr/amination to install the protected amine, (3) global deprotection to the free 2-aminopyrimidine—is reasonable and reasonably short. Key weaknesses: (a) the bis-PMB protecting strategy is heavier than necessary; a direct displacement of the 2-chloro with ammonia, or use of benzophenone imine/Buchwald, would shorten the route and avoid a potentially sluggish double deprotection; (b) steric congestion from the bulky 1-naphthyl adjacent to the reaction center may slow the amination, possibly requiring Pd-catalysis rather than thermal SNAr; (c) Suzuki mono-selectivity and protodeboronation of the hindered naphthylboronic acid need careful optimization. The stereocenter on the saturated ring (the methyl-bearing carbon) is set by the starting material and not controlled in the route, which is acceptable if a racemate is targeted. With modest modifications to the amination/protection strategy, the route should deliver the target.

The overall strategy is sound and reaches commercially available building blocks (1-naphthylboronic acid, the dichloropyrimidine fused system, and bis-PMB amine). The fused dichloropyrimidine starting material's true commercial availability should be verified; if not available it would need its own synthesis. With the suggested simplification of the amination/protection strategy, this is a viable and reasonably efficient route.

The overall strategy is logical and reaches commercially available or accessible building blocks: 1-naphthylboronic acid (commercial), a 2,4-dichloro fused dihydroquinazoline-type core, and bis-PMB amine. The overall strategy is reasonable and reaches commercially available building blocks: a 2,4-dichloropyrimidine fused with the cyclohexane ring, 1-naphthylboronic acid, and bis(4-methoxybenzyl)amine. With the amination simplification, this becomes a short, convergent, and scalable 2-3 step route. Weaknesses/modifications needed: (1) The demethylation step (908078287c290d7b817f995a8d900918975502a10f18e57e28da516c27859635) is potentially problematic given the free benzylic alcohol and amine; milder conditions or a protecting group strategy should be employed, or sourcing the phenol directly would simplify the route. The overall strategy is logical and linear, building the target from a readily accessible tetrahydroisoquinoline/benzazepine-type core. The retrosynthesis correctly disconnects: (1) the 3-fluoropropyl aryl ether via Williamson etherification, (2) the N-phenylbutyl chain via N-alkylation, and (3) the phenol via demethylation of a commercial methyl ether. All terminal building blocks (1-bromo-3-fluoropropane, (4-bromobutyl)benzene, and the methoxy bicyclic amino alcohol) are commercially available or accessible, so the route reaches building blocks. Strengths: short (3 steps), uses cheap alkylating agents, sensible order (demethylate, then selectively alkylate N before O). Key concerns/modifications: (a) chemoselectivity between phenol and the secondary aliphatic alcohol during the final O-alkylation - mild base (Cs2CO3) exploiting the phenol's higher acidity should favor aryl ether formation, but mono-O-alkylation of the secondary OH is a possible minor pathway; (b) the demethylation step with a free secondary alcohol present may require careful reagent choice (BBr3 can be problematic) - consider doing N-alkylation first or protecting the secondary alcohol; (c) the order could be reconsidered to improve selectivity. This is a concise, linear 3-step route to a complex aminotetralin/benzazepine-type target from a commercially available methoxy aminotetralin precursor. The overall strategy—demethylation to reveal the phenol, N-alkylation to install the 4-phenylbutyl chain, then O-alkylation to install the fluoropropyl ether—is logical and reaches in-stock building blocks. The principal weakness is the absence of a protecting group strategy. The target bears three reactive handles (secondary amine, phenol, secondary benzylic alcohol) and several steps face chemoselectivity challenges: (1) the demethylation in the presence of a free amine and benzylic alcohol, (2) N-alkylation competing with phenol O-alkylation, and (3) final phenol O-alkylation competing with the secondary alcohol. Reordering and/or selective protection (e.g., temporarily protecting the secondary alcohol, or performing N-functionalization via reductive amination with 4-phenylbutanal for cleaner selectivity) would significantly improve the route. Stereochemistry of the benzylic alcohol is not addressed but appears to be racemic/unspecified in the target. With minor modifications to address chemoselectivity, the route is feasible and uses readily accessible materials.

The overall strategy is a linear, logical sequence: (1) demethylation of a commercially available methoxy-aminotetralinol to reveal the phenol, (2) N-alkylation of the secondary amine with (4-bromobutyl)benzene, and (3) O-alkylation (Williamson) of the phenol with 1-bromo-3-fluoropropane.
