This is a concise, linear 3-step synthesis of an [18F]-labeled stilbene radiotracer (structurally reminiscent of an amyloid-imaging or florbetapir-type agent). The overall strategy is sound: (1) Heck coupling to build the E-stilbene core, (2) SNAr radiofluoroethoxylation displacing an activated ortho-nitro aryl fluoride, (3) nitro reduction to the aniline. Strengths: good convergence at the Heck step, use of commercially accessible building blocks (vinyl arene, aryl bromide, fluoroethanol), and well-activated SNAr. Key weaknesses/modifications needed: (a) The FINAL nitro reduction (4509ebbaf0b8d1d617ca1baf6208285ba23da9e41a90e6d09417de52dbf2d273) is chemoselectively problematic in the presence of the stilbene alkene—catalytic hydrogenation would reduce the double bond, so a selective reductant (Fe/AcOH, SnCl2, Na2S2O4, or Zn) is mandatory. (b) From a radiochemistry standpoint, performing the [18F] labeling at the penultimate step followed by an additional reduction step is suboptimal given F-18's 110 min half-life; reordering to make the [18F]-fluoroethoxylation the absolute last step on a nitro/amino-protected precursor would improve radiochemical yield and reduce synthesis time. Consider Boc-protection of the aniline to allow late-stage labeling. Overall the disconnections are chemically valid and the route should deliver the target with these refinements.

This is a radiolabeled ([18F]) stilbene tracer synthesis (structurally reminiscent of amyloid/florbetaben-type PET agents). The overall strategy is logical: build the stilbene core via Heck coupling, install the [18F]fluoroethoxy group, then reduce the nitro to the aniline. Strengths: convergent Heck disconnection from commercial-type building blocks; clear linear logic. Key weaknesses: (1) For PET radiochemistry the [18F] should be incorporated as late as possible to minimize decay losses; here a nitro reduction follows the [18F] step, adding a time-consuming manipulation to a t1/2~110 min isotope — not ideal. (2) The SNAr using [18F]fluoroethanol as nucleophile is non-standard; the conventional and more robust approach is O-alkylation of a phenol with [18F]fluoroethyl tosylate, which would require revising the precursor to a protected phenol (and likely protecting the aniline/amine). (3) Chemoselectivity in the nitro reduction must avoid reducing the stilbene alkene (use Fe, SnCl2, or Na2S2O4 rather than H2/Pd). Recommended modifications: redesign so that radiofluorination is the final or penultimate step (alkylate a phenolic precursor bearing the already-formed aniline, suitably protected, with [18F]fluoroethyl tosylate), thereby avoiding post-label reduction. With these adjustments the route is viable.

The overall strategy builds a substituted trans-stilbene (a resveratrol/combretastatin-like scaffold) bearing a 2-[18F]fluoroethoxy ether and an aniline, useful as a PET tracer. The carbon framework assembly via Heck coupling (a6c509ed4533ddc9c9533e88ba9fd8b081edc56863eb7072e499e4081efca39b) is sound, and the SNAr ether installation (1aefe644f0fd6763bfd1c3ed488c52da648ee3b1652c71aac44051b711268e94) and nitro reduction (4509ebbaf0b8d1d617ca1baf6208285ba23da9e41a90e6d09417de52dbf2d273) are individually reasonable transformations. The MAJOR strategic flaw concerns the radiochemistry: 18F has a half-life of ~110 min, so the [18F] label must be introduced in the FINAL (or near-final) synthetic step. In this route, [18F]fluoroethanol is introduced two steps before the end (SNAr), followed by an SNAr reaction and a nitro reduction — this is impractical and would result in massive radioactive decay losses and difficult radiosynthesis logistics. A redesigned route should: (1) build the full non-radioactive precursor bearing a -OCH2CH2-OTs (or OMs) leaving group (or a -OCH2CH2[18F] precursor), and (2) introduce [18F]fluoride by nucleophilic displacement of the tosylate as the last step, optionally followed by a quick deprotection. Additionally, the nitro reduction (4509ebbaf0b8d1d617ca1baf6208285ba23da9e41a90e6d09417de52dbf2d273) needs chemoselective conditions to preserve the stilbene alkene, and the SNAr step requires controlling alkoxide vs amine chemoselectivity. The non-radioactive chemistry is feasible; the radiolabeling sequence ordering requires substantial revision. Building blocks (fluoronitrostyrene, 4-bromo-N-sec-butylaniline) are accessible.

The overall strategy assembles a [18F]-labeled fluoroethoxy stilbene aniline PET tracer (structurally reminiscent of florbetaben/AV-class amyloid tracers). The core C-C disconnection via Heck coupling (a6c509ed4533ddc9c9533e88ba9fd8b081edc56863eb7072e499e4081efca39b) is excellent and convergent. The main strategic flaw is the placement of the 18F label EARLY in the sequence: 1aefe644f0fd6763bfd1c3ed488c52da648ee3b1652c71aac44051b711268e94 uses pre-labeled 2-[18F]fluoroethanol and 4509ebbaf0b8d1d617ca1baf6208285ba23da9e41a90e6d09417de52dbf2d273 performs a nitro reduction AFTER labeling. For 18F radiochemistry (t1/2 ~110 min), the 18F-fluorination MUST be the final or penultimate step to minimize decay losses and handling. The standard and superior approach: (1) construct the full stilbene scaffold bearing a 2-(tosyloxy)ethoxy (or 2-hydroxyethoxy then tosylate) group and a PROTECTED aniline (e.g., Boc or via the nitro as a masked amine), (2) perform [18F]fluoride displacement of the tosylate as the LAST radiochemical step, (3) deprotect. Additionally, chemoselective nitro reduction in the presence of the stilbene alkene requires a non-hydrogenative reductant (Fe, SnCl2, Na2S2O4). The SNAr etherification (1aefe644f0fd6763bfd1c3ed488c52da648ee3b1652c71aac44051b711268e94) is chemically valid but should be reordered. Building blocks (4-vinyl-2-fluoronitrobenzene, 4-bromo-N-sec-butylaniline, fluoroethanol) are accessible. With reordering of the labeling step and choice of chemoselective reduction, the route becomes viable.

The overall route is short (3 steps), convergent at the final Suzuki coupling, and reaches commercially available building blocks (2-bromothiophene, the fluorinated/methoxylated benzoyl chloride, and 2-hydroxyphenylboronic acid). The strategy is sound: build the diaryl ketone via Friedel-Crafts acylation, install the second aryl via Suzuki coupling, and reveal the phenol by demethylation. Strengths: good step economy, logical use of a methyl protecting group on the phenol to survive Friedel-Crafts and coupling, sensible halide handle for cross-coupling. Weaknesses/modifications: (1) The order of demethylation (879cfee7869fc3ee13513515d02ec42edfc7fc05ab6b5fb7bf10dc54b93e18ae) before the Suzuki coupling (8447e9bcb249b27d84a47cf23cd99b7a86a564f16f3bef6ab09f9fe877744dcb) means the free phenol is present during the Suzuki step on the thiophene partner - this is generally tolerated but consider performing the demethylation as the LAST step to minimize phenol interference and protodeboronation risk. (2) Friedel-Crafts conditions must be chosen to avoid demethylation of the aryl OMe. (3) Ortho-hydroxyphenylboronic acid is prone to protodeboronation - the boronic ester (e.g., pinacol or the dibenzofuran-forming cyclic variant) or careful mild conditions should be used. With these adjustments the route should deliver the target.

The overall route is short (3 steps), convergent at the final Suzuki coupling, and reaches commercially available building blocks (2-bromothiophene, the polyfluorinated methoxy-benzoyl chloride, and 2-hydroxyphenylboronic acid). Strengths: good step economy, reliable, well-precedented transformations, and the bromide serves dual purpose (regiodirecting in F-C acylation and cross-coupling handle). Minor considerations: (a) the order of demethylation before Suzuki is reasonable since BBr3 conditions are harsh and best done before introducing the sensitive 2-hydroxyphenyl group; alternatively demethylation could be performed last to simplify, but the current order is acceptable. (b) 2-Hydroxyphenylboronic acid is prone to protodeboronation/boroxine formation—use of the pinacol ester or controlled conditions may improve yield. (c) Free phenols in both coupling partners are tolerated but excess base should be moderated. Overall the route is feasible essentially as drawn with only minor optimization needed.

The overall route is a logical and reasonably short (3-step) linear sequence: (1) Friedel-Crafts acylation to build the diaryl ketone with a bromothiophene handle, (2) demethylation to reveal the phenol, and (3) Suzuki coupling to install the 2-hydroxyphenyl group. The strategy is sound and uses commercially available building blocks (2-bromothiophene, the polyfluorinated benzoyl chloride, and 2-hydroxyphenylboronic acid). Strengths: convergent final coupling, well-precedented reaction types, short sequence. Weaknesses/modifications needed: (1) The Suzuki coupling employs a 2-hydroxyphenylboronic acid which is prone to protodeboronation - consider using the corresponding pinacol boronate or a MIDA boronate, or reverse the coupling polarity (boronate on thiophene, aryl halide as 2-bromophenol). (2) The order of operations is questionable - the demethylation (879cfee7869fc3ee13513515d02ec42edfc7fc05ab6b5fb7bf10dc54b93e18ae) is performed before the Suzuki coupling, leaving a free phenol during the cross-coupling, which is tolerable but could complicate purification. It may be preferable to keep the methyl ether through the Suzuki step and demethylate last, OR to install the free phenol differently. (3) The methyl ether is a non-optimal protecting group requiring harsh BBr3 conditions; a more labile group could improve efficiency. With these adjustments (particularly addressing the protodeboronation-prone boronic acid and the deprotection timing), the route should deliver the target.

The overall strategy is sound and reasonably convergent. The overall strategy targets an acyclic nucleoside phosphonate (a cyclopropyl diaminopyrimidinone bearing a phosphonomethoxyethyl chain), structurally analogous to antiviral agents like tenofovir/adefovir. The convergent logic (heterocycle + phosphonate fragment) and final TMSBr-mediated phosphonate deprotection (a22fd8283408cd0c44ae089956f0060a291d0d47224337c11511215b86a42516) are sound and well-precedented. However, the route has several significant weaknesses: (1) The protecting-group strategy via methyl ether (5f151bdae6486403d78ef6acb50a190227c2a6fe6264d5db104670b92f9cdca0) followed by harsh O-demethylation (62586090b7c21dffdf2dc968c78788bbb738dae9a9ede1f1e7aa6603d4f9bba6) is inefficient and chemically risky in the presence of free amines — a silyl/THP protection of ethanol, or direct use of a protected hydroxyethyl unit, is preferable. (2) The PBr3 bromination (2d0ef01aa227c3da18cfc84e8d79ba5432e17fc1366039b5a1d2588614b3a6b6) and the subsequent ether-forming alkylation (9e24c72895f0821d6adb41aa64966ff40bd4c0312620fd2d9eaf6cb3a598fa02) both suffer from chemoselectivity problems because of the unprotected diaminopyrimidinone, which is highly nucleophilic and prone to competing N-alkylation/cyclization. (3) The N1-regioselective alkylation of the diaminopyrimidinone (5f151bdae6486403d78ef6acb50a190227c2a6fe6264d5db104670b92f9cdca0) is a recognized difficult step. The far more robust and literature-aligned approach would be to first construct the phosphonate-bearing side chain (e.g., diethyl (2-bromoethoxymethyl)phosphonate or its tosylate) and alkylate the protected heterocycle in a single coupling, then deprotect — closely mirroring the established ANP (acyclic nucleoside phosphonate) syntheses. The starting materials (COCCBr, diethyl hydroxymethylphosphonate, the diaminopyrimidinone) are commercially accessible, so the building-block endpoint is reached. With reordering of steps and proper amine protection, the route could be made viable.

The target is an acyclic nucleoside phosphonate (ANP) bearing a 2,6-diamino-5-cyclopropyl-pyrimidin-4(3H)-one core with an O-CH2-P(O)(OH)2 phosphonomethyl ether side chain — a recognizable nucleotide analogue class. The overall strategy (build heterocycle N-alkylation → install hydroxyethyl chain → activate → couple with hydroxymethylphosphonate → deprotect) is the standard ANP retrosynthetic logic and is sound in its broad outline. However, the route has two major weaknesses. (1) Protecting group strategy: a methyl ether is used to mask the hydroxyethyl group (5f151bdae6486403d78ef6acb50a190227c2a6fe6264d5db104670b92f9cdca0/62586090b7c21dffdf2dc968c78788bbb738dae9a9ede1f1e7aa6603d4f9bba6), but methyl ethers cannot be cleaved selectively under conditions compatible with this sensitive diaminoheterocycle. A better approach uses a directly installed 2-acetoxyethyl or THP/benzoyl-protected chain, or alkylation with a chain already bearing the phosphonate. Overall the strategic skeleton is correct but requires substantial protecting-group and selectivity revisions.

The overall strategy is recognizable and conceptually sound: it builds an acyclic nucleoside phosphonate (structurally analogous to cidofovir/adefovir-class ANPs) bearing a cyclopropyl-substituted 2,4-diaminopyrimidinone base, by N-alkylation with a 2-hydroxyethyl tether, conversion to a leaving group, ether coupling with diethyl (hydroxymethyl)phosphonate, and final TMSBr-mediated phosphonate deprotection. The endgame (9e24c72895f0821d6adb41aa64966ff40bd4c0312620fd2d9eaf6cb3a598fa02 coupling and a22fd8283408cd0c44ae089956f0060a291d0d47224337c11511215b86a42516 deprotection) is well-precedented and strong. However, the route has several serious flaws in its protecting-group and alcohol-introduction strategy: (1) 62586090b7c21dffdf2dc968c78788bbb738dae9a9ede1f1e7aa6603d4f9bba6 invokes a methyl-ether-to-alcohol 'demethylation' that is chemically impractical and incompatible with the heterocycle — methyl ether is a poor choice here. The route should instead introduce a 2-haloethanol or a readily-removable protected hydroxyethyl group directly, eliminating 62586090b7c21dffdf2dc968c78788bbb738dae9a9ede1f1e7aa6603d4f9bba6 and 5f151bdae6486403d78ef6acb50a190227c2a6fe6264d5db104670b92f9cdca0's awkward methyl ether. (2) Throughout the sequence the two free exocyclic amines are never protected, creating chemoselectivity problems for both the PBr3 bromination (2d0ef01aa227c3da18cfc84e8d79ba5432e17fc1366039b5a1d2588614b3a6b6) and the alkylation/coupling steps (regioselective N1 vs exocyclic-N alkylation in 5f151bdae6486403d78ef6acb50a190227c2a6fe6264d5db104670b92f9cdca0, and side reactions in 9e24c72895f0821d6adb41aa64966ff40bd4c0312620fd2d9eaf6cb3a598fa02). A protecting-group strategy for the amines (or use of an aminopyrimidinone synthon that masks them) is strongly advised. (3) Regioselectivity of the initial N-alkylation (5f151bdae6486403d78ef6acb50a190227c2a6fe6264d5db104670b92f9cdca0) onto N1 versus the exocyclic amines is a key risk requiring optimization. With redesign of the hydroxyethyl introduction (avoiding methyl ether) and incorporation of amine protection, the core convergent ANP strategy is viable and scalable. Starting materials (diethyl hydroxymethylphosphonate, methoxyethyl bromide, PBr3) are commercial; the diaminocyclopropyl-pyrimidinone base may require independent verification of availability.

The target is an acyclic nucleoside phosphonate (ANP) of the diaminopyrimidinone/cyclopropyl class, bearing a phosphonomethyl ether side chain — chemically related to known antivirals. The overall strategy (build pyrimidinone core, install N-(2-hydroxyethyl) side chain, attach phosphonomethyl ether, deprotect phosphonate) is conceptually sound and the final TMSBr deprotection (a22fd8283408cd0c44ae089956f0060a291d0d47224337c11511215b86a42516) is standard. However, several disconnections are non-optimal or problematic: (1) The protecting-group/installation strategy for the hydroxyethyl chain is wasteful — alkylating with bromoethyl methyl ether then demethylating (62586090b7c21dffdf2dc968c78788bbb738dae9a9ede1f1e7aa6603d4f9bba6) to reveal the alcohol is impractical (methyl ether is hard to cleave under conditions tolerated by this scaffold). Instead, directly alkylate with a hydroxyl-protected (e.g., THP, acetate, or benzyl) 2-haloethanol. (2) The PBr3 bromination (2d0ef01aa227c3da18cfc84e8d79ba5432e17fc1366039b5a1d2588614b3a6b6) and the alkylations (5f151bdae6486403d78ef6acb50a190227c2a6fe6264d5db104670b92f9cdca0, 9e24c72895f0821d6adb41aa64966ff40bd4c0312620fd2d9eaf6cb3a598fa02) all suffer from chemoselectivity problems because the two free exocyclic amino groups and the lactam are unprotected and will compete. The amines should be protected (e.g., as acetamides or with a benzoyl/transient TMS strategy) before these steps. (3) The phosphonate ether-forming step (9e24c72895f0821d6adb41aa64966ff40bd4c0312620fd2d9eaf6cb3a598fa02) uses an inverted, less-precedented disconnection (hydroxymethylphosphonate as nucleophile against the alkyl bromide); the more reliable route installs the phosphonate via a tosyloxymethyl/chloromethyl phosphonate electrophile reacting with the side-chain alcohol. Overall, the building blocks are reasonable and the endgame is solid, but the middle of the route needs substantial redesign around protecting groups and the order/mode of side-chain and phosphonate installation.

This is a well-conceived, convergent route built around the differential reactivity of the three positions on a 1,3,5-triazine core. The strategy sequentially functionalizes cyanuric chloride: (1) Suzuki coupling to install the 3-pyridyl group, (2) SNAr with 4-morpholinopiperidine, and (3) SNAr with the aminoethylmorpholine. This exploits the classic temperature-controlled, stepwise substitution of cyanuric chloride, which is a textbook and robust strategy. All three building blocks (cyanuric chloride, pyridin-3-ylboronic acid, 4-morpholinopiperidine, 2-morpholinoethylamine) are commercially available. The main practical considerations: (a) achieving clean mono-selectivity at each triazine substitution requires careful temperature control (0 °C, RT, then heat for the three positions respectively); (b) protodeboronation risk for the 3-pyridylboronic acid in the Suzuki step; (c) ensuring the order of operations places the least nucleophile-demanding substitution last. No protecting groups are needed because all nucleophilic partners contain only the intended reactive sites. The route is short (3 steps from cheap materials), scalable, and the chemoselectivity is governed by the inherent electronic deactivation of the triazine after each substitution. Overall a sound and efficient design.

The overall strategy is sound and convergent in spirit: build a trisubstituted pyrimidine from 2,4,6-trichloropyrimidine via (1) Suzuki coupling to install the 3-pyridyl group, (2) SNAr with 4-morpholinopiperidine, and (3) SNAr with 2-morpholinoethylamine. All starting materials are commercially available and inexpensive. The sequence exploits the differential reactivity of the three chloride positions, which is a classic and effective approach for polychloropyrimidine functionalization. The main risks/required optimizations are: (a) achieving mono-selective Suzuki coupling on the trichloropyrimidine without bis-arylation/protodeboronation; (b) controlling the regiochemistry of the two sequential SNAr steps so that the correct positions are functionalized in the right order (typically the most electrophilic position reacts first—careful temperature/stoichiometry control needed); and (c) chemoselectivity of the primary amine vs morpholine nitrogens, which is generally favorable. The order of operations (Suzuki first, then the more nucleophilic secondary amine, then the primary amine last) is logical. No protecting groups are needed, which is efficient. With careful optimization of the Suzuki selectivity and SNAr regiocontrol, the route should deliver the target. Overall a practical, short (3-step) route to building blocks.

The overall strategy is logical and convergent in concept: build the heteroaromatic core, install the aryl group via Suzuki coupling, then sequentially displace two chlorides with two different amines (4-morpholinopiperidine then 2-morpholinoethylamine). Starting materials (trichloropyrimidine/cyanuric chloride, pyridin-3-ylboronic acid, 4-morpholinopiperidine, 2-morpholinoethylamine) are all commercially available and inexpensive, which is a strength. The principal challenge is selectivity control across the three sequential functionalizations of the polychlorinated core. A more robust ordering exploits the differential reactivity of the chlorines: typically perform the SNAr aminations first (which are exquisitely temperature-selective on cyanuric-type cores: first substitution at 0 °C, second at RT/elevated), then the Suzuki coupling last on the least reactive remaining chloride. The current sequence places the Suzuki first, where chemoselective mono-coupling on a tri/dichloro electron-poor ring is harder and risks over-arylation and protodeboronation. Reordering steps and tight stoichiometry/temperature control would improve robustness. No protecting groups are needed, which is efficient. Overall a viable medicinal-chemistry route with minor optimization of step order and conditions.

The overall strategy is logical and convergent in concept: build a trisubstituted triazine by sequential functionalization of cyanuric chloride. The order of operations is sensible—Suzuki arylation first, then two stepwise SNAr reactions exploiting the increasing deactivation of the triazine as more electron-donating amines are installed. Starting materials (cyanuric chloride, 3-pyridylboronic acid, 4-morpholinopiperidine, aminoethylmorpholine) are all commercially available and inexpensive. The main weakness is the first step (bcaf61641a41e59b9aaca3c7cd6af581d4caf930b1a2dc865b0f4ed5c8d8f033): achieving mono-Suzuki coupling on cyanuric chloride is selectivity-challenging and may suffer from over-coupling and protodeboronation of the electron-poor pyridylboronic acid. A common practical alternative is to perform one or both SNAr aminations first (which are easier to control by temperature) and reserve the Suzuki coupling for a less reactive intermediate, or to use a pre-formed dichloro-pyridyltriazine. The SNAr steps (2e5fb5a62dde514f85186a8bedb1431ecd3adf3247c61140451840e12b7f58e1, d0298681d44e5cadd45874cee8025fa71cfc6d8869979c9e891f7ed15632a25d) are well-precedented and exploit the natural reactivity gradient of triazines. With reordering or careful optimization of the cross-coupling step, the route should deliver the target efficiently.

The overall strategy is sound and well-conceived. It builds the trisubstituted triazine core via sequential, selectivity-controlled functionalization of cyanuric chloride: (1) Sonogashira to install the naphthyl alkyne, (2) low-temperature SNAr with a primary amine, (3) SNAr with a secondary amine, and finally (4) hydrogenation of the alkyne to the ethylene linker. All starting materials (cyanuric chloride, 1-ethynylnaphthalene, isobutylamine, N-methylisobutylamine) are commercially available and inexpensive. The sequence exploits the well-known graded reactivity of chlorotriazines, which is a strong, classic strategy. Key concerns/modifications: (a) the order of operations matters - performing the Sonogashira first on cyanuric chloride risks competing amination and mono-coupling selectivity; an alternative order (install amines first via temperature-controlled SNAr, then Sonogashira on the remaining chloride) might give cleaner selectivity, though Pd-catalyzed coupling on an aminotriazine chloride is less activated. (b) Glaser homocoupling and over-substitution must be controlled with careful stoichiometry and temperature staging. (c) Final hydrogenation is chemoselective and reliable. Overall the route is convergent enough, step-economical, and scalable, requiring only minor optimization of reaction order and selectivity control.

The overall strategy exploits the well-known sequential, temperature-controlled SNAr chemistry of cyanuric chloride (triple displacement with decreasing reactivity), which is a sound and scalable approach for trisubstituted triazines. The two amine displacements (isobutylamine then N-methylisobutylamine) and the final alkyne hydrogenation are all reliable. All terminal building blocks (cyanuric chloride, 1-ethynylnaphthalene, isobutylamine, N-methylisobutylamine) are commercially available, and the route is short and reasonably convergent. The principal weakness is the FIRST step (a59c04b0bdff7fcd63476f3ae36387152809e1295ac0b0959ade76e277a9fd6f): performing a mono-selective Sonogashira coupling on cyanuric chloride is problematic both in terms of chemoselectivity (three reactive chlorides) and competing reactivity of the terminal alkyne/Cu-acetylide with the electrophilic triazine, plus possible Glaser homocoupling. RECOMMENDED MODIFICATION: reorder the sequence so that the alkyne is installed after one or two amine substitutions have reduced the number/reactivity of remaining chlorides (e.g., do the SNAr aminations first, then Sonogashira on a mono- or di-chloro aminotriazine), which greatly improves selectivity. With this reordering the route should perform well. Stereochemistry is not an issue (no stereocenters). Purification at each SNAr stage is standard.

The overall strategy is logical and convergent at the triazine core, exploiting the well-precedented stepwise SNAr chemistry of cyanuric chloride (sequential displacement of the three chlorides, temperature-controlled for selectivity) combined with a Sonogashira coupling to install the naphthalenyl-ethynyl unit, finished by alkyne hydrogenation to the ethylene linker. All building blocks (cyanuric chloride, isobutylamine, N-methylisobutylamine, 1-ethynylnaphthalene) are commercially available, and the route is short and reaches stock materials. The principal weakness is the order of operations: performing the Sonogashira coupling on the fully chlorinated cyanuric chloride (a59c04b0bdff7fcd63476f3ae36387152809e1295ac0b0959ade76e277a9fd6f) risks poor mono-selectivity, Glaser homocoupling, and competing chloride hydrolysis. A more robust sequence would carry out one or both aminations first to attenuate triazine electrophilicity before the Pd/Cu-catalyzed alkynylation, or perform the hydrogenation/alkyne installation at a different stage. With this re-sequencing, the route should be quite practical and scalable. Final hydrogenation chemoselectivity over the naphthalene is good with mild Pd/C conditions.

The overall strategy is sound and convergent on a 1,3,5-triazine core, exploiting the well-known sequential, temperature-controlled SNAr chemistry of cyanuric chloride to install the two distinct amine substituents, with a Sonogashira coupling to install the naphthylethynyl group and a final alkyne hydrogenation to give the ethylene linker. The principal weakness is the ORDER of operations: performing the Sonogashira coupling on cyanuric chloride first (a59c04b0bdff7fcd63476f3ae36387152809e1295ac0b0959ade76e277a9fd6f) risks poor mono-selectivity and competing SNAr by the alkyne/amine base on the highly electrophilic triazine. A more robust sequence would install the two amines first (using temperature control: ~0 °C for the first amine, RT for the second), then perform Sonogashira on the remaining, now less-activated mono-chlorotriazine, and finally hydrogenate. This reordering would substantially improve selectivity and overall yield while retaining the same disconnections. With that modification the route is very practical and scalable.

The overall strategy aims to construct a complex oxabicyclo[2.2.1] core bearing a trisubstituted alkene (via Suzuki coupling on a vinyl triflate), a catechol monosulfonate, an aryl amide tethered to a suberic acid, and a 4-hydroxyphenyl group. The retrosynthetic logic is internally consistent: late-stage Suzuki coupling, tBu ester as carboxyl protection, benzyl as catechol-phenol protection, amide coupling from suberic acid mono-tBu-ester. The starting materials at the leaves (boronate, BnBr, oxalyl chloride, mono-tBu suberate) are commercially available. However, several serious issues undermine the route as written: (1) The route is NOT solved to building blocks — the key advanced intermediate 'O=[N+]([O-])c1ccc(...vinyl triflate...sulfonate...)cc1' is shown as in_stock:False with no further disconnection, so the construction of the central oxabicyclic core, the vinyl triflate, and the sulfonate ester is never addressed. This is the most complex part of the molecule and is left unsolved. (2) Major chemoselectivity/compatibility conflicts: the persistent vinyl triflate is base-sensitive (benzylation), and the alkene/triflate/benzyl ether are all incompatible with catalytic hydrogenation used for both the nitro reduction and the debenzylation. These two steps would destroy the core. (3) The protecting-group plan is internally inconsistent: a benzyl ether that must later be removed without hydrogenation, plus a nitro reduction that also cannot use hydrogenation, suggests the benzyl group is a poor choice — a TBS or other non-hydrogenolytic phenol protection would be more compatible. (4) The order of operations leaves a vinyl triflate intact through many steps (amidation, deprotection, reduction), risking decomposition. To salvage the route: solve the core synthesis to true building blocks, replace benzyl phenol protection with a fluoride/acid-labile group, use chemoselective (non-hydrogenation) nitro reduction (Fe/SnCl2), use peptide-coupling rather than acid chloride for the amide, and perform the Suzuki coupling earlier or with full protection of acid/phenols. Overall the central disconnections have merit but the route requires substantial reworking and completion.

The overall strategy is to assemble a highly functionalized 7-oxabicyclic core bearing a vinyl triflate, an aryl (catechol) sulfonate ester, a secondary alkyl sulfonate, a nitro/aniline, and an amide-linked suberic acid. The retrosynthesis is internally chained but suffers from several fundamental problems. (1) Orthogonality failure: the route relies on benzyl protection of the catechol phenol AND on hydrogenolytic debenzylation/nitro reduction, yet the molecule carries a vinyl triflate and a tetrasubstituted alkene that are NOT compatible with H2/Pd. The nitro reduction (70b0ea6a94b6f5f78b3da5ae861fcc4252784603df02b8c7ef12d2f54b182419) and debenzylation (4fd64c8b4dd5bd605c94cb6212c509f965f9310d18a5727c20c35ff85756b36f) directly clash with these sensitive groups. (2) The vinyl triflate is carried through many steps (amide coupling, deprotections, benzylation) - triflates on enol systems are labile to base, nucleophiles, and reducing conditions and are unlikely to survive. (3) Chemoselectivity in the final Suzuki coupling (f198d0c3f6e8bbcf7f7bdfe2decb8869db479b4250243c790294feb9094d7f8f) is questionable because two sulfonate electrophiles are present plus an unprotected acid and an electron-rich (protodeboronation-prone) p-hydroxyphenyl boronate. (4) The most strategic disconnection (installing the aryl groups by cross-coupling) is reasonable, but the timing/order is poor: the sensitive vinyl triflate should be installed and coupled at the very last possible moment, not carried through reductions and deprotections. Overall, while the bond disconnections are individually conventional, the protecting-group and functional-group compatibility logic is broken, making the route as written not feasible without a significant redesign (e.g., late-stage triflate formation/Suzuki, avoid hydrogenolysis, use non-reductive nitro reduction or pre-installed aniline, protect the carboxylic acid throughout). Note the route is also flagged is_solved:false.

The overall strategy builds a complex oxabicyclic/cyclopentene core bearing a vinyl triflate, an aryl sulfonate ester (catechol monosulfonate), two aryl substituents, and a suberic acid amide chain. The retrosynthesis is linear, not convergent, and—more importantly—does NOT reach the actual core building block: the synthesis is not solved to commercial materials for the central bicyclic sulfonate scaffold (the starting nitro-aryl oxabicyclic vinyl triflate sulfonate is simply listed as a precursor without further disconnection). Thus the route is effectively incomplete at the key fragment. Major concerns: (1) the molecule simultaneously contains a vinyl triflate AND an aryl sulfonate ester—both are Pd cross-coupling electrophiles, so the late-stage Suzuki coupling (f198d0c3f6e8bbcf7f7bdfe2decb8869db479b4250243c790294feb9094d7f8f) faces serious chemoselectivity problems; (2) several redox steps (nitro reduction 70b0ea6a94b6f5f78b3da5ae861fcc4252784603df02b8c7ef12d2f54b182419, O-debenzylation 4fd64c8b4dd5bd605c94cb6212c509f965f9310d18a5727c20c35ff85756b36f) would, under standard H2/Pd conditions, reduce the strained alkene and cleave the vinyl triflate—non-hydrogenolytic alternatives are mandatory; (3) carrying a free carboxylic acid/phenol into the Pd step (f198d0c3f6e8bbcf7f7bdfe2decb8869db479b4250243c790294feb9094d7f8f) risks catalyst poisoning. The protecting-group logic (tBu ester, Bn ether) is reasonable, but the sequencing should place the sensitive Suzuki coupling before installing/exposing the competing sulfonate or use orthogonal coupling partners. Overall the strategy has merit for assembling the periphery but requires substantial reordering, chemoselective reagent choices, and completion of the core synthesis to be viable.

The overall strategy assembles a complex, highly functionalized target containing a 7-oxabicyclo[2.2.1] core bearing a vinyl triflate, an aryl sulfonate ester (catechol-derived), a stilbene-type tetrasubstituted alkene, an amide-linked carboxylic acid chain, and multiple phenols. The retrosynthesis has a logical backbone: late-stage Suzuki coupling to install the hydroxyphenyl group, amide bond formation to attach the diacid chain, and protecting-group manipulations. However, there are pervasive functional-group compatibility problems: (1) The vinyl triflate must survive numerous steps including a nitro reduction and a benzyl deprotection - both classically done with H2/Pd, which would destroy the triflate. Orthogonal, non-hydrogenolytic conditions must be specified. (2) The benzyl protecting group on the catechol is a poor choice given the triflate sensitivity. (3) The presence of TWO sulfonate/triflate electrophiles raises chemoselectivity concerns in the Suzuki step. (4) The order of operations - keeping the highly reactive vinyl triflate intact while doing nitro reduction, amide coupling, and acid deprotection - is fragile. A key concern not addressed retrosynthetically is HOW the central oxabicyclic core with the tetrasubstituted alkene and vinyl triflate is constructed; the tree never disconnects this core (it is carried through as an intact, complex fragment requiring the unprotected/protected versions to be commercially available, which they are NOT). The route also does not reach genuine building blocks for the most complex fragment - the nitro-substituted oxabicyclic sulfonate is shown as a leaf 'in_stock: False' without further disconnection. Recommendation: (a) replace benzyl with an acid- or fluoride-labile catechol PG; (b) use a chemoselective nitro reduction or install the amine differently; (c) move the vinyl-triflate-dependent Suzuki coupling as early as feasible; (d) provide a genuine retrosynthesis of the oxabicyclic core (e.g., Diels-Alder/oxa-bridge construction). As drawn, the core strategy has merit but requires substantial revision.

The overall convergent strategy—building the methoxypyrrole/azafulvene core, brominating at the alpha position, and joining the second pyrrole ring by Suzuki coupling, then deprotecting—has a sensible logic and reasonable convergence. The aryl–aryl (pyrrole–pyrrole) Suzuki disconnection is the strategic highlight and is appropriate for assembling the bis-heterocyclic system. However, there are major weaknesses: (1) The terminal two steps (9adb64aec42f442569c52b916935e6ab790682f5bcf63ea41e9f9d56846dd48e/3e7e498fccb33584f19478d2cdbda11c3dfaeff3380f7f6e83c3a6c2146645da) introduce a wasteful and chemically inconsistent methyl ester -> carboxylic acid -> ethyl ester interconversion. If the ethyl ester is the target, an ethyl ester should be carried throughout; these two steps should be collapsed/eliminated. (2) The whole route relies on a highly conjugated, electron-rich, acid- and oxidant-sensitive azafulvene/dipyrrin-like chromophore being subjected to NBS bromination, Pd coupling with an unstable N-Boc-pyrrol-2-ylboronic acid (protodeboronation prone), Boc deprotection (acid), and ester hydrolysis/esterification (acid/base). Cumulatively this poses serious functional-group-compatibility and selectivity risks for the sensitive core. (3) The exocyclic alkene geometry (E/Z) must be preserved through several steps; conditions like strong acid or radical bromination risk isomerization. Recommended modifications: carry an ethyl ester from the start (delete 9adb64aec42f442569c52b916935e6ab790682f5bcf63ea41e9f9d56846dd48e/3e7e498fccb33584f19478d2cdbda11c3dfaeff3380f7f6e83c3a6c2146645da redundancy), use a more robust boron source (MIDA/pinacol) or reverse the Suzuki coupling partners, and consider performing the C–C coupling before installing the sensitive azafulvene/condensation, i.e., construct the bipyrrole earlier and form the methylidene bridge late to protect the chromophore. Starting materials (NBS, Boc-pyrrole boronic acid, ethanol) are commercially available. Net: core strategy has merit but needs substantial reordering and protecting-group rationalization.

The overall strategy assembles a dipyrromethene/azafulvene-type bis-heterocycle bearing an enol ether and an ethyl ester, with the key disconnection being a Suzuki coupling to join the two heteroaromatic rings. The convergent biaryl disconnection (Suzuki) is strategically sound, and Boc protection of the pyrrole-boronic-acid partner is reasonable. However, the route has clear weaknesses: (1) An unnecessary and wasteful ester interconversion sequence (methyl ester -> carboxylic acid (3e7e498fccb33584f19478d2cdbda11c3dfaeff3380f7f6e83c3a6c2146645da) -> ethyl ester (9adb64aec42f442569c52b916935e6ab790682f5bcf63ea41e9f9d56846dd48e)). The ethyl ester should be carried throughout or installed at the start, eliminating two steps and avoiding exposure of a sensitive chromophore to harsh hydrolysis/Fischer conditions. (2) Regioselectivity of the NBS bromination (e1c846e295a864b25b3d1b9a8370577d7088213565e034d2c65c0cf555b1da4d) on a highly activated, multi-nucleophilic substrate is questionable; bromination earlier in the synthesis (before assembling the full conjugated system) would be safer. (3) The Boc-pyrrole-2-boronic acid (47825577bde9cde6833b0c5404527504e912898c54a9b70985f4e65531300fcb) is prone to protodeboronation; a more robust boron source (MIDA/pinacol) is advised. (4) The exocyclic methine (azafulvene) geometry must be preserved; many of these steps risk E/Z isomerization. The route does reach in-stock building blocks (EtOH, NBS, Boc-pyrrole boronic acid, succinimide), so it is solved to building blocks, but the strategy needs reordering and reagent upgrades. Most critically, the redundant ester cycle should be removed.

The overall strategy targets a dipyrrin/azafulvene-type molecule (resembling a prodigiosin-like or pyrromethene chromophore) and uses a sensible key disconnection: a Suzuki cross-coupling to forge the central bipyrrole C-C bond, with bromination to set up the coupling partner. These core disconnections (47825577bde9cde6833b0c5404527504e912898c54a9b70985f4e65531300fcb, e1c846e295a864b25b3d1b9a8370577d7088213565e034d2c65c0cf555b1da4d) have merit. However, the route has serious efficiency problems. The most glaring issue is the redundant oxidation-state/ester shuffle at the end: a methyl ester (3e7e498fccb33584f19478d2cdbda11c3dfaeff3380f7f6e83c3a6c2146645da) is hydrolyzed to the carboxylic acid, then re-esterified to the ethyl ester (9adb64aec42f442569c52b916935e6ab790682f5bcf63ea41e9f9d56846dd48e). This is wasteful and chemically illogical—the ethyl ester should be installed directly or carried throughout, eliminating two steps. Additional concerns: (1) the entire sequence is conducted on a substrate bearing a highly sensitive, acid- and base-labile azafulvene/dipyrrin chromophore with free pyrrole NH groups, raising compatibility concerns with the Fischer esterification (strong acid) and saponification (base) conditions; (2) regioselective pyrrole bromination (e1c846e295a864b25b3d1b9a8370577d7088213565e034d2c65c0cf555b1da4d) and N-Boc-pyrrolylboronic acid coupling (47825577bde9cde6833b0c5404527504e912898c54a9b70985f4e65531300fcb, protodeboronation prone) are both yield-limiting steps requiring optimization; (3) the route was not fully solved to building blocks—the starting bromo-azafulvene precursor (COC(=O)C1=C(C)/C(=C/c2[nH]ccc2OC)N=C1C) in e1c846e295a864b25b3d1b9a8370577d7088213565e034d2c65c0cf555b1da4d is marked not in stock and has no further children, so the retrosynthesis is incomplete. Recommendations: eliminate the 9adb64aec42f442569c52b916935e6ab790682f5bcf63ea41e9f9d56846dd48e/3e7e498fccb33584f19478d2cdbda11c3dfaeff3380f7f6e83c3a6c2146645da ester interconversion redundancy, use a stable MIDA/pinacol boronate for the coupling, and complete the retrosynthesis of the azafulvene core. Starting materials that are in stock (EtOH, NBS, Boc-pyrrole boronic acid) are commercially available, but the key azafulvene fragment needs further disconnection.

The overall strategy of building a substituted pyrromethene/azafulvene system via Suzuki coupling to install the bipyrrole linkage, with Boc protection of the coupling partner, is sound and convergent in concept. The Suzuki disconnection (47825577bde9cde6833b0c5404527504e912898c54a9b70985f4e65531300fcb) and Boc deprotection (93c6ef4f668fb90dd8c35565c7099715b97e29070e1c9a165c8b4d72b2265289) are reasonable. This methyl->acid->ethyl ester sequence is illogical and inefficient. The target is the ethyl ester, so the entire synthesis should carry an ethyl ester from the start (or use direct transesterification), eliminating two redundant steps. Additionally, the NBS bromination (e1c846e295a864b25b3d1b9a8370577d7088213565e034d2c65c0cf555b1da4d) faces real regio/chemoselectivity challenges given the highly electron-rich, extended conjugated system, which could brominate the methine bridge or undergo polybromination. The acid/base conditions in the hydrolysis/esterification steps also risk degrading the sensitive azafulvene framework. Finally, the route terminates at a non-stock pyrrole-azafulvene starting material (COC(=O)C1=C(C)/C(=C/c2[nH]ccc2OC)N=C1C in e1c846e295a864b25b3d1b9a8370577d7088213565e034d2c65c0cf555b1da4d) that is not resolved to commercial building blocks - this intermediate itself requires synthesis (e.g., a Knoevenager/condensation between a pyrrole-3-carbaldehyde derivative and a pyrrolenine ester). Recommend: (1) carry ethyl ester throughout, removing 9adb64aec42f442569c52b916935e6ab790682f5bcf63ea41e9f9d56846dd48e/3e7e498fccb33584f19478d2cdbda11c3dfaeff3380f7f6e83c3a6c2146645da; (2) optimize/validate the bromination regioselectivity; (3) extend retrosynthesis to true commercial building blocks for the core.

The overall strategy is reasonable and converges on a sulfonylation endgame using a commercially available sulfonyl chloride. The core bicyclic diamine-lactam is built via an intramolecular N-alkylation (b572a37ba5f5aebb791645587ba5297332ad2157e15dd418b778f8471feff981) from an aryl-tethered bromide, which is a sensible ring-forming step. Key weaknesses: (1) The protecting-group logic in a1513e17aa2e75487eb45453762d568371a096bc2d2530a170ee3a695c57d9ae is non-optimal — converting an N-benzyl amine to an N-Cbz carbamate via chloroformate is not a clean operation; it would be far more efficient to simply debenzylate the N-benzyl bridgehead amine directly (H2/Pd-C) and proceed to sulfonylation, removing two steps (Cbz install + remove). (2) a3756a869cb1996b0dec2ebb42375394bcde9b90666b921d0c17c842b7d6bbcc specifies CBr4 alone for the alcohol-to-bromide conversion; this needs PPh3 (Appel) or an alternative reagent. (3) Most critically, the route is NOT solved to commercial building blocks — the deepest precursor (the amino-alcohol bicyclic lactam, COc1cc(CCO)c(C2NC(=O)C3CCCC2N3Cc2ccccc2)c(OC)c1) is marked not in stock and has no further disconnection. The construction of this complex fused/bridged azabicyclic lactam bearing the dimethoxyaryl and N-benzyl groups is the true synthetic challenge and is left unaddressed. Stereochemistry of the multiple ring-fusion stereocenters is also not controlled in any step. The endgame is sound, but the route needs the core scaffold synthesis defined and the PG/reagent fixes applied.

The overall strategy is logical for assembling this complex bridged bicyclic system: late-stage sulfonylation of the bridgehead amine, a protecting-group regime on the bridging nitrogen, and intramolecular N-alkylation to close the dihydroisoquinoline ring. Strengths: the sulfonamide is correctly installed last (it would not survive hydrogenolysis or alkylation conditions); the alcohol-to-bromide-to-cyclization sequence is reasonable. Weaknesses: (1) The protecting-group strategy is redundant — benzyl is installed, then swapped to Cbz, then removed. A single protecting group (Cbz from the start) would eliminate one step (a1513e17aa2e75487eb45453762d568371a096bc2d2530a170ee3a695c57d9ae) and the awkward N-benzyl to N-Cbz interconversion. (2) The CBr4 reagent in a3756a869cb1996b0dec2ebb42375394bcde9b90666b921d0c17c842b7d6bbcc needs PPh3 to be valid (Appel). (3) Most critically, the retrosynthesis is INCOMPLETE — the key intermediate 'COc1cc(CCO)c(C2NC(=O)C3CCCC2N3Cc2ccccc2)c(OC)c1' (the bridged bicyclic lactam core bearing the alcohol tether and N-benzyl) is marked NOT in stock and is NOT broken down further. This molecule contains the entire stereochemically dense aza-bicyclic skeleton, which is the principal synthetic challenge and is not addressed at all. The route therefore does not reach commercial building blocks for its hardest fragment. The stereochemistry of the multiple ring-fusion stereocenters is also not considered. Overall: the endgame is sound but the route does not solve the core problem and has an inefficient PG strategy.

The overall strategy builds the fused diazabicyclic/lactam core via an intramolecular N-alkylation and caps the bridgehead amine as a sulfonamide in the final step, which is a sound endgame. Strengths: the final sulfonylation (162e844b1660e318ba23e0497e3713fc29c3fa5b3f9be5ca6602df8887a39063) and the hydrogenolytic deprotection (17a42fbb0dde9d6bab8e139ebd01484e986a7721abaefb0d40890f87f553cf60) are robust; starting materials such as 4-cyanobenzenesulfonyl chloride and benzyl chloroformate are commercial. Weaknesses requiring attention: (1) The route is NOT solved to commercial building blocks — the deepest intermediate, the amino-alcohol-containing diketopiperazine/bicyclic lactam bearing the N-benzyl bridgehead (precursor in a3756a869cb1996b0dec2ebb42375394bcde9b90666b921d0c17c842b7d6bbcc), is shown as in_stock:false and its synthesis (including establishment of the bicyclic stereochemistry and the aryl tether) is not addressed. The complex stereodefined core is essentially assumed. (2) The Appel step (a3756a869cb1996b0dec2ebb42375394bcde9b90666b921d0c17c842b7d6bbcc) lacks PPh3. (3) The protecting-group logic in a1513e17aa2e75487eb45453762d568371a096bc2d2530a170ee3a695c57d9ae is redundant/awkward — converting N-Bn directly to N-Cbz with CbzCl is not a clean operation; it would be more efficient to carry a single removable group (either Bn or Cbz) throughout and avoid the swap, then deprotect/sulfonylate. (4) Stereochemical control across the multiple ring fusions and bridgehead centers is not analyzed; the intramolecular alkylation (b572a37ba5f5aebb791645587ba5297332ad2157e15dd418b778f8471feff981) and the core assembly need defined stereochemistry that this tree does not establish. Overall the late-stage steps are credible, but the route stops short of true building blocks and contains a non-optimal reagent and a redundant protecting-group manipulation.

The overall strategy — building the bridged diazabicyclic lactam core, closing the fused ring by intramolecular alkylation, then installing the sulfonamide last — is reasonable and the late-stage sulfonylation is a good endgame choice. However, the route has notable weaknesses: (1) The Cbz protection step (a1513e17aa2e75487eb45453762d568371a096bc2d2530a170ee3a695c57d9ae) is mechanistically flawed as drawn — you cannot acylate a tertiary N-benzyl amine to a carbamate; a debenzylation must precede Cbz installation, and indeed the entire benzyl→Cbz→H exchange is redundant (direct hydrogenolysis of the N-benzyl group would suffice, eliminating two steps). (2) The Appel bromination (a3756a869cb1996b0dec2ebb42375394bcde9b90666b921d0c17c842b7d6bbcc) omits the required phosphine reagent. (3) The intramolecular N-alkylation (b572a37ba5f5aebb791645587ba5297332ad2157e15dd418b778f8471feff981) on an amide nitrogen risks elimination and modest reactivity, and the regiochemistry/stereochemistry of forming the bridged system needs careful control. This densely functionalized, stereochemically complex diazabicyclo[2.2.1] lactam is the true synthetic challenge and is left undisclosed. The route therefore is not solved to building blocks for its most difficult core, and the protecting-group logic should be streamlined. With removal of redundant PG steps, correction of reagents, and a defined synthesis of the bicyclic core, the strategy could work.

The overall strategy is reasonable and convergent in parts: building the 2,4-disubstituted thiazole via Hantzsch synthesis (76726b47749c2fc03796974930d154f043d5134c4d739e58a01a6e4f7dc569ef) and thioamide formation via Lawesson's (98532d3c173f0087efe94199d5ad9ff1058ce2c001c580d42a516a372055ce68) are sound, well-precedented transformations. However, the route has several significant problems. (1) The route is marked 'is_solved: False' and the terminal amide precursor (NC(=O)C(Cc1ccc(Br)cc1)c1ccc(OC(F)(F)F)cc1) is not disconnected to commercial building blocks — the synthesis is incomplete. (2) Step 095a967fb4ccd60d78add131ad909e56003dcc89926e4e151463c82d3f732f4d uses phosphoric acid as an 'oxidant' for aldehyde-to-acid, which is chemically incorrect; a proper oxidation (Pinnick, KMnO4) must be specified. (3) Step 1885ce9407b24a786c6dcfaeece72cc5c61eb0b63492e6004bdd213c66b7c88d invokes ArBr -> ArCHO formylation, but organolithium-based metalation is incompatible with the acidic benzylic position, the metalatable thiazole, and the ArCl; a Pd-catalyzed carbonylation route would be safer. (4) Step 65a7212a299a447c1890736238efa8e3d6d2ded0f48d57ea89a87116488b565f couples a free aryl acid to a methyl ester amine, requiring an unshown final ester hydrolysis to unveil the target carboxylic acid — a protecting group/deprotection step is missing. (5) Stereochemistry at the central benzylic CH is unaddressed throughout (the target appears racemic). Recommendations: complete the retrosynthesis of the amide precursor to commercial materials; replace the phosphoric acid oxidation with Pinnick conditions; replace the lithiation formylation with Pd-carbonylation or carry the aldehyde/acid functionality earlier; add an explicit final ester hydrolysis (LiOH) step. With these modifications the strategy is workable.

The overall strategy builds the thiazole core via a sound Hantzsch synthesis (76726b47749c2fc03796974930d154f043d5134c4d739e58a01a6e4f7dc569ef) from a thioamide (98532d3c173f0087efe94199d5ad9ff1058ce2c001c580d42a516a372055ce68, Lawesson's) and an alpha-bromoketone, which is convergent and uses accessible building blocks. However, there are several serious problems. (1) 1885ce9407b24a786c6dcfaeece72cc5c61eb0b63492e6004bdd213c66b7c88d: the conversion of ArBr to ArCHO via 'DMF' alone is not viable as written - it requires an organolithium/Grignard or Pd-carbonylation, which would be incompatible with the thiazole, OCF3, aryl chloride, and acidic benzylic proton. This is the weakest link. (2) 095a967fb4ccd60d78add131ad909e56003dcc89926e4e151463c82d3f732f4d: phosphoric acid is not an oxidant; an aldehyde-to-acid oxidation needs a proper oxidant (Pinnick/NaClO2). (3) f840bf3054b85269d235dced0f10c67137c41753d0c65a50ca595f6dba8daf60/65a7212a299a447c1890736238efa8e3d6d2ded0f48d57ea89a87116488b565f: the final amide coupling uses the methyl ester of beta-alanine but the target is the free acid, so a saponification step is missing, and the aryl acid would need to be activated for coupling. Additionally, building the late-stage aldehyde/acid on the same ring as the alpha-bromobenzyl introduces selectivity questions. A cleaner route would install the carboxylic acid functionality earlier (e.g., starting from a 4-substituted benzaldehyde/benzoic acid derivative bearing the desired CH(thiazole) center) rather than relying on a non-feasible ArBr->CHO step. Core thiazole disconnection is good, but the functional group interconversions need substantial revision.

The overall strategy is reasonable and convergent in its final amide coupling, with a solid foundation in the Hantzsch thiazole synthesis (76726b47749c2fc03796974930d154f043d5134c4d739e58a01a6e4f7dc569ef) and Lawesson thionation (98532d3c173f0087efe94199d5ad9ff1058ce2c001c580d42a516a372055ce68) at the core - both of which are well-precedented and use accessible building blocks (2-bromo-4'-chloroacetophenone, Lawesson's reagent, beta-alanine methyl ester are all commercial). However, several significant problems undermine the route as written: (1) A terminal mismatch: the target bears a free carboxylic acid but the amine building block is a methyl ester, so a final ester hydrolysis step is missing entirely. (2) 095a967fb4ccd60d78add131ad909e56003dcc89926e4e151463c82d3f732f4d lists phosphoric acid as an oxidant for the aldehyde->acid conversion; this is incorrect - a proper oxidant (e.g., NaClO2 in a Pinnick oxidation) is needed. (3) 1885ce9407b24a786c6dcfaeece72cc5c61eb0b63492e6004bdd213c66b7c88d is the weakest step: converting an aryl bromide to an aryl aldehyde using only DMF is not feasible without a metalating reagent (n-BuLi) or a Pd/CO carbonylation system, and such harsh lithiation would be incompatible with the thiazole/OCF3 functionality. A better overall plan would install the para-substituted benzaldehyde/benzoate functionality earlier (e.g., via a pre-functionalized building block or cross-coupling), rather than relying on late-stage bromide-to-CHO conversion. The first amide is also unprotected as the precursor amide before thionation (98532d3c173f0087efe94199d5ad9ff1058ce2c001c580d42a516a372055ce68), which is fine. With correction of the oxidant, the bromide-to-aldehyde strategy, and addition of a final saponification, the route could become viable. The core thiazole-forming chemistry is sound.

The overall strategy has a logical core: build the 2,4-disubstituted thiazole via Hantzsch (76726b47749c2fc03796974930d154f043d5134c4d739e58a01a6e4f7dc569ef) from a thioamide (98532d3c173f0087efe94199d5ad9ff1058ce2c001c580d42a516a372055ce68, Lawesson's), then elaborate the benzylic aryl-bearing fragment. The thiazole-forming steps are sound and well-precedented. However, there are several serious issues: (1) The final amide coupling (f840bf3054b85269d235dced0f10c67137c41753d0c65a50ca595f6dba8daf60) uses a methyl ester-protected amine but the target bears a free carboxylic acid, so an explicit ester hydrolysis step is missing and the route as drawn does not deliver the target. (2) The aldehyde-to-acid oxidation (095a967fb4ccd60d78add131ad909e56003dcc89926e4e151463c82d3f732f4d) mislabels phosphoric acid as the reagent; a proper oxidant (Pinnick conditions) is needed. (3) The ArBr -> ArCHO step using DMF (1885ce9407b24a786c6dcfaeece72cc5c61eb0b63492e6004bdd213c66b7c88d) is questionable on this polyfunctional substrate (thiazole, OCF3, acidic benzylic position incompatible with organometallic formylation), and the regiochemistry between the bromide and the introduced aldehyde appears inconsistent. To improve: replace the late-stage aryl formylation with a pre-installed aldehyde/ester building block (e.g., couple a 4-formyl/4-carboxy aryl fragment earlier), clarify the oxidation conditions, and add/clarify the saponification step or use beta-alanine with proper protecting-group logic. The building blocks reached (alpha-bromoacetophenone, Lawesson's reagent, methyl 3-aminopropanoate, DMF) are commercial, but the primary amide precursor (98532d3c173f0087efe94199d5ad9ff1058ce2c001c580d42a516a372055ce68 product) is not traced to building blocks, so the retrosynthesis is also incomplete at that branch.

This retrosynthetic route contains multiple fundamental flaws making it unfeasible as proposed. Key problems: (1) Several disconnections are chemically impossible (e2e61a2532a8040f640a8b7d7a94a2797d9eb2b0f909f9c5566e1a3278326aa2: SNAr of unactivated aryl fluoride by MOM-oxygen; 3fbcf2972821fc846c8dd287af1b723a6ef760227b91cfd10878ad2feffa87fa: making MOM-OH from DCM + methanediol; 9df9b851e26c143661b430d089a4e10bded22161ad5eb713b9908f89915269ad: O-methylation of phenol by methanol). (2) The protecting group strategy (PMB/MOM manipulations in 01e859b2f30d4c5769296b84f66d56a0ff23fc6b47ef405649844c27e061a7e3-e2e61a2532a8040f640a8b7d7a94a2797d9eb2b0f909f9c5566e1a3278326aa2) is convoluted, adds numerous unnecessary steps, and provides no clear strategic advantage - and the oxidative PMB removal would be incompatible with the sensitive sulfide and quinone functionalities. (3) The final-step late-stage nitration (d9d26074adaa97cbc132a2683d4314346183364615d595feec2cd4bd03ad9a6e) of a highly functionalized, redox-sensitive molecule containing a thioether and quinones risks oxidation and decomposition; the nitro group should be introduced via a 4-nitrophenylhydrazine building block early. (4) The route is not solved to reasonable commercial building blocks for the core thiophene-fused quinone/urazole system - the most complex and challenging bond constructions (the spirocyclic core, the C-S bonds, the urazole ring formation, the pyridine-quinone) are never disconnected. The retrosynthesis essentially performs cosmetic peripheral manipulations while leaving the genuinely difficult ring system intact and undefined. A productive retrosynthesis should disconnect the urazole (from a hydrazide/isocyanate), the thioether ring, and the quinone-forming steps, while sourcing the nitrophenyl group from commercial 4-nitrophenylhydrazine. As written, this route should be substantially redesigned.

The overall strategy has major problems. (1) The terminal late-stage nitration (d9d26074adaa97cbc132a2683d4314346183364615d595feec2cd4bd03ad9a6e) with HNO3 on a highly sensitive substrate containing a sulfide and a fused quinone/diketone is likely to cause oxidation/decomposition and regioselectivity issues; the p-nitrophenyl group should instead be introduced via a pre-nitrated building block (e.g., 4-nitrophenylhydrazine) during construction of the urazole. (2) The bulk of the route (01e859b2f30d4c5769296b84f66d56a0ff23fc6b47ef405649844c27e061a7e3–3fbcf2972821fc846c8dd287af1b723a6ef760227b91cfd10878ad2feffa87fa) is an elaborate and self-defeating protecting-group sequence on a benzyl substituent: a PMB/MOM/O-methyl 'protection of a protecting group' chain that ultimately yields a free urazole NH that was apparently never required to be protected in the first place. These steps add no synthetic value and several are chemically invalid: e2e61a2532a8040f640a8b7d7a94a2797d9eb2b0f909f9c5566e1a3278326aa2 (SNAr on an unactivated aryl fluoride) and 3fbcf2972821fc846c8dd287af1b723a6ef760227b91cfd10878ad2feffa87fa (nonsensical formation of methoxymethanol from CH2Cl2 + formaldehyde hydrate) are not real transformations, and 9df9b851e26c143661b430d089a4e10bded22161ad5eb713b9908f89915269ad uses methanol as a methylating agent which will not work. (3) Critically, the retrosynthesis does not converge to reasonable commercial building blocks — the deepest precursors are still complex, fully elaborated heterocyclic intermediates (the spirocyclic thiophene-fused pyridinedione/urazole core) with no disconnection of the core ring systems. The route is therefore both not solved to building blocks and contains several impossible steps. A complete redesign is recommended: disconnect the spirocyclic core (e.g., via a thia-Michael/Diels-Alder or condensation to assemble the dithiole/thiophene-fused quinone), construct the urazole from a 4-nitrophenyl semicarbazide/hydrazide directly, and avoid all the redundant protecting-group chemistry.

This route contains multiple fatal flaws and is not feasible as proposed. Key problems: (1) Several disconnections are chemically invalid - e2e61a2532a8040f640a8b7d7a94a2797d9eb2b0f909f9c5566e1a3278326aa2 (aryl-F to MOM-ether via hemiformal) and 3fbcf2972821fc846c8dd287af1b723a6ef760227b91cfd10878ad2feffa87fa (MOM precursor from DCM + methylene glycol) are not real reactions; 9df9b851e26c143661b430d089a4e10bded22161ad5eb713b9908f89915269ad (O-methylation from methanol without a methylating agent) is also invalid. (2) The protecting group strategy is internally inconsistent and circular: the phenol is protected as MOM, then converted to a methyl ether, then deprotected to phenol again, serving no coherent purpose - the para-hydroxy/methoxy/MOM benzyl group ultimately appears to be removed entirely (compare to the final N-phenyl target), suggesting it functions as an N-protecting benzyl group, but the manipulations are scrambled. (3) The final nitration (d9d26074adaa97cbc132a2683d4314346183364615d595feec2cd4bd03ad9a6e) is performed on an extremely sensitive substrate containing an oxidation-prone thioether and a fragile azaanthraquinone, risking decomposition. (4) The route is NOT solved to building blocks - the core tricyclic thiophene-fused azaanthraquinone-spiro-triazinanedione scaffold appears intact at the deepest node (the fluorobenzyl precursor in e2e61a2532a8040f640a8b7d7a94a2797d9eb2b0f909f9c5566e1a3278326aa2) and is simply assumed available, never disconnected. Recommendation: completely redesign. Introduce the nitro group at the aniline building-block stage; build the spirocyclic urea/triazinanedione and the thiophene-azaanthraquinone core through real disconnections (e.g., spirocyclization, Knoevenagel/condensation to form the quinone); and choose a single rational protecting group if needed. As drawn, the strategy cannot be executed.

The overall route contains multiple fundamental flaws that render the strategy unfeasible. The most serious problems lie in the protecting group cascade (steps 9df9b851e26c143661b430d089a4e10bded22161ad5eb713b9908f89915269ad-3fbcf2972821fc846c8dd287af1b723a6ef760227b91cfd10878ad2feffa87fa): the synthesis invokes an unstable, non-isolable 'methoxymethanol' reagent prepared by a nonsensical route (formaldehyde + DCM), proposes an implausible SNAr displacement of an unactivated aryl fluoride, and includes a pointless and impossible phenol-to-methyl-ether conversion using only MeOH. These steps form a self-defeating, illogical protecting group sequence (install MOM, remove MOM, methylate, then fully debenzylate) that adds no synthetic value. Furthermore, the terminal nitration (d9d26074adaa97cbc132a2683d4314346183364615d595feec2cd4bd03ad9a6e) on this highly sensitive, electron-poor, sulfur-containing polyheterocycle raises serious chemoselectivity concerns (thioether oxidation, over-nitration, scaffold decomposition). The retrosynthesis also does not reach sensible commercial building blocks for the core azaanthraquinone-spiro-thiophene-triazinedione scaffold - that complex core is essentially carried unchanged throughout, so no real disconnection of the difficult ring systems is achieved. A viable approach would: (1) introduce the nitro group early on a simple arylhydrazine building block, (2) eliminate the entire MOM/PMB cascade, and (3) construct the spiro-thiophene and triazinedione rings via rational annulation disconnections. As presented, the route should be rejected.

A far better strategy would disconnect at the piperidine nitrogen (reductive amination of a 4-substituted piperidine with cyclohexanecarboxaldehyde) and use a preformed piperidine ring rather than building it by acyclic double alkylation, plus install the oxime late and reduce the nitro group before introducing the alkyl halide. The target is a 4-substituted N-(cyclohexylmethyl)piperidine bearing an aryl O-methyl oxime ether with aniline, chloro, and methoxy substituents. The overall strategy attempts to construct the piperidine ring late via double N-alkylation, but the key weakness is the reliance on differentiating two nearly equivalent primary leaving groups (an alkyl bromide and an alkyl mesylate) for sequential, chemoselective amination then cyclization (steps 1b3e857ca542ad75bd317d42279d6866d6d62efa22dcbb0731bf2e0c2ec21d71 and 8c5ea146d998b718ad21ff505929cccc1f2ba099797f1dad4e2856aa02f560c9). This selectivity is unrealistic and would lead to mixtures, oligomerization, and premature cyclization. Additionally, the free aryl-NH2 is an unprotected competing nucleophile throughout the alkylation/mesylation sequence, which is problematic and is unmasked too early (67342e89cf256506f2f86201d3cd378491660d19c746fa237fb6baf0a7df808c) when it would be better kept as the nitro group until after C-N bond-forming steps. The nitro reduction (67342e89cf256506f2f86201d3cd378491660d19c746fa237fb6baf0a7df808c) as default hydrogenation is incompatible with the alkyl bromide, aryl chloride, and oxime ether—chemoselective reduction (Fe, Zn, SnCl2) is required. The MsCl synthesis (33cef9e576b26567d1395c55155c567aaf291958528c8f85868335ba05c72671) is an unnecessary step. STRONGLY RECOMMENDED: build the piperidine ring from a preformed 4-substituted piperidinone or via a clean intramolecular reductive amination of a keto-amine, install the N-cyclohexylmethyl group by reductive amination (cyclohexanecarbaldehyde + secondary amine) rather than alkyl halide displacement, and keep the aniline masked as nitro until the final step. The oxime ether (CO/N=C) geometry must also be controlled. With these substantial redesigns the core target is reasonable, but the proposed disconnections as written are not robustly feasible. Note also the route is not fully solved to building blocks (the nitro alcohol precursor CO/N=C(\CCC(CCO)CCBr)... is marked not in stock with no further children).

The overall strategy targets a 4-substituted N-(cyclohexylmethyl)piperidine bearing a substituted aryl O-methyl oxime ether. The retrosynthetic logic of disconnecting the piperidine ring to an acyclic amino-mesylate and using THP protection/mesylation is conceptually reasonable, but the route has several serious issues: (1) Chemoselectivity problems dominate — the intermediates carry simultaneously a primary alkyl bromide AND a primary mesylate (1b3e857ca542ad75bd317d42279d6866d6d62efa22dcbb0731bf2e0c2ec21d71/ccd64bdf697e16f51b5a1a89c79d1e9abd1605f0b6705917939eb7ce82bade0e), making selective amine alkylation and cyclization difficult; the route never clearly differentiates these two leaving groups. (2) The free aniline is unprotected during mesylation (ccd64bdf697e16f51b5a1a89c79d1e9abd1605f0b6705917939eb7ce82bade0e) and amine alkylation (1b3e857ca542ad75bd317d42279d6866d6d62efa22dcbb0731bf2e0c2ec21d71), where it would compete as a nucleophile and lead to side reactions. A logical fix is to keep the nitro group through the alkylation/cyclization steps and reduce it last, or to protect the aniline (e.g., as an acetamide/Boc) during these steps. (3) The nitro reduction (67342e89cf256506f2f86201d3cd378491660d19c746fa237fb6baf0a7df808c) is performed while the alkyl bromide and oxime ether are present, requiring carefully chosen chemoselective conditions (SnCl2, Fe/NH4Cl) rather than hydrogenation. (4) The piperidine-forming cyclization (8c5ea146d998b718ad21ff505929cccc1f2ba099797f1dad4e2856aa02f560c9) needs two leaving groups but only one (mesylate) is present in the drawn precursor; the disconnection bookkeeping is inconsistent. (5) The MsCl-from-MsOH step (33cef9e576b26567d1395c55155c567aaf291958528c8f85868335ba05c72671) is unnecessary since MsCl is commercial. A more robust route would: protect the aniline (or carry the nitro to the end), use a bis-electrophile (e.g., a diol bis-mesylate or a 4-substituted glutarate-derived dihalide) for clean double N-alkylation to build the piperidine in one operation with cyclohexylmethylamine, and avoid carrying a reactive bromide through a nitro reduction. Starting materials (cyclohexylmethylamine, DHP, MsCl, MsOH, oxalyl chloride) are commercial. The retrosynthesis is technically reaching building blocks but is marked unsolved; with the modifications above the core strategy could be salvaged.

The target is an O-methyl oxime ether bearing a 4-substituted N-(cyclohexylmethyl)piperidine and a chloro/methoxy/amino aromatic ring. Overall, the convergence is poor (essentially linear), and the protecting-group strategy is flawed. A redesign is recommended: assemble the N-(cyclohexylmethyl)piperidine first (e.g., from a 4-substituted piperidine via reductive amination with cyclohexanecarbaldehyde), install the aryl/oxime portion, and reduce the nitro group at a stage free of alkyl halides. Building blocks (cyclohexylmethylamine, MsOH, oxalyl chloride, DHP) are commercial, but the upper aryl-oxime fragment is not traced to building blocks and the retrosynthesis is marked unsolved.

The overall strategy is sound and reasonably short: the key disconnection is an amide bond between the 4-(trifluoromethyl)indoline (commercially available) and a pyrimidinone-acetic acid fragment, which is logical and convergent. The pyrimidinone-acetic acid is accessed by ester hydrolysis of a readily available ethyl ester. The main weakness is the unnecessary and problematic detour through the acyl chloride (steps 640c5d262fa9f2126b8718f81693e177edd03ec5df48d9ac2cc863111902b811 and 92ed09f3254cae63270b66407728138bedd7b4a162d57dc16329c71a9a2f10ab). Converting the acid to an acyl chloride with oxalyl chloride risks chlorination of the pyrimidinone ring and O-acylation/self-condensation, and the acyl chloride is likely unstable. The route should be simplified by performing a direct amide coupling of the carboxylic acid with the indoline using a peptide coupling reagent (HATU, EDC/HOBt, or T3P) with a mild base. This eliminates one step and avoids the chemoselectivity hazards. With this modification, the route is practical and scalable, terminating at commercially available building blocks (4-CF3-indoline, ethyl pyrimidinone-acetate, oxalyl chloride). Purification of the polar pyrimidinone intermediates may be challenging but manageable.

The overall strategy is logical and reasonably short: a key amide bond disconnects the target into a commercially available indoline (5-CF3 indoline) and a heterocyclic acetic acid fragment derived by hydrolysis of an in-stock ethyl ester. The recommended modification is to skip the acid chloride and perform a direct amide coupling of the carboxylic acid with the indoline using HATU/T3P/EDC-HOBt with a mild base. This would collapse two steps into one, improve chemoselectivity, and avoid heterocycle chlorination. With this modification the route is sound and scalable. Starting materials (oxalyl chloride, 5-CF3 indoline, and the ethyl ester precursor) are commercially accessible.

The overall strategy is sound and reasonably short: build the carboxylic acid by ester hydrolysis, then form the amide bond to the 4-(trifluoromethyl)indoline. The main weakness is the choice to proceed through the acid chloride intermediate. Given the unprotected pyrimidinone NH (lactam) and the morpholine, the acid chloride route presents significant chemoselectivity risks (O-acylation, chlorination of the lactam, ketene/self-condensation from the activated alpha-CH2). The route would be substantially improved by replacing the oxalyl chloride/acid chloride sequence with a direct amide coupling of the free carboxylic acid using EDC/HOBt or HATU with a base, which tolerates the free NH and morpholine. With this single modification, the route is practical and scalable. Building blocks are reached (ethyl ester, oxalyl chloride, CF3-indoline all in stock), so the retrosynthesis is complete.

The overall strategy is short and convergent: build/obtain the pyrimidinone-acetic acid core, activate the carboxylic acid, and couple to the trifluoromethyl-dihydroindoline amine to form the target amide. The disconnections are logical and the terminal building blocks (ethyl ester precursor and the CF3-dihydroindole) are commercially reasonable. The carboxylic acid bears an acidic pyrimidinone NH, a basic morpholine, and a doubly-activated alpha-CH2; oxalyl chloride risks chlorodehydroxylation of the pyrimidinone and ketene/self-condensation pathways, and the zwitterionic acid may be poorly soluble. RECOMMENDATION: Replace 640c5d262fa9f2126b8718f81693e177edd03ec5df48d9ac2cc863111902b811 (acid chloride formation) and the subsequent coupling with a direct amide coupling using HATU, T3P, or EDC/HOBt on the free acid, which avoids the unstable intermediate and improves chemoselectivity. With this modification the route should perform well. The final amide bond formation onto a hindered secondary aniline-type nitrogen may still require optimization (T3P or acid chloride at low temperature). Overall a sound, efficient 3-step plan needing reagent refinement.

The overall strategy is fundamentally flawed. The target is a rhodanine (2-thioxo/imino-thiazolidinone) bearing an arylidene (Knoevenagel) exocyclic alkene, an N-aryl imine, a p-dimethylaminostyryl group, and a guaiacol-type phenol. Instead the route builds the dimethylamino group by late-stage Buchwald amination of an aryl bromide (3c217b1efcd131c22be5cc2f32f8d9123a8faf524094bc18cabf1a734ff87376), which is itself proposed via non-selective NBS bromination of an unactivated phenyl ring (fb4550d4deebd5e915c35d7bfacdbc7b78faf7967ad2573d71669dab2ac32fea). This route contains multiple fundamental flaws and an inefficient overall strategy. The target is a 5-arylidene-2-(arylimino)thiazolidin-4-one (rhodanine-type) scaffold. The thiazolidinone core can be assembled from a thiourea/isothiocyanate and a haloacetic acid derivative. The current route does not reach proper building blocks productively and is not feasible as written.

The overall strategy has fundamental flaws. The target is a benzylidene-rhodanine bearing a 4-(dimethylamino)phenyl group, a 2-aryl imine, and a 3-methoxy-4-hydroxyaryl (vanillin-derived) substituent. The most logical and convergent synthesis is a Knoevenagel condensation between a rhodanine (or 2-imino-thiazolidinone) and 4-(dimethylamino)benzaldehyde, with the N-aryl imine installed from the corresponding 2-imino-thiazolidinone and an aniline (e.g., from 4-amino-2-methoxyphenol/vanillin-derived amine). The retrosynthesis is also not solved to building blocks (the central benzylidene-rhodanine core 'COc1cc(/N=C2...c3ccccc3)S2)ccc1F' is left as a non-stocked leaf with no further disconnection). The far superior approach is forward-synthesis convergence: condense N-aryl-2-imino-4-thiazolidinone (rhodanine imine) with commercially available 4-dimethylaminobenzaldehyde under Knoevenagel conditions (piperidine/AcOH), avoiding all the problematic late-stage functionalizations and protecting groups. As written, this route is unfeasible.

The overall strategy contains several fundamental flaws that make it unworkable as drawn. (1) The protecting-group strategy is built on an impossible SNAr step (af133b73429531ef163e26c846288b4a37171cf02acaf98271375715d1ec3de6): displacement of an aryl fluoride by benzyl alkoxide on an electron-rich methoxy-substituted ring will not occur, and the benzyl protection is unnecessary in the first place. The N-aryl imine/amine portion should be derived from commercially available 4-amino-2-methoxyphenol. This avoids all the protecting-group and selectivity problems.
